The C64 mainboard skips the entire through-hole plating sequence a via board runs: hole desmear, electroless copper seed, electrolytic copper build, nickel, gold. None of that equipment ever saw this board, and any account that puts electroless copper into a C64 mainboard is describing a different machine.

#### Epoxy solder mask on both sides `mb.pcb.mask` _(medium)_

Green epoxy ink is screen-printed over the whole board with apertures left over every pad and hole. It is the green the C64 has always been. Without it the board shorts from a fingerprint, a solder splash or a screw, and the white legend would disappear under bare copper. Period inks were solvent-based epoxies cured in infrared or hot-air ovens; modern liquid solder mask is still screen-printed and cured far more cleanly, and liquid solder mask plus ENIG is now the standard pairing.

#### White silkscreen legend and compartment boxes `mb.pcb.legend` _(medium)_

Reference designators, block outlines and assembly notes are printed in white epoxy ink over the cured mask through a tensioned fine-mesh screen, then baked to cure the ink onto the mask. Commodore drew boxes around functional blocks, the so-called compartments, and used extra ink colours in bands and outlines to colour-code regions of the board and mark the television standard. Each extra colour is a separate screen pass with its own screen, squeegee and cure, which is a real cost and a real time step on the line.

##### Screen printing and bake `mb.pcb.legend.screen` _(medium)_

A fine-mesh screen coated with photosensitive emulsion is stretched and tensioned over the board, epoxy ink squeegeed through, and the board then baked to cure the ink onto the mask.

##### Coloured silkscreen bands `mb.pcb.legend.colour` _(low)_

A separate pass in each extra colour, with its own screen, to draw the colour bands and outlines that mark functional regions and the PAL or NTSC variant. A modern cosmetic imitation of this is a coloured solder mask; in 1983 it was extra ink passes.

#### Electrical test of the bare board `mb.pcb.inspection` _(medium)_

Before any component goes on, the blank is checked for shorts between nets and for opens in the artwork. In 1983 this was a continuity and insulation-resistance tester plus a careful visual check under a lamp and a loupe. Automated optical inspection existed by 1983 but was a line investment rather than an assumption on a commodity board.

#### Finished bare board, fab no. 250406 `mb.pcb.bareboard` _(medium)_

A drilled, etched, stripped, masked, legended and finished blank ready for component insertion. At 1983 commodity prices a two-layer 1.6 mm consumer board of this size cost on the order of one to two dollars.

### MOS 6510 CPU, 40-pin DIP `mb.cpu`

8-bit NMOS microprocessor at U7 of the C64 mainboard, clocked at 1.022727 MHz NTSC (0.985248 MHz PAL). It is the 6502 core plus an 8-bit I/O port on pins 9/10 (address 0000 data-direction, 0001 output latch). The MOS/CSG datasheet calls it 'HMOS, silicon gate, depletion load technology' - i.e. an N-channel silicon-gate double-polysilicon process with depletion-mode load devices, roughly a 2 um minimum feature. Fabbed in-house by MOS Technology (later Commodore Semiconductor Group) at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown, Pennsylvania.

#### Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `si.wafer` _(medium)_

The starting substrate every die in the machine is cut from: a 4-inch (100 mm) Czochralski-grown, boron-doped p-type silicon wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, mirror-polished on one face, 300-350 um thick, with a primary flat and a small secondary orientation flat. 125 mm was not standard until about 1986, and by 1982 every logic die in the C64 was patterned on one of these.

##### Polysilicon ingot and rod, 9N `metal.silica.polysilicon`

Shiny grey metalloid deposited as a polycrystalline boule on electrically heated silicon seed rods and then sawn into chunks. The chunks are the cathode-grade feedstock that the crystal puller charges. In 1982 the world outside Japan consumed polysilicon as an expensive specialty chemical, not as a commodity. The 6510 is an NMOS part, so its 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown oxide rather than a polysilicon gate; this branch is the industry feedstock route behind that, and it is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

###### Siemens deposition on UHF-heated rods `metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition`

Trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow over silicon rods held just below their melting point by radio-frequency induction, and silicon atoms drop out as polycrystalline growth. Rod temperature is the whole ballgame: too cold and you get powder, too hot and you get liquid droplets that fall into the bed. Two temperature measurement methods were in use - an optical pyrometer sighted on a blackened patch of rod, and a movable thermocouple in the gas stream - and calibrating that pyrometer was a plant secret worth millions.

###### Doped vs undoped polysilicon `metal.silica.polysilicon.doping` _(medium)_

Two grades were produced side by side in the same plant. UNdoped polysilicon went to the crystal puller for Czochralski ingots. Heavily doped material - p-type with boron or phosphorus, n-type with phosphorus or arsenic - went to subcollector plugs, to doped polysilicon films in later processes, and, most importantly, to the heavily doped epi and subcollector wafers that the NMOS logic was built on. In 1982 the dopant was dosed into the trichlorosilane stream as phosphine or the corresponding trichloride.

###### Crushing, flaking and acid etching of the rod `metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking` _(medium)_

The deposited rod is sawn with a slurry-impregnated circular saw, then the pieces are fractured and leached in hot hydrochloric-nitric acid to strip near-surface contamination from the seed end. What the puller wants is small pieces with clean fracture faces, because every surface is a chance to recontaminate. Rod ends were also ground back and reused as seed.

###### Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N `metal.silica.tcs`

Colourless fuming liquid, the money molecule of the whole silicon industry. Made by chlorinating impure silicon with hydrogen chloride in a fluidised bed, then purified to 11 nines purely by fractional distillation, because every one of the metal impurities that matter happens to be a chloride with a different boiling point from HSiCl3.

###### Fractional distillation of HSiCl3 `metal.silica.tcs.distillation`

Tall, stainless, pressure-rated columns that separate trichlorosilane from its neighbours purely on volatility. The separation is the entire purification strategy: nothing clever happens chemically, the same material is simply re-fractionated until the boron is gone.

###### Fluid-bed chlorination of silicon at ~300 C `metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination`

Metallurgical silicon is fluidised with nitrogen and metered HCl gas at 290-320 C. Silicon converts to trichlorosilane with hydrogen off; a large fraction of the feed instead goes to silicon tetrachloride, because the oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals push the stoichiometry. The bed is a tall stainless vessel with a distributor plate, and the reaction is exothermic enough that cooling coils matter.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `metal.silica.mgsi`

The commodity-grade output of a submerged arc furnace: a grey-black brittle lump material about the density of bone. In 1982 a Japanese or Taiwanese silicon plant bought it as if it were ore. The specification that matters is not the silicon but the boron - anything above roughly 20 ppm boron cannot reach electronics grade, which is why the silicon furnace takes a low-ash petroleum coke and not the 10-12% ash coke the steel industry uses.

###### Submerged-arc furnace reduction at 1800-2000 C `metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace`

A three-phase submerged arc furnace drops quartz, coal and woodchips down between graphite electrodes into a molten carbide bath at 1800-2000 C, and carbothermic reduction strips the oxygen off silica. Chemical silicon came to dominate this furnace by the late 1970s because the copper-clad electrode could then be pushed to a much higher current density. The off-gas, silicon monoxide at 400-1000 C, carries the energy away and is what lets the furnace run near-thermoneutral on the electrode side.

###### Carbothermal reductant: coke and woodchips `metal.silica.reducer` _(medium)_

The silicon furnace burns roughly one tonne of high-ash-reduction carbon per three tonnes of silicon, and the recipe is a tight compromise: too much ash and you get slag, too much volatile and the furnace fumes. Producers blend low-ash petroleum coke or anthracite with a proportion of woodchips, because the wood brings in hydrogen and potassium that volatilise out and are quietly useful, and because the porosity of the burnt wood helps the charge breathe. The same class of carbon, at different purity, is the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, ferrosilicon, ferromanganese and ferrochrome branches of this file.

###### Calcined petroleum coke for silicon `metal.silica.petcoke` _(medium)_

Delayed-coker green coke calcined in a rotary or shaft kiln to 2200-2800 C and quenched. The silicon grade is chosen for low ash, low vanadium and low sulphur, which is a narrow slice of the coke market - needle coke and sponge coke are the mainstream products and both carry more vanadium than the silicon furnace wants.

###### High-grade quartzite (97-99% SiO2) `metal.quartzite`

A metamorphosed, recrystallised quartz sandstone that is quarried rather than deep-mined. The chemical silicon industry does not use beach sand at all - it uses very low iron, very low aluminium quartzite, because Al and Fe are the impurities that survive the entire chain into the crystal. Two regions have essentially all of it. Note this is a DIFFERENT rock from the industrial silica sand used for glass, foundry moulds and copper-smelter flux, which is a much more common material.

###### Quartzite quarry, ~100,000 t/year `metal.quartzite.quarry` _(medium)_

The Norwegian quartzite quarry is a bench mine in metamorphosed sandstone: drilling, blasting, a primary jaw crusher, and a sorting step where workers - and, later, optical sorters - remove the visibly iron-stained lumps by hand. The rock is then crushed, washed on a sluice or in a scrubber, dried and size-graded, because a single grain of iron left in the batch makes a bad day of the whole furnace.

###### Quartz sandstone protolith (metaquartzite) `metal.quartzite.rock` _(medium)_

The rock as a geologist would name it: a quartz-rich sandstone or siltstone, now a hard white metaquartzite of interlocking quartz grains with the bedding picked out by iron oxides. Some of the Norwegian material is a hydrothermal replacement body in a metasedimentary sequence. Either way the leaf of the silicon chain is a sedimentary or metamorphic rock exposed at the surface and dug out of a hillside.

###### Silicon tetrachloride by-product and recycling `metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle` _(medium)_

Roughly half to two thirds of the silicon fed to a fluidised-bed chlorinator leaves as SiCl4 instead of HSiCl3, because oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals conspire. SiCl4 boils at 57.6 C and separates easily; it was largely dumped in the 1970s and later re-admitted as a chlorinating agent. The stoichiometric route that lets a plant recycle SiCl4 back into HSiCl3 by adding hydrogen and more silicon is the reason modern plants get the yields they do.

###### Hydrochloric acid (commercial 32-37%) `metal.hydrochloric-acid` _(low)_

The hydrochloric acid that chlorinates metallurgical silicon. Industrial acid is made by burning hydrogen in chlorine, both products of the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the silicon plant's feedstock chain runs back through a 1970s chlor-alkali plant and, behind that, a salt mine or a solar salt pan. The same acid is used for galvanising pickling, for the stainless pickling line, for the tinplate line, and for regenerating ferric chloride etchant at the board fab.

###### HCl synthesis and absorption `metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis`

Chlorine and hydrogen are fed to a steel burner with a plug of graphite or a water film that quenches the flame - a free gas-phase hydrogen-chlorine reaction is not something you leave unattended. The hot HCl gas is then absorbed in a water scrubber to make the azeotrope, and the acid is pumped out to wherever it is going: the fluidised bed, the pickle line, the tankhouse.

##### Sawing the ingot and laser-scribing the flats `si.wafer.slicing`

The boule is ground round, a sapphire-orientation-reference crystal is used to find the (100) direction, and the wafer flats are laser-scribed with a ruby or Nd:YAG laser before cutting. Slicing was by OD saw, with blades up to 2.2 m in diameter turning at 2000 rpm for a 0.30 mm kerf, or on more advanced 1982 machines by ID saw, with the blade inside the crystal for a 0.25 mm kerf. The result is a 0.7 mm wafer, far too warped and marked to print on.

###### Diamond-impregnated saw blade `si.wafer.saw` _(medium)_

A thin steel or resin-bonded wheel whose rim carries a diamond grit. Slicing 100 mm silicon at two to three wafers a minute relies on that grit: 20-40 um for a roughing cut and 3-5 um for the finish cut. Resin-bonded blades were introduced in the mid 1970s and gave a thinner kerf and less bow than the metal bond.

###### Industrial diamond from graphite `si.wafer.diamond` _(medium)_

Saw-grade industrial diamond in 1982 was mostly synthetic: graphite pressed and sintered with a diamond-metal catalyst (Fe, Co or Ni) at 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C in a belt press. Natural diamond - the harder, scarcer gem and industrial grade - came from kimberlite pipes in South Africa, Botswana and Russia.

##### Lapping, chemical polish and edge rounding `si.wafer.finish`

Saw-cut wafers are lapped double-sided on a rotating cast-iron plate against a conditioning plate, in a slurry of colloidal silica or alumina in water, taking them to about 300 um with several micrometres of total thickness variation left across the wafer. They are then polished chemically in hot alkaline peroxide or in HNO3/HF/acetic acid, which removes the last 10 um or so of saw damage and leaves an atomically flat surface, and finally the razor edge is rounded by a brief hot KOH or NH4OH etch so that photoresist cannot build up on it and so the wafer will not chip in handling.

##### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `si.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles rather than yield models set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic at 1.6 MHz in deionised water, a hot Piranha of 3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, then RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O 1:1:5 at 75-80 C) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. Between every mask level the same sequence ran again.

#### Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop `si.litho` _(medium)_

Every layer of every die is defined the same way. The wafer is coated on a spinner at 2000-5000 rpm to 1-3 um of positive photoresist, soft-baked at 90-100 C, aligned to the mask on a 1:1 contact or proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate at 30-50 mJ/cm2, spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard-baked, stripped, and cleaned. Shipley AZ-1350 was the workhorse thin-film resist of the whole industry and the higher-solids AZ-1354 was used wherever the film had to stand up to a deep etch.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `si.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer, followed by a convection hot plate or an infrared bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed at a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified nitrogen purge and amber-safe lighting.

##### Contact and proximity mask aligner `si.litho.aligner`

A 1:1 mask aligner: mercury or xenon source, a 20x-100x binocular microscope, a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and either hard vacuum contact with the mask pressed straight down onto the resist, or a 100-500 um proximity gap. Typical 1982 units were the Coburn 2400, the Kasper 2400, the Universal Exposure Systems machines, and the Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2, whose 5x optical projection removed the "mask lifts off the wafer" failure mode that plagued pure contact printing. Mask work in the 1980s was often done on the same machines, by flashing an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster.

        - *Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic* `si.clean` *(seen above)*
#### Photomask set, ~10 levels `mb.cpu.mask-set` _(medium)_

The set of 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates the 6510 pattern was cut into: nine or ten levels - n+ source/drain, field, contact, poly, second contact, metal, passivation and pad, plus alignment and test structures. For a device this small the fab printed 1:1 with contact or proximity printing; 10x steppers were brand new in 1982 and not used for this part. The plates are made by the fabrication branch below.

##### Chrome-on-glass photomask plate `si.mask.plate`

The physical plate a 1982 fab printed from: 5x7 inch of 1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz, coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, then exposed and developed in positive photoresist, the exposed chrome etched away in hot perchloric or sulfuric-perchromate acid, washed, inspected on a Zeiss comparison tool against the design database, and defect-repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle. Chromium was the universal absorber from the 1960s onward because of its opacity in the deep UV and its resistance to wet cleaning.

###### Electrolytic chromium metal from chrome alum `metal.chromium.metal` _(medium)_

Pure chromium metal - for the chromium plating chemistry and for chromium sputtering targets - is made the opposite way to ferrochrome: hydrometallurgically. Chromite is roasted with soda ash to a water-soluble sodium chromate, the chromate is leached, the hexavalent chromium is reduced to trivalent in an acid solution, and the metal is electrowon onto a lead cathode to 99.9%. It is a short, small industry - a few thousand tonnes a year of a metal worth a great deal. The chrome alum the world consumed came largely from chemical processing plants, and the sulphur dioxide from the roast was a nuisance that pre-1950 plants simply released. The same hydrometallurgical route also produced the sodium chromate that went into the chromate conversion coatings of the zinc and tin plating branches.

###### Hexavalent chromium electroplating bath `metal.hex-chrome-plating`

The classic chromiumic acid bath: CrO3 at 50-250 g/L in dilute sulfuric acid at 100-250 g/L, run at 45-60 C, 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2, with a lead-lead dioxide anode. A special steel anode is used and the bath is extremely hard to waste-treat: the chromium has to get from Cr(VI) down to Cr(III) before it can be precipitated. Cr(VI) is acutely and cumulatively toxic with a demonstrated carcinogenicity, and the 1971 OSHA standard for airborne hexavalent chromium was one of the first such rules in the United States. A C64's hard chrome on the switch contacts, the case hinges and the shield-contact points would have been plated in a plant subject to it.

###### Chromium electrowinning cell and the diaphragm `metal.chromium.metal.cell` _(low)_

Chromium is electrowon from a trivalent chromium sulphate solution at 5-8 V with a lead or lead-alloy cathode, in cells separated by a diaphragm - traditionally asbestos cloth, later a synthetic fibre - because the anodic chlorine would otherwise oxidise the trivalent chromium back and the two would meet and precipitate. The product is 99.9% chromium at 80-90% current efficiency. The cell room is the most noxious part of the whole chromium industry: hexavalent chromium in the feed, acidic mist, and an operator who must be in a respirator.

###### The diaphragm and the asbestos inheritance `metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm` _(low)_

The cell needs the anodic chlorine kept away from the trivalent chromium in the catholyte, and the membrane that does that was, until the 1980s, asbestos cloth - the same asbestos as the chlor-alkali diaphragm cells. So the chromium and chlor-alkali industries of the early twentieth century share a materials problem that was only being dealt with in the 1980s, in both cases by a conversion programme driven by worker exposure rather than by metallurgy. The 1982 answer was a synthetic fibre diaphragm, which worked and cost more.

##### Cutting, inspecting and repairing the mask plates `mb.cpu.mask-set.fabrication` _(medium)_

The 6510 layout existed as polygons on a Calma or Computervision workstation. It was checked against the design rules, extracted to a mask database and written to tape, and a mask data preparation program merged the layout with the process layers, the alignment marks and the die boundary to produce the flat rectangle-and-trapezoid format the pattern generator consumed. The generator then flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or a 1:1 mask writer exposed the blank plate directly. Each plate was developed in positive resist, the exposed chrome etched away, inspected on a Zeiss or KLA comparison tool against the database, and defect-repaired with a gallium or indium needle or by lifting and re-exposing the film. This data-reduction step, not the exposure, was where most mask errors were caught.

###### Pattern generator driving a mask exposure `mb.cpu.mask.plotter` _(medium)_

In 1982 most masks of this size were made by a numerically controlled pattern generator that flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or by a 1:1 mask writer that exposed a blank plate directly. Electron-beam mask writers (EBG, Santa Clara) existed but at roughly US$1-2 million were not typical in a small internal device fab.

###### Mask inspection and defect repair `mb.cpu.mask.inspection` _(medium)_

Masks were checked on a Zeiss or KLA comparison mask inspection tool against the design database, printing defect-free chrome checkouts. Opaque defects on clear areas were repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle or by lifting the film and re-exposing; clear defects in a chrome line were patched with deposited carbon. Pellicles - 1-2 um Mylar membranes mounted in a frame - protected final production masks from dust, though they were less common for 1:1 contact printing, where the mask still touched the wafer. Inspection was the last gate before a plate went into the mask library, because one bad plate silently ruins a whole wafer run.

##### The 10x stepper arriving at the end of the period `mb.cpu.mask.stepper` _(medium)_

Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, and later ASML) that printed a 10x-reduced reticle with a +-0.2-0.3 um overlay and broke the industry below the 1 um limit. By 1982 a 1:1 contact printer could just barely hold a 2 um line, so a 2 um 6510 was still printable 1:1; the steppers were arriving for the next generation, not for this part. Canon FPA-series 10x machines were among the first installed.

#### 2 um NMOS front end: the layer stack `mb.cpu.front-end` _(medium)_

A silicon-gate, double-polysilicon NMOS process flow on p-type (100) CZ silicon: heavily doped n+ source/drain first, LOCOS field oxide, heavily n-doped polysilicon gate, self-aligned arsenic source/drain, contact cuts, aluminium metallization, then phosphosilicate glass plus a plasma nitride seal. Ten mask levels, ~50 major process steps, roughly 6-8 weeks of fab cycle time.

##### 1. n+ source/drain pre-diffusion `mb.cpu.fe.nplus` _(medium)_

A thermal phosphorus diffusion: the wafer is coated with a phosphosilicate glass (PSG) doped by PH3 or by a PBN (pyrolytic boron nitride) solid phosphorus source, then held at 900-950 C for 30-60 minutes to push phosphorus about 0.5-1 um into the silicon. The result is a heavily doped (10^20 cm^-3) n+ region that will become the bit-line/tap contact landing areas and the bases of the load and driver devices.

##### 2. LOCOS field oxide `mb.cpu.fe.locos`

The active-area mask is defined in photoresist over the grown oxide, and field oxide grown by two-step thermal oxidation: a dry O2 pass at ~1000 C to lay down the thin masking oxide, then steam at the same temperature for ~2 hours to reach 6000-8000 A of field oxide. Field oxide was the isolation, the mask for the self-aligned source/drain implant, and the thickest feature on the die.

##### 3. Deposition and doping of the polysilicon `mb.cpu.fe.poly`

Polysilicon was deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition in a heated-wall tube furnace from silane (SiH4) at 800-850 C or from dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) at ~1000 C, giving 4000-8000 A of polycrystalline film. For gates it was deposited heavily n-doped in the same step by adding phosphine to the silane flow. Undoped poly, or lightly doped poly, was also deposited in the same furnace as the load resistors and as the depletion-mode loads the 6510 datasheet describes.

##### 4. Poly gate oxidation (the real '3.5 V' gate dielectric) `mb.cpu.fe.polyoxide`

After the undoped polysilicon is patterned, the whole wafer is re-oxidised: the bare silicon is left capped by the 400 A screen oxide, while the poly itself grows its own oxide. Dry O2 at 1000-1100 C for 30-90 minutes grows ~350-450 A of silicon dioxide on the poly, converting it into a depletion-mode MOSFET with the same gate dielectric as the silicon. This is why 'the gate oxide was grown in an oxygen furnace' is literally true of silicon-gate NMOS - but on the poly, not on the channel.

##### 5. Self-aligned source/drain implant `mb.cpu.fe.self-aligned`

With the poly gate and field oxide standing up, the wafer is ion-implanted with arsenic (or phosphorus) at 50-150 keV. The gate poly and the field oxide act as their own masks, so the source and drain edges are formed automatically under the poly edges with no alignment tolerance at all. The implanted arsenic is then annealed at 1000-1100 C in dry O2 or N2, which also drives it under the gate edge and repairs implant damage.

##### 6. Contact cut and aluminium metallization `mb.cpu.fe.contacts`

Contact windows are cut in the field oxide with an HF dip masked by photoresist (silicon dioxide etches fast in HF), then the wafer is coated by vacuum evaporation or DC sputtering with 1-2 um of aluminium containing 0.5-1% silicon to stop aluminium spikes punching through thin junctions. The aluminium is patterned by a hot phosphoric-acid etch (H3PO4:HNO3:acetic acid/water at ~50-80 C) or, from the late 1970s, by a CF4/O2 plasma in a barrel etcher.

##### 7. Passivation and pad opening `mb.cpu.fe.passivation` _(medium)_

The aluminium is sealed under a phosphosilicate glass overcoat grown by CVD from TEOS and phosphine at 700-800 C, and in 1982-84 plants increasingly by plasma-enhanced CVD silicon nitride (~700 C, SiH4/NH3 or SiCl4/NH3 in a low-frequency glow discharge). Pad windows are opened with a hot phosphoric acid etch of the nitride followed by a buffered HF dip.

##### Positive photoresist: spin, soft-bake, expose, develop `mb.cpu.fe.photoresist` _(medium)_

Wafer coated on a spinner (2000-4000 rpm) to 1-2 um of AZ-1350, dried 90-100 C for 20-30 min on a hot plate, aligned to the mask in a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 optical proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate, then spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. Between every step: megasonic clean, dilute H2SO4:H2O2, and a hard bake.

##### Oxidation and diffusion tube furnaces `mb.cpu.fe.furnace`

Quartz or fused-silica tube furnaces, horizontal, 5-6 inch ID, with 2-4 zone radiant or resistance heating to 1100 C, a boat of silicon-carbide or quartz carrying 25-50 wafers, and gas flow panels with wet/dry mixing valves. These did the field oxide, gate oxide, poly anneal and the source/drain drives.

##### Polysilicon LPCVD furnace and aluminium sputterer `mb.cpu.fe.deposition`

A second tube furnace, plumbed for silane/phosphine or dichlorosilane, for poly deposition. Aluminium went on in a separate vacuum tool: a DC magnetron sputter chamber (Balzers, Perkin-Elmer, Leybold) or a resistive evaporation chamber, both with turbomolecular pumps and a rotary fixture.

##### Wet etch bench and plasma etcher `mb.cpu.fe.etcher` _(medium)_

Wet etches in quartz or PVDF tanks: HF for oxide, hot H3PO4 for aluminium, buffered oxide etch (HF:NH4F) for fine oxide patterning. By 1982 many fabs had added a barrel-type CF4/CF4+O2 plasma etcher (e.g. the Plasma Technologies PT etch, or an ASM) for aluminium and for poly etching.

##### Low-energy ion implanter `mb.cpu.fe.implanter` _(medium)_

A small Van de Graaff or mass-separated implant source (High Voltage Engineering, Extrion, or Veeco) accelerating arsenic to 50-150 keV, with a beam scanning and dose measurement unit. Implantation of the source/drain had largely replaced diffusion by 1982 in a well-equipped shop.

#### Wafer probe (electrical die sort) `mb.cpu.probe` _(medium)_

Before dicing, each die is probed on a wafer with a probe card: a printed-circuit board with 40 microscopic tungsten or rhenium needles, one per 6510 bond pad. A Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST automated tester drives a test program and logs wafer coordinates, so only known-good dice go to assembly. Probe cards in 1982 were hand-drilled needle cards; automatic stepping probes were still rare.

##### Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board `si.probe-card` _(medium)_

Before dicing, every die is probed on the wafer through a probe card: a fibreglass or ceramic substrate with a pattern of gold-plated tungsten or rhenium needles on 0.1 inch centres, hanging on a probe ring over the die and stepping down with a few grams of force. In 1982 cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated; automatic stepping probe stations were still a novelty at these pad counts.

#### Die separation: scribe and break, or diamond-wheel saw `mb.cpu.dicing`

The wafer is flipped onto a vacuum chuck, scored along the scribe lines with a diamond scriber or, in the more expensive method, cut with a resin-bonded diamond wheel on a saw, leaving a kerf of 50-100 um. Small dies like the 6510 (about 3.5 x 3.9 mm) were often diced by scribing and snapping, then washed dry.

##### Diamond scriber and dicing saw `mb.cpu.dice-tool`

A small die like the 6510 (roughly 3.5 x 3.9 mm) was separated either by scoring the wafer's back-side scribe lines with a diamond scriber and snapping the wafer along them, or by cutting with a resin-bonded diamond wheel leaving a 50-100 um kerf. The wafer was then washed dry, and a final microscopic inspection checked each die's edges and surface before it went to bonding - a chip on a pad would cost a whole package.

#### Stamped DIP lead frame `si.leadframe`

The die and its leads emerge from a stamped, plated strip. Frames were made from FeNi 42/58 (C4-29) alloy 0.15-0.20 mm thick by progressive die stamping on a 400-800 ton press, then plated - a nickel strike and gold for hermetic parts, or a matte tin or tin-lead plate over nickel for plastic parts. The strip is indexed on a 0.3 inch tape through the bonder and the moulder, and a 40-pin DIP cavity set produces dozens of packaged parts per moulding cycle.

##### FeNi 42/58 lead frame alloy strip `si.leadframe.alloy` _(medium)_

The standard low-CTE frame alloy: 42% nickel, 58% iron, with a coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of the die, so the bond survives temperature cycling. Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed to 0.15-0.20 mm. Copper alloy C194 with 2.3% lead, and nickel itself, were the alternatives.

##### Nickel strike and gold or tin plating of the lead frame `si.leadframe.plating` _(medium)_

A nickel strike first, because gold will not adhere directly to the iron-nickel alloy and the leads have to solder. Hermetic parts get a heavier gold plate over the nickel; plastic parts get tin or tin-lead over the nickel so the leads solder into the machine's sockets. The bonding tab is always gold-plated, because the die is eutectic-bonded to it.

#### Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound `si.emc`

What actually seals a 1982 plastic IC. A thermosetting epoxy or phenolic compound of novolac resin plus 60-75% crushed quartz filler, a small amount of silicone release agent, catalyst and pigment, compounded on a two-roll mill under heat and then transfer moulded at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for one to three minutes, with a post-mould bake at 175 C. A 6510 uses on the order of 0.3-0.5 g of it; a 4164 about 0.1-0.2 g.

##### Epoxy novolac resin from phenol and epichlorohydrin `si.emc.resin`

Phenol and formaldehyde condensed under acid to a novolac resin, which is then reacted with epichlorohydrin and caustic soda to give the epoxy novolac that forms the backbone of the moulding compound. Phenol itself came from cumene-process oxidation of benzene - overwhelmingly a coal-tar derivative in 1982 - or from chlorobenzene hydrolysis.

##### Crushed quartz filler from quartz sand `si.emc.silica` _(medium)_

The single largest mass ingredient in any plastic package: 60-75% by weight of angular fused or ground silica of 0.5-3 um mean size, made by firing and grinding high-purity quartz. It is there to control the shrinkage coefficient and the thermal expansion, and it is why a decapsulated die sits in a white ceramic-looking blob.

#### Die attach to the lead frame `si.attach` _(medium)_

The die is placed circuit-side-up on a pre-plated gold lead frame tab and swept through a die bonder. The hot-tool bond raises die and frame to about 400-450 C: gold and silicon melt together at 361 C and, on cooling, form a hard Au-Si eutectic weld roughly 25-50 um thick. That is both the mechanical bond and the die's low-resistance thermal path out to the frame. The diced dice are inspected under a stereomicroscope at 20-50x, and under dark-field illumination for particles, before they are attached: a chip on a pad costs the whole package.

#### Gold wire wedge bonding `si.bond` _(medium)_

A wire bonder pulls 25-30 um diameter gold wire from a spool through a ceramic capillary and welds it to the aluminium bond pads: a first wire from each pad out to the frame lead, then interconnect wires pad to pad for internal bussing. Gold is soft, so a wedge-shaped tool presses the wire flat rather than using the ultrasonic ball bond of aluminium bonding. A single 6510 carried about 60 wires, roughly 1.5 m of 25 um gold in total.

#### Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy `si.mould` _(medium)_

The bonded frame sits in a multi-cavity transfer press and is encapsulated in silica-filled epoxy moulding compound. A typical cycle is 150-180 C at 700-1000 psi for one to three minutes per cavity, and plaques of flash at the parting line are trimmed off in a second press operation. The alternate route for hermetic parts is sintering an alumina ceramic shell at about 850-950 C with a glass frit seal - slower, more expensive, and used for military and aerospace grades.

##### Hydraulic transfer moulding press `si.mould.press` _(medium)_

A 50-100 ton multi-cavity transfer press with a heated upper platen, a pot and plunger that pre-form the compound pellet, and the encapsulated lead-frame strip in the cavity. Cycle: close the press, 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, one to three minutes dwell, then open and eject the encapsulated part still on its frame rail.

#### Trim, form, mark and final electrical test `si.trim`

After moulding the leads are formed on an 8-16 station trim-and-form press - trimmed, bent to the package pitch, flattened, and dipped in a tin or tin-lead solder pot - the body is marked with a dot-matrix ink printer or a Nd:YAG laser with part number, lot code and date code, and the part is dropped into a socket on an automatic tester and run against a final test program.

#### Burn-in and final test `si.burnin` _(medium)_

Assembled parts were run at elevated voltage - typically 7-9 V on a 5 V part - at 100-125 C for 24 to 168 hours in an oven loaded with sockets on a board, to weed out early-failure parts with contaminated junctions before they reached the customer. The C64 itself needed no burn-in: the chips were simply inserted into the board sockets.

#### 40-pin plastic DIP package `si.package.40` _(low)_

The package the 6510 CPU, the 8562 VIC-II and the 6526 CIA shipped in on the C64 mainboard: a 0.6 inch pitch, 40-leaded stamped lead frame with the die eutectic-bonded on its tab, gold wire to the pads, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. A ceramic hermetic version existed for industrial and military customers. The 6581 SID is not in this package: it shipped in a 28-pin DIP, and the service manual's parts list carries 16-pin, 28-pin and 40-pin IC sockets for the board.

        - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
        - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
##### Hermetic ceramic DIP sintering `si.package.ceramic` _(medium)_

For hermetic parts the die went into a 96% alumina ceramic shell, sealed with a devitrifying glass frit in a belt furnace at about 850-950 C, and the metal flange was brazed or glass-sealed to the header. Ceramic was slower and costlier than plastic and was used for military and industrial grades - but MOS shipped ceramic 40-pin parts of this kind, which is where the collectors' market for them comes from.

###### Alumina ceramic DIP shell `si.package.ceramic.shell` _(medium)_

A 96% alumina header: alumina powder pressed and sintered into a gas-tight body with a metallised cavity floor for the die, a glass-frit seal ring, and a flange carrying the frame leads. Alumina powder comes from bauxite, and that chain lives in the metals and packaging trees.

#### MOS Technology / CSG plant, 950 Rittenhouse Road `mb.cpu.fab`

The place these chips were born. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, moved to 950 Rittenhouse Road in the Valley Forge Corporate Center off Trooper Road near Norristown, and was bought by Commodore Business Machines in 1976, becoming the Commodore Semiconductor Group. It was a small but complete device plant: design, mask making, wafer fabrication on 4- and 5-inch wafers, assembly and final test all under one roof, which is why a single address appears on every C64 chip marking. It closed in 1992 and the site became an EPA Superfund site from leaking underground storage tanks.

##### Class 10 cleanroom bays with HEPA filtration `mb.cpu.fab.cleanroom`

Wafer processing in yellow-lit laminar-flow bays fed by fan filter units, with a class 1000 corridor outside; 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases distributed on stainless steel panels from bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen tanks; resist and wet chemistry in stainless or quartz benches; photomasks brought in through a pass-through hatch and never returned dirty.

##### In-house or commissioned mask shop `mb.cpu.fab.maskshop` _(low)_

A device plant of this size either cut its own masks or bought them from a regional mask shop. The work involved taking the layout database to a numerically controlled pattern generator, exposing and etching 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates, inspecting them on a comparison tool, and repairing defects - a few weeks and a few thousand dollars per mask level, ten levels per part. Commodore's mask-making capability is asserted in some histories but not documented to this level.

##### Assembly and test lines in the same building `mb.cpu.fab.assembly` _(medium)_

Die sort, sawing, die bonding, wire bonding, transfer moulding, trim-and-form, marking and final test all ran on the site behind the fab. The gold bonder room was kept dry and at constant humidity (roughly 40% RH) because gold wire and epoxy bonding are moisture-sensitive; the moulding presses were hydraulic, 50-100 ton, multi-cavity transfer presses.

### Four/eight 4164 64Kbit DRAMs = 64 KB RAM `mb.ram`

The C64's dynamic memory. The breadbin mainboard (PCB 326498-01) carries EIGHT 4164 64Kbit x 1 DRAMs, each holding 8 KB, giving 64 KB total; the address bus is multiplexed row/column through two 74LS257 multiplexers. Early prototypes used 4116 16-pin parts. The 4164 is a single-transistor single-capacitor (1T1C) dynamic cell, needs only +5 V because the 8-pin version generates its own -5 V substrate bias internally, and runs a two-level polysilicon process.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### The 1T1C memory cell `mb.ram.cell` _(medium)_

Each of the 65,536 bits is one access transistor plus one capacitor. The cell uses THREE polysilicon layers: poly 1 is the word line crossing the device, poly 2 is the overlapping plate of the storage capacitor (the plate is doped n+ and shared with the bit line), poly 3 is the bit line itself. Around 3.5 um x 8 um per cell in 1982 - big compared with modern trench/stacked cells. Double-diffused poly (DDP) cells, where the source and drain are separately implanted so the cell can be offset, were used by several 64K DRAM makers.

##### Second polysilicon layer: the storage capacitor `mb.ram.cell.doublepoly` _(medium)_

The key DRAM process problem in 1982. A second conformal polysilicon layer had to be deposited and patterned so that its edge was razor sharp and its overlap onto the access transistor was tight. Deposition was LPCVD silane at ~800-850 C; the plate was doped n+ with a phosphorus implant and annealed. Refractory metal silicides (WSi2, TiSi2) were being introduced on gates in 1983-84 but were not universal in 1982 64K DRAMs.

#### On-chip -5 V substrate bias charge pump `mb.ram.vbb` _(medium)_

The 4116 needed +5, +12, -5 and a boosted write supply, which is why it had a VBB pin and why the C64 prototype had extra regulators. The 4164 collapsed this to +5 V alone by generating the negative substrate bias on chip: an on-chip oscillator drives a capacitor, and the resulting AC is rectified to about -5 V and fed to the substrate, which also forward-biases the pn junction between the substrate and the n+ wells. Sense amplifiers bootstrap the bit line to +7-8 V during restore, and a second internal supply raises the word line above VDD.

#### Two-level polysilicon NMOS DRAM process `mb.ram.process`

Same basic silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU but heavier: thicker field oxide, more polysilicon depositions (three), a heavier arsenic source/drain, a thicker aluminium (2-3 um) for the bit lines that have to survive repeated bootstrapped swings, and usually two mask levels for bit-line precharge and sense amp. Eight to ten mask levels and 100-150 process steps, versus ~50 for the CPU.

##### Projection printing the poly 2 and bit-line levels `mb.ram.photolitho` _(medium)_

The tight overlays in a 4164 (bit line over capacitor plate, poly 2 over poly 1) were what finally forced 5x reduction step-and-repeat printing rather than 1:1 contact printing, because 1:1 contact printing of a 4 um bit line over a 4 um plate feature was too lossy. Typical 1982 DRAM mask lines ran GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers, with hard-baked 2 um Shipley AZ-1354 resist and a 5x reticle on a 3x3 inch quartz plate.

#### 4164 photomask set `mb.ram.mask` _(medium)_

A 64K DRAM needed eight to ten mask levels: active area, n+ field, contact, poly 1 (word line), poly 2 (capacitor plate), poly 3 (bit line), the second diffusion, metal, and passivation pad - plus gate-2 test structures. The poly 2 and bit-line levels are what forced 5x step-and-repeat printing; most 4164 wafers in 1982-83 went through GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers with 3x3 inch quartz reticles, and a handful of lines were still on 1:1 proximity aligners.

##### 5x reticle: chrome on quartz `mb.ram.mask.reticle`

A 3x3 inch fused-quartz or borosilicate plate coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, exposed from a 10x or 20x artwork intermediate by a mask stepper, developed, the chrome etched in perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected against the database on a Zeiss comparison tool, and mounted in a reticle cassette. Because quartz has a thermal expansion near zero, the reticle pattern stays put through a mask-level thermal cycle - the reason quartz beat glass once steppers became common.

          - *Chrome-on-glass photomask plate* `si.mask.plate` *(seen above)*
#### Alpha-particle and latch-up protection `mb.ram.protection`

DRAM soft errors from alpha particles emitted by radon daughters in the mould compound were a real field-failure mode in 1982. Mitigations used then: a sintered alumina or silicon-nitride chip cover potted over the die in a hermetic package; 'getter' compounds in the cavity; and softer, minimum-area bit-line and capacitor geometries to increase the stored charge margin.

##### Sintered chip cover over the die `mb.ram.package.cover` _(medium)_

On many 64K DRAMs the mould compound was not allowed near the die: instead a small alumina or silicon-nitride lid was diffusion-bonded to the lead frame cavity and the cavity then filled with a low-alpha moulding compound or left in a hermetic ceramic package. Alpha emission rate of the compound was a purchased specification in units of alphas per cm2 per hour.

#### 8-pin plastic DIP package `si.package.8`

The smallest and most common package in the machine: eight 4164 DRAMs, each a die on an 8-leaded lead frame with about eight frame bonds plus a dozen internal wires for the sense amps, transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy. A 16-pin version of the same die exists for stackable C128 memory.

        - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
        - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
      - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Die attach to the lead frame* `si.attach` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold wire wedge bonding* `si.bond` *(seen above)*
      - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `si.mould` *(seen above)*
      - *Trim, form, mark and final electrical test* `si.trim` *(seen above)*
#### Wafer sort and final test of the 4164 `mb.ram.sort` _(medium)_

Every die is probed with an 8-needle probe card and tested on an automated memory tester that runs a march-type pattern (write a checkerboard, read it, invert, repeat) through all 65,536 cells, then a refresh test holding 128 RAS cycles. Assembled parts go back into a socket on the same tester for a signature/AC timing check at 150 ns. Timing bins came out of this test - the C64 does not need the fastest grade, but the drive and the C128 memory expansions did.

        - *Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board* `si.probe-card` *(seen above)*
#### RAS-only refresh `mb.ram.refresh` _(low)_

The 4164 has no refresh counter: the row address must be presented on RAS every cycle to stay alive. On the C64 the counting is done by the VIC-II, not by the CPU and not by a CIA. While the VIC has the bus it multiplexes refresh row addresses onto its own video-RAM address bus, generating RAS itself; AEC going low is what takes the bus away from the 6510, so refresh is transparent to the processor. The KERNAL's part is only to write the raster counter at $D012, which steps the VIC through its refresh addresses.

### U6 2114L colour RAM (1K x 4 static) `mb.color-ram`

The C64's screen colour memory at U6, decoding to $D800-$DBE7: 1024 words of 4 bits each, i.e. one colour nibble for each of the 40x25 text screen's 1000 cells. The VIC-II reads these nibbles during the visible portion of every scanline and presents them to the 4-bit colour DAC, so the memory must be fully static with no clocks and no refresh - unlike the eight 4164 DRAMs sitting next to it. Period part numbers are 2114L (MOS Technology / other MOS vendors), MM2114 (National Semiconductor) and plain 2114; the C64 BOM lists 2114L-30, the -30 being a 300 ns speed grade. 18-pin DIP, single +5 V, TTL-compatible bidirectional I/O, about 225 mW.

#### Why static rather than dynamic `mb.color-ram.why-static`

The DRAMs beside it get a refresh cycle roughly every 2 ms because the 6510 can be held off the bus while the KERNAL's refresh routine runs. The colour RAM has no such luxury. The VIC-II fetches a colour nibble out of this chip in the middle of drawing each character cell, within a few hundred nanoseconds of the start of the scanline, from an address counter the VIC owns - there is no software window in which the chip could be taken off to rewrite it. So the cell has to hold its state indefinitely. That is the whole reason for the part: it is a static latch array, and it draws more power (225 mW) than one DRAM chip as a result.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### NMOS silicon-gate front end `si.front-end`

The flow every simple logic part in the machine ran: n+ source and drain pre-diffusion, LOCOS field oxide grown in dry O2 and then wet H2/O2 at about 1000-1050 C, LPCVD polysilicon gate from silane at 800-850 C, a self-aligned arsenic source/drain implant with a 1000-1100 C anneal, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium sputtered with 0.5-1% silicon and etched in hot phosphoric acid, then PSG and nitride passivation. Ten mask levels, printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner. The 6510 branch under the CPU carries the layer-by-layer version with every temperature; this node is the same flow stated once for the parts that did not need the detail.

#### Six-transistor NMOS static cell `mb.color-ram.cell`

Each of the 1024 nibbles is six transistors: two cross-coupled NMOS inverters forming a bistable latch, plus two NMOS pass transistors that connect the latch to the bit line when the address decoder enables that column. Because it is NMOS, each 'inverter' of the latch is a pull-down transistor in series with a load - which is where the load scheme matters. The latch holds its state for as long as power is applied, with no refresh and no clock, and has to keep roughly 2 V of noise margin at 5 V supply despite sharing a die and a substrate with 1024 other cells that all switch at once.

##### The load device: polysilicon resistor or depletion transistor `mb.color-ram.cell.load` _(low)_

This is the real difference between a 2114 and a CMOS SRAM, and it is an extra process step. A ratioed NMOS latch needs something in series with the pull-down transistor to act as a load: on 1982 parts this was typically an undoped or lightly doped polysilicon resistor deposited in the same LPCVD step as the gate, or a depletion-mode NMOS transistor (gate tied to source, threshold deliberately shifted negative by an extra implant) acting as a current source. The depletion option needed one more implant than the resistor option. Not established: which option the C64's 2114 used.

##### Pass transistors and the two-decoder structure `mb.color-ram.cell.access` _(medium)_

A 1024 x 4 array is decoded as a 32 x 32 matrix: a six-to-64 row decoder from A0-A5 and a five-to-32 column decoder from A6-A9, each a NAND-type NMOS decoder built from series pull-down strings. Each cell therefore needs two access transistors, one gated by a row line and one by a column line. The decoders are the only clocked-looking part of the chip, but they are combinational - there is no clock input pin at all, which is exactly what makes it static.

#### The 2114 mask set `mb.color-ram.mask` _(medium)_

Eight or nine 1:1 levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon (gate and, if used, the load resistor pattern), self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad, and alignment/test levels, printed from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment.

        - *Chrome-on-glass photomask plate* `si.mask.plate` *(seen above)*
#### How the VIC-II reads it during raster `mb.color-ram.vic-interface`

The VIC-II owns an internal video address counter that runs ahead of the beam. For each character cell in the visible portion of a scanline it drives the ten colour-RAM address lines and /CS low, and the chip returns the 4-bit colour on D0-D3 within about 300 ns; those four bits go straight to the 6-bit-per-channel RGB DAC and out through the 18-resistor palette on the mainboard. When the VIC releases the bus, the 6510 can access the same memory as ordinary RAM at $D800. That single-ended, mid-scanline, few-hundred-nanosecond read is the electrical reason the part had to be a static latch array with roughly 2 V of noise margin.

#### 18-pin plastic DIP package `si.package.18`

The package of the 2114L colour RAM: an 18-leaded stamped lead frame at 0.6 inch pitch, about 18 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and compound stories are the same as every other DIP in the machine.

        - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
        - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
      - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Die attach to the lead frame* `si.attach` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold wire wedge bonding* `si.bond` *(seen above)*
      - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `si.mould` *(seen above)*
      - *Trim, form, mark and final electrical test* `si.trim` *(seen above)*
#### Probe, sort and final test `mb.color-ram.test` _(medium)_

Probed on the wafer with an 18-needle probe card running an address/data checker over all 4096 bits in a marching pattern, then retested after moulding. Because the part has no refresh, its main failure modes are stuck cells from particles and defective decoders, both of which a walking-one/walking-zero pattern catches quickly - which is why the C64's most common colour-RAM symptom, a garbled or shifting character colour, is a die or socket fault rather than a marginal-timing one.

        - *Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board* `si.probe-card` *(seen above)*
### 901226-01 BASIC, 901227-03 KERNAL, 901225-01 character ROM `mb.roms`

The three mask-programmed NMOS ROMs on the C64 mainboard, all in 24-pin DIP: 901226-01 is the 8 KB (2364-compatible pinout) Commodore BASIC V2 interpreter at $A000; 901227-03 is the 8 KB KERNAL at $E000 (901227-01/-02 in earlier lots, and 901229-0x is the 1541 drive's KERNAL, not this one); 901225-01 is the 4 KB (2532-compatible) character generator ROM at U5. Mask ROMs are programmed by deleting or adding metal at one point in the flow, which means a whole extra mask set cut for each ROM revision.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### NMOS mask ROM front end `mb.roms.process` _(medium)_

The same silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU - n+ source/drain diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium, PSG/nitride passivation - with one extra mask level for the ROM programming pattern. A 24-pin DIP ROM die is small (a few mm2) and yields well; the constraint was mask cost, not yield.

#### Mask programming: one mask set per ROM revision `mb.roms.programming` _(medium)_

An NMOS mask ROM of 1982 was an NMOS transistor array with a decoder, programmed by removing or adding contacts/metal at the array intersections. The usual 1980s implementation was contact programming: the programmer and sense-amp metal were left unconnected at a bit=1 location, and the ROM-only mask plate was drawn with those contact cuts simply omitted - or, in the opposite polarity, extra contact cuts were added for every 0. The array is arranged 32 bit lines (or 24, using 6 cells of 4 transistors) across 2048 words for the 8 KB parts.

##### Bit-line sense amplifiers `mb.roms.sense` _(medium)_

A masked bit line is precharged high and then a dummy word is selected to develop a voltage across the bit line; a differential sense amplifier (a latch of four NMOS transistors plus a pair of cross-coupled load devices, exactly the same topology as the 6510's logic) amplifies the millivolt difference and latches it. The sense amps were the largest block in a mask ROM die - typically 10-15% of the area - because each needed a perfect match.

#### The ROM-only mask plate `mb.roms.mask` _(medium)_

Because the ROM pattern is a physical edit to the flow, Commodore held a separate chrome-on-glass plate for each ROM number. It was cut from the ROM's bit map by the same pattern generator used for the logic masks, inspected against the database, and stored in a mask library; 901226-01 and 901227-03 each required their own.

        - *Chrome-on-glass photomask plate* `si.mask.plate` *(seen above)*
#### 24-pin plastic DIP package `si.package.24`

The package of the BASIC, KERNAL and character ROMs: a 0.6 inch pitch, 24-leaded stamped lead frame, die eutectic-bonded on its tab, 25 um gold wedge bonding, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. On the C64 mainboard these three were the only chips soldered in rather than socketed, because they cannot usefully be replaced - though owners have socketed them since day one.

        - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
        - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
      - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Die attach to the lead frame* `si.attach` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold wire wedge bonding* `si.bond` *(seen above)*
      - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `si.mould` *(seen above)*
      - *Trim, form, mark and final electrical test* `si.trim` *(seen above)*
#### Verifying every ROM bit `mb.roms.verify` _(medium)_

A mask ROM cannot be re-programmed, so its contents are verified twice. On the wafer, a 24-needle probe card runs a read-only pattern through the 8192 or 4096 addresses and sums the data; after assembly, the part goes into an automatic tester that reads the whole array and checks it against a resident signature and, for the C64's BASIC and KERNAL, the published checksum. Any failure meant a defective mask or a contamination particle, and the whole mask set had to be re-run.

        - *Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board* `si.probe-card` *(seen above)*
#### ROM revisions are mask revisions `mb.roms.revisions`

Every fix to the C64's firmware cost a new mask set and a new wafer run. The BASIC ROM has exactly one version, 901226-01; the KERNAL went through 901227-01, -02 and -03, the last of which fixed a tape-loading bug and is what nearly every C64 shipped with; the character generator is 901225-01, with national variants 325018 (Swedish) and 325056 (Spanish C64C). A mask-ROM run also had to be large enough to fill the order, so a small revision could mean waiting weeks for wafers.

### 8562 VIC-II video chip, 40-pin DIP `mb.vic`

The C64's video, colour and sprite chip at U19, in a 40-pin DIP. The 8562 is the C64-specific part number for the NTSC VIC-II (the 6567/6569 are the Max Machine / PAL parts); it is an NMOS silicon-gate chip of the same generation as the 6510. The die contains the 40x25 text/bitmap video matrix, the 8 sprite (hardware sprite/clogger) engine, the colour-latch RAM interface, the 6-bit DAC colour outputs, the interrupt and border logic, the ~18 colour PAL palette resistors, and the 5-bit VIC-II colour registers. It reads VIC bank colour RAM through 8 pins and does no pixel-to-PAL conversion itself.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### NMOS front end for a large analog-plus-logic die `mb.vic.process` _(medium)_

The same silicon-gate NMOS sequence as the CPU, with extra care because the VIC-II mixes digital logic, a 6-bit DAC and analogue comparators on one die: 2 um minimum feature, ~400 A poly-oxide, LOCOS field oxide, self-aligned n+ source/drain, single 1-2 um aluminium layer, PSG plus plasma nitride passivation. The colour DAC outputs were open-source n-channel pull-downs that the external resistor ladder on the mainboard pulled up to +5 V.

#### The VIC-II colour output network on the mainboard `mb.vic.palette` _(low)_

The VIC-II does not name colours; it emits a set of analogue colour levels that circuitry on the mainboard has to turn into a usable video signal, and that circuitry is the physical interface between this die and a television. The specific network is not settled by the documents read: the 1992 service manual's 326298 parts list carries a 74LS373 octal latch at U26 together with resistor packs, and no resistor ladder or 74LS175 appears in that manual, in either Anatomy volume, or in the C128 Internals text.

#### VIC-II photomask set `mb.vic.mask` _(medium)_

The 8562's mask set was nine or ten levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, second diffusion, metal, ROM-programming (none here), passivation pad and the alignment/test levels. A 1982 small fab of this sort typically printed 1:1 on a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner with AZ-1350, using 1 mm chrome-on-glass plates about 5x7 inch. Overlay was held to +-0.5 um by a deliberate 'grid-broken' mask design: the layout broke the grid lines over active regions and added dummy structures so the stepper could align on a broken main grid rather than a continuous one.

        - *Chrome-on-glass photomask plate* `si.mask.plate` *(seen above)*
      - *40-pin plastic DIP package* `si.package.40` *(seen above)*
      - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
      - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Die attach to the lead frame* `si.attach` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold wire wedge bonding* `si.bond` *(seen above)*
      - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `si.mould` *(seen above)*
      - *Trim, form, mark and final electrical test* `si.trim` *(seen above)*
#### Wafer probe and pattern test of the 8562 `mb.vic.test` _(medium)_

The VIC-II is probed with a 40-needle card and a test program that exercises the character generator, the sprite pointers, the colour registers and the interrupt logic - and, on the analogue side, checks that all six colour outputs swing the full 0-5 V and that the 18-bit colour latches all decode. Assembled parts run the same program in a socket, often while a technician watched a test pattern on a monitor plugged into the tester's video output.

        - *Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board* `si.probe-card` *(seen above)*
### 6581 SID sound chip, 40-pin DIP `mb.sid`

The C64's sound generator at U18: three analogue subtractive-synthesis voices (two oscillators plus a noise source through a 12-bit DAC, one extra-noise-only channel for percussion), a ring modulator, a resonant multimode filter with a self-oscillating VCA, external-to-internal feedback volume routing, two pulse-width modulators and a hard sync. It is an NMOS hybrid - digital logic and poly counters driving an analogue poly on the same die - which is why it is noisy, why R4, R4AR, R5 and R6 differ, and why a 8580 (made on a newer process) sounds cleaner.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### NMOS hybrid process: digital counters on an analogue poly `mb.sid.process` _(medium)_

The 6581 was not a purely digital NMOS part. Its 24-bit phase accumulators, the noise LFSR and the envelope generators are ordinary silicon-gate NMOS with depletion loads, the same technology as the 6510. Its DACs, the filter and the VCA are analogue: long polysilicon resistors laid down in the same polysilicon deposition, a large-area common-emitter output transistor, and a big p-diffused 'pump' resistor in the VCA. All of it in one 2-4 um process with a single aluminium layer, and with the analogue section laid out shielded inside its own p-epitaxial tub.

##### Polysilicon load resistors `mb.sid.poly-res`

The 6510 and the SID both use undoped or lightly doped deposited polysilicon as a resistor, deposited in the same LPCVD silane step as the gate and left unetched between two aluminium contacts. Sheet resistance was 30-100 ohm/sq in 1982 and the resistance was trimmed, if at all, by laser or by anodising the surface - the 'thin-film resistor' trimming industry existed for exactly this.

#### External components the SID needs from the board `mb.sid.external`

The 6581 does not make sound by itself. The C64 mainboard provides the 14.31818 MHz colour clock, which is the frequency of crystal Y1 itself rather than a divided or multiplied derivative, two 4066 CMOS bilateral switches and a 7406 hex inverter to control filter routing and to stabilize the output (a documented MOS workaround that varies with chip revision), the 470 ohm/1 kohm output network, and the 4066-switched external-to-internal feedback path. Those are separate parts in the board and interconnect trees.

#### SID photomask set `mb.sid.mask` _(medium)_

Nine or ten levels for the 6581: n+ field, LOCOS active area, base/well, contact, polysilicon (including the poly resistor pattern that is the DAC), second diffusion, metal, passivation pad, plus alignment. Printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plates, with the grid-broken alignment scheme. The analogue poly resistor pattern was itself a mask level, and trimming it by laser was an option some makers used.

        - *Chrome-on-glass photomask plate* `si.mask.plate` *(seen above)*
      - *40-pin plastic DIP package* `si.package.40` *(seen above)*
      - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
      - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Die attach to the lead frame* `si.attach` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold wire wedge bonding* `si.bond` *(seen above)*
      - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `si.mould` *(seen above)*
      - *Trim, form, mark and final electrical test* `si.trim` *(seen above)*
#### Wafer probe and audio test of the 6581 `mb.sid.test` _(medium)_

Probe testing a SID meant electrical tests (register access, oscillator counters, envelope thresholds, DAC linearity, filter self-oscillation) plus, on the better lines, a functional audio test: a short score stepped through the chip and the output listened to or measured on a spectrum analyser. Final test repeated it in a socket. This is why 6581 revisions are dated and marked (R4, R4AR, R5, R6) - each was a measured change to the analogue thresholds. The threshold voltages of the envelope generators and the VCA had to be trended, because the whole reason the 8580 sounds different is that its analogue section was redesigned and its thresholds tightened.

        - *Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board* `si.probe-card` *(seen above)*
#### SID revisions as an analogue-process story `mb.sid.revisions` _(low)_

The 6581 shipped in an unsuffixed NMOS form from 1982, then as R3, R4 and R4AR between 1985 and 1987. Later parts changed the analogue behaviour - supply voltage on pin 28 and the value of the four filter capacitors - but the familiar account of each revision being a discrete change to the analogue block found by listening to parts on probe is not established here. The 8580 arrived in 1987 as an R5, built on an HMOS-II process rather than a later NMOS one, with 9 V on pin 28 and 22 nF filter capacitors in place of the 6581's 470 pF; it is generally regarded as the cleaner and quieter part.

### Two 6526 CIA complex interface adapters `mb.cia`

CIA 1 at U17 and CIA 2 at U18 (PLA at U17 on some board revisions) provide the C64's two 8-bit parallel ports, the keyboard/joystick matrix scanning, the two 16-bit interval timers with one-shot/underflow interrupt, the shift register used for the serial (IEC) bus, and TOD (time-of-day) clocking derived from AC mains. Each 6526 is a 40-pin DIP NMOS part; CIA 1 sits at $D400 and reads port A from the VIC colour register file, while CIA 2 sits at $DC00 and drives the user port and serial bus.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### Time-of-day clock `mb.cia.tod`

The CIA's time-of-day clock is a 17-bit counter clocked from the serial pin, which the C64 mainboard drives from one side of the AC line through a 470 kohm resistor. The resulting clock is therefore a divided version of the mains frequency, trimmed per unit at final test by selecting a film capacitor. The timer counters themselves are static CMOS-style ripple counters, so they hold their count with the clock stopped - which is why a dead battery or a flat mains filter freezes the clock.

#### Serial shift register `mb.cia.serial`

The CIA's 8-bit shift register is what makes the Commodore serial bus work at all. Software sets a bit, shifts it out under CIA timer control with the handshake lines driving the ATN and CLK/CB lines, and reads bits back the same way; the VIC-II's serial output is decoded separately. This is a purely digital function built from ordinary NMOS flip-flops, but its timing jitter is the reason the KERNAL's serial routines are as delicate as they are.

      - *NMOS silicon-gate front end* `si.front-end` *(seen above)*
#### CIA photomask set `mb.cia.mask` _(medium)_

Nine or ten levels - n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad and alignment levels - printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from chrome-on-glass plates, using the grid-broken alignment scheme with dummy structures and stepper/diffusion checks. The two CIAs and the VIA were almost certainly the same process with three different mask sets.

        - *Chrome-on-glass photomask plate* `si.mask.plate` *(seen above)*

      - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Die attach to the lead frame* `si.attach` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold wire wedge bonding* `si.bond` *(seen above)*
      - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `si.mould` *(seen above)*

#### Wafer probe and final test of the 6526 `mb.cia.test` _(medium)_

Probe with a 40-needle card and a program that clocks both 16-bit timers against a reference, steps the serial shift register through a byte, checks the interrupt priority logic and the port handshake, and measures the TOD chain. Assembled parts repeat it in a socket. Because the TOD is clocked from the AC line, the accuracy test needed a calibrated frequency standard, not just a functional pass.

        - *Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board* `si.probe-card` *(seen above)*
### 6522 PPI/VIA, 40-pin DIP `mb.ppi`

The 6522 Versatile Interface Adapter at U15 on the C64 mainboard: two 8-bit parallel ports (the user port at $D420 and the cassette port at $D800), two 1-bit handshake lines, an 8-bit shift register for the cassette serial interface, two 16-bit timers with pulse output, four interrupt inputs and an I/O port with three latched control bits. It is the same 40-pin DIP silicon-gate NMOS part as the CIAs, from the same mask-family era and almost certainly the same process.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
      - *NMOS silicon-gate front end* `si.front-end` *(seen above)*
#### Parallel ports and handshake lines `mb.ppi.userport` _(low)_

The 6522's parallel ports are the C64's only general-purpose parallel I/O, and they appear on the 12-way cartridge edge as the user port for printers, samplers and third-party cartridges, and on the mainboard as the cassette port. The user port carries one 8-bit port, not two: on the cartridge edge it presents PB0-PB7 together with PA2 alone. CIA 2 sits at $DD00, and the lines are open collector with internal pull-ups rather than quasi-bidirectional TTL, so driving them from two cards at once was a hardware error rather than a negotiated one.

#### 6522 photomask set `mb.ppi.mask` _(medium)_

Nine or ten levels - n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad and alignment - printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment. As with the CIAs, the process is the CSG standard flow; only the layout differs.

### U17 PLA 906114-01 (mask-programmed NMOS) `mb.pla`

The C64's Programmable Logic Array at U17: it decodes the 6510's address lines and generates the chip-select and bank-switching strobes for every other chip on the board - RAM, ROMs, VIC-II, SID, CIAs, VIA, colour RAM - which makes it the single point of failure for the whole machine. Commodore part number 906114-01, alternate designation MOS 8700-001, die marked MOS 7700R1 / 8700R2. It is a mask-programmed NMOS clone of the Signetics 82S100 bipolar array, in a 28-pin 600 mil epoxy DIP, and it is by far the most failure-prone and most counterfeited part in the machine.

#### What a PLA physically is `mb.pla.array`

Two arrays of transistors and a set of 'links'. The fixed AND array is a matrix of diode or transistor junctions arranged so that each row implements one product term - every possible AND of a subset of the 16 inputs. The programmable OR array adds up to eight of those product terms per output. Each product-term-to-output connection is a physical link in that array, and 'programming' the part simply means deciding which links exist. Commodore's version is pure combinational logic with no registered terms, which is why it is fast enough to sit directly on the 6510's address bus and settle inside a 6510 cycle.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### NMOS process for the 906114-01 (node not claimed) `mb.pla.process` _(low)_

The device-level facts are solid: it is NMOS, mask programmed, made at Norristown, and running a lower VOH than the bipolar original. The process details are not published anywhere. On the evidence of die markings, the era and the same fab, it is almost certainly the house silicon-gate NMOS flow used for the 6510, 6522 and 6526 - n+ diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, LPCVD polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, one aluminium layer, PSG or nitride passivation - run at whatever line width that flow was at the time. No specific figure is asserted for that line width, because no source states one for this part.

#### Mask programming of the link pattern `mb.pla.mask-programming`

This is the practical heart of a mask-programmed PLA. The AND array, the OR array and the decoders are all routine NMOS layers, but the pattern of which links exist is frozen into a single additional mask level - drawn as one extra colour plane in the layout database and cut like any other plate. That one extra mask is what makes each unique logic function expensive: artwork generation, mask fabrication and inspection all have to be repeated, and the wafer run cannot be short because the lot must be big enough to be worth the NRE. The whole array is physically small, so a 4-inch wafer holds many thousands of dies - the constraint on order size is mask and engineering cost, not silicon.

#### Fusible-link and antifuse PLAs `mb.pla.alternatives` _(medium)_

The two field-programmable routes a PLD could have taken instead, and the reason a mask-programmed part is a different commercial animal. A fusible link is a real wire of chromium or nichrome, 1-3 um thick, burned out by a laser programmer through the package's FE/NE pin - this is how the PAL 16L8 and 20L8 worked, and why a PAL is a catalogue part you can buy in thousands of functions. An antifuse starts as a conducting amorphous-silicon or silicon-dioxide film which a 20-40 V pulse converts into high-resistance insulation; it needs no laser but was slower to program and harder to test. Commodore could use neither for a part sold in the millions at commodity logic prices.

#### PLA versus PAL: why the name misleads `mb.pla.vs-pal`

The C64's part is called a PLA, but the parts most readers know by that name - the 16L8, 16R8, 20L8 - are PALs, and the two are not interchangeable in sourcing or programming. A PAL is a generic catalogue device: every 16L8 from every vendor is the same silicon, and the buyer programs it. A mask-programmed PLA is a custom device: the buyer cannot program it, and nobody else ever made this function. That is the whole reason fakes are so common - the SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton and PLAtinum parts sold as replacements are typically GAL/EPROM emulations or freshly mask-programmed parts from a third party, and the C64's PLA is precisely the component where a substitute can fail in ways that are hard to trace.

#### Reverse-engineered from a Signetics 82S100 `mb.pla.provenance`

Early C64s shipped with a bipolar Signetics 82S100, or the Fairchild 93459 clone of it; Signetics was acquired by Philips, which renamed the part PLS100. Commodore's engineers then decapped the bipolar part, photographed it with a Polaroid camera and rebuilt the function as a mask-programmed NMOS design - Bil Herd's recollection is 'We reverse engineered the PLA from Signetics using a polaroid camera'. The resulting die is marked MOS 7700R1 or 8700R2, and it runs at a slightly lower VOH than the bipolar original (about 3.7-3.8 V against 4.2 V), which is part of why early and late C64s behave marginally differently.

#### The economics of one custom mask set `mb.pla.economics` _(medium)_

The 906114-01 encodes the entire C64 memory map in a die smaller than the fingertip, and Commodore sold millions of C64s, so once the mask was paid for the part was dirt cheap per unit. But the flip side is that the function exists nowhere else in the world. Any machine needing a different bank-switch map needs a different mask, a different lot and a different lead time - which is why C64Cs needed a different PLA (MOS 8721) to support the cartridge port's new banking. It is also why the cost of a single counterfeit or of a dead original is disproportionate to the value of the silicon inside it.

#### 28-pin 600 mil DIP package `si.package.28`

A wide-body package, because the PLA needs 16 inputs, 8 outputs, an output enable, the unused FE/NE pin, VCC and VSS. Die attach is a gold-silicon eutectic bond on a gold-plated tab, about 28 pad bonds on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy, with the leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch in a 28-socket trim-and-form operation. A ceramic variant exists but is uncommon on a C64.

        - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
        - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Stamped DIP lead frame* `si.leadframe` *(seen above)*
      - *Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound* `si.emc` *(seen above)*
      - *Die attach to the lead frame* `si.attach` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold wire wedge bonding* `si.bond` *(seen above)*
