      - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `si.mould` *(seen above)*
      - *Trim, form, mark and final electrical test* `si.trim` *(seen above)*
#### Why it fails more than anything else in the machine `mb.pla.failures`

Three reasons stack up. First, it is a single point of failure: if any of its eight strobes misbehaves, the symptom is a dead or misbehaving machine rather than one dead chip. Second, its output enable and eight outputs switch hard on every 6510 cycle against the capacitive load of the whole board, so it is the highest-current part on the bus and the one that sees the worst ringing. Third, and decisively for longevity, it is the one chip that cannot be replaced: a dead 6510 can be bought new; a dead 906114-01 cannot, so in practice a dead PLA means a dead machine unless it is re-masked or emulated.

#### Probe, truth-table test and final test `mb.pla.test` _(medium)_

A PLA is uniquely testable because its specification is a truth table rather than a waveform. On probe, a stored truth table is stepped through all 16 inputs x /OE combinations on all 8 outputs - a few thousand vectors - which catches a stuck link, a shorted link or a bad decoder in seconds. Assembled parts get the same vector set in a socket on an automatic tester, plus a timing check that the address decode settles inside a 6510 cycle.

### Discrete semiconductors on the board `mb.discretes` _(medium)_

The handful of non-IC semiconductors in the machine: small-signal NPN and PNP planar transistors (2N3904, 2N3906, 2N4124) for the serial/parallel port buffers, the colour-amplifier and video-driver stages and the cassette/joystick input switching; higher-voltage NPN power transistors (2N3055, 2N3792) in the power supply's regulator and short-circuit crowbar; rectifier, switching and zener diodes (1N4001, 1N4148, 1N47xx); one or two indicator LEDs; and a metal-oxide varistor across the AC input. Each of these was made in a bipolar or compound-semiconductor plant completely unrelated to the Norristown logic fab.

      - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
      - *Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop* `si.litho` *(seen above)*
#### Planar epitaxial small-signal BJT process `mb.discretes.bjt`

The 2N3904, 2N3906 and 2N4124 are all the same architecture, differentiated by polarity and voltage rating: a p-type substrate, a heavily arsenic- or phosphorus-doped n+ subcollector, then a 1-3 um epitaxial n collector layer grown in an ATCP radiant-heated reactor at ~1150-1250 C with AsH3 or PH3 in H2. Isolation diffusions of boron create the tub, then the base (boron, ~0.5-1 um deep) and finally the emitter (arsenic or phosphorus, heavily overdoped to a low base resistance) through separate photolithography steps. Aluminium metallization is deposited by evaporation, alloyed at 400 C to make ohmic contacts, then the wafer is probed.

#### Radiant-heated epitaxial reactor `mb.discretes.epi` _(medium)_

After the n+ subcollector diffusion, a 1-3 um n-type epitaxial layer was grown in a radiant-heated vertical reactor: the wafers sat on a graphite susceptor inside a quartz bell jar, inductively heated to 1150-1250 C, with AsH3 or PH3 in H2 flowing over them. Epitaxy gave the collector the uniformity and the carrier concentration that a diffusion simply could not, which is what made the 2N3904's gain and its saturation voltage repeatable.

#### Isolation diffusion and its moat `mb.discretes.isolation`

A boron diffusion deep enough to reach the subcollector creates a p-type tub around each transistor, isolating it from its neighbours through reverse-biased pn junctions rather than an oxide. The same oxide that covers the tub is later cut away in the base and emitter windows - this is the 'planar epitaxial' process invented at Fairchild in 1959 and still the standard discrete recipe in 1982.

#### TO-92 epoxy mould package `mb.discretes.bjt-package` _(medium)_

Discretes were diced, attached to the tab of a stamped lead frame, wire bonded or solder dipped, and transfer moulded in a black epoxy (a filled phenolic or epoxy compound loaded with carbon black for colour) with the leads formed to a 0.25 inch pitch. The 2N3904's die is under 1 square mm; the package volume is almost all mould compound.

##### Discrete lead frame, 0.25 inch pitch `mb.discretes.leadframe`

A transistor's leads are a stamped 0.25-0.30 mm strip of nickel or copper alloy, plated with tin or tin-lead so they solder into a phenolic or epoxy-moulded phenolic board. The C64 mainboard is a solder-through board, so lead-frame plating was the difference between a working assembly and a cold joint.

#### Rectifier, switching and zener diodes `mb.discretes.diodes` _(medium)_

Three diode families with completely different construction. The 1N4001 is a diffused rectifier: an n- epitaxial layer on an n+ substrate with a heavily p-doped anode, rated 1 A / 50 V. The 1N4148 is a planar switching diode: a small npn with a Schottky-clamped base shorted to the cathode, rated 200 mA / 100 V, fast enough for 300 ns recovery. The 1N47xx is a zener: a heavily doped junction with a knee of 2.4-75 V, usually a diffused planar or, in the low-current versions, a temperature-compensated bandgap reference. All three were made by alloying or diffusing junctions into small silicon dice and moulding them in DO-35 glass or DO-41 plastic.

#### Indicator LED (red/green/amber only) `mb.discretes.led`

The C64's power indicator is a 3 mm or 5 mm epoxy-domed LED: a liquid-phase epitaxially grown GaP or GaAsP junction die, die-bonded into a reflector cup on the cathode post, wire bonded to the anode, and encapsulated in a semi-transparent epoxy lens that also acts as a light pipe. Red (GaAsP, ~660 nm) and green (GaP, ~555 nm) were common; amber (GaAsP ~590 nm) and the increasingly cheap GaP red were also in use. Blue LEDs did not exist in 1982 at any price - the first practical blue GaN/InGaN device was 1993, and an efficient one 1995.

##### Liquid-phase epitaxy of the GaP junction `mb.discretes.led.epi` _(medium)_

A GaP or GaAsP wafer is dipped in a molten, boron-doped Ga/GaP/P solution in a horizontal tilting boat inside a long quartz tube furnace at ~850-900 C. The substrate is swept through many alternating supersaturated melts so that dozens of GaP layers a few microns thick grow in, alternating p-type (Zn-doped) and n-type (S-doped) to form the double-heterostructure junction that makes the bright 1980s LED. The process is epitaxial in the strict sense - it is the same technique used for GaAs microwave chips.

##### Refined gallium `mb.discretes.led.gallium` _(medium)_

Gallium refined from bauxite residue or from zinc residues by repeated ion-exchange in alkaline solution or by amalgam/hydroxide extraction, to 99.9-99.99% metal, then to GaP by reaction with high-purity phosphorus at 1000-1100 C in a sealed quartz ampoule.

##### GaP or GaAsP substrate wafer `mb.discretes.led.substrate` _(medium)_

The LPE junction layers grow on a polished, Czochralski-grown substrate of n-type or semi-insulating GaAs, or on GaP grown by the same kind of pull used for silicon. GaAs itself is made by liquid-phase or VGF growth from a melt of gallium and arsenic, with the arsenic fed from a boiler of high-purity arsenic metal in hydrogen.

#### Zinc oxide varistor disc `mb.discretes.varistor` _(medium)_

A MOV disc across the mains input: a disc of ZnO powder mixed with a few percent of glass and pressed and sintered at 1000-1200 C in air. Its resistance is nonlinear - about 1 kohm/mm at low voltage, collapsing to tens of ohms at the 275 V clamping point - because the grain boundaries are thin depleted zinc-oxide grain-boundary phases that break down. Organic or glassy coating and epoxy moulding complete the disc.

##### Zinc oxide powder from zinc concentrate `mb.discretes.varistor.zinc` _(medium)_

Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed at 900-1000 C to zinc oxide, then reduced with carbon in a shaft or electrothermic furnace at 900-1100 C to zinc metal, burned back to ZnO, and purified to high-purity ZnO for the varistor mix.

#### Probe, gain binning and final test of the discretes `mb.discretes.test` _(medium)_

Discretes are probed on the wafer with a 3- or 10-needle card, then tested after packaging on a curve tracer or a dedicated bin tester. Bipolar small-signal parts are binned by hFE and by VCEO - the 2N3904's hFE spread runs roughly 100-300 - so a given lot is graded, and the C64's assembly only ever saw parts within the standard bin. Rectifiers are tested for reverse leakage and forward drop at rated current.

### 74-series glue logic `mb.logic`

The off-the-shelf logic chips on a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 that are not Commodore's own designs - thirteen positions according to the service-manual parts list, plus an LM556 timer alongside them. They do no arithmetic and no video: they multiplex addresses, latch bytes, decode chip selects, count, generate the video dot clock and invert the cassette port. Ten are 74-series in black epoxy DIP, three are CMOS 4000-series, and the U8 is an older non-Schottky 7406. Individually each was a commodity costing tens of cents.

#### 7406 hex inverter buffer, open collector (U8) `mb.logic.u8-7406` _(medium)_

Six inverting buffers whose outputs are open collectors rather than totem poles, in a 14-pin DIP. On the 250407 they invert and buffer the 6510's cassette-port output lines (CASS MOTOR, CASS SENSE, CASS WRITE, CASS DATA) and the shared user-port / serial lines. Open-collector outputs with pull-ups are how those lines could be wired-OR and level-shifted without contention, and a pin that shorts to ground leaves the CPU reading the defined 'off' state rather than floating.

##### How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL) `mb.logic.bipolar` _(medium)_

The 74LS family was not built on the same kind of line as the Commodore custom chips. This is a junction-isolated, collector-diffused bipolar process: an n+ buried-and-collector structure grown epitaxially on p-type silicon, four thermal diffusion cycles, a sputtered NiCr resistor level, one level of aluminium metallisation, about eight mask levels and sixty to a hundred process steps. Minimum drawn features were 3-5 um - twenty times coarser than a 1983 dynamic RAM - which is exactly why a logic chip cost a fraction of what a 6510 or a 4164 cost.

###### The junction-isolated bipolar flow `mb.logic.bipolar.process`

The sequence that turns a plain slice of silicon into a chip of interconnected bipolar transistors. Four diffusion cycles do all the work: an n+ isolation diffusion to separate each transistor into its own island; a p base diffusion under the island to form the transistor base; an n+ emitter diffusion into the base to form the emitter; and the Schottky-barrier levels that give the 'LS' in 74LS its name. Between and inside those cycles sit an epitaxial growth, a thin-film resistor deposition, a metallisation and a passivation.

###### p-type starting wafer `mb.logic.bipolar.process.substrate`

A slice of p-type silicon, lightly doped so that it is a good insulator between transistor islands and does not leak much reverse current. Everything the tree contains - the transistors, the resistors, the isolation - sits on this one piece of crystal.

              - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
###### Epitaxial growth of the collector `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi`

The single most distinctive step of the bipolar process. The wafer is placed in a horizontal reactor and a few micrometres of lightly doped n-type silicon is grown on top of it in a hydrogen atmosphere at about 1100-1200 C. The growing layer inherits the crystal lattice of the wafer below, so the n-type collector sits on the p-type substrate as a perfect single crystal - a vertical diode. Without epi, a vertical bipolar transistor would be impossible.

###### The horizontal epitaxial reactor `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.reactor` _(medium)_

A quartz or silicon-carbide tube with a graphite susceptor that is heated by a radio-frequency induction coil. Silane or trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow past; the silicon atoms deposit on the hot wafer. Inductors rotate the wafer and provide the radiant heat. Loaded by hand or by a cassette elevator; a batch of 20-30 wafers takes an hour or two.

###### Growth of the field oxide `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation`

Silicon dioxide grown by passing steam over the wafer at 900-1050 C. This thick oxide is the field oxide: it covers everything except the windows that are later cut for diffusion and metallisation, and it is what electrically and physically isolates one transistor island from the next, in the same way the oxide isolates a MOS gate.

###### The oxidation furnace `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.furnace`

A horizontal tube furnace, quartz or silicon-carbide, heated to 1000 C, with wet oxygen or steam flowing through. The wafer rides on a quartz boat pushed in and out by a loader. Oxidation is the slowest step in a bipolar line and the furnaces are the bottleneck.

###### Deionised process steam `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam`

Ultra-pure water turned to vapour in the furnace inlet. The water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold. Fab water came from municipal supply through a chain of reverse osmosis and ion exchange. Steam is an ingredient of the oxidation step, not a component of the furnace, so it hangs off `inputs` rather than as a child.

###### Fused quartz tube and boat `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quartz`

The tube the wafer sits in is fused quartz, because quartz holds up to about 1100 C and is chemically inert to the oxidising atmosphere. Quartz is itself manufactured from high-purity silicon, so the tube and the silicon it processes came from related chemistry.

###### Collector-collector isolation `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation`

The first diffusion. Where the field oxide has windows, phosphorus is driven in to make a heavily n-doped region that runs all the way down to the p-type substrate. Everything inside a window is now n-type; the n+ walls around and between windows cut the wafer into separate n-type islands, each with a p substrate beneath it. Two n+ islands separated by a p-substrate region form back-to-back diodes, and those diodes are the isolation - a device made entirely of unwanted junctions doing an essential job.

###### Diffusion into the window `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diffusion`

The wafer is coated with a phosphorus-bearing dopant source - a spun-on emulsion or a deposited glass - then pushed into a furnace at 1000-1150 C. Heat alone moves the phosphorus atoms down into the silicon, opening up and closing the junction as it goes. Diffusion, not implantation, because diffusion gives the smooth graded junctions that give a transistor its gain.

###### Guard rings around the islands `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guardring` _(medium)_

A ring of n+ material, often tied to the most positive supply, laid around each sensitive island. It intercepts stray minority carriers and surface charge before they can reach the isolation junction, and it raises the breakdown voltage of the isolation. Guard rings are one of the oldest tricks in the planar process and were still drawn on a 1983 logic layout.

###### What a guard ring physically is `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guardring.how` _(medium)_

Not a new material - just the same n+ diffusion, but drawn as a closed loop around the transistor instead of a small dot. The mask for the isolation diffusion draws the guard ring at the same time as the island, so it costs one more shape on one mask and no extra process step. That is the whole elegance of it.

###### Dielectric isolation (Fairchild's alternative) `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.dielectric` _(medium)_

Instead of relying on reverse-biased isolation diodes, the islands can be sunk into a solid thermally grown oxide so each is completely surrounded by insulating oxide. The wafer is oxidised, then diffusion (or epitaxy) is done into small windows in the oxide; the oxide under the silicon is never removed, so no vertical isolation junction exists at all. This gives lower capacitance and better speed but is much harder to make, because the silicon has to be grown in a hole in oxide without lifting it.

###### Deep trench isolation (later, and now extinct in logic) `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trench`

For the highest-performance bipolar processes - the ones behind linear amplifiers and the last power logic - isolation was cut as a deep trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide or polysilicon, then buried. This gives near-vertical isolation walls and far lower capacitance than the lateral isolation diffusion. It was expensive and it is now essentially extinct in merchant logic.

###### The base diffusion `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base`

A second diffusion. Through a new mask, boron is driven into each n-island to make the p-type base of the transistor. The base is the thinnest and most tightly controlled region in the whole structure - roughly half to one micrometre deep - because the transistor's gain and its maximum speed both come from how narrow the base is. Every minute the base is too wide, the transistor is slow.

###### Boron as the p dopant `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron`

Boron, the p-type dopant, came either as diborane gas or as a thin boron-doped oxide or boron nitride wafer, and was the standard acceptor for base diffusions throughout the era. It is an ingredient of the diffusion, so it hangs off `inputs` (chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane) rather than as a child.

###### Boron oxide (B2O3) solid source `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.borax` _(medium)_

For thermal diffusion, boron was often carried in a boron-doped oxide or a boron nitride wafer placed face-to-face with the silicon in the diffusion boat. Cheaper and easier to handle than gas. The active species is boron oxide, B2O3; the name previously used here said 'borax', which is the sodium tetraborate and a different - and not the standard - source.

###### The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it `mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter` _(medium)_

The third diffusion. Through a finer mask, a very heavily doped n+ region is driven into the boron base, forming the emitter. Because the n+ emitter is so much more heavily doped than the p base, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased at only 0.7 V and injects enormous current gain - but only as long as the emitter does not punch through the thin base under the reverse bias of the collector. Pushing gold into the emitter diffuses the emitter junction forward slightly, making the junction harder for holes to reverse-inject, which suppresses punch-through and the associated capacitance, and raises the gain. This is the 'gold-doped emitter'.

###### The gold in the emitter `mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold` _(medium)_

A fraction of a percent of gold, introduced by co-doping the emitter source and driven in with the emitter diffusion. Gold is a deep acceptor-diffusing substitutional impurity in silicon; it behaves in the base like a recombination centre. In the emitter-base junction it forward-shifts the junction for electrons and suppresses hole injection into the emitter, which is what raises gain and kills the reverse gain of the transistor.

###### The Schottky clamp - the S in LS `mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky`

In standard 7400-series TTL a transistor saturates when it is driven hard: both junctions forward-biased, charge stored in the base, and the transistor slow to turn off. A 74LS puts a small Schottky diode - metal to lightly doped n-type, with no forward drop - from each transistor's base to its collector. When the base tries to go more forward than a silicon junction would allow, the Schottky diode conducts first and steals the excess, pinning the collector voltage just above saturation. The transistor never saturates, so it turns off in a couple of nanoseconds instead of twenty. That is the whole 'Schottky' idea, and it is why an LS gate is fast and still low-power.

###### The NiCr thin-film resistor level `mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr` _(medium)_

A 74LS is full of resistors - the pull-ups, the current-limiting elements, the bias network. On a junction-isolated bipolar logic line they were made as a deposited thin film of nickel-chromium alloy, sputtered onto the wafer, patterned by one extra mask, and annealed. This is the one mask level that separates the 74LS flow from a plainer bipolar analog flow, and it is why an 'LS' logic wafer and an analog bipolar wafer had different mask counts.

###### The nickel-chromium sputtering target `mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target`

A block of 80/20 nickel-chromium alloy that the sputter gun erodes. High-purity nickel and chromium are the two metals that dominate this one thin film; the chromium is what gives the film its near-zero temperature coefficient, and the nickel is what makes it resistive rather than metallic.

###### The RF/DC sputterer `mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.sputter`

A vacuum chamber pumped to a low argon pressure, a cathode holding the NiCr target, the wafer as the anode. An RF or DC glow discharge strikes the target, argon ions knock nickel and chromium atoms loose, and they deposit onto the wafer. It is a slow, line-of-sight, unidirectional process - which is why sputtered NiCr resistors are behind the same shadow problems as sputtered metal interconnect.

###### The contact window `mb.logic.bipolar.process.contact`

One more mask, which cuts small windows in the field oxide wherever a metal film needs to reach the silicon underneath - the collector, the base, the emitter. Each window is a hole a few micrometres across. The oxide elsewhere is untouched, and it is the oxide that keeps the aluminium from shorting to the substrate everywhere except where you wanted it to.

###### Aluminium metallisation `mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal` _(medium)_

The final mask. A layer of aluminium about 1 micrometre thick is deposited over the whole wafer - sputtered or evaporated - and a mask removes it everywhere except the wires. Those wires connect the transistor terminals, the resistors, and the bonding pads around the edge of the die. One single metal level, no vias, no second layer. This is the single biggest reason a 1983 logic chip was so simple to make: routing was almost free because the cells were small.

###### Sintering the metal into the contacts `mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter` _(medium)_

After aluminium is deposited, the wafer is pushed briefly to 400-450 C in hydrogen or forming gas. This melts the aluminium into the contact windows, welding it to the silicon and lowering the contact resistance, and it anneals out the sputter damage in the silicon. It is a short, cheap step and it is the reason the metallisation recipe ends with a hydrogen firing.

###### Passivation over the metal `mb.logic.bipolar.process.passivation`

A final film - silicon dioxide, usually with a nitride cap - deposited over the finished aluminium, opened again only at the bonding pads and along the scribe lanes. It seals the chip against moisture and mobile ions, which is what lets a 1983 logic part hold a 15-year life in a consumer television.

###### Eight masks, eight photolithography cycles `mb.logic.bipolar.litho`

A full bipolar logic cycle is repeated for each of its eight mask levels, and each cycle is the same eight or nine operations: clean, dehydrate, spin-coat resist, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse and dry, hard-bake, then inspect - before the wafer goes back to the furnace, the etcher or the implanter. Eight masks times about nine operations is roughly seventy lithography operations, plus oxidation, etching and deposition steps that need no resist, giving the sixty-to-a-hundred total front-end steps.

###### The mask set `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks`

A set of eight photomasks, one per level, each a square of glass about 15 cm on a side with the pattern for that level in opaque chrome. They are made once from the circuit layout, then used to print thousands of wafers. Making the mask set - patterning, mask inspection, and a few days of lead time - was itself a multi-thousand-dollar, multi-week undertaking, and the masks were the physical embodiment of the design.

###### The mask blank (soda-lime glass) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank`

A plate of low-expansion borosilicate or soda-lime glass, polished flat to a few micrometres over 150 mm. Low-expansion glass (LE glass) was preferred for masks because it did not change size with temperature. Both the blank and the pattern ultimately derive from fused silica.

###### The opaque chrome layer `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome`

A layer of chromium, evaporated or sputtered onto the glass and then patterned by a mask writer. Chrome is used because it is opaque to the deep-UV and because it survives repeated contact printing without wearing. The clear areas are just bare glass, which is why a mask is easy to inspect: you look through it.

###### The reticle (1:1 mask) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle` _(medium)_

A bipolar logic wafer of 1983 was almost always patterned 1:1 by contact or proximity printing, so the mask carried the pattern at full size - a 100 mm wafer printed from a 100 mm mask. Reticles in the sense of 4x or 5x reduction masks were for steppers and mostly for the finer NMOS and DRAM processes, not for the coarse logic line.

###### The mask writer `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer` _(medium)_

A computer-controlled plotter that draws the pattern onto the chrome layer - a direct-write electron-beam or laser writer, or a mask stepper using photographic reduction for the simpler logic geometries. The mask set for one part number was the output of days of the mask shop's finest-resolution tool, and it was checked by eye under a microscope before use.

###### Spinning on the resist `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat`

The wafer is put on a vacuum chuck in a bowl, a few millilitres of resist is dispensed, and the bowl spins at several thousand rpm, flinging the resist into a film of a chosen thickness - thicker where a thick layer is needed to etch deep, thinner where fine resolution is needed. The film is then soft-baked to drive off solvent and stabilise the image.

###### The coater/developer track `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.spinner`

A machine with hot plates and spray-heads that automates spin-coat, soft-bake, develop, rinse and bake for a whole cassette of wafers in one pass. The track was the workhorse of the photomask bay: an operator loaded a cassette and pushed a button, and the bay's lithography throughput was set by how many tracks it had.

###### Dehydration bake before the resist `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration`

Resist will not stick to a wet wafer, so before every coat the wafer goes on a hot plate or in a dehydration oven at 150-250 C to drive off the adsorbed water from the previous wet step. Skipping it causes the single most common resist defect - the film lifting off in patches during development. Every one of the eight cycles repeats this.

###### The dehydration hot plate `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.hotplate` _(medium)_

A temperature-controlled aluminium or ceramic plate the cassette sits on for a minute or two at 150-200 C. Cheap, essential, and present at every wet bench in the bay.

###### Aligning the mask to the wafer `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align`

The wafer is dried, loaded onto a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and the mask is laid directly on top of it - contact printing - or held just above it with a controlled air gap - proximity printing - or imaged one-to-one through a lens. The machine's job is to align each feature on the mask to the feature already printed on the wafer, usually by optically reading alignment marks etched into the previous level. At 3-5 um, alignment tolerance was generous; at DRAM geometries it was brutal.

###### The contact/proximity mask aligner `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.printer`

A granite or cast base, a Chuck/Hamble wafer stage with micrometer knobs for theta and X-Y, a vacuum frame to pull the mask down onto the wafer, a mercury lamp below, and a pair of binocular microscopes to watch the alignment marks. One operator could run one or two of these, spending most of the cycle walking up and down the level stack.

###### The 1:1 projection stepper `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.stepper`

A mask aligner that images the mask through a fixed 1:1 lens onto the wafer with a small gap, so there is no contact and no wear, and no mask-defect printing. TI's Micralign and Perkin-Elmer's units of the late 1970s and early 1980s brought this to the logic lines. It was the technology that eventually killed contact printing entirely.

###### The mercury lamp `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.lamp`

A 1000 W high-pressure mercury arc with a quartz envelope. Its spectrum peaks at 365, 405 and 436 nm; optical filters select one line, almost always 436 nm (g-line) for the finest resolution the era could reach. Newer deep-UV lamps added 248 nm. The lamp is run at constant power because the resist's exposure depends on its intensity, and lamp ageing was a constant yield headache.

###### Developing the image `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop`

The exposed wafer is sprayed with an alkaline developer - for a positive resist, a solution of tetramethylammonium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide; for a negative resist, an organic solvent. The unexposed (positive) or exposed (negative) resist dissolves, leaving the pattern in hardened resist. Then a rinse in deionised water, a dry, and a hard-bake to cross-link the remaining resist so it survives the etch that follows. TMAH was preferred because it left no metal ion residues that would poison the device.

###### Etching the oxide window `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch`

The patterned resist is the stencil; the wafer goes into an etchant. Buffered oxide etch - hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride - attacks the silicon dioxide where the resist is gone, opening the window, and stops at the silicon or at the oxide-nitride beneath. The wafer comes out with resist still on it, which is stripped next. In this era the oxide etch was still wet chemistry; dry plasma etching had not yet replaced it for the bulk oxide.

###### Stripping the resist `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip` _(medium)_

With the etch done, the resist has served its purpose and is removed. In this era, because resist was often negative and organic, a chlorinated solvent strip in a hot bath was standard - historically xylene, then trichloroethylene, boiling at 87 C. Solvent stripping leaves ionic residue, which had to be followed by a piranha clean, a rinse, and a dehydration bake before the next coat. Trichloroethylene was ubiquitous as a resist strip and a vapour degreaser in this period and was being phased out for toxicity and ozone reasons through the 1980s, replaced by perchloroethylene and then by piranha wet strips.

###### Cleanroom air, filtration and the wet bench `mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom`

The whole front end runs in filtered air with positive pressure, and the wet benches - the sinks where wafers are etched and cleaned - were the dirtiest place in the fab and the reason it needed a Class 100 (ISO 5) hood over every one. HEPA-filtered air was blown down continuously; nitrogen and dry air purged the tool chambers; and huge volumes of deionised water and process chemicals flowed through the sinks.

###### The HEPA fan filter unit `mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu`

A box of pleated glass-fibre or PTFE media in a sheet-metal housing, blowing filtered air down over the tool at 20-40 air changes an hour. It is the single most numerous object in a 1980s fab - one every few square metres of ceiling - and it is why the whole building was pressurised and why the electricity bill was dominated by fan motors.

###### The wet bench `mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench`

A row of acid-resistant sinks - quartz or polypropylene - where wafers are rinsed and wet-etched. Because wet chemistry releases acid mist and organic solvent vapour, every wet bench sat under a Class 100 laminar-flow hood and exhausted to a scrubbed stack. The wet bench is the reason a 1980s logic line was not as cheap to run as the 'it is just photolithography' story suggests.

###### The merchant logic fab that ran the process `mb.logic.bipolar.fab` _(medium)_

A 1983 merchant logic line was a long building with a linear flow: wafers came in at the front and moved one way through cleaning, oxidation and diffusion, photolithography, etch and metallisation, then out to probe, then to assembly and test at the back. Because a logic process was so repeatable, one fab ran dozens of different part numbers on the same flow, changing only the mask set - which is exactly why the 74LS catalogue was so cheap.

###### Oxidation and diffusion bay `mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baydiffusion`

The hot end of the fab: tube furnaces for oxidation, source drive-in and anneal, plus the epitaxial reactors. This bay determined the cycle time of the whole line, because a diffusion push is hours and a furnace boat takes 20-40 wafers. An operator loaded boats in and out at a slow, deliberate rhythm all shift.

###### Metallisation bay `mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baymetal` _(medium)_

The vacuum tool room: the sputterers that lay down the NiCr resistors and the aluminium metal, the evaporation stations, the sinter furnace, and the ion-implantation machines. Vacuum and cleanroom in one room; argon flows constantly.

###### Fab utilities: water, power, scrubbers `mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities` _(medium)_

A logic fab in 1983 drew tens of megawatts and consumed tens of millions of gallons of ultrapure water a year, and every acid vapour had to be scrubbed. The ultrapure water plant - reverse osmosis then ion exchange, then a final 0.2 um filter - was as large and as capital-intensive as any single machine in the fab.

###### What happened to bipolar logic afterwards `mb.logic.bipolar.now`

The 74LS line described here is essentially extinct as a manufacturing process. CMOS won because it drew almost no static power, scaled, and could hold a whole microprocessor on one die, which bipolar could never do economically. Bipolar survives only in niches - power regulators, high-voltage controllers, low-dropout rectifiers, precision amplifiers, the front end of high-speed analog, microwave amplifiers, Hall sensors - where the transistor's current handling and gain are still hard to beat, and those parts are still grown epitaxially and still use guard rings and deep-trench isolation at the leading edge: the process family survived, the market for plain logic gates in it did not. The two families briefly merged in BiCMOS, which built CMOS logic and bipolar output drivers on the same die for gate arrays and for the output stages of older CPUs; it was abandoned once CMOS could drive high current on its own, and is largely gone from production. And the geometry is unrecognisable: the 3-5 um feature of this line put of the order of 10^1 to 10^2 transistors on a die, where a modern GPU puts about 10^10, on 300 mm wafers. Nothing about the aluminium DIP package, the epoxy, the lead frame or the 0.1 in pitch changed at all through that entire scaling - only the silicon inside.

##### The black epoxy DIP `mb.logic.package`

Nearly every 74-series chip Commodore bought arrived in a black moulded dual in-line package: a lead frame carrying sixteen to twenty pins on 0.1 in centres, a piece of die glued to the frame's centre paddle, a fan of 0.5 mil gold wires, and about a third of a gram of filled epoxy poured over the whole thing and cured. This is the single most replicated package in electronics history.

###### Why 0.1 inch and 0.3 inch `mb.logic.package.geometry`

The two dimensions that made the DIP work at all, and the reason for both. The 0.100 in (2.54 mm) lead pitch was chosen so a cheap single-row socket, and a hole in a piece of perforated board on the same grid, would accept the part. The 0.3 in (7.62 mm) row spacing was a compromise: close enough that a 14-pin body clears a 0.05 in hole-pad on 0.1 in centres, far enough apart that the leads are stiff enough to survive insertion into a socket and that the part can sit on the older, wider 0.6 in grid alongside the 40-pin devices. Bodies too wide for 0.3 in moved to 0.6 in rows.

###### 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) lead pitch `mb.logic.package.geometry.pitch`

The distance between adjacent pins on one row of the DIP. It is the same pitch as the holes on a piece of perforated board, and it is the reason a 74LS04 could be dropped into a socket or a perfboard without any special tooling. The pin itself is a 0.25 x 0.5 mm rectangular wire, the narrow dimension facing the chip.

###### 0.3 inch row spacing and its wider variants `mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing` _(medium)_

The distance between the two rows of pins. Standard JEDEC practice in 1983 was 300 mil for packages up to 24 pins and 600 mil for 28-pin and 40-pin parts, so a 40-pin device and a 16-pin device could share a footprint grid. A 900 mil (22.9 mm) body was used by some hermetic and high-current ceramic parts but was never common in merchant logic.

###### Nickel-iron lead frame `mb.logic.package.leadframe`

A continuous strip of metal, punched and formed into a repeating chain of DIP skeletons joined by tie-bars. It arrives at the assembler as a reel of maybe 3000 frames; the frames are cut out one at a time, plated, and then become the skeleton of the package - the seventeen or more separate pins, the two rows, and the little central ledge the die sits on.

###### Progressive-die stamping of the frame `mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp`

The strip is fed through a sequence of steel dies on a mechanical press. Each station cuts, pierces, forms and bends a little more; by the last station the strip has a repeating row of completed DIP skeletons still joined by their tie bars. Ten to twenty tonnes of press capacity for a strip that is a tenth of a millimetre thick and has to be dimensioned to a few microns.

###### The progressive die set `mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.tool`

A stack of hardened tool-steel plates, each with apertures and forming punches cut by wire EDM or grinding, bolted into a set between the press bolster and the ram. Making the tooling for one frame number was a days-to-weeks job and was why a lead frame number was never changed casually: the tooling, the mould, the socket and the board artwork all had to change together.

###### Lead plating: tin, gold flash, nickel `mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating`

Bare nickel-iron leads solder badly and gall when the DIP is pushed into and out of a socket, so every logic lead frame came out of the stamping press already plated. The common 1983 finish was an electroless or electrolytic nickel pre-plate followed by a matte tin or tin-lead overlay; gold flash over nickel was used where a part had to survive many insertions. A small fraction of frames used silver.

###### Tin plating bath `mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin`

A chemical or electrolytic tin deposit, typically 1-3 micrometres thick, over a nickel underlayer. Tin is soft, wets solder readily and costs almost nothing, and it is why a logic chip could be soldered onto a two-layer board with a plain iron in an automated wave-solder machine with no special flux. The refined tin came from cassiterite smelted in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand or Bolivia.

###### Copper-clad C4 lead frame (later, not 1983) `mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4` _(medium)_

A lead frame fabricated not from a bulk alloy strip but from an aluminium or copper leadframe clad on both faces with a controlled thickness of copper, so the surface the solder sees is copper rather than a flash plate. Known by the trademark C4. It solved the tin-whisker and solderability problems at once and became standard for fine-pitch packages from the late 1980s onward.

###### The separated, tested die `mb.logic.package.die`

Between the diffusion bay and the packaging line, the wafer is scribed into rectangles, diced, and every rectangle is probed while still in wafer form. The die that arrives at the assembly line is a bare rectangle of silicon, perhaps 1.5 by 2.5 mm, with a scratched pattern of aluminium bonding pads on one face and a bare oxide film over the circuitry on the other.

###### Scribing and dicing the wafer `mb.logic.package.die.scribe`

A diamond stylus is dragged along the scribe lanes between dies, not to cut through but to fracture the crystal along the damage tracks buried in the oxide. For the narrow lanes the wafer is turned edge-on and run through a rotating diamond blade, or more recently a tensioned wire loaded with abrasive, which leaves far less chipping than a blade.

###### The glass over the aluminium `mb.logic.package.die.passivation`

After metallisation the whole wafer is coated in a thick film of silicon dioxide, usually with a plasma-deposited nitride cap. This passivation layer is what protects a 1983 logic die from the humidity and mobile ions that would otherwise creep under the aluminium and shift the threshold of a transistor. Openings in it are the bonding pads and the scribe lanes.

###### Why 4164 DRAMs die but 74LS parts mostly do not `mb.logic.package.die.hardtest` _(medium)_

A 74LS gate is a handful of transistors with enormous margin; it either works or the diffusion is cracked. A 64Kx1 DRAM stores charge in a capacitor about 100 femtofarads across a transistor with a leakage path, and it has to be refreshed every few milliseconds. That is why the eight 4164s on the C64 are the board's failure-prone chips and the 74-series glue is almost always fine.

###### Die attach, wire bond, moulding `mb.logic.package.assembly`

Three operations turn a loose die and a loose lead frame into a component. The die is brazed to the frame's central ledge. Twenty-ish gold wires are ball- or wedge-bonded from pads on the die to the inner ends of the pins. Then about 0.3-0.5 g of filled black epoxy is transfer-moulded over everything and cured.

###### Die attach to the frame paddle `mb.logic.package.assembly.attach`

The die is placed face-down onto a small ledge in the middle of the lead frame and brazed there with a preform of gold-silicon eutectic at 350-400 C. The eutectic melts before the silicon itself does, so the joint is made without heating the chip to a temperature that would damage it. Cheap parts instead used a silver-filled organic paste cured on a hot plate, or conductive epoxy, and some logic used glass-frit die attach for thermal cycling.

###### Gold wire bonding `mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond`

A machine called a wedge bonder presses a hair-thin gold wire onto an aluminium bonding pad with a tungsten or ceramic tool while a hydrogen torch or arc welds them together, then repeats at the inner end of the pin. Each joint is a small aluminium-gold intermetallic wedge, and the wire is parted by tearing it rather than by cutting it. It is the cheapest way ever devised to connect a chip to the outside world, and it is why every 1983 logic chip has that characteristic fan of gold legs.

###### The wedge bonder `mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.bonder`

A two-station machine that draws wire from a spool, forms a loop, drives a wedge onto the die pad under a hydrogen flame, swings 90 degrees, and drives the second wedge onto the pin, then snaps the wire. Twenty or forty of these sat in a row along a packaging line, each attended by one operator feeding frames in and taking packaged parts out.

###### Transfer moulding the black epoxy body `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould`

A slab of thermosetting epoxy loaded with 75-85 percent spherical silica is melted at 175 C and forced through a small orifice into a multi-cavity steel mould - the transfer mould - that holds the wired frame in one cavity per die. The compound flows around the wire loops, fills voids, and cures in three to five minutes. Because it is filled with silica it is not really a plastic in the loose sense: it is a ceramic-filled thermoset whose job is to hold the die in place, carry heat away, and keep moisture out. Moulding compounds are incompletely polymerised at the mould temperature, so the parts are then baked for hours at 175 C to complete the cure and drive off the last of the residual stress - a batch operation, thousands of parts in a tray, on a schedule that ran overnight.

###### The transfer press `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.press`

A heated platen press with a pot and plunger that transfers melted compound into the mould. Modern machines are multi-cavity and run at thousands of shots an hour; a 1980s line used 20- to 100-shot multi-cavity tools and got through a few hundred thousand DIPs a month.

###### Epoxy moulding compound `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound`

A blend of roughly 15-20 percent resin system and 80-85 percent filler by weight. The resin is an epoxy-novolac cured by a phenolic novolac; the filler is spherical fused or precipitated silica graded from a few microns up to about 100 microns so the compound can be both thin enough to flow around a 25 um wire and stiff enough to survive handling; and there is a trace of carbon black pigment to make the part black, plus a trace of mould release. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s.

###### Epoxy cresol novolac resin `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin`

The workhorse of chip packaging in every decade since 1970. Cresol-formaldehyde epoxy novolac is made from epichlorohydrin and a cresol-formaldehyde novolac; cured with a phenolic novolac and catalysed with a small amount of hexamethylenetetramine, it cures without volatiles and without ionising anything, so it does not damage the die. The epoxy end comes from epichlorohydrin, which industry has always made by chlorohydrination of propylene - propene plus hypochlorous acid to 1,2-dichloropropane, then base dehydrochlorination to close the epoxide ring - so the propylene came off a steam cracker, the chlorine out of a chlor-alkali cell, and the caustic soda out of the same cell: the plastic body of every 74LS chip traces back to salt and to crude oil.

###### Carbon black pigment `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.pigment` _(medium)_

About half a percent by weight of furnace black, dispersed into the compound, to make the package opaque black. Black rather than natural-coloured because a black package hides internal voids, and because it was what the whole industry had standardised on since the first plastic DIP.

###### The mould cavity and ejector pins `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.tool`

A hardened, polished steel block with one to hundreds of identical cavities. For a DIP the cavity is a rectangle with fourteen to twenty pin-shaped slots; the mould also carries the moulded cavity number, the vendor's part-number embossing, and ejector pins that push the finished part out without scuffing it. Moulds lasted a few hundred thousand to a few million shots.

###### Probe test before packaging `mb.logic.package.probe`

Die that fail are thrown away before they are worth a lead frame. The wafer is loaded onto a probe stage, a probe card with one needle per bonding pad is lowered onto it, and a tester runs every pattern and every DC parameter. Only known-good die are cut. This is why probe test and not final test is what sets the economics of a logic wafer: a yield loss after packaging has already cost you the moulding and the wire bonds too.

###### The wafer probe station `mb.logic.package.probe.prober` _(medium)_

A heavy cast stage that steps the wafer die by die under a fixed probe card: a vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, a microscope to line the card up, and a needle interface to the tester. An operator loads a cassette of up to 25 wafers and unloads it at the end; everything in between was automatic.

###### The probe card `mb.logic.package.probe.card` _(medium)_

A ceramic or printed-circuit substrate carrying one cantilever needle per bonding pad, cantilevered down from an epoxy or quartz shell so the needles survive hundreds of thousands of touches on hard silicon. Building a card for a new part number took days and cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, which is why a device that sold for thirty cents could not afford a new probe card per variant.

###### The logic tester `mb.logic.package.probe.tester`

An automated test system running a stored functional pattern and a set of DC limit tests per device type: propagation delay, fan-out current, input current, output high and low voltage, and the truth table at the functional corners. A 74LS04 has a few hundred such tests. The tester was the expensive part of probe test and was amortised across every device type on the line.

###### The ceramic DIP (mostly not used here) `mb.logic.package.ceramic`

For military and extended-temperature parts the epoxy was replaced by a package made of alumina ceramic, sealed hermetically with a glass frit or a metal lid. It could be baked out, leak-tested, and taken from -55 to +125 C without the epoxy softening. It was also more expensive and much larger, so merchant logic in a home computer was always plastic: the C64's own 74-series parts are all black epoxy, with the ceramic version only appearing in industrial or aerospace equipment.

###### Alumina ceramic body `mb.logic.package.ceramic.body`

A package shell made of 95-99 percent alumina, formed by pressing or by tape-casting a green body in a serpentine conductor pattern and firing it at 1500-1600 C. Alumina was chosen because it matches silicon and the glass seal closely in expansion, is cheap, and is a good thermal conductor compared with any polymer.

###### Kovar lid and nickel seal ring `mb.logic.package.ceramic.lid`

For parts sealed with metal rather than glass, a lid of Kovar (iron-nickel-cobalt, chosen for its matching expansion) is brazed or welded to a nickel ring around the ceramic. Kovar is the same idea as the lead frame alloy: pick the expansion coefficient of the metal so it matches the ceramic and the seal does not crack.

###### Glass frit sealing `mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal` _(medium)_

A paste of powdered borosilicate glass with a small amount of binder is applied around the rim, the lid is set on it, and the assembly goes through a sealing furnace. The glass melts, wets the metallised ceramic and the metal lid, and on cooling forms a hermetic, dimensionally matched bond. The temperature profile - ramp, soak around 700-750 C, controlled cool - is the whole art of it.

###### Marking the top of the package `mb.logic.package.marking`

Ink printing was still the norm in 1983: a pad or a dot-matrix printer lays the part number, the manufacturer's mark, a date code (year and week, e.g. 8341) and a lot or assembly code on the moulded surface. Laser marking was beginning to appear, mostly for military parts, and would take over within a decade because a laser-marked part cannot be relabelled.

###### Marking ink `mb.logic.package.marking.ink` _(medium)_

A phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, laid on and baked, or cured by UV. Cheap and utterly routine - but it is why an original C64 chip is still readable today and a modern BGA is not. (Ink marking was also curable by laser ablation of the mould compound, which is the mechanism the laser marking route exploits.)

#### 74LS257 quad 2-to-1 multiplexer (U13 and U25) `mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257`

Two identical 16-pin packages, each holding four independent 2-to-1 data selectors with non-inverting outputs. They exist for one reason: the 4164 DRAMs are multiplexed parts with only nine address pins, taking a row address first and a column address a few hundred nanoseconds later on the same wires. The CPU has sixteen address bits to deliver, so eight of them have to be time-division multiplexed onto four wires. One 74LS257 multiplexes four bits; two are needed for eight.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS258 quad multiplexer with three-state outputs (U14) `mb.logic.u14-74ls258`

The same four 2-to-1 selectors as the 74LS257 but with outputs that can be switched into a high-impedance state. This is the bus arbiter for VIC-II memory access: when the VIC-II is allowed to take the bus, the multiplexer's outputs are disabled so the VIC-II's own address pins can drive directly instead of fighting them. A failed U14 shows up as the VIC-II being unable to fetch screen data from RAM.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS139 dual 1-of-4 decoder (U15) `mb.logic.u15-74ls139` _(medium)_

Two independent four-way decoders with common active-low enables and active-low outputs, in a 16-pin DIP. Given four address bits and an enable, each half asserts exactly one of four outputs. Commodore uses it to expand the sparse decode coming out of the PLA into individual chip selects - VIC-II banking, the I/O devices - and to qualify them with the read/write phase. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the house-number part 7708/7711.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS373 octal D latch, three-state (U26) `mb.logic.u26-74ls373`

Eight transparent D-type latches with three-state outputs in a 20-pin DIP. The VIC-II has only eight address pins but must reach two different memories - the 1 KB screen/bitmap RAM and the character-generator ROM - so it puts one byte on its own pins while this latch holds the other byte. The three-state outputs let the CPU read the latched byte back whenever the VIC is not driving. A dead U26 corrupts text and bitmap graphics but leaves everything else alive, which is why it is the classic 'screen is garbage but the machine boots' fault.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS08 quad 2-input AND gate (U27) `mb.logic.u27-74ls08` _(medium)_

Four independent two-input AND gates in a 14-pin DIP - the most ordinary chip on the board and the one that does the most unglamorous work. ANDing is how the machine makes qualified control signals: a decode line ANDed with a clock phase becomes /RAS, /CAS or /WE for the DRAMs, and ANDed with the read/write phase becomes the chip select for the VIC-II, SID or CIA. Commodore also second-sourced it as house-number part 7712.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS74 dual D-type flip-flop (U29) `mb.logic.u29-74ls74` _(low)_

Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with asynchronous preset and clear, in a 14-pin DIP. In the C64 they sit in the DRAM timing chain: shaping and stretching the column strobe and dividing or retiming the phase clock so the 4164s get a valid /CAS pulse on the right edge. A flip-flop is what turns a combinational AND into a one-shot wide enough to meet the memory's timing spec.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS193 synchronous 4-bit up/down counter (U30) `mb.logic.u30-74ls193` _(low)_

A four-bit presettable binary counter with separate up and down clocks and a clear, in a 16-pin DIP. It sequences the multiplexed dynamic-RAM cycle - stepping through address states and generating the refresh strobes - and helps step the VIC-II's raster counters. This is the chip that turns 'one address bit is high right now' into 'we are on the nth step of a cycle'.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (U31) `mb.logic.u31-74ls629` _(medium)_

Two voltage-controlled oscillator sections plus an enable and a range control, in a 14-pin DIP. The C64 has no crystal governing its video dot clock: one half of U31 amplifies the colour-subcarrier reference coming out of the video circuitry, the other half generates a free-running dot clock whose frequency is pulled by a control voltage. That is the oscillator half of the phase-locked loop completed by the MC4044 at U32. Despite the 'LS' prefix this part is CMOS internally, not bipolar TTL.

##### The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629 `mb.logic.cmos` _(medium)_

Three of the C64's glue chips are CMOS, and they were made on a completely different line from the 74LS parts. Instead of four diffusion cycles and an epitaxial collector, a CMOS line does a p-well and an n-well implant, grows a field oxide between them by LOCOS, grows a hundred-nanometre gate oxide, deposits polysilicon, and uses that same polysilicon as its own mask for the source and drain implant. Roughly ten mask levels, no epitaxy, no gold, no NiCr resistor film, and a static power consumption of nanowatts instead of milliwatts. That combination is why CMOS took the whole logic business within fifteen years.

###### The twin-tub CMOS flow `mb.logic.cmos.process`

The order of a CMOS process is dictated by one rule: you can never put anything back into silicon after a high-temperature step, so everything that must survive later furnace work is done first, in descending order of temperature. Wells, then field oxide, then thin gate oxide, then polysilicon, then the self-aligned source/drain implants at a low temperature, then metal.

###### p-type substrate (and the tub) `mb.logic.cmos.process.substrate`

The wafer is p-type, lightly doped. On top of it two wells are implanted: a deep n-well and a somewhat shallower p-well. The n-well holds every p-channel transistor; the p-well (or the substrate itself, on simpler parts) holds every n-channel transistor. Two tubs, two polarities, one chip - that is the 'twin tub'. The wells must be deep enough that they do not punch through into each other and short the two transistor types together.

              - *Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer* `si.wafer` *(seen above)*
###### n-well and p-well implants `mb.logic.cmos.process.wells`

Two masked implants. Phosphorus (or arsenic) goes into the n-well; boron into the p-well. At 3-5 um these were thermal diffusions or, increasingly, implantations - by the early 1980s medium-current implanters were displacing diffusion in CMOS, the opposite trend to bipolar, where diffusion survived much longer. An implantation is done cold and fast: the dopant is accelerated into the surface at tens of keV and stops almost where it is put.

###### The medium-current ion implanter `mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter` _(medium)_

A big steel vacuum chamber with a source, an analysing magnet, an accelerating column and a beamline down to a scan platter that holds the wafer. The dopant is ionised, selected by mass, accelerated to tens of keV, and swept across the wafer. Implanters were expensive, and CMOS was the process that made them a standard line tool rather than a special one.

###### LOCOS isolation `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos`

Locally Oxidised Silicon. Where two transistors must not touch, the field oxide is simply grown. A layer of silicon nitride is deposited and patterned; the wafer is oxidised in steam, so oxide grows everywhere the nitride is absent; the nitride is stripped off in hot phosphoric acid, leaving a thick field oxide behind. It is isolation by oxidising rather than by doping, and it is the reason a CMOS chip looks like a quilt of raised oxide platforms.

###### The silicon nitride masking film `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride`

A layer of amorphous silicon nitride, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition from silane and ammonia at about 800 C. It is used in three places in a CMOS line: as the mask that protects active areas during field oxidation, as the encapsulant under the nitride passivation at the end, and as a spacer. Nitride is chosen because it is immune to hot steam - which is precisely why it is a good mask for something that is about to be steamed. Its two feed gases are named in `inputs`: monosilane (chem.silane.monosilane) for the silicon, and electronic-grade ammonia (chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide, delivered as anhydrous NH3 sparged into ultrapure water) for the nitrogen. In 1983 essentially all industrial ammonia was made by Haber-Bosch - nitrogen from the air plus hydrogen from steam-reformed natural gas over an iron catalyst at 400-500 C and 200-300 atm - so the film that defines a CMOS transistor's isolation runs, indirectly, on natural gas.

###### Hot phosphoric acid `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric` _(medium)_

Silicon nitride is attacked by hot concentrated phosphoric acid and by nothing else practical, so a boiling phosphoric acid bath is the standard way to remove it - which is why LOCOS needs an acid tank that no other step in the line does. The acid was made by burning phosphorus, itself from phosphate rock, in excess air and absorbing the oxide in water.

###### The gate oxide `mb.logic.cmos.process.gateoxide`

Inside the active windows the thin gate oxide is grown, by dry oxidation in oxygen at about 1000 C. On a 3-5 um part it is 80-120 nm thick - a few hundred atom layers. This film is the transistor: its thickness sets the threshold voltage and its capacitance sets the drive current, and it is the thinnest and most fragile thing on the chip. At 1983's feature sizes it was still thick by modern standards, which is one reason CMOS of that era was not yet faster than bipolar.

###### The polysilicon gate `mb.logic.cmos.process.poly`

A layer of polycrystalline silicon is deposited over the whole wafer, then doped (usually with phosphorus from phosphine, or with POCL3 in a furnace) so that it conducts, then patterned. That patterned polysilicon is the gate. Crucially, it is also used as the mask for the source and drain implant immediately afterwards - so the gate aligns itself, and no extra mask is needed. The self-aligned gate and source/drain, invented at Fairchild in the late 1960s, is the single idea that made CMOS manufacturable at all.

###### The self-aligned source and drain `mb.logic.cmos.process.sd` _(medium)_

With the gate already patterned in polysilicon, the source and drain are implanted straight through the exposed silicon beside it, and the gate itself blocks the implant everywhere it is. No alignment mask is needed: the gate defines the gap between source and drain by its own edge. Two implants, phosphorus for the n-channel source/drain and boron for the p-channel, each masked by the opposite field oxide. This is 'self-aligned', and it is the reason a CMOS transistor's channel length is set by a printed line width and nothing else.

###### The source/drain anneal `mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal` _(medium)_

After the implant the wafer goes back into a furnace briefly to heal the crystal damage and to activate the dopant atoms into substitutional positions. This is the one remaining high-temperature step, and it is why CMOS still used a furnace in the era when bipolar was moving to implantation.

              - *The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter` *(seen above)*
###### Contact and aluminium interconnect `mb.logic.cmos.process.contact` _(medium)_

The field oxide is etched away over the source, drain and gate to expose silicon, then aluminium is deposited and patterned into one single layer of interconnect. Exactly the same metallisation as the bipolar line, exactly the same problems (step coverage over the oxide steps, electromigration under current) and exactly the same solution in this era: one level, because at 3-5 um the cells were big enough to route around with a single layer.

              - *Aluminium metallisation* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal` *(seen above)*
###### Passivation, and why CMOS needed less of it `mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation` _(medium)_

An interlayer oxide and a final nitride cap, opened only at the pads and scribe lanes. A CMOS device is far less sensitive to mobile ions than a bipolar one, because a CMOS gate draws no gate current and its threshold is set electrostatically rather than by charge state; so the passivation job is easier and the nitride does most of the work.

###### The photolithography is the same, but the resist is positive `mb.logic.cmos.litho` _(medium)_

A CMOS line of 1983 reused the same mask aligners, coaters and developers as the bipolar line next door. The one substantive difference is the resist: by the end of the 1970s the NMOS and CMOS lines had already switched to positive resists such as Shipley's AZ-1350, while bipolar logic was still often running negative resists. Positive resists tolerate the small misalignment that LOCOS bird's-beak and oxide steps cause better, which is part of why MOS won.

###### CMOS transmission gate (bilateral switch) `mb.logic.cmos.switch`

The 4066's four bilateral switches are the canonical CMOS cell: two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel between two nodes, each with its gate driven by one of the two control inputs. When the control is high the pair conducts in both directions; when it is low the pair is off and the terminals float. It is two transistors. That is the whole reason CMOS logic is cheap - there is no junction isolation, no epitaxy, no resistor film and no gold-doped emitter to reproduce for every function, just NMOS and PMOS. It is also why the 4066 could be used as an analogue multiplexer at all: the on-resistance of a few hundred ohms to a few kilohm was low enough to route luma, chroma and audio, where a single bipolar pass transistor would have cost more than the rest of the gate.

###### What CMOS became `mb.logic.cmos.now`

The same n-well/p-well/twin-tub idea, shrunk by a factor of thousands. Every design rule changed. The bird's beak - the way LOCOS field oxide grew sideways and swallowed the active area - became a scaling killer, and shallow trench isolation, in which a narrow trench is etched into the substrate and filled with oxide over a nitride liner, gave a much sharper boundary and became universal from the late 1980s onward; STI is itself a direct descendant of the deep-trench-isolation idea that appeared at the high-performance end of the bipolar branch, so the two halves of this tree converged on the same solution. STI in turn gave way to fin-shaped gates and gate-all-around. The gate material changed from polysilicon to metal. The number of copper interconnect layers went from one to a dozen. The light source went from a mercury lamp at 436 nm to an argon-fluoride excimer laser at 193 nm, and then to extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, which needs a vacuum. A 3-5 um logic gate became a nanometre-scale device with billions of its relatives.

        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### CMOS logic on the board: 4066 switches and MC4044 `mb.logic.cmos-4000`

Four of the C64's glue chips are CMOS rather than bipolar TTL: two 4066 quad bilateral switches (U16, U28) and one MC4044 phase/frequency comparator (U32), plus the 74LS629 above. The 4066 is four independent CMOS transmission gates used as analogue multiplexers to route luma, chroma and audio and to hand the shared pins between the VIC-II and the outside world. The MC4044 compares the VCO's phase against the colour-subcarrier reference and generates the control voltage that locks the dot clock. Both were Motorola/RCA 4000-series parts, normally sold as CD4066B and CD4044B.

        - *The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629* `mb.logic.cmos` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
##### LM556 dual timer (U20) - adjacent, not a logic part `mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556`

Two 555-class monostable timers sharing one package, in a 14-pin DIP. It sits in the analogue paddle-input path, producing the timed pulse whose width the SID measures to report joystick and paddle position. Included here for completeness because it is off-the-shelf, because it is bipolar, and because it was made on the same diffusion lines as the TTL glue - just a different circuit on them.

#### 74-series parts that are NOT on a C64 `mb.logic.not-on-this-board` _(medium)_

A warning about the part list, kept so a reader can trust the sibling nodes. Frequently published lists of '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' include 74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125 and 74LS181. None of those are on the ASSY 250407. They belong to other machines - the 74LS181 look-ahead carry and the 74LS165 shift registers are Apple II parts, the 74LS157 multiplexers are VIC-20 and BBC Micro parts - and they are almost always the result of copying a generic 'TTL in home computers' list rather than reading a parts list. This is commentary about the supply chain, not an entity, so it is a note.

      - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
      - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
      - *The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629* `mb.logic.cmos` *(seen above)*
#### Merchant logic supply to Commodore `mb.logic.sourcing` _(medium)_

Commodore did not fab logic. It bought merchant 74-series parts from the American and Japanese vendors, and because a machine built in millions cannot wait for a part number to be on allocation, it also ran second sources of its own - internal house-numbered equivalents made at other plants, marked 7701, 7707, 7708, 7711, 8712 and so on. An original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore number, all mixed on the same board, all doing the same job. This branch describes Commodore's procurement rather than a physical process: the vendors are companies, the second-source parts are a real component family, and the distribution chain is a sentence about how parts travelled rather than a thing.

##### The merchant logic vendors `mb.logic.sourcing.makers`

Five or six companies made the overwhelming majority of the world's 74-series logic in the early 1980s. Between them they ran the same public process to the same design rules, which is why a 74LS08 from any of them was interchangeable. What they did not share was quality: this is the core of the C64's running joke that some boards need three attempts before they work. The companies themselves are the entities here; this framing paragraph is commentary, so the node is a note that keeps them as children.

###### Texas Instruments `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti` _(medium)_

The company that invented the 7400 series in 1964 and the Schottky TTL in 1964-65, and the largest supplier of the 74LS catalogue. It ran its own fabs (among them Dallas, Sugar Land in Texas, and Niceville in Florida) and also did foundry work for others - the fab-forum business was a real cash generator in the era.

###### Fairchild `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild` _(medium)_

The company where Faggin invented the silicon-gate technology that made CMOS practical, in 1968, and which shipped the first commercial silicon-gate MOS ICs. Fairchild went bankrupt in 1985 and its remaining operations were absorbed by National and by a French group, so by 1983 a Fairchild-branded 74LS was already a slightly awkward purchase.

###### National Semiconductor `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national` _(medium)_

A major second-source supplier of 74LS logic throughout the period, and the company that published the 74HC/74HCT databooks that turned high-speed CMOS into a genuine 74-series replacement. It later absorbed much of Fairchild.

###### Motorola `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola` _(medium)_

The dominant supplier of the 4000-series CMOS parts on this board: the MC4044 phase comparator at U32 and the two MC4066 bilateral switches. The MC prefix on those parts is Motorola's, which is why the C64's glue logic is not entirely a 74-series story. Motorola also ran one of the merchant 74LS lines, and in 1969 it licensed and cross-supplied with Signetics, so the two names turned up in the same catalogue and the same distribution literature of the era.

###### Signetics `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics` _(low)_

An early Silicon Valley logic house that second-sourced the 74 series through the 1960s and 1970s, and that had been owned by Philips since 1975. It is not attested by name on surviving ASSY 250407 boards. It appears in this branch only because it shared a licensing and cross-supply arrangement with Motorola from 1969, which is why the two marks appear together in period catalogues and why repair literature treats them as a pair.

###### Hitachi, Toshiba and the Japanese suppliers `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan` _(low)_

By the mid-1980s Japanese and then Korean vendors had taken a large share of world logic volume, and they were undercutting American silicon hard. C64 boards are also found with Hitachi-branded parts. Commodore bought early and often, and the rising Japanese share was one reason the C64's own bill of materials got cheaper every year of its life.

##### Commodore's house-numbered second sources `mb.logic.sourcing.second-source` _(medium)_

To avoid single-supplier risk Commodore had equivalents of several glue parts made for it and marked with its own house numbers: 7701 and 8701 in place of the PLA family, 7707 for the 7406 hex inverter, 7708 or 7711 for the 74LS139 decoder, and 7712 for the 74LS08 quad AND. These were contracted from other fabs under Commodore's specification. They are functionally equivalent and reliably much worse - the MOS-made decoder and inverter parts are among the most failure-prone components on a C64. This node records the practice and the part numbers rather than being one of the parts itself: the four house numbers are four different devices in four different packages, so there is no single object here to put in a box.

##### How the chips physically arrived in 1983 `mb.logic.sourcing.distribution` _(medium)_

Nobody at Commodore's Pennsylvania assembly plant picked up a telephone and ordered from Texas Instruments. There was a distribution chain, and where a part sat in that chain decided both its price and whether it was genuine. Buying from the manufacturer's own sales arm or a franchised distributor got you an authorised part with a full warranty and a date code. Buying from a broker or an independent distributor got you the same silicon much cheaper, with no guarantee of origin at all. Three mechanisms made the difference. Allocation: when demand exceeded supply - and in 1982-84 it very often did, because the whole consumer electronics industry was recovering from the 1980-81 recession simultaneously - a manufacturer rationed, a computer maker with a purchase order got whatever share the vendor allocated pro rata, and production had to be scheduled around delivery dates rather than around its own. That is why the price of a commodity 74LS was set by the market's shortage rather than by what it cost to make. Pulls: parts that reached a buyer through anything other than a franchised distributor were, in the trade's language, 'pulled', which could be entirely innocent - a company over-ordered and released surplus, a broker bought at auction - or diverted from a competitor's own allocation. Because a 74LS08 has no serial number, no authentication and no visible origin, nobody could tell the difference; the industry's response through the 1980s and 1990s was a growing formal apparatus for tracking authorised distribution, and the counterfeiting industry grew alongside it. And incoming inspection: every shipment of semiconductors was counted and checked against the bill of materials before the parts went near a board, with non-matching parts quarantined - which is worth noting because the components on a C64 mainboard are not hand-selected, so the board either works with whatever chip arrived in the box or it is reworked, which is a large part of why surviving C64s need a recap and a chip-sorting pass before they will run.

#### What a 74LS is made of, and what it cost `mb.logic.economics` _(low)_

The whole point of the comparison. A 74LS chip is a few milligrams of silicon, a few milligrams of metal, a third of a gram of epoxy, and a couple of hundred person-minutes of work spread across a fortnight of factory flow time. It sold for a few tens of cents. The 6510 on the same board, a thousand times more transistors on a finer process, cost several dollars. Commodore's entire bill of materials for the electronics was a small fraction of the machine's retail price. The bill of materials for one 74LS04, with the arithmetic: about 3 mg of silicon in a roughly 3.6 mm2 die cut from a 300 um wafer - the '3-5 um' figure usually quoted is the depth of the active junctions, not the mass; 10-30 mg of aluminium on the die from one 1.0-1.5 um level over about half the die area, which is an order of magnitude below the 0.3 g often quoted and is probably a wafer-level inventory figure rather than a per-chip one; under a milligram of gold in total, from about sixteen to twenty 0.5-1.0 mil wire bonds (0.2-0.4 mg) plus the die-attach preform (0.2-0.5 mg of Au-Si); under a milligram of sputtered NiCr; about 100 mg of nickel-iron in the lead frame at roughly 42 percent Ni, most of that mass being the iron half; and 0.3-0.6 g of silica-filled epoxy, three quarters of it fused silica. So the total is roughly half a gram per DIP-14, of which about 100:1 by mass is polymer, and the thirteen glue-chip positions on a C64 together weigh about six grams. The labour figure of roughly 200 person-minutes per finished chip is an order-of-magnitude estimate and worth unpacking, because it is not 200 minutes of one person's attention: it is direct operator and technician time amortised across the whole flow, roughly 20-30 operator touches across the 60-100 front-end steps, plus probe test, assembly, final test and inspection. Flow time is not touch time - a batch of wafers spends a week and a half moving through the fab, almost all of it waiting in a furnace, in a queue or in a cassette under a nitrogen purge, and what costs money is the twenty or thirty separate occasions when somebody has to be present and paying attention, which over a fortnight is a couple of hours. On price: a commodity 74LS gate was priced against a cost of a few tens of cents and a price in the same range, falling year on year as the industry learned; a merchant part's cost is amortised across every customer in the world and over a mask set that runs on a flow making dozens of other part numbers, so Commodore was buying a fraction of the output of a factory that existed whether or not Commodore existed, with a mask set it did not pay for and a design it did not own. The 6510 was the opposite on every count - one mask set, one customer, one buyer, a design that had to be paid for before it shipped a single unit - which is why Commodore's engineers minimised custom silicon and spent money freely on merchant glue, and also why the later C128 could add a second 6510 and a bank-switching PLA without touching the price of the machine.

### Commodore RF modulator module (VHF/UHF TV) `mb.rf-modulator`
