###### Ink pigment `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pigment` _(medium)_

The value marking pigment is carbon black for dark parts and azo or phthalocyanine colour for bright ones, in a resin vehicle that will not be attacked by the board cleaning solvents.

###### Printed PVC sleeve `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.pvc-sleeve` _(medium)_

Film capacitors arrived in a printed plastic sleeve printed with the value, the rating and the maker. Sleeve polymer is the same PVC family as the case and the cable jacket.

### Master clock crystal and oscillator `mb.crystal`

Y1, a hermetically sealed HC-49/U quartz crystal, plus the four glue-logic chips that turn it into the machine's entire timing reference: a colour subcarrier crystal oscillator, a PLL that quadruples it, a divider chain, and a phase/frequency detector that locks the dot clock to the colour clock. Every clock edge in a C64 descends from this one 11 mm metal can.

#### Y1 quartz crystal, HC-49/U `mb.crystal.y1` _(medium)_

A plano-convex quartz plate, 0.07 mm thick, with electrodes fired on its two faces, held on supports inside a small metal can filled with argon and sealed by a crimped, resistance-welded cap. The quartz is the oscillator's frequency-setting element: the whole machine's timing accuracy is the accuracy of one cut and lapped slice of Brazilian or synthetic silicon dioxide.

##### Natural rock crystal `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz` _(medium)_

Gem-quality clear quartz for crystal units came historically from the rock-crystal veins of Minas Gerais in Brazil, prized for natural faces that need no lapping and for the very low defect density that makes a low-phase-noise oscillator possible. By the early 1980s this was being displaced by hydrothermal synthetic quartz, which is chemically identical and far more uniform.

##### Hydrothermal synthetic quartz `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic`

Because natural quartz is limited and variable, industry moved to growing it: an autoclave is charged with silica (often crushed natural quartz) in a hot sodium-hydroxide solution and heated at around 400 C and 150 MPa. Quartz grows on seed crystals hung in the solution, growing the rough in days rather than geological time. This is the source of nearly all quartz crystal blanks made from about the mid-1970s onward.

###### Steel autoclave with seed crystals `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.autoclave` _(medium)_

A filled, sealed pressure vessel - usually Hastelloy or 17-4PH steel liner - held at high temperature and pressure so an alkaline solution dissolves silica from the feed and re-deposits it on thin zoned seed plates hung in the vessel. Temperature gradients create the supersaturation that drives growth, and the growth zones themselves are what later become the tuned crystal resonators.

###### Alkali solvent `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.autoclave.caustic` _(medium)_

The growth solution is hot concentrated sodium or potassium hydroxide, which dissolves silica at the elevated temperature while quartz re-deposits on the seeds. The alkali is made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the crystal ultimately touches rock salt as well as quartz sand.

###### Quartz sand / crushed quartz feed `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.silica-feed` _(medium)_

The silica feedstock for the autoclave is cleaned quartz sand or lumps of milky quartz. Natural quartz sand is a common beach and dune sand: essentially SiO2, left behind as quartz survives weathering while everything else dissolves and washes away.

##### Sawing, lapping and X-ray orienting the blank `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation`

Rough crystal is sawn into blanks, then the cut face is lapped to about 0.15 mm and X-ray diffracted to find its crystallographic orientation. Orientation is everything: only an AT-cut at the right angle gives the flat temperature curve a frequency-stable oscillator needs.

###### X-ray orientation and AT-cut angle selection `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.xray-orienting` _(medium)_

A synthetic rough is indexed by X-ray diffraction so its Z axis and X axis are known, then sawn at a chosen angle to the X axis (the 'AT-cut'). The mid-1980s standard for general-purpose oscillators was about 35 degrees; this angle is chosen because it lands the resonance on a flat, temperature-insensitive point in the quartz stiffness-temperature curve.

###### Lapping and double-lap polishing `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping` _(medium)_

The cut blank is lapped on rotating cast-iron plates with progressively finer abrasives (aluminium oxide, then colloidal silica) down to about 0.15 mm, then double-lapped against a second plate to remove bow and damage left by the saw. Crystal blanks for a 1982 oscillator were lapped on plates run by lapidary and lapping shops, not in the same plant that makes the finished crystal.

###### Final lapping abrasive `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping.colloidal-silica` _(medium)_

The last lapping stage uses a colloidal silica slurry, which polishes rather than cuts. Colloidal silica is precipitated from a dilute sodium silicate solution, itself made from silica sand and sodium carbonate.

##### Grinding the lens shape `mb.crystal.y1.grinding` _(medium)_

The face is bevelled and the outline ground so the finished blank is a lens or plano-convex dome rather than a flat slab. The convexity is deliberate: it makes the crystal's resonant frequency less sensitive to surface damage and to where the mounting points press on it.

###### Diamond grinding wheel `mb.crystal.y1.grinding.diamond-wheel` _(medium)_

A resin-bonded diamond wheel, used wet, that bevels the plate edge and cuts the lens curvature. In 1982 diamond abrasive was largely synthetic, made from graphite under a shock wave; natural diamond was reserved for dressing the wheels.

##### Mounting and soldering of the crystal `mb.crystal.y1.supports` _(medium)_

The four HC-49 leads are formed to a right angle and soldered onto the board in a wave-solder pass. The crystal's case sits at the board's natural mechanical frequency well below the circuit's operating frequency, which is deliberate: an HC-49 body has several overtone resonances that would otherwise produce spurious oscillator modes.

##### Metal electrodes on the blank faces `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes` _(medium)_

Chromium is evaporated or sputtered onto both faces as an adhesion layer, then gold or silver is deposited over it as the conductive electrode, through a shadow mask that defines the electrode area. Chromium-gold is the classic 1980s crystal electrode stack: Cr to bond, Au to conduct.

###### Chromium adhesion layer `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium` _(medium)_

Chromium is evaporated as the adhesion layer because bare quartz will not hold gold by van der Waals forces alone. Chromium wets both the quartz surface and the gold film, and it is itself a hard, chemically inert metal.

###### Gold electrode film `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film` _(medium)_

Gold evaporated through a shadow mask to give the electrode its final geometry and conductivity. The mask pattern fixes the electrode area, which together with the plate thickness is what sets the crystal capacitance.

###### Evaporation shadow mask `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film.mask` _(medium)_

A thin metal mask placed above the rotating blank during evaporation so the electrode pattern is defined. The mask is made from a drawn stainless or nickel strip, chemically etched to the electrode shape.

##### Cutting the plate and vacuum baking `mb.crystal.y1.cutting` _(medium)_

The plated blank is cut with a diamond wheel into individual resonator plates, then the plates are vacuum-baked at around 400 C to drive off adsorbed moisture and contaminants. That vacuum bake is what removes the piezoelectric pyroelectric drift and the 'dope' effect - the stress-induced frequency shift as a crystal heats - and it is why a crystal that has been opened is never a good crystal.

###### Diamond dicing saw `mb.crystal.y1.cutting.dicing-saw` _(medium)_

A thin resin-bonded diamond wheel, ~0.03-0.05 mm thick, cutting the plated blank into resonators. The wheel has to be extremely thin and extremely flat to avoid chipping a 0.07 mm plate.

###### Cleaning between steps `mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom` _(medium)_

Every step from lapping onward is done washed and clean: a fingerprint on a 0.07 mm plate changes the frequency. Crystal preparation is one of the few wet, cold, dirty-looking processes in electronics.

###### Deionised rinse water `mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionised-water` _(medium)_

Every crystal process rinse uses deionised water, because a single dissolved ion on a resonating plate changes the frequency measurably. City water is nowhere good enough.

##### HC-49/U case: crimp, weld and argon fill `mb.crystal.y1.case` _(medium)_

The plate sits on a pair of wire supports in a crimped and welded nickel can, filled with argon or krypton at a few kPa. The can is drawn from nickel-plated steel or brass, and its small welded lid is what makes the unit hermetic - the reason a 1982 crystal does not drift as the humidity of an attic changes.

###### Nickel can stock `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can` _(medium)_

HC-49/U cans were drawn from nickel or nickel-plated strip steel, or from brass with a nickel finish. Nickel is used because it matches the thermal expansion of the quartz and the electrode leads closely enough that the mounting stress does not drift the frequency.

###### Drawn can stock `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock` _(medium)_

The HC-49/U can is deep-drawn from thin nickel-plated strip in a progressive tool, then the crimped collar is rolled and the lid welded on. Both operations happen before the plate goes in - the can is made empty and loaded later.

###### Welded lid and crimped collar `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld` _(medium)_

The lid is spot-welded or resistance-welded to the collar in an atmosphere of dry hydrogen or forming gas, which keeps the internal oxide clean and lets the fill gas stay inert. Hermeticity is what makes a forty-year-old crystal hold its frequency.

###### Forming gas for welding `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.gas` _(medium)_

A mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen used as a cover during the lid weld. Hydrogen also diffuses any internal oxide onto the getters, which is why a well-made can can have a getter mirror at the bottom after opening.

###### Argon or krypton fill gas `mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill` _(medium)_

The can is filled with a chemically inert gas before welding. Argon is preferred because it does not react with the electrode and cannot outgas; krypton was used where a slightly more hermetic atmosphere was wanted. The gas also damps acoustic vibration in the plate.

###### Spring-wire supports `mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire` _(medium)_

Two short wires spot-welded to the plate's major faces at the nodal points. Because quartz is piezoelectric, mechanically stressing it shifts its resonant frequency, so the supports must sit where the strain of the vibrating mode is smallest - the whole reason the plate is bevelled and domed.

###### Gold or nickel support wire `mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.wire` _(medium)_

Fine wire, 0.1-0.2 mm, spot-welded to the plate electrodes. Gold is preferred where maximum Q is needed; nickel is the cost-driven choice for the volume 1982 HC-49.

#### Oscillator and PLL circuitry `mb.crystal.oscillator`

The crystal is only the frequency reference. Turning it into the machine's clocks takes a 74LS629 dual VCO crystal oscillator, a Motorola MC4044 phase/frequency detector, a 74LS193 divider, and a 74LS74 flip-flop, with R27 or a trimmer capacitor setting the exact pull.

##### Pierce oscillator and load capacitors `mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce`

The crystal acts as a negative-resistance element in a Pierce oscillator with a small load capacitor at its CL and the drive level set by a series resistor. Its frequency is set by the crystal's CL, the load capacitors and the transistor's input capacitance all in series: at 14 MHz with a few tens of picofarads involved, a fraction of a millimetre of stray copper shifts the trim range, which is why the C64 needed an adjustable element here rather than a fixed capacitor. The oscillator is a high-gain positive-feedback amplifier at all frequencies until the crystal's impedance peaks at the design frequency, so the circuit is designed to start on noise and settle; a badly driven crystal never settles, which is the classic symptom of a cracked plate.

##### PLL: MC4044 into the 74LS629 VCO `mb.crystal.oscillator.pll` _(medium)_

The 74LS629's second oscillator is a voltage-controlled oscillator. The MC4044 phase/frequency detector compares a divided colour clock against the VIC-II's phase clock and returns a DC control voltage on pin 8, which the 74LS629's frequency-control pin steers. That is the whole of the C64's PLL: a crystal oscillator holding the exact subcarrier frequency, and a tracking VCO running SLOWER than it at 8.1818 MHz, locked to it, for the dot clock.

###### Why a trim is required at all `mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.trim-range` _(medium)_

The NTSC colour subcarrier is specified to about 5 parts in 10^7, and an untrimmed crystal and oscillator would wander far more than that over temperature and supply. The trim element (R27 on breadbin boards, a capacitive trim later) lets the whole PLL be pulled onto the exact frequency at the factory and then holds it there.

###### PAL crystal, 17.734475 MHz `mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.pal-variant`

The PAL machine uses a 17.734475 MHz crystal (four times the 4.433619 MHz PAL subcarrier) in the same circuit, and the 74LS193 divider is switched to divide by nine instead of seven. Later C64B/C boards moved to a 16 MHz crystal and a dedicated clock-generator IC, dropping the discrete VCO.

### Soldering the C64 mainboard `mb.solder` _(medium)_

Every joint on the C64 mainboard is made with 63/37 tin-lead alloy activated by rosin flux: about 600 in one pass through a wave-soldering machine, the rest by hand afterwards on the connectors, fuse clips, big electrolytics and wire jumpers. This branch follows the machines, the settings and the bench that make those joints; the alloy itself, its wire and its bar, are the shared node metal.solder.

#### Wave-soldering machine `mb.solder.wave` _(medium)_

A conveyorised machine that drags the underside of the board through a standing wave of molten solder. Components are all inserted from the top so they point the same way, and the wave only ever touches leads and pads. It is why a 1983 line could put hundreds of sound joints on a board for the price of the solder. A single long wave exerts a strong forward drag that tears fine-pitch parts sideways, so any serious machine of this era used a twin-wave or double-peak former: a main wave plus a smaller, faster secondary wave that cuts the drag while still filling holes. That same drag, made worse by lead-free's higher melting point, is what pushed through-hole assembly off wave soldering and onto selective solder a decade later.

##### Welded machine frame and shell `mb.solder.wave.frame` _(medium)_

The pot, tunnel and conveyor sit in a welded mild-steel frame that also carries the fume hood and the flux plumbing. The mass of the frame is what keeps the wave flat while the pot runs. The steel is arc- or induction-furnace steel from the same iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

##### Preheat tunnel `mb.solder.wave.preheat` _(medium)_

An oven before the wave that brings the whole board to roughly 120 deg C so the thermal shock of hitting 250 deg C solder is spread out. It also drives off moisture, which would otherwise spit solder out of the holes as the board hits the wave.

###### Recirculating hot-air preheat `mb.solder.wave.preheat.air` _(medium)_

Preheating is by moving air or radiant tubes, with the zone held below the solder melting point so nothing melts early. Too little preheat gives thermally shocked joints; too much dries the resin and lifts pads off the laminate. A board full of large electrolytics takes a long time to come through, and preheater capacity is usually what sets the conveyor speed for the whole line.

##### Flux foamer `mb.solder.wave.foam` _(medium)_

Just before the wave, a bank of porous stone immersed in rosin flux bubbles air through it and lays a thin, even, pre-activated film on the board's underside. Foaming gives uniform coverage a spray or brush never does, and it is where the smell of boiling pine on a board line comes from.

###### Sintered porous stone `mb.solder.wave.foam.stone` _(medium)_

A sintered polyethylene or polyurethane stone whose pore size is chosen to bubble air finely through the flux. It clogs with crystallised flux and has to be soaked out on a schedule.

##### Conveyor chain and fixtures `mb.solder.wave.conveyor` _(medium)_

A stainless or phenolic chain carries boards through the machine, held by their edge in fixtures spaced along the chain. Chain pitch and fixture design, not the pump, set the real throughput. The fixtures were often the board's own edge, which is one reason board edge quality was a production concern.

##### Nitrogen blanket over the pot `mb.solder.wave.nitrogen` _(medium)_

Many machines piped nitrogen over the solder surface to keep the oxide skin thin and stop dross forming. It also stops the skin from insulating the pot from the wave, which makes the wave itself erratic. Cheaper machines ran open to air and simply lived with the dross.

##### Cooling zone `mb.solder.wave.cooling` _(medium)_

After the wave, boards sit in moving hot air before leaving the machine. Hot air rather than cold, because chilling a freshly soldered joint around a large thermal-mass lead is how you get a cracked solder fillet.

#### The wave-soldering profile `mb.solder.profile` _(medium)_

The machine is set by five numbers together: pot temperature, conveyor speed, preheat temperature, preheat time and flux concentration. Get them wrong in a specific way and you get a specific, diagnosable defect. A joint cools from 250 deg C to 183 deg C in about a second; if the board and the lead start cold the joint solidifies from the outside inward and you get the dull, grainy, poorly wetted fillet a line inspector rejects, which is the entire point of the preheat tunnel. Large thermal-mass leads - the big axial electrolytic, the tabbed regulator - heat far more slowly than the solder around them, so the line runs the conveyor slowly enough that the solder stays molten until the lead is hot, which in turn slows every board on the machine.

##### Why preheat sets joint quality `mb.solder.profile.thermal` _(medium)_

The thermal-shock argument for the preheat tunnel, in one place. Starting the joint at 120 deg C lets the alloy flow and wet before it freezes; starting cold does not.

##### Heavy leads set the slowest joint `mb.solder.profile.thermalmass` _(medium)_

Why the big electrolytics are among the joints most often hand-touched after the wave, and why the instruction to go back and check them existed at all.

##### Joint defects and what causes them `mb.solder.profile.defects` _(medium)_

The diagnostic vocabulary a line supervisor used in 1983, and it has barely changed since. Dull grainy joints mean a dirty pad or too little preheat. Dry joints and unfilled holes mean a hole too tight for the lead or a wave too slow. Solder balls and spatter mean moisture in the board. Bridging between fine pads means too much flux, a pot too hot, or a wave too shallow. Blowholes in the joint mean damp.

#### Copper-tin intermetallic at the pad `mb.solder.reliability` _(medium)_

Solder does not merely sit on a pad, it reacts with it. Within seconds of contact, tin and copper fuse at the surface into Cu6Sn5, and a Cu3Sn layer follows as the joint ages. That intermetallic is the actual metallurgical bond holding the joint, and because its growth is limited by diffusion through itself, higher-temperature solders containing silver or gold exist purely to slow the reaction at the pad. Fully intermetallised joints are brittle, which is the origin of solder fatigue and the reason a leaded joint is forgiving in a way a lead-free one is not.

#### Hand soldering on the line `mb.solder.hand` _(medium)_

Soldering iron, solder wire and pliers on a bench under a smoke extraction arm. Used for the connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers, the big electrolytics and every joint the inspector rejected. A small minority of joints, but where the line rejects come from too. A small hand-held solder pot or a solder fountain was used for the fuse clips and heavy connector leads where a wave cannot reach.

##### Soldering iron and tip `mb.solder.hand.iron` _(medium)_

A nichrome or cartridge heater in a barrel with a replaceable copper tip. The tip has to be kept tinned; a dry tip oxidises and then stops transferring heat at all, which is the real reason beginners conclude solder will not melt on a joint.

##### Fume extraction `mb.solder.hand.extraction` _(medium)_

An arm or hood over the bench draws off the flux smoke. The smoke is resin vapour, not tin vapour, but it is unpleasant and it is the reason every solder bench in 1983 had a hood over it.

#### Connectors, fuse clips and heavy joints `mb.solder.selective` _(medium)_

The parts that cannot simply be taken through the wave in the usual way: the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers and the large electrolytics. The board-mount connectors on this board are right-angle types with solder tails projecting out of the back of the shell, so they were soldered from the underside with the shell already in place - a short working time and a hot iron in a cramped space, which is why so many surviving C64 boards show resoldered connector joints. Inside a shell, solder wicks along a pin and jumps the gap to the next pad, and the bridge cannot be seen happening; the 1983 countermeasures were flux plus a steady iron, then a probe and a rework iron to break the bridge. For genuinely heavy joints the answer was a second iron on the lead to keep it at temperature while the solder melted, so the solder wetted the lead instead of freezing a cold slug around it. Slower per joint, but the only way to get a sound joint onto a big thermal-mass part.

### Populating, cleaning and finishing the C64 mainboard `mb.assembly`

What happens between the bare board and the tested machine. Components are inserted, a few hand-fitted wires and jumpers are added, the board is soldered, cleaned, shielded and screwed into the case. On this board the whole operation is through-hole and hand-and-machine insertion: there is no surface-mount reflow anywhere in the C64 mainboard assembly. The connectors, the fuse clips and the keyboard ribbon were all fitted and hand-soldered rather than waved, because a conveyorised wave cannot hold them; the keyboard ribbon in particular is a delicate soldered joint and a classic failure point on surviving machines.

#### Component insertion `mb.assembly.insertion` _(medium)_

Every part goes into the board from the top. Because there are no vias and no bottom-side components, the whole machine is one-sided: one operator can see every joint from the solder side and there is no second-side insertion operation at all. Axial parts are cut to length and formed to a right angle or a left-right offset so they drop into a fixed hole pitch, and radial parts are spread to the board's lead spacing, usually 0.1 or 0.2 in; the forms are set in the machine and are a real cost, because a wrong form is a board that will not insert. Everything the machine could not do - the fuse clips, the connectors, the small-signal parts in awkward places, the wire jumpers - was worked by hand at the line from a traveller's list. Mixed human-and-machine insertion on one board is a recipe for a part inserted twice or missed entirely, so the line had a checking station: a verifier that confirms every part is present and seated before the board goes into the wave.

##### Component spacing dictated by the insertion machine `mb.assembly.insertion.layout`

Component spacing on this board was dictated by the insertion machine rather than by the circuit designer, which is exactly the argument Commodore had with its Japanese plant and lost. The same board could not be hand-inserted efficiently and machine-inserted efficiently at once.

##### Insertion engine and its cycle time `mb.assembly.insertion.engine` _(medium)_

A machine with a magazine per part type picks a part, leads it to the right hole and pushes it in, typically in 0.3-0.6 s per component. On a board of about 90 parts that is roughly half a minute of machine time, which is why insertion engines paid for themselves on volume this high. The bedplate is cast iron or welded steel, because its flatness is the limit on how accurately a lead can be placed in a hole.

###### Part magazines and vibratory feed `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines` _(medium)_

Radial magazines shake components down a track to a pick head. Cut, formed axial leads are the hardest part to feed; resistors and capacitors with wide leads feed easily.

##### Insertion fixture and board handling `mb.assembly.insertion.fixture` _(medium)_

The board is held in a jig with locating pins while components go in, and the same family of jig carries the board through the wave and into test. Every fixture on the line solves the same problem: the board has to land in exactly one position, every time.

#### DIP sockets as the C64 serviceability choice `mb.assembly.sockets` _(medium)_

This is the single most underappreciated decision on the board. The C64 sockets its integrated circuits rather than soldering them directly, which means any chip can be swapped in the field - and it means the number of joints roughly doubles, because each socket has two contacts per pin. A home computer with unfield-serviceable ROM or SID chips would generate warranty returns, so Commodore accepted the socket money and the extra joints.

#### Wire jumpers and configuration links `mb.assembly.jumpers` _(medium)_

Because the board has no vias, the few places where a connection must cross between the two copper layers with no component to do it are bridged with a short tinned copper wire, hand-fitted into two holes and hand-soldered after wave soldering. These are the E1 and E2 links on the 250407 layout, and there are exactly two of them.

##### Tinned single-core jumper wire `mb.assembly.jumpers.wire` _(medium)_

A short length of fine tinned copper wire, cut and formed to the two holes, fitted and soldered by hand. It is the mechanical ancestor of the jumper link on every later board.

#### No surface-mount parts and no reflow on this board `mb.assembly.reflow`

A deliberate absence, recorded here so it does not read as an omission. It is worth being explicit that the C64 mainboard has no surface-mount parts and no reflow step: everything is through-hole, everything is either waved or hand-soldered. Reflow ovens were already known in 1983, but they were used for flat-pack IC packages and for small daughterboards. The analogue RF modulator is one of those daughterboards - a separate small board, covered by the mb.rf-modulator branch of this tree, not part of the main logic board. Any account that reflows the C64 mainboard is describing a different machine.

#### No conformal coating on this board `mb.assembly.conformal` _(medium)_

A deliberate absence, recorded here so it does not read as an omission. The C64 mainboard was not conformally coated. Conformal coating existed in 1983 for military and automotive work and was increasingly common in commercial electronics, but not for a home computer in a dry indoor case.

#### EMI shield bonding `mb.assembly.shield` _(medium)_

The metal shield around the video and audio circuitry is bonded to the board's ground so that the enclosure is actually part of the ground return. Without a real bond the shield picks up the very signals it is there to contain. On this board the bond is a combination: a small tab on the shield soldered to a ground pad, and a plated hole into which a shield screw goes. Either way it is one of the joints most often disturbed by owners, and its condition is worth checking before blaming the video circuit.

##### The VIC-II heat-sink tab `mb.assembly.shield.tab`

A metal tab welded inside the shield lid pressed against the top of the video chip package, so the shield doubled as a heat sink for the chip that dissipated about 1.5 W. This was a deliberate design fix for a real heat problem, not a later addition, and it is a neat example of the enclosure, the ground return and the thermal path being one part.

#### Board-level rework and repair `mb.assembly.repair` _(medium)_

Bad joints are reworked on the line: the joint is reflowed with an iron, the part is replaced, and a full set of consumable tips is kept to do it. Commodore's own engineering position was famously to ship rather than to hold back, which shows up here as rework being a normal, high-volume operation rather than an exception.

#### Volume and yield reality of the line `mb.assembly.volume` _(low)_

Commodore sold on the order of two million C64s a year at the 1983-84 peak, on a production cost that started near 130 dollars and fell as volume rose. Every board here was one of millions per year through the same line, which is the context that explains every process decision in this branch: a two-layer board with no vias and no plated barrels has very few ways to fail, so board yield was high and the cost stayed near a dollar or two.

### Factory test of the C64 mainboard and machine `mb.test` _(medium)_

How a populated C64 board was proved working before it left the factory. Electrical test on the bare board, then a functional test that boots the machine from a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port and checks it against a monitor and a test cradle, then burn-in, then final test and packing. The practice was mostly manual, and Commodore's own engineers admitted it was thinner than it should have been.

#### In-circuit electrical test `mb.test.ict` _(medium)_

A bare populated board is checked electrically before it is ever plugged into a machine. The point is to catch a missing component, a shorted pad or a broken trace while it is still trivially fixable. The board is pressed down onto a bed-of-nails fixture whose probes touch every node of interest, so the tester can measure each net without a probe being placed by hand; on a board with no vias and only DIP footprints the fixture is comparatively simple to design and to wire, though it still has to be cut for the artwork, which is why fixtures were an expensive per-part-number investment.

##### Continuity, resistance and short detection `mb.test.ict.measure` _(medium)_

The tester looks for opens in the artwork and for shorts between nets that should be isolated, and on some fixtures measures absolute values. On a simple two-layer board with no vias, continuity checking is very nearly the whole job.

##### Component-presence and seating check `mb.test.ict.presence` _(medium)_

Checking that the right part is in the right place is a distinct and important test on a board with thirty sockets and a hundred passive parts. A missing, reversed or half-seated socketed IC is the single most common fault on any 1980s logic board. Verifiers that push each socket to confirm its pins are actually in the hole were in use in this era, alongside visual and continuity checks.

##### The tester itself `mb.test.ict.tester` _(medium)_

A rack of switching electronics driving the fixture, with a go or no-go readout and a reject bin. It is ordinary 1980s digital test equipment: a small computer, a relay matrix and a display, all built from the same logic families the C64 itself uses.

#### Functional test with a test ROM `mb.test.functional`

The populated board is mounted in a test cradle with a power supply and a monitor, and the machine proves itself by running a diagnostic program from the cartridge port. This exercises the real boot path - CPU, ROM, RAM, character ROM, VIC, SID and the I/O chips - all in the configuration they will ship in. Using the cartridge port as the test-vector delivery mechanism is an elegant piece of period engineering: no extra fixture hardware, and it tests the bus the machine actually uses.

##### Diagnostic and dead-test ROM `mb.test.functional.rom` _(medium)_

A small EPROM in a cartridge shell which, on power-up, prints a screenful of named tests and runs each one, reporting RAM, ROM and video faults by pattern rather than by instrument. The operator's job is to look at the picture and read the verdict. These test ROMs were so successful that Commodore later sold the same idea to the public as the Dead Test cartridge, which is why they are so well documented today.

##### Test cradle `mb.test.functional.cradle` _(medium)_

A jig that holds the board on locating pins, presents a regulated 5 V and 12 V, routes the video and audio outputs to a monitor and speaker, and presents the cartridge and edge connectors. The C64's 5 V and 12 V came from its external supply, so the factory had to prove both the board and that supply; testing the power supply itself belongs to the power branch of this tree.

###### Test power supply `mb.test.functional.cradle.psu` _(medium)_

A regulated supply with a current limit, so a shorted board does not destroy it. This is a bench instrument, not the machine's own power brick.

##### Keyboard and ribbon test `mb.test.functional.keyboard` _(medium)_

Because the keyboard connects to the mainboard through a soldered ribbon on this design, the functional test has to cover that joint: every key is checked, which is a simultaneous test of the connector, the ribbon, the keyboard matrix and the CPU's scanning routine.

#### CRT display test `mb.test.video`

The machine's own composite video output is fed to a test monitor and the inspector reads the picture. Nothing instruments this: the pass criterion is that the picture is correct, which means the human being in the loop is doing the measuring. The engineering team said outright that testing colour quality automatically was effectively impossible, and that line workers were told to adjust a colour control until they saw colour. Several thousand machines shipped with garish colours as a result, and the instruction itself was the cause.

##### Test monitor `mb.test.video.monitor` _(medium)_

A small composite monochrome monitor, or a colour television, used as the reference picture. Each is a cathode-ray tube: drawn glass envelope, phosphor coating, deflection yoke and a high-voltage supply.

#### Burn-in `mb.test.burnin` _(medium)_

Finished machines are powered up under load, often at elevated temperature, for an extended period. This was originally to weed out infant-mortality failures in the custom chips, which is exactly where the C64's problems were, and it is why there had to be a diagnostic ROM that could run unattended. Heat is the cheap accelerator of every silicon and soldering defect there is, which is why burn-in exists at all. The ROM is left to run so a machine that fails on its own gives a visible failure, freeing the line from one operator per machine - which is why the dead-test ROM's pattern output mattered as much as its pass-or-fail verdict. Racks were moved in and out of the oven on a schedule, which is a lot of manual handling for what looks like a passive wait.

##### Burn-in oven or rack `mb.test.burnin.oven` _(medium)_

A room or cabinet holding powered machines on racks, warmed to speed up failure. The heat comes from nichrome resistance elements, an alloy of nickel and chromium that resists oxidation at red heat, so the oven is a consumer of both metals in small but real quantity. It is also one of the largest electricity loads in the plant.

###### Burn-in rack `mb.test.burnin.oven.rack` _(medium)_

A steel frame carrying a shelf of machines, ventilated so the heat is actually reaching them. The rack had to carry a full load of powered machines for hours at temperature, so the frame is structural steel rather than sheet-metal convenience.

#### Final test and packing `mb.test.final` _(medium)_

A last pass over the complete machine in its case: keyboard, control ports, serial port and a final power-on. Surviving machines are packed with the cord and the manual for shipment, in corrugated board with a printed outer. The packaging branch has its own industrial chemistry under c64.packaging; this node marks only where the tested board leaves the factory.

##### Control and serial port check `mb.test.final.ports` _(medium)_

The two control ports and the serial port are exercised with known-good peripherals or loopback plugs. These are the connectors most often left untested on a line that was under pressure, and it is where the documented field failures of this era cluster.

### Phototooling: how C64 copper artwork became an etched board `mb.photo`

The chain that turns a board database into a resist image. The 250407 artwork is number 251137. It was drawn on a design workstation, reduced to aperture-table plot files, plotted onto photographic film at a jobbing house, developed, checked on a test coupon, and used as the mask that prints the board's dry-film resist before etching.

#### The board database on the design system `mb.photo.design` _(medium)_

In 1983 the layout lived on the CAD vendor's own workstation, not in a modern repository. Traces, pads, components and drill data were edited on the machine and periodically written out as plot files on nine-track tape and then on 8-inch floppy disks. Copying it to the jobbing house was a physical act of transporting magnetic media, and a lost tape meant the whole panel waited.

##### PCB CAD workstation `mb.photo.design.workstation` _(medium)_

A dedicated 16-bit microcomputer or small minicomputer with its own storage and a high-resolution monochrome display, often with a pen plotter and a digitizer on the desk. The digitizer mattered as much as the plotter: designers drew and revised artwork on mylar overlays and digitised the changes back into the database. Interactive PCB CAD in the 1980s was a commercial market dominated by a handful of vendors, and the C64 layout predates every open format and tool used today.

###### Monochrome CRT display `mb.photo.design.workstation.display` _(medium)_

A high-resolution green or white phosphor CRT on which the layout was examined trace by trace. This is a designer's tooling CRT, not the machine's own video output.

###### CRT envelope glass `mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glass` _(medium)_

The bulb is soda-lime glass formed on a glass lathe from the same kind of batch as the reinforcing cloth: silica sand plus limestone plus alkali. A design workstation's screen is a small consumer item, but it is the terminal through which every copper trace of the board was examined.

###### Plot-file storage media `mb.photo.design.workstation.storage` _(medium)_

Plot files and library data were written to nine-track tape, then to 8-inch floppy disks. The magnetic oxide on a thin polymer backing is the physical carrier the jobbing house receives. This is the handover point between design and fabrication.

##### Backannotation from a drawn overlay `mb.photo.design.backannotation` _(medium)_

The designer taped mylar over the plotted printout, drew routing changes with a special pen, and passed the overlay through a digitizer that read the new lines and apertures back into the database. Some of the most awkward-looking copper on a 1983 board is the residue of this workflow: a routing decision made on a sheet of plastic and converted by an encoder.

#### Data reduction and CAM `mb.photo.cam` _(medium)_

The database is converted into per-layer plot files. This is where a net becomes copper, a component pin becomes a pad, and the drill hits are separated out; autorouters handled most of the bulk in 1983 and a human cleaned up the critical nets, which is why the copper on a 1983 board looks the way it does. Automated checks for minimum track width, minimum spacing and pad-to-pad clearance ran here too; on a board with no vias the annular-ring check has almost nothing to check, but spacing between fine pads on the IC footprints still matters. Errors at this stage are replicated across a whole panel, which is why the step is done once, carefully, for hundreds of boards.

##### Aperture table `mb.photo.cam.apertures`

Every distinct pad shape and track width is assigned an aperture in a table the plotter reads, so a 1.0 mm round pad and a 0.3 mm track are drawn as repeated simple shapes rather than as free curves. The Gerber format was invented at this time to carry exactly this table, which is why it is still about apertures and flashes rather than geometry, and why it is still the universal interchange format for board artwork today.

#### Photoplotting the artwork film `mb.photo.plotter` _(medium)_

The plot files drive a photoplotter that draws the copper artwork onto a transparent film. In 1983 these machines lived at the fabricator, not the design office, and were the company's most valuable single asset.

##### Electrostatic plotter `mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic` _(medium)_

The dominant plotting technology of the era. A fine wire or shaped electrode is stepped across the film under computer control and a corona discharge exposes the emulsion wherever copper is wanted. Flatbed machines laid a film flat and exposed quickly, which is why they became the standard for two-sided work. Gerber Scientific commercialised these plotters and the aperture-table format that drove them, so the format the industry still uses is a direct inheritance of this machine.

##### Artwork film stock `mb.photo.plotter.film` _(medium)_

A high-contrast, dimensionally stable photographic film that the plotter exposes and the shop develops into a finished mask. It must hold its geometry over a store door and be opaque where there is copper. The base is a dimensionally stable polyester, the same polymer family as the dry-film resist carrier used on the board itself.

##### Pen plotter `mb.photo.plotter.pen` _(medium)_

A carriage carrying a light-sensitive pen draws the artwork directly on film or mylar. Simple and reliable, but slow, with real line-width variation, so it was being displaced by the electrostatic plotter through the early 1980s. Still used for check plots and for prototype single-layer boards well into the 1980s.

##### Laser plotting, arriving later `mb.photo.plotter.laser` _(medium)_

An argon-ion or, later, a diode laser writes the film or the photoresist directly. Sharper than corona discharge and faster, but in 1983 it was still being adopted and the electrostatic plotter was not yet history. This is the last piece of 1980s phototooling equipment before direct imaging replaced film entirely in the 1990s - an aside on where the technology was heading, not a step in this board's own process.

#### Developing and fixing the film `mb.photo.develop` _(medium)_

The exposed film is developed, fixed, washed and dried before it can serve as a mask. The chemistry is ordinary silver-halide photographic processing, run as a short line of tanks.

##### Photographic developer (hydroquinone) `mb.photo.develop.developer` _(medium)_

The film emulsion is silver halide; hydroquinone reduces the exposed grains to metallic silver, giving the opaque image that will block the resist. The reducing agent is itself an aromatic chemical made from benzene, so the mask chemistry is a petroleum chain like almost everything else in this branch.

##### Fixer (ammonium thiosulfate) `mb.photo.develop.fixer` _(medium)_

The unexposed silver halide is dissolved away and the image made light-stable, so the film can be handled, stored and re-exposed without latent-image changes.

#### Rephotography, the master, and the coupon `mb.photo.rephoto` _(low)_

The plotted working film is rephotographed onto a higher-quality film to get a sharper, dimensionally stable master. Before a whole panel is committed, a test coupon is exposed and etched with every line width the panel uses, and the widths are measured under a measuring microscope. This is how a shop proves its process still holds tolerance, and it is the quiet heart of 1980s board making: a cheap, fast way to prove that the narrowest trace the designer asked for is still coming out, before a hundred boards are committed to it.

##### The artwork master `mb.photo.rephoto.master` _(medium)_

The film treated as the authoritative copy of the design, stored flat and handled by the edges. It is the board's master record, and losing it means paying for the panel again.

#### Printing the artwork onto the resist `mb.photo.mask` _(medium)_

The artwork film is laid against the exposed dry-film resist on the board and exposed in the vacuum frame. Where the film is clear, the resist hardens and resists the etch; where it is opaque, the resist stays soft and the copper beneath is etched away. This is the moment the phototooling chain finally touches the board, and every solder joint on the finished machine is located by this exposure.

#### Panelising the order `mb.photo.panel` _(medium)_

The board is one part out of a panel of identical boards nested in a sheet large enough for the process equipment. The panel gets tooling holes for registration and for the drill, and the boards are held together by small perforated mouse-bite tabs that are broken out by hand or by a router after the panel is finished. Those tabs leave a characteristic rough edge on the board outline, visible on a 1983 board if you look for it. This is where the layout cost of an order is amortised, and why a two-layer panel in 1983 could hold a surprising number of boards.

## Commodore 64 external 'brick' power supply `c64.psu`

A sealed black ABS box roughly 150 x 100 x 60 mm that sits under the C64 and converts wall mains into 5 V DC for the logic plus unfiltered ~9 V AC for the cassette motor, the RF modulator, the VIC-II's CAN +5 V rail, the SID's +12 V doubler and the 50/60 Hz time-of-day clock. It is a linear supply: an iron-core transformer, two rectifier diodes, one 4700 uF electrolytic, one three-terminal 5 V regulator and a folded aluminium heatsink, all buried under a minty-green epoxy pour from 1983 on.

### Mains transformer, 40-46 VA `c64.psu.transformer`

The whole of the supply's energy conversion. One primary on 117 V mains, a centre-tapped ~18 V secondary feeding the 5 V regulator, and a separate ~9 V winding feeding straight out to the C64. The two secondaries are galvanically isolated from each other as well as from the primary - that isolation is what lets the C64 tie their grounds together only at the rectifier. Every wound transformer is proved before it is potted or assembled: a 1500-2500 V AC dielectric withstand between primary and all secondaries, an insulation-resistance check at 500 V DC, a turns-ratio and phasing check between the taps, and a loaded run at nominal line voltage.

#### E-I laminated silicon-steel core `c64.psu.transformer.core`

A stack of punched E and I laminations with interleaved joints, taped along the yoke edges with a single wrap of masking or Kapton tape. For a 40 VA unit at 60 Hz the stack is maybe 25-35 mm tall in 0.35-0.5 mm plate, and it is clamped hard enough that the laminations must be isolated from each other by the oxide scale left on the punched edges.

##### Punched E and I lamination `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination`

One E and one I punched from a strip of grain-oriented electrical steel by a high-speed progression press, roughly 200-600 strokes per minute. The die is a hardened tool-steel stamping die with a compound profile; the strip is fed on a roll and the interlamination burr left by the punch is small enough not to short adjacent plates.

###### High-speed stamping press `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punch` _(medium)_

A vertical crank or hydraulic press with the compound E+I die in the lower ram and a blanking punch above. In a 1982-era plant the strip ran on a powered roll feed with a pilot pin for registration; the same press also cut the mounting-hole side features and the interleaving key.

###### Hardened tool-steel stamping die `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punch.die` _(medium)_

Tungsten-chromium or high-chromium tool steel, hardened and ground, with the compound E and I outline in the same 25-40 mm stroke. Dies lasted millions of hits before the cutting edge rolled and the burr grew past the electrical-steel tolerance.

##### Core stack assembly and clamping `c64.psu.transformer.core.stack`

E and I plates are stacked in alternating layers with the joints staggered so no section of the stack has an unbroken air gap, then clamped end to end by angle plates and bolts or by rivets through the yoke. The joints are the dominant core loss, so the assembler has to keep the interleaving sequence right by hand.

###### Clamp bolts and angle plates `c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.clamp-hardware` _(medium)_

Mild steel angle plates bolted across the yokes, or two long tie bolts through the core legs, with the axial clamp force chosen so the interlaminar pressure is roughly 3-10 kg/mm2 - enough to stop the stack buzzing at 50 Hz, not so much that the punched edges crack.

##### MnZn ferrite E-core alternative `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative` _(medium)_

Later Commodore bricks and the C64C/Plus4 supplies switched to a pressed manganese-zinc ferrite core. Ferrite has much higher resistivity than silicon steel so it can be used as a solid moulded shape with no lamination joints, giving lower core loss at 60 Hz and a much lighter assembly - at several times the material cost, and with a supply chain in Japan or Germany rather than the local steel mill.

###### E/EI/EE core geometry and the transformer `metal.ferrite.e-core` _(medium)_

The shape is dictated by the winding, and the 1982 supply for small switchers was a pair of E cores with a centre leg and a window, assembled 'E-E' or interleaved 'EI' so that the joint is staggered and the effective air gap is halved. The window has to fit the magnetising inductance and the wire; the cross-section is set by the core loss target. The same ferrite pressing produces E, EI, EE, U, toroid, drum and bobbin cores, and the shapes are made by different tools in the same press. The C64's transformer is one of the smallest: perhaps 25 mm across, 30-40 turns of 0.3 mm magnet wire on a bobbin, and a gap cut into the centre leg with a scraper to set the inductance.

###### Cutting the air gap in the centre leg `metal.ferrite.gap-scrape` _(medium)_

An ungapped ferrite E core has a very high inductance and would not regulate a switch-mode supply; the switcher's magnetising current would be wrong and the whole design fails. So the gap is made deliberately, and on a 1982 E core it was cut with a carbide-tipped scraper - literally a hand blade run along the face of the centre leg - to 0.2-1.0 mm. Cutting rather than inserting a gap material keeps the inductance high and spreads the gap's fringing over an area, and it does it with a machine a ferrite buyer can operate. The tolerance of that hand cut is what sets the inductance tolerance, and the whole thing is one of the more beautiful pieces of 1980s manufacturing: a blade and a number.

#### Enamelled copper winding `c64.psu.transformer.winding` _(medium)_

The primary, the 18 V centre-tapped secondary and the 9 V output secondary are wound in layers on a moulded bobbin, with a few hundred turns of 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper wire. Layer insulation between each pass and interleaved padding between the primary and the secondaries carry the 1000-1500 V RMS of the mains.

##### Enamelled magnet wire `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire`

Bare copper rod drawn down to 0.25-0.4 mm through a series of tungsten-carbide or diamond dies, then coated in two or more passes of a thermosetting enamel - typically polyester-imide (Grade 2 / THEIC) - and baked to cure it. Each coat adds roughly 5-10 um, so a double-grade wire has 25-40% more copper per given window area than bare wire.

###### Wire drawing `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing`

A 8 mm copper cathode rod or coil is pickled in sulphuric acid, washed, annealed in a continuous bright-annealing furnace at 500-700 C, then pulled through progressively finer dies with a phosphated soap lubricant. Ten or more die passes take 8 mm to 0.3 mm, and the die temperature is water-cooled to keep the copper from work-hardening to failure.

###### Polyester-imide enamel coating `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel`

The wire runs continuously through a die-casting oven where a 25-30% solids solution of the modified polyester-imide resin in cresol/xylene is applied, then through a 350-450 C curing oven, and through the same pair again for a second coat. The thermal cure crosslinks the resin to a hard film that resists varnish, oil and coolant.

###### Polyester-imide resin `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel.resin`

The workhorse magnet-wire enamel of the 1980s. The base is a polycondensation of dimethyl terephthalate (or trimellitic anhydride) with polyols; the imide is introduced with a polyamide of trimellitic anhydride and a diamine such as ethylenediamine, which is what raises the class to H (180 C).

##### Moulded nylon bobbin `c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin`

A spool-shaped coil former in glass-filled or unfilled nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, with cheek flanges that locate it on the core leg and a continuous slot that keeps the layer insulation in place. Bobbins were (and still are) a Miles-Platts product line, which fits the 'MP' mark found on this transformer.

###### Injection moulding the bobbin `c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.moulding` _(medium)_

Nylon is hygroscopic so the pellets are dried at 80 C for 4-8 h before moulding, then injection moulded at 240-280 C into a multi-cavity tool with hot runners and a mould temperature of 60-90 C. The mould cavity is polished because a flash of loose fibre on the winding slot would be a turn-coat defect.

##### Layer and interwinding insulation `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation`

Crepe paper or glass-cloth tape between winding layers, a wide kraft or composite tape wrap between the primary and the secondaries, and in the potted builds strips of polyimide (Kapton) film around the whole winding. The 1983-84 bricks visibly used masking tape on the core yoke edges and something like Kapton over the coil to keep the epoxy pour off the windings.

###### Crepe paper insulation `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.crepe-paper`

A lightly crinkled, unbleached kraft paper that stretches to follow the winding contour without bunching. Made on a Fourdrinier machine from a dilute suspension of long-fibre softwood pulp.

###### Mechanical wood pulp `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.crepe-paper.pulp`

Softwood (spruce/fir) is debarked, chipped, steamed and refined in a disc or refiner mill; the long fibres are ideal for electrical insulation paper because they give high dielectric strength and mechanical strength in the thin sheet.

###### Softwood pulp `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.crepe-paper.pulp.softwood` _(medium)_

The species matters as much as the process: long-fibre softwood pulp from spruce, fir or pine gives the dielectric strength and tear resistance that electrical insulation paper needs, while hardwood pulp from birch or aspen gives opacity and printability and is used in the thinner papers. Softwood is bought as chips or as market pulp.

###### Glass-cloth insulation tape `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.glass-cloth`

Woven E-glass yarn cloth, ~0.1 mm thick, silane-sized for adhesion, wound in the last layer before the outer tape. Glass has no moisture absorption and much higher dielectric strength than paper, which is why the safety-approved design puts it nearest the primary.

###### Polyimide (Kapton) film `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.kapton`

A 12-25 um amber polyimide film used as the barrier between the coil and the epoxy pour and, in later builds, as the layer insulation. Its value is that it does not soften, dissolve or outgas in a hot epoxy cure.

###### Pyromellitic dianhydride monomer `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.kapton.pyromellitic-dianhydride`

The diacid anhydride half of Kapton is made by air oxidation of pseudocumene to trimellitic acid and then dehydrating it - a petroleum-aromatics chain. The diamine half is 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine, both aromatics intermediates.

##### Interwinding earth screen `c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen` _(medium)_

The protective-earth conductor is bonded to an aluminium or copper foil laid between the primary and the secondary windings - or sometimes to the transformer frame bolt. It does not leave the transformer: the earthing path is closed inside the potted block and never reaches the plastic case or the computer. The foil is plain rolled aluminium or copper, lapped and left uncut so it cannot tear, and it is deliberately insulated from both windings.

##### Layer winding on a coil winder `c64.psu.transformer.winding.process` _(medium)_

A single-spindle or two-spindle coil winder turns the bobbin while traversing the wire, and the operator lays interleaved insulation between each layer with a slow-moving 'paper feeder'. Bobbin layers are counter-wound to flatten the coil, and the leads are brought out through the bobbin flange and dressed so they cannot chafe on the core.

###### Lead termination and crimped flag terminals `c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.lead-termination` _(medium)_

The winding leads are soldered or, in the 1983-84 bricks, soldered directly to the transformer's own pins; the line cord and interwinding conductors terminate in tin-plated brass crimp flags. Under the epoxy pour the crimps are the weak link - they can anneal and let go - and the PVC of the line cord is visibly browned right at the pin.

##### Polyester varnish impregnation and oven cure `c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation`

The finished assembly is vacuum impregnated with a thermosetting polyester or epoxy varnish so the winding becomes a solid block and cannot move at 50 Hz. Viscous impregnating varnishes were standard by the early 1980s; the alternative is dip-and-bake in an epoxy or a polyurethane.

###### Impregnating varnish `c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.varnish` _(medium)_

A low-viscosity, high-solids unsaturated polyester resin dissolved in styrene, with an organic peroxide cure catalyst. It cures by crosslinking rather than by solvent loss, so it shrinks very little and fills completely.

#### Transformer pin terminal board `c64.psu.transformer.pinboard`

A row of brass pins on a small phenolic or nylon board carrying the primary, the interwinding earth, and all the secondary taps. The rectifier diodes and fuses in the 1983-84 bricks are soldered straight onto these pins, which is why the schematic 'terminals' that appear in a teardown are the transformer's own pins rather than a separate board.

##### Phenolic laminate board `c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.phenolic`

Paper or cotton-linen web impregnated with phenol-formaldehyde resin under heat and pressure. Cheap, dimensionally stable and self-extinguishing, which is why it was the default material for transformer terminal boards and fuseholders.

### Rectifier diodes, 400GI / 1N5400 `c64.psu.rectifier`

Two or four stud-less axial rectifier diodes convert the 18 V centre-tapped secondary into pulsating DC. The 902503-02 uses two General Electric 400GI silicon rectifiers in a full-wave centre-tapped configuration, which saves the two extra dice of a bridge; other builds use four 1N5400s or a moulded bridge. The diodes are soldered directly onto the transformer pins.

#### Axial rectifier diode `c64.psu.rectifier.diode` _(medium)_

A single silicon junction in an axial package with a formed lead, cathode band marked with a stripe. Inside: a die a few hundred microns across with a heavy anode metallisation, a glass passivation, and epoxy or a voidless glass body filled with silicone stress-relief gel to survive the power cycling.

##### Silicon rectifier die `c64.psu.rectifier.diode.die`

A 100-150 mm wafer ground to a die typically 2 x 2 x 0.3 mm, with a diffused N-type cathode and metallised anode. The same Czochralski silicon as the VIC-II and the 6510; the detailed wafer process belongs to the silicon branch of this tree.

###### Die attach, wire bond and axial encapsulation `c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging` _(medium)_

The die is die-attached to the anode lead with silver-loaded glass or a soft solder, one or two aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the cathode metallisation to the cathode lead, then the whole assembly is transfer-moulded or cast in an epoxy body filled with silicone gel to relieve the thermal cycle between the glass and the leads.

##### Moulded bridge rectifier alternative `c64.psu.rectifier.bridge-alternative`

Some builds and most replacement supplies use a packaged bridge: four dice mounted on a common ceramic or moulded body with the terminals formed into the four corners. Commodore's own choice of two discrete diodes over a bridge saved two dice and one package, at the cost of a centre tap on the transformer.

### 5 V linear voltage regulator `c64.psu.regulator`

The pass element that turns roughly 8-10 V of pulsating DC into 5.00 V. Three different implementations appear in C64 bricks inside two years, and the choice of which one determines how much heat has to be removed. At full load the drop across the pass device is 3-5 V at 1.5 A, so 4.5-7.5 W has to go into the heatsink - which is why these supplies run hot and why the electrolytics above them cook.

#### 7805-class three-pin regulator `c64.psu.regulator.variant-7805`

The simplest form: a monolithic regulator containing the reference, error amplifier, current limit and the pass transistor, in a TO-220 or TO-3P-like plastic body with a tab bolted to the heatsink. In the 251053-02 brick it is a three-legged part with rectangular legs, screwed straight into the folded aluminium plate under a blob of epoxy.

#### Sanken SI-3052P integrated regulator `c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p`

The regulator in the later 902503-02, which many hobbyists misidentify as a transistor because it is moulded in a TO-3P-looking package. It is a 5 V / 2 A linear regulator with an internal error amplifier and a foldback current limit that kicks in at about 2.4 A. The datasheet explicitly warns that the output must not be raised by inserting a resistor in the ground pin - and Commodore inserted a 300 Ohm resistor in the ground pin anyway, to make up for the drop in the output cable.

##### Output stability capacitor `c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p.stability-cap`

A small electrolytic or tantalum directly across the regulator's input and output pins. The datasheet requires it for loop stability; a 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum appears on some 902503-02 builds and the 3-83 version has the holes for it but does not populate it, which suggests it was a late cost change.

#### Discrete 2N3055 / 2N3792 series-pass regulator `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete` _(medium)_

The earliest 'repairable' silver-label brick used a discrete design: an NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can bolted to a heatsink as the series pass, a smaller driver transistor, a zener or low-current regulator as the reference, wirewound resistors in the emitter and base for current limiting, and a thermal shutdown in contact with the heatsink. It is the arrangement the 902503-02's monolithic regulator replaced.

##### 2N3055 / 2N3792 power NPN `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn`

A triple-diffused planar NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can: a bolted metal header with an isolation disc, the die brazed or soldered to the header, one or two emitter bonds, and a hermetic can with a glass-sealed pin feedthrough. The 2N3055 is grossly oversized for a 1.5 A load (15 A, 60 V, 115 W dissipation capability), which is exactly why it was chosen: it could not fail thermally even when the circuit was badly designed.

###### Triple-diffused planar process `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn.triple-diffusion`

Three sequential dopings - collector-base, base-emitter, and a deep collector-emitter - through a photolithographically masked oxide. The heavy collector-emitter diffusion carries the load current while the shallow, tightly controlled base-emitter diffusion sets the gain and the breakdown voltage. This is the process that made 15 A transistors possible at all.

###### Die attach and hermetic TO-3 sealing `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn.die-attach`

The die is brazed to the header in a hydrogen atmosphere at 700-800 C with an active-metal braze, or soldered with a 50Pb-50Sn or AuSn preform at 220-300 C; the header is then nickel-plated. The can is crimped or cold-welded onto the header with an annular glass or ceramic feedthrough insulator; mica or a thin mica-fibre washer goes between the can and the heatsink to isolate the collector while conducting heat.

###### Emitter wire bonds `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn.wire-bond`

Two to four 100-200 um aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the emitter metallisation to the emitter lead to carry the full emitter current; the collector current flows through the die's back contact straight into the header. Ultrasonic wedge bonding at 50-250 g per wire was the universal method - ball bonding was for fine-pitch.

##### Driver / error-amplifier transistor `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.driver` _(medium)_

A small-signal NPN whose job is to supply the ~0.7 V of base drive plus the feedback signal the pass transistor needs. In a 1982 discrete supply this is typically a TO-92 part with hFE around 100-400, or one half of a matched pair. Its collector dissipation is small but its junction temperature is close to the pass transistor's, so it shares the same heatsink metal.

##### Voltage reference `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.reference` _(medium)_

In a 1982 discrete supply the reference is either a 5.1-6.2 V zener diode biased from a constant-current source, or a low-current three-terminal regulator such as a TL431 or a small 7805 in a TO-92 used purely as a reference. The zener route needs a stable bias current; the temperature coefficient of an ordinary zener is poor, which shows up as output drift with case temperature.

##### Emitter ballast resistors `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitter-ballast` _(medium)_

One to three wirewound resistors in series with the pass transistor's emitter. Their purpose is to develop a signal proportional to output current for current limiting and to force a standing current through the pass transistor so its hFE and therefore the loop gain do not collapse at light load. Wirewound rather than film because the dissipation is fractional watts but the temperature rise has to stay small.

###### Manganin wire `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitter-ballast.manganin-wire`

A copper-manganese-nickel alloy (typically 86% Cu, 12% Mn, 2% Ni) whose resistivity barely changes with temperature. A spiral-wound wirewound resistor is made by winding manganin or constantan wire onto a ceramic or plastic former and baking it under high tension so the winding stress-relaxes and stays against the form.

##### Thermal shutdown `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.thermal-shutdown` _(medium)_

A temperature-sensitive element in contact with the heatsink - a thermistor or a bimetallic thermal switch - that shorts or removes the driver bias when the sink passes roughly 90-110 C, so the supply folds back rather than destroying itself. Commodore's bricks more often relied on a thermal fuse in the primary and on the epoxy pot for heat retention, which is the root of their reputation.

###### NTC thermistor `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.thermal-shutdown.thermistor`

A bead or disc of semiconducting metal oxide whose resistance falls steeply with temperature (10 kOhm at 25 C, ~1 kOhm at 100 C for the standard 10K curve). Glued or bolted to the heatsink and shunting the driver bias, it gives a soft, non-resetting protection that must cool before it re-conducts.

#### Bolting the regulator to the heatsink `c64.psu.regulator.mounting`

The regulator tab or TO-3 can is bolted to the folded aluminium plate with a thin layer of thermal compound - in 1982 typically a zinc-oxide paste in a silicone or hydrocarbon base, or sometimes simply a piece of thin copper foil. The thermal interface matters more than the compound brand: dry metal-to-metal contact is roughly ten times worse than a properly filled joint.

### Folded aluminium heatsink `c64.psu.heatsink`

A thin aluminium plate folded into a U so that one leg clamps under the case and the other presents an area against the regulator. There are no fins: the design relies on the natural convection of a brick sitting under a desk. It is the reason the case runs at 60-70 C and the epoxy never fully cools. The sheet is commercial-purity aluminium folded on a press brake and tapped for the regulator screw, usually left mill finish or painted, occasionally black anodised.

#### Sheet folding and tapping `c64.psu.heatsink.forming` _(medium)_

Strip or sheet is blanked, then folded on a press brake to a U; the mounting hole is punched or drilled and tapped with a thread-forming tap. Aluminium's low modulus means the fold must be given a generous inside radius or the sheet tears, and the tapped hole must be at least 1.5 diameters from the bend.

### 4700 uF 16 V aluminium electrolytic `c64.psu.bulk-cap`

The single reservoir capacitor on the rectifier output. It is the part that has killed the most C64s: as the electrolyte dries out the ripple current is no longer smoothed, the series regulator loses headroom and starts pumping 100/120 Hz ripple onto the 5 V rail, and eventually the cap leaks current into the regulator's ground reference and pushes the output up past 5.5 V. Replacements are still sold as the C64 'fix' four decades later.

#### Aluminium anode foil `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil` _(medium)_

The anode is a 12-20 um aluminium foil that has been chemically etched in a hot chlorate or permanganate bath to roughen the surface into a high-area sponge. Because capacitance is proportional to real surface area, the etch multiplies the effective area by 30-100x and is the entire reason a 4700 uF part fits in a 25 mm can. The foil gauge, the rolling lubricant and the last work-hardening pass matter as much as the etch: at 12 um the metal is barely thicker than the oxide skin on it, so a single pinhole becomes a short. The stock foil and its rolling chain are the shared metal.aluminum.foil line, from the rolling ingot down to the slitter.

##### Aluminium foil, 6-25 um, for capacitors `metal.aluminum.foil`

The C64's power supply is full of electrolytic capacitors, and every one of them is an aluminium foil sandwich: a thin cathode foil wound with a thicker anode foil and a paper separator soaked in electrolyte. Making 6 um foil is a genuinely hard rolling problem - at that gauge the metal is thinner than the oxide skin that forms on it, so the rolls and the housekeeping are the whole technology. This is a deliberate convergence node: the foil branch, the anode-foil etch branch and the rolling-mill branch all hang off it.

###### DC casting to a rolling ingot `metal.aluminum.dc-casting`

Molten aluminium at 700-750 C is poured into a steel mould that is being withdrawn by a hydraulic jack at a controlled few millimetres per second, so the metal freezes progressively behind a solidification front instead of all at once. The front is water-cooled and the emerging surface is squirted with a water mist to control its shape. This produces a big flat rectangular billet - typically 500-1000 mm wide, 600 mm thick, 5-25 t - with a fine equiaxed chill zone at the surface. Because it is a continuous process, a 1980s smelter and a modern one produce ingots of essentially identical shape.

###### Homogenising soak `metal.aluminum.homogenising` _(medium)_

A long hold in a gas- or electrically-heated pit furnace, typically 12-24 h at 450-600 C, whose only job is to let the alloying elements diffuse evenly. Without it a slab rolled on one edge behaves differently from the same slab rolled on the other and the foil tears. It also rounds the dendritic structure into equiaxed grains, which is what makes the achievable surface quality possible.

###### Hot rolling to 2-6 mm `metal.aluminum.hot-rolling` _(medium)_

The ingot is preheated to 300-400 C for wide slab or 450-550 C for narrower, thicker slab, and a reversing hot mill takes it down to 2-6 mm in one or two passes. Aluminium's rolling window is famously narrow - too cold and it tears at the edges, too hot and the ingot surface oxidises and scales - so a 1980s reversing hot mill had two or three stands and quite tight control. Scale is removed with hot descaling rolls, which presses a rolled-in oxide pattern into the surface that later helps the lubricant out of the pores.

###### Mill scale (iron-bearing aluminium oxide) `metal.aluminum.mill-scale` _(medium)_

Hot rolling oxidises the surface and the scale is knocked off by the descaling rolls. The chips that fall are a mix of alumina and iron oxides pulled in from the ingot surface, and they are the same material the ferroalloy and cement industries fought over - and, ground and magnetically separated, the raw iron oxide for soft ferrites. In 1982 most was dumped.

###### Cold rolling on a Sendimir high-roll mill `metal.aluminum.cold-rolling`

The 2-6 mm hot strip goes to a multi-high cold mill - a Sendimir 20-high or 24-high arrangement where a small work roll is backed by many intermediate rolls, giving the enormous rolling force needed at a small gap without a mill body the size of a building. The work rolls are hardened tool steel, 100-300 mm diameter, with a chasing finish that the operator keeps polished with emery and a lint-free cloth while the mill runs; at 6 um a single fingerprint is a visible defect. Between passes the strip is annealed at 200-400 C in a gas-fired or electric furnace, because the roll gap cannot take the whole reduction in one pass and because that anneal is what resets the rolling texture. The finished 1-2 t coil, 400-1300 mm wide, is then slit into customer widths with tungsten-carbide or ceramic-coated knives and re-spooled, which is the least forgiving part of the whole operation: at 6 um the foil has almost no stiffness and simply tears on a blunt knife. From 1980 onwards the Sendimir Z-High mill, which adds separate work-roll bending and flattening control, was the state of the art for aluminium foil width.

###### Aluminium rolling oil and the degreaser `metal.aluminum.rolling-oil` _(medium)_

Cold rolling of aluminium would tear without a lubricant: a water-in-oil emulsion or a neat mineral oil with fatty-acid esters, applied by nozzles at order 0.1-1 g/m2. The oil is what lets the gauge get down without the surface tearing, and it has to be removed afterwards - a few grams of oil left on capacitor foil ruin the capacitor, because the electrolyte chemistry and the oxide interface are that sensitive. Foil mills ran a dedicated degreasing line with naphtha or trichloroethane and a 200-300 C bake.

###### Fatty-acid esters from tallow and palm fat `metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow` _(medium)_

The ester lubricants are made from animal or vegetable fats - tallow, palm, rapeseed - hydrolysed to fatty acids and re-esterified, on a paraffinic mineral base or a synthetic ester. This is the one place in the aluminium chain where biomass chemistry is genuinely load-bearing: an aluminium rolling lubricant is a soap-and-fatty-acid chemistry, not a petrochemical one. In 1982 tallow was still the dominant base; vegetable ester formulations grew through the 1990s.

###### Etched aluminium anode foil `metal.aluminum.anode-foil` _(medium)_

The trick that made a decent electrolytic fit into an 8 mm diameter can. Plain anode foil etched in a hot acid bath grows an aluminium oxide/hydroxide layer over essentially the whole surface - up to about a hundred times the geometric area, and therefore a hundred times the capacitance per unit of volume. The 1980s etching chemistry was a chloride bath or, in the Japanese-dominated high-end market, a chlorate bath with acetic acid; the etch pits are then hardened with a phosphate or chromate formation treatment and the surface is impregnated with the electrolyte. The chloride ion eats its way into the foil along the grain boundaries and leaves a field of round tunnels 0.1-2 um across; oxidation inside those tunnels is what multiplies the area. A formation step then grows oxide in a controlled taper so the weakest point - the mouth of each pit - is the first to fail if the etch is wrong, which is why a 1982 capacitor that failed early failed as a short circuit and a vent rather than as a slow leak.

##### Chemical etching of the anode foil `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching` _(medium)_

The foil is threaded continuously through an etch tank at 70-80 C. Sodium chlorate with hydrochloric acid, or potassium permanganate, dissolves aluminium faster where the surface is already rough, so the etch runs away into a deep microscopic pore structure rather than eating away uniformly. The etched foil is rinsed, dried and cut to length.

###### Potassium permanganate etchant `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.permanganate` _(medium)_

An alkaline potassium permanganate bath oxidises the aluminium surface; the loose MnO2 sludge is removed by brushing or a nitric acid dip. The alternative chlorate chemistry was being phased out for safety and environmental reasons through the 1980s because chlorate/dioxide is toxic.

##### Electrolytic formation of the anode oxide `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation` _(medium)_

The wound wet cell is energised from a DC source at a voltage ramped up to the rated working voltage. At the anode the aluminium oxidises to a dense amorphous alumina film only a few nanometres thick - the dielectric. Raising the voltage thickens the film; raising the temperature thickens it faster but also lets it dissolve, which is why forming is done hot and forming voltage is always lower than the operating voltage.

#### Electrolytic electrolyte `c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte` _(medium)_

An aqueous solution of an ammonium or amine salt - ammonium pentaborate was the classic low-voltage recipe - that forms the counter-electrode ion layer against the oxide. In an aluminium electrolytic the cathode reaction deposits a hydrated aluminium oxide or tin layer from the metal ion, and the leakage current is exactly that reaction rate.

#### Cell separator `c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator`

A porous dielectric sheet between the anode and the cathode foil, keeping them apart without shorting. Low-voltage parts in 1980-82 used cellulose (paper) separators, which is the direct cause of the decades-later failure: paper is hygroscopic and absorbs electrolyte, and the carbonisation of that paper when leakage current rises shorts the cell.

##### Polypropylene separator `c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene` _(medium)_

A microporous isotactic polypropylene film, 12-25 um thick and about 35-45% porous, made by extruding a film and stretching it or by solvent extraction so that the electrolyte fills the voids while the sheet still keeps the electrodes apart.
