###### Lubricated nylon 6,6 bushing resin `c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.resin` _(medium)_

A lubricated or unfilled nylon grade, chosen for low friction against steel. The base polymer is nylon 6,6 from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid; caprolactam is the route to nylon 6, a different grade. The joystick contains nylon in this bushing, in its microswitch cases and in its gate.

###### Friction pad `c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad` _(medium)_

A small felt or fibre pad under the gate that sets the lateral friction. Felt pads need almost no oil, dry-run cleanly, and shed a black dust that eventually gums the gate if the stick is never cleaned.

###### Wool felt `c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool` _(medium)_

Pressed wool felt sets the lateral friction of the gate. Unlike an oiled pad it needs no lubricant, which matters because an oiled pad in a 1982 joystick attracts dust and eventually gums.

#### Four miniature microswitches `c64.joystick.microswitches`

Four sealed miniature switches under the gate, one per direction. Each is a plastic case with a plunger and a fixed leaf plus a sprung leaf, gold-plated so the contact resistance stays low through millions of actuations. The plunger is depressed by a rib on the gate as it slides.

##### Sprung leaf contact `c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves` _(medium)_

Inside each switch a formed leaf is bowed against a fixed contact; pressing the plunger straightens the leaf onto it. The contacts are gold-plated over nickel because a joystick switch is a low-current, high-cycle signal contact where a stable millivolt-level resistance matters, and because the leaf is wiped clean on every actuation.

###### Gold plating of the microswitch leaf `c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-plating` _(medium)_

The contact is gold-plated over nickel so its resistance stays at the millivolt level through millions of cycles. Gold leaf contacts in this class of switch were a real reliability advantage over the silver and nickel contacts used in cheaper equivalents.

##### Switch case polymer `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case` _(medium)_

A small moulded case in a filled thermoset or a glass-filled nylon, chosen so the case survives being dropped off a desk with the stick still in hand - which, for a joystick sold with a computer, was a frequent event.

###### Glass-filled nylon case `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.nylon` _(medium)_

A glass-filled nylon case gives a microswitch enough stiffness to keep its contact force with a thin wall, and enough toughness to survive being dropped. It is the standard material for that class of switch through the 1980s.

###### Nylon-6-6 resin `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.nylon.nylon-6-6`

The base polymer of the glass-filled nylon case, made from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid. Caprolactam is the route to nylon 6, a different grade. A single C64 contains nylon in its switch housings, its joystick bushings and its microswitch cases.

###### Through-hole mounting and solder lugs `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.solder-lugs` _(medium)_

The switches are pushed into holes in the joystick's printed board and their pins soldered from underneath. Positioning them on that board is what sets how far the gate has to travel before a direction registers - the mechanical timing of the whole joystick.

#### Steel shaft and ball top `c64.joystick.shaft` _(medium)_

A cross-section steel shaft pressed into the gate, rising through the chassis with a moulded ball or ball-and-paddle top at the user end. The ball is the most-comforted part of the design and is also the part that wears smooth or cracks in old machines.

##### Cold-drawn steel bar `c64.joystick.shaft.steel` _(low)_

Mild or low-alloy steel, cold-drawn to a square section and cut to length. The gate's press fit is what locates the shaft; the steel is unplated except where it passes through the chassis, where corrosion is a genuine failure mode on a machine stored in a damp shed. The steel begins as sintered hematite-magnetite pellets and lump ore charged with coke and limestone, and the bulk of world steel in 1982 was made that way, so rust and pitting on a forty-year-old joystick shaft is this ore still trying to get out.

#### ABS knob and top button `c64.joystick.knob` _(medium)_

The moulded handle on the top of the shaft. On a 2-button unit it is a plain grip knob; on a 3-button unit a fire switch is moulded into the shaft and a third button into the knob's top, sprung against the shaft and actuated by a rod inside it. Black ABS, textured on the grip faces.

##### ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene) `c64.joystick.knob.abs`

The workhorse thermoplastic of consumer electronics housings in 1982: injection mouldable to a hard gloss surface, tough enough for a hand-held knob, and cheap. The same material as the keycaps, and largely the same hydrocarbon feedstock.

###### Pigments and fillers in the ABS knob `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler` _(medium)_

The knob is black because of a pigment - usually a carbon black or an iron oxide - dispersed in the ABS before moulding, and it is stiffened with glass or mineral filler. Where a lighter colour was wanted the whitener was rutile titanium dioxide from ilmenite, which is the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.

###### Pigment dispersion in the ABS `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dispersion` _(medium)_

The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press. A black joystick knob therefore contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package.

###### Titanium dioxide whitener `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dispersion.tio2` _(medium)_

Where a lighter colour was used, the whitener was rutile TiO2 from ilmenite - the same titanium chain as the barium titanate powder.

###### Injection moulding of the knob `c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding` _(medium)_

The knob is a two-shot or single-shot ABS moulding, often with a moulded-in texture or a soft overmould. It has to be comfortable and it has to stay on the shaft for decades.

###### Knob mould tool `c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool` _(medium)_

A hardened steel cavity tool, polished so the knob has a gloss finish. Thousands of knobs per tool life; the polish is the difference between a shiny knob and a matt one.

###### Fire button on shaft and knob `c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button` _(medium)_

On 3-button sticks a fire switch is moulded into the shaft itself and a third button into the knob top, actuated by a rod inside the shaft. Each is a miniature microswitch of the same family as the direction switches.

#### Coiled cable and DE-9 plug `c64.joystick.cable` _(medium)_

A coiled cable of seven or nine conductors leaving the chassis bottom, terminating in a DE-9 male plug that looks mechanically identical to the socket it plugs into but has male pins. The plug's contacts are gold-flashed brass, made the same way and by the same stamping and plating route as the socket contacts on the machine.

##### DE-9 male plug contacts `c64.joystick.cable.plug` _(medium)_

Stamped brass pins, gold-flashed over nickel, moulded into a thermoplastic D-shell that keys to the socket's D-shape. Because the D-shell is polarised, the plug physically cannot be inserted backwards - the same mechanical trick as the moulded keyway on a D-sub generally.

###### Cable assembly and strain relief `c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly` _(medium)_

The conductors are crimped into the DE-9 pins and the cable is clamped by a moulded strain relief at the shell, so bending the cable does not work the pin out of the crimp. Strain relief is the single cheapest thing that decides whether a peripheral cable survives five years of use.

###### Stranded conductor `c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor` _(medium)_

Fine-stranded copper, tinned, for flexibility. Seven or nine of them, depending on the joystick model - the C64 reads five signals plus the common and the fire button.

###### Tinning of the conductor `c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinning` _(medium)_

The stranded conductor is tinned so the crimp barrel grips cleanly and the joint is solderable. Tin from cassiterite, in a peripheral cable a few centimetres from the machine.

  - *Joystick controller* `c64.joystick` *(seen above)*
## Where every branch terminates `c64.bottoms-out` _(low)_

Everything above ends in one of three trunks: refined metals, petrochemicals, and the plants and utilities that supply both. Most component subtrees carry their own shorter copy of the relevant chain - a capacitor really does carry its own aluminium, and an ABS case really does carry its own acrylonitrile - so these are the canonical, deepest versions of the same chains, kept together so that one can be read end to end.

### Metals, ores and industrial minerals `metal` _(medium)_

Every mineral stream behind a 1982 Commodore 64: the quartzite that becomes silicon, the bauxite and cryolite that becomes aluminium foil, the porphyry copper that becomes PCB track and transformer magnet wire, the tin and lead that become 63/37 solder, the iron ore and coke that become the steel chassis and the transformer laminations, and the specialty metals - gold, silver, nickel, tantalum, zinc, chromium, manganese, cobalt, tungsten - that end up plating contacts, filling ceramic capacitors, binding carbide cutters and drawing the filament in a television's gun. The rare earths are here too, as oxides rather than metals, because they arrive as oxides and are only a few hundred tonnes of them. Each branch runs from the finished metal down to the quarry, the open pit, the evaporite bed or the seabed.

#### High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon) `metal.silica`

The refined element every chip in the machine is cut from. A 1982 Commodore 64 mainboard carried a handful of silicon dies and one quartz crystal, both traceable to this chain: quartzite or silica reduced to 96-99% metallurgical silicon, chlorinated to trichlorosilane, distilled to 9-nines, deposited as polysilicon, then pulled as a single Czochralski crystal. Two corrections to what this node previously said. The board's crystal Y1 is 14.31818 MHz, not 2 MHz; the 2 MHz line is a divided output of the clock circuitry, not a separate crystal, and the 6510 runs at about 1.02 MHz. And the 6510 is an HMOS part - silicon gate, depletion load - so its 1982 die does use a polysilicon gate, not aluminium gate metal; the polysilicon branch below is the route the machine's own chips were made by, not merely the wider industry's.

        - *Polysilicon ingot and rod, 9N* `metal.silica.polysilicon` *(seen above)*
##### Czochralski monocrystalline ingot `metal.silica.czochralski`

Where the polysilicon chain ends and the semiconductor business begins. A 2 kg charge is melted at 1414 C in a silica crucible over a seed crystal, and a slow pull at 0.5-2 mm/min with rotation grows a 75-150 mm boule under high-purity argon. Every defect the 6510 die carried - dislocations, oxygen precipitates, the dopant gradient along the length of the ingot - was frozen in during this pull. The ingot is then sawn, lapped and polished into wafers, and the MOS structure is grown and etched on the wafer.

###### Fused quartz growth crucible `metal.silica.czochralski.crucible` _(medium)_

The crucible the melt sits in is made from the same silicon chain one step further down, from high-purity quartz fused in vacuum or wet hydrogen to knock out the alkali that would poison a p-type wafer. It is expensive, fragile, and replaced every few hundred pulls.

###### Thermally grown silicon dioxide (SiO2) `metal.silica.field-oxide` _(medium)_

The gate oxide, the field oxide and the photoresist mask oxide of a 1982 NMOS die are not bought - they are grown out of the silicon itself. A wafer goes into a 1000-1150 C steam or dry-oxygen furnace for an hour and a half and roughly a thousand angstroms of SiO2 comes off the wafer, consuming about 0.1% of its thickness. The machine's entire insulation is therefore chemically the same element as the chip, oxidised in place, and the 6510's gate dielectric is aluminium on oxide rather than a polysilicon gate.

##### 14.31818 MHz quartz clock crystal (Y1) `metal.silica.quartz-crystal` _(medium)_

The C64's timing reference is a 14.31818 MHz quartz crystal, designated Y1 and listed in the service-manual parts lists as part 900558-01 and as 251467-01, both described as 'Crystal 14.31818 MHz'. It feeds the 74LS629 voltage-controlled oscillator, whose output on pin 10 is itself a 14.31818 MHz colour clock, while the dot clock comes out at 8.1818 MHz; the divider and flip-flop chain beyond it produces the 2 MHz and 1 MHz lines and the 6510 runs at about 1.02 MHz. There is no 2.048 MHz crystal in this machine. Quartz is the only material with a usable temperature-stable mechanical resonance that cheap. The C64B changed the arrangement rather than the outcome: its manual section describes a 16 MHz fundamental feeding a clock-generator IC that still delivers the same 8.1818 MHz dot and 14.31818 MHz colour clocks.

###### Grow the clock crystal hydrothermally `metal.silica.quartz-crystal.synthetic` _(medium)_

A seed of vein quartz hangs in aqueous sodium hydroxide in a steel autoclave at 380-450 C and 100-200 bar, and quartz grows on the seed at 1-3 mm a day until a synthetic boule of a few kilograms is complete. The advantage over mined Brazilian rock is that the growth conditions are repeatable, so the Q and the defect density of every boule match. By 1982 synthetic quartz had displaced natural rock for essentially all consumer resonator production, because natural material had to be hand-selected for Q and the supply of good vein quartz was small and variable.

###### Natural vein quartz `metal.quartz` _(medium)_

Vein and pegmatite quartz, of which Brazil's Minas Gerais was the world source for the resonator industry. In 1982 it had two jobs: the seed for hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz, and, in small volume, high-stability resonators for frequency standards where natural material genuinely beat synthetic on Q. A computer clock did not need that. The industrial silica sand and the silicon-grade quartzite elsewhere in this file are processed rocks; this is crystal-grade rock.

#### Sodium compounds: caustic soda and soda ash `metal.sodium`

Sodium is not in the machine as a metal, but the C64 could not exist without it: caustic soda dissolves bauxite to make alumina, and the same chlor-alkali industry that makes the caustic soda also makes the chlorine and hydrogen that become the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Behind both sits a bed of rock salt or a bucket of evaporite from a solar salt pan.

##### Caustic soda (NaOH), 50% solution `metal.caustic-soda` _(medium)_

Two entirely different consumers in this tree. The Bayer process digestion liquor, where a caustic grade tanker holds roughly 300-400 t of 50% solution and a refinery's caustic and steam costs dominate its operating cost. And the chlor-alkali industry, where the same product comes out of the same cell as the chlorine and hydrogen that make the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Cost accounting in aluminium is dominated by caustic and steam; every tonne of caustic lost to red mud is recovered by lime in the causticisation circuit or bought.

###### Chlor-alkali electrolytic cell `metal.chlor-alkali`

2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2. In 1982 almost all of it was a diaphragm cell or a mercury cell. The diaphragm cell - an asbestos-cloth cathode separator - gave low-purity caustic loaded with salt and was steadily displaced through the late 1970s and 1980s by the membrane cell, which delivers 50% NaOH essentially free of salt. Mercury cell caustic went to a short finishing step, causticisation with sodium carbonate, to strip the last mercury; the Hooker Chemical conversion of its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984 is the emblematic date.

###### Chlorine gas (Cl2) `metal.chlorine` _(medium)_

A pale yellow-green gas denser than air, made in the chlor-alkali plant and piped or tanker-shipped to the hydrochloric acid synthesis unit. Around 1982 much of it went to solvent makers and to water treatment as chlorinated organics; only a fraction ever reached a silicon plant, and silicon-grade chlorine must be bone dry, because water plus trichlorosilane gives hydrochloric acid and hexasiloxane gel that plugs the fluidised bed.

###### Electrolysis hydrogen from the chlor-alkali cathode `metal.hydrogen` _(medium)_

The wet hydrogen off the cathode goes to acid synthesis, and in a silicon plant it also goes to the Siemens reactor as the carrier that carries trichlorosilane to the rod and strips the chlorine off. The purification train is a caustic scrubber, then a drying tower, and the carbon monoxide has to be taken below a few ppm or the polysilicon comes out with carbon in it. The same hydrogen, purified a stage further, is what a stainless bright-annealing line uses.

###### The diaphragm cell and the asbestos problem `metal.chlor-alkali.digram-cell`

The 1980s chlor-alkali cell was a rectangular steel box, 2-3 m long, with an anode compartment of brine and a cathode compartment of water separated by an asbestos cloth diaphragm deposited on a wire gauze. The diaphragm was cheap, durable and effective, and it was the reason the world's chlor-alkali industry had a mesothelioma problem. The cell voltage was low, 3.0-3.5 V, and the caustic carried 10-15 g/L of salt because the diaphragm let chloride through. The Hooker Chemical conversion at Niagara Falls in 1984 to a membrane cell was the moment the asbestos diaphragm began to disappear from the industry.

###### Dechlorination and the brine circuit `metal.chlor-alkali.dechlorination` _(medium)_

The brine leaving a cell still has hypochlorite in it, because chlorine dissolves in the caustic. It is treated with sodium sulphite and then acidified, the brine is re-saturated with salt and re-purified on a soda ash and barium carbonate cycle, and it goes back to the cell. So a chlor-alkali plant also consumes sodium carbonate and barium carbonate - the latter being, note, the barium carbonate from the barium branch of this file. The barium carbonate is there to remove the sulphate from the brine as barium sulphate, which is filtered off and, until the 1980s, dumped.

###### Ceramic-grade barium carbonate `metal.barium-carbonate`

A fine white powder, 99%+ BaCO3, and the actual commodity that the barium titanate maker buys. Its iron and sulphur contents are the specification that matters, and both come back from the reduction step. It is also used directly - in the glass frit of the ferrite coat, in the barium ferrite magnet, in the dielectric of the lower-value ceramic capacitor grades, and in the ferrite itself.

###### Calcine the carbonate to a reactive powder `metal.barium-carbonate.calcination` _(medium)_

The barium carbonate that comes out of the carbonation tank is 99.0-99.5% pure but coarse and dense, and barium titanate needs a reactive powder. So the carbonate is calcined at 1000-1200 C to break it down to the oxide and then re-carbonated lightly, or it is ground extremely fine. Either way it is a chemical-material step rather than a smelting one, and it is where a lot of the ceramic-grade versus technical-grade distinction is made.

###### Iron and sulphur in the ceramic grade `metal.barium-carbonate.contamination` _(medium)_

The ceramic-grade barium carbonate specification is essentially a statement about two impurities. Iron, carried through from the barite and from the flue of the reduction kiln, if it survives into barium titanate, acts as an acceptor and shifts the Curie point and the dielectric constant and hurts the loss - so iron has to be below a few hundred ppm. Sulphur, carried from the reduction and not removed by the carbonation, sits at the grain boundary of the fired ceramic and hurts the breakdown voltage. Both of them are the same answer as in the ferrite branch: wash, precipitate, and calcine in a controlled atmosphere. It is a recurring theme in ceramics that the last hundred ppm is the whole specification.

###### Rock salt and solar salt brine `metal.salt-brine` _(medium)_

Two very different-looking things that are the same feedstock. Rock salt is a bed of halite pushed up by evaporation of a restricted sea and then mined; solar salt is the same chemistry done in the sun, in shallow evaporation ponds that turn a square mile of bay into a crystalliser. The chlor-alkali cell does not care which it gets: what matters is a saturated brine with the calcium and magnesium removed, because both precipitate as scale in the diaphragm cell and would otherwise carry oxygen into the chlorine.

###### Halite bed: Wieliczka, Michigan, the saltbelt `metal.salt-rock` _(medium)_

Salt deposited in an evaporating sea and buried later; mined by room-and-pillar, with the salt crushed and screened for the brine saturator. The Wieliczka mine in Poland is the oldest deep salt mine still working, and Polish rock salt was the classic feed for the eastern European chlor-alkali industry.

###### Halite evaporite: the rock `metal.salt-evaporite`

The leaf of the sodium branch: a bedded evaporite sequence of halite with interbedded gypsum and clay, laid down when a restricted sea evaporated. Nothing chemical about it - just a dried-up ocean.

###### Evaporate brine in a solar salt pond `metal.salt-solar-pan` _(medium)_

A series of shallow ponds, from 2 m down to 30 cm, through which seawater is stepped down in salinity, precipitating gypsum first and then halite. A hectare of pond evaporates tens of thousands of tonnes of salt a year. The leaf is a solar pond on a coastal lagoon.

##### Soda ash (Na2CO3) `metal.soda-ash`

Sodium carbonate, the second half of the sodium story. It goes into glass (a huge 1980s user, though the glass agent owns that branch), into detergents, and into the Bayer plant as the carbonate that lime converts back into caustic. The Solvay process, still the dominant route in 1982, makes it from salt, limestone and coke in a solution-and-precipitation tower - no molten salt, no electrolysis.

###### Carbonation tower and the rotary calciner `metal.soda-ash.ammonia` _(medium)_

A 20-30 m steel tower with a conical bottom, fed at the top with ammoniated brine and in the side with CO2 from the lime kilns. Sodium bicarbonate precipitates as a fine white slurry in the upper third and settles into the cone; the temperature is held near 40 C because below that the ammonium chloride in the liquor crystallises out and fouls the tower. Bicarbonate is then calcined at 200-250 C in a rotary kiln to soda ash.

###### Make ammonia from coke in the gasworks `metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source` _(medium)_

In 1982 most ammonia in the soda industry still came from the gasworks: coke plus steam and iron passed over a hot carbonaceous catalyst, then cracked to nitrogen and hydrogen. Natural gas-based steam reforming had largely displaced this in North America and Western Europe, but coke-based ammonia remained standard in India, China and much of Eastern Europe - which is where much of the world's soda ash, and hence much of its glass, was made.

###### The lime kilns that feed the Solvay tower `metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln` _(medium)_

The Solvay process needs carbon dioxide and it gets it by burning limestone in a shaft kiln beside the tower, in the same way a sugar mill burns bagasse. The kiln gas, after the dust is knocked out and the gas is cooled and scrubbed, is about 40-45% carbon dioxide on a dry basis - lower than the 98% a dedicated CO2 plant would produce, but it came free with the lime the process also needed. The Solvay works was therefore a self-contained chemical plant that took limestone and salt and made soda ash, calcium chloride and CO2 in one site.

###### Limestone (CaCO3) quarry `metal.limestone` _(medium)_

High-calcium limestone for the Solvay towers, the blast furnaces, the Bayer plant, the lead sinter and the lime kilns. Quarried by bench mining with a face shovel or a chain dragline, crushed, and graded; a blast furnace wants roughly a third of a tonne of limestone per tonne of hot metal. The same rock is the flux in the copper flash furnace, the causticisation reagent in alumina refining, and the neutraliser at the board fab.

###### Carbonate platform limestone `metal.limestone.bed` _(medium)_

The leaf: a fossiliferous carbonate rock, mostly calcite, laid down on a shallow warm sea floor and now quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face.

###### Limestone quarry and crushing plant `metal.limestone.quarry` _(medium)_

A 5-15 m bench taken out of a 10-40 m face with a face shovel or a chain dragline, drilled and blasted where the rock is competent, then a primary jaw or gyratory crusher to 50-150 mm and a crushing and screening plant that produces three fractions: 0.5-5 cm for the sinter plant, 5-40 mm for the blast furnace and the kilns, and a fines fraction that goes back. A limestone quarry is one of the least complicated mines there is, which is why lime is cheap everywhere and why the Bayer process's caustic and lime costs are the alumina industry's real cost base.

###### Causticise the spent brine to recover the salt `metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery` _(medium)_

The Solvay process does not consume the salt: the ammonium chloride in the spent brine is causticised with lime back to ammonia and sodium chloride, and the brine is re-saturated. The plant therefore closes its salt loop, and its only real consumption is limestone and energy and the ammonia. That closure is the whole reason Solvay was so cheap for a century and why it was so hard to displace until the chlor-alkali-soda ash route had caught up.

#### Lime (CaO) and calcium `metal.lime` _(medium)_

Lime is one of the most-used industrial chemicals there is, and this tree touches it in four places: the Bayer plant uses it to desilicate and to causticise, the blast furnace uses limestone directly as flux, the PCB fabricator regenerates ferric chloride etchant and neutralises with it, and the metallurgical silicon and tin circuits use lime as a flux and a scavenger. Lime is roasted limestone; limestone is quarried rock.

##### Shaft and rotary lime kilns `metal.lime.kiln`

Limestone plus coke or coal in a vertical shaft 20-40 m tall, or on a rotary kiln, at 1000-1100 C. The vertical kiln - a stack of alternating layers of 250 kg limestone and 40 kg coke in a 2.5-4 m shaft, fired from the bottom - makes the good lime, because the counter-current gas gives a soft, well-calcined product; the rotary kiln makes it faster and is what a captive lime plant at a steelworks or a Bayer refinery used. A 300 t/day shaft kiln is a small plant by industrial standards and there were thousands of them.

###### The counter-current shaft kiln `metal.lime.shaft-kiln` _(medium)_

Because limestone goes in at the top at ambient temperature and lime comes out at the bottom at 1000 C, the shaft has to be a heat exchanger as well as a kiln, and that is why a shaft kiln makes a better lime than a rotary one. The gases go up, the stone goes down, and the last of the fuel burns out in the upper third. Below the burn zone the calcination is isothermal, so the lime is not over-heated and does not shrink the kiln's yield.

###### The rotary kiln and the preheater `metal.lime.rotary-kiln` _(medium)_

A 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long rotary kiln, inclined a few degrees, turning 1-3 rpm, heated by a burner at the lower discharge end with coal, coke or gas, and fitted at the upper end with a preheater or a flash dryer for the limestone. The rotary kiln makes worse lime than the shaft kiln - the residence time varies through the bed and the lime is over- and under-burnt - but it makes it faster and it copes with a variable feed, so a captive plant at a steelworks or an alumina refinery used one. A 2000 t/day rotary lime kiln is the sort of thing that sits next to a coke-oven battery.

###### Overburnt lime and the clinker problem `metal.lime.kiln-clinker` _(medium)_

If a lime kiln burns a stone too hot for too long, the lime grains sinter together into hard 'clinker' and the lime is unusable: it slakes too slowly and lumps in the mixer. Overburnt lime is a real fraction of the output of a poor kiln and it has to be screened out or ground. The same failure happens in a captive lime kiln feeding a blast furnace, where the operator is watching the furnace's slag chemistry and the lime plant's temperature curve at the same time. It is a small thing and it is a good illustration that lime is a feed, not a commodity.

###### The lime kiln gas and its CO2 `metal.lime.kiln-gas` _(medium)_

A lime kiln makes carbon dioxide as its main product, roughly 0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, and in 1982 that gas was usually burnt or dumped because there was nowhere to put it. Its two real uses were the Solvay tower, which is built beside its lime kilns, and - much later - the emerging practice of feeding kiln gas to a nearby chemical plant. So the limestone quarry behind a C64's case carries a hidden carbon footprint that did not become an engineering problem until the 1990s.

##### Slaking: quicklime to hydrated lime `metal.lime.slaking`

CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing about 65% more mass and enough heat to boil water. Slaking is done in a pan with a rotating rake, or in a ball mill in the paper industry, and the product is a fine white powder or a milk. It is done at the steelworks, at the water treatment plant and at the board fab's causticisation circuit. The safety point that every plant's training programme is about is that a lump of quicklime dropped into a drum of water will split the drum.

###### Lime in Portland cement `metal.lime.cement`

By far the largest single use of lime in the world, and the reason the business had a global price: about 90% of all lime produced goes into cement, and cement is the second-largest industrial material after steel. The route is the one already in this branch - limestone, kiln, CaO - and then the clinker: 75-80% limestone with 20-25% clay or shale in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, and the resulting clinker ground with 3-5% gypsum. A C64's case was painted, not cemented, but the cement industry is the reason lime is cheap, and it is a legitimate side door out of this branch.

            - *Limestone (CaCO3) quarry* `metal.limestone` *(seen above)*
##### Causticise and desilicate the Bayer liquor `metal.lime.bayer-uses` _(medium)_

Two unrelated jobs in one plant. Lime added during digestion converts reactive silica (kaolinite) into an insoluble calcium silicate, which would otherwise lock up alumina permanently - the single most important reason a high-silica bauxite is unprocessable. Lime also drives the causticisation step, converting the sodium carbonate that accumulates in the Bayer liquor back into caustic, and it helps precipitate iron and titanium as hydroxides. Dosage was order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite digested.

###### Causticise the carbonate back to caustic soda `metal.lime.causticisation` _(medium)_

The Bayer liquor's sodium carbonate is converted back to caustic with lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, and the calcium carbonate drops out as a filter cake that is a by-product of every tonne of alumina. The cycle is the industry's real control loop, because the caustic that leaves in the red mud is replaced by buying new caustic or by buying lime and causticising it, and the choice is mostly about what lime is available near the refinery. It is also why a bauxite refinery is nearly always built next to a limestone quarry.

###### Pre-desilicate the ore by attrition washing `metal.lime.pre-desilication` _(medium)_

By 1982 the more elegant answer to high-silica bauxite had arrived and it needs no lime at all: wash the ore. An attrition scrub and a desliming step take out the kaolinite clay before the ore ever meets the caustic, and a gibbsitic ore washed this way can digest without lime at all. The cost of the process is a lot of water and a lot of clay tailings - and the tailings are the same red mud, just produced earlier and with less soda in it. So the industry moved from a chemistry problem to a solids-handling problem, which is a recurring theme in aluminium refining.

##### Flux the blast furnace slag with limestone and lime `metal.lime.blast-flux` _(medium)_

The furnace needs its slag liquid at 1450 C, and calcium is how you get there: CaO absorbs silica into a calcium silicate slag whose liquidus is around 1300-1400 C, so the slag runs off the tuyeres before the iron does. The burden carries roughly 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal, deliberately paired with a silica content of about 0.4-0.6 mass units of SiO2 per unit of CaO.

##### Regenerate ferric chloride etchant with lime `metal.lime.pcb-etch` _(medium)_

At the board fab the copper etchant is ferric chloride: CuCl2 + FeCl3 -> CuCl + FeCl2, and the ferric is regenerated by blowing air through the spent bath, which is where a great deal of the chlorine chemistry of PCB etching comes from. Lime then raises the pH and drops the copper out as copper hydroxide so the iron can be reclaimed, and lime also neutralises the acid process streams downstream of the etcher. The board's own etch chemistry belongs to the board subsystem; what matters here is that the reagent traces back to a limestone quarry.

##### Lime as a slag flux in tin, lead and silicon smelting `metal.lime.scavenger` _(medium)_

Beyond alumina and iron, lime shows up as a cheap flux wherever a siliceous slag has to stay liquid and the impurity has to be dumped: tin smelting adds lime to pull silica and some tungsten into the slag, the lead sinter and blast furnace charge roughly 15-25% limestone, and calcium compounds are added to the silicon furnace feed to mop up alumina. It is the general-purpose garbage collector of the metals industry.

#### Potassium chloride (KCl) for tantalum reduction `metal.potassium`

Not a C64 component - potassium never appears in the machine - but it is a mandatory reagent in the tantalum branch, because the metal is won as a fluoride salt and reduced with metal, not from an oxide. Potassium also divides tantalum from niobium in the fluoride chemistry. It is included so the tantalum branch reaches a real, mined leaf instead of stopping at an implied reagent.

##### Sylvinite (KCl + NaCl) `metal.sylvinite`

The ore of the Devonian Prairie Evaporite in Saskatchewan, mined underground at 800-1100 m by potash shafts where the ground is artificially frozen so the salt stays put, or by solution mining in Ontario. Run of mine is about 8-14% K2O; it is beneficiated by flotation or hot leaching and sold as muriate of potash.

###### Potash evaporite bed `metal.potash.evaporite`

The leaf: a buried evaporite sea - sylvinite interbedded with halite, carnallite and mudstone, formed by the same evaporation of a restricted sea that made the salt used in chlor-alkali. The Colville and Hatchet lakes area of Saskatchewan sits over one of the largest.

###### Freeze the ground around the potash shaft `metal.sylvinite.freezing`

The Saskatchewan potash ore is 800-1100 m down in a bed that is 30-40 C and gassy, and it is a weak, water-bearing shale-like rock that would flow into the shaft. The solution since 1967 has been to freeze it: brine is circul through freeze pipes in the shaft and the decline for two to three years before sinking, turning the ground into a self-supporting frozen plug of ice and salt. It works, and it is one of the more unusual pieces of mining engineering anywhere - and it is the reason the Saskatchewan potash industry looks the way it does.

###### Potash flotation and hot leaching `metal.sylvinite.beneficiation` _(medium)_

Run-of-mine sylvinite is about 12% K2O with a lot of NaCl and clay. Beneficiation is by flotation of the sylvinite in a saturated KCl-brine solution (because sylvinite is barely soluble while halite is much more so, so the brine selectively wets the sylvinite), or by hot leaching at 85-100 C which dissolves the potassium chloride and leaves the salt. For the tantalum industry the relevant product is not potash at all - it is the KCl that goes into the K2TaF7 precipitation.

###### Muriate of potash and its tailings `metal.potash-product` _(medium)_

The product is 60-95% KCl, bagged or bulk, and the waste is a slurry of NaCl and clay that goes into a tailings pond impoundment. Two points of interest for this tree: the potassium chloride that ends up in a potassium fluoride bath for the tantalum reduction is bought from this industry, and the tailings pond is a genuinely large hole in the ground - the Belle Plaine potash mine near Esterhazy had a tailings pile that became, by the 1980s, a place people went to watch birds. So a fertilizer industry byproduct is where the tantalum industry gets its potassium.

###### Move the potash out by unit train to the port `metal.potash.stockyard` _(medium)_

Saskatchewan potash moved to world markets by unit train - a dedicated train of a hundred or more hopper wagons - to Vancouver, Prince Albert or Minneapolis, and then by ship from Vancouver or by barge and lake freighter to Chicago. So the potassium in a 1982 tantalum capacitor travelled down a potash shaft, through a washer and a flotation plant, into a bulk railcar, onto a ship, and into a plastics extruder. It is the most ordinary logistics chain in the tree and it is the shortest path from a geological process to a metal part.

###### Solution mining of potash `metal.sylvinite.solution-mining` _(medium)_

Where the potash seam is deeply buried and thin - as at Thames, Ontario - the shaft is not worth sinking. Instead two horizontal wells are drilled into the seam, one to inject hot water and one to draw the resulting brine, and the potash is recovered from the brine by evaporation. Two wells can produce a million tonnes a year. It is a solution-mining technique borrowed from the salt industry and it works because sylvinite dissolves in hot water while the clay it sits in does not.

###### The injection and recovery well pair `metal.solution-mining.well` _(medium)_

Solution mining is two wells and a plant. A cemented well is drilled horizontally into the potash seam and a casing is set with a perforated liner; hot water at 80-90 C is injected at a pressure of a few hundred psi, the seam is about 1-3 m thick and dissolves over a 30-200 m horizontal section, and a second well 500 m away draws the brine back. The well field is fracked between the wells to connect the fracture, and the plant evaporates the brine in a multiple-effect evaporator. It is a genuine engineering oddity - a mine with no mine - and it works because potash dissolves in hot brine and clay does not.

##### Potassium chloride as the tantalum flux `metal.potassium.flux` _(medium)_

The only reason potassium is in this tree. Potassium chloride is added to the tantalum fluoride solution to precipitate K2TaF7, and potassium fluoride is used as a flux in some silicon and aluminium processes. Both are bought from the potash industry as a commodity, in tonnes. So a handful of grams of tantalum in a C64's capacitors required a few grams of potassium chloride, which required a shaft in Saskatchewan or a pond on the Dead Sea, which required a bed of evaporite. It is the shortest branch in this file and the funniest, because it starts with an ocean drying up.

#### Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion `metal.aluminum`

Where the C64's aluminium comes from. Bauxite is dug, digested in caustic soda to alumina, and electrolysed in molten cryolite to 99.7% metal - about 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne, the largest single industrial electricity draw anywhere in this tree. The ingot is then DC-cast to a rolling ingot and rolled down to 6-25 um foil for the electrolytic capacitors in the power supply, to sheet for the case and shield cans, and extruded for the heat sinks. Note that the capacitor foil and the plain foil are different jobs for the same rolling mill.

##### Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5% Al2O3 `metal.alumina` _(medium)_

A white, sandy, hygroscopic powder delivered to the smelter in railcars or 1-2 t bags. The contract is brutal: 99.5% Al2O3 minimum, loss on ignition below about 1%, total iron below 0.02%, because every gram of iron that reaches the cell ends up in the metal and the ingot stops being 99.7%. In 1982 this was a global commodity with about a dozen producers - Alcoa, Alcan, Kaiser, Norsk Hydro, Sumitomo, and the Australian and Jamaican national producers. This is the deliberate convergence point for the bauxite and the pot branch: both hang off it.

###### Bauxite (hydrated alumina ore) `metal.bauxite`

A soft, red-brown, pisolitic or clayey laterite, 45-60% Al2O3, still essentially the ore it was before anybody wanted it. Ore below about 180 C of gibbsite digest easily at low temperature and is called low-temperature bauxite; ore with diaspore and boehmite needs 240-280 C and is called high-temperature bauxite, which costs much more in steam. The three great districts in 1982 were Boke and Kindia in Guinea, the Weipa and Gove platforms in northern Australia, and the Clarendon and Saint Ann parishes in Jamaica.

###### Open-cast bauxite mine with dragline `metal.bauxite.mine` _(medium)_

Strip mining on a 10-20 m bench height, with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline stripping 10-50 m of overburden and then a bench of bauxite perhaps only 3-6 m thick. The dragline is the point: it digs the bauxite, swings and dumps it onto a ramp, and strips the next strip of cover, all in one machine. Loading is by conveyor, almost never by truck. The Weipa and Gove operations were built this way.

###### Lateritic bauxite profile `metal.bauxite.laterite` _(medium)_

The leaf: a 3-12 m pisolitic blanket of iron-stained bauxite nodules sitting on a Cretaceous or Tertiary lateritic surface above a kaolinitic clay. Guinea's deposits are the classic tropical pisolite; the Australian Weipa and Gove ores are flat-lying terrace deposits on Cretaceous sediments. Either way the rock outcrops at the surface and is dug, not tunnelled.

###### The kaolinite and gibbsite beneath the bauxite `metal.bauxite.kaolinite`

The leaf of the aluminium branch, and the reason the alumina process exists in the form it does. The economic bauxite is a 3-12 m blanket of iron-stained nodules sitting directly on kaolinite clay, and the kaolinite is the reactive silica that has to be neutralised by lime or washed out. Below that is the saprolite, the partly-weathered parent rock. So the aluminium in a C64 case began as an oxide that precipitated in a tropical weathering profile above a clay, on top of Cretaceous or Tertiary sediment, and the silica problem is a mineralogical fact about the same profile rather than an impurity someone failed to remove.

###### Wash the bauxite in a creek sluice `metal.bauxite.creek-wash` _(medium)_

The last leaf of the aluminium branch. In the Weipa and Gove deposits on the Cretaceous laterite surface, bauxite is dug in the wet season and the clay is washed out of it in a creek: a 200 m long, 30 m wide sluice excavated along the edge of the terrace, into which the bauxite is tipped and a stream of water is run, and the light clay washes away over a long distance while the pisolitic bauxite nodules, 5-50 mm and iron-stained, stay behind and are recovered by hand or by a mechanical rake. It is a 1980s technology on a Cretaceous rock surface in tropical Queensland, and it is the reason those deposits look the way they do.

###### The Cretaceous laterite surface `metal.laterite-terrace` _(medium)_

The leaf, geologically: a flat, deeply weathered surface on Cretaceous sandstone where a tropical lateritic profile has developed over tens of millions of years, with a bauxite horizon at the top, kaolinite below it, and the saprolite and fresh rock beneath. The flatness is the point - it is why the pits are cheap and the ore is shallow - and it is a direct consequence of the rock type and of the extraordinarily long, warm, wet chemical weathering that made it.

###### Bauxite crushing, washing and drying `metal.bauxite.beneficiation` _(medium)_

The Bayer plant does not want a 300 mm boulder and it certainly does not want the clay. The run-of-mine ore is crushed in a gyratory or a jaw crusher to 25-50 mm, and then - in the wet-grinding route that became standard for high-temperature bauxite - it is ground in a ball mill in a rod or a wet scrubber to a slurry, and that slurry is screened and washed to remove the clay, which is called 'desilication by attrition washing'. The under-0.5 mm clay is discarded as tailings, and it is often 15-30% of the mass. What goes into the digestor is a 40-50% solids slurry of 25-50 mm lumps with the reactive silica taken out, and the moisture matters because every kilo of water into the autoclave is a kilo of steam wasted.

###### Bayer process `metal.bayer`

A 110-year-old caustic-leach purification that every tonne of aluminium still goes through. Five steps: crush and wash, digest in caustic at pressure, clarify and throw away the red mud, cool and precipitate pure aluminium hydroxide, calcine to alumina. It works because the alumina in bauxite is amphoteric - it dissolves in hot caustic as sodium aluminate - while the iron and titanium oxides are not, and silica is neutralised by lime into a harmless calcium silicate.

###### Caustic digestion in autoclaves `metal.bayer.digestion` _(medium)_

Bauxite slurry and 150-300 g/L free caustic (as Na2O) are charged into stirred autoclaves and held at temperature for 30-90 minutes. The alumina dissolves as NaAl(OH)4; the iron oxide stays as a red slurry. Older low-temperature plants used a bank of horizontal autoclaves with indirect steam heating; high-temperature plants used vertical autoclaves. The pressure was only 5-15 bar because the vessel was not a modern high-pressure autoclave but a horizontal drum with a vapour space.

###### Reactive silica and the lime reaction `metal.bayer.desilication` _(medium)_

The killer impurity in bauxite is reactive silica - kaolinite clay and opal - which dissolves in the caustic and then reacts with aluminate to form a non-redissolving kaolinite-nepheline hydrate that permanently traps alumina. Two defences. In low-temperature digestion the clay is left undissolved by keeping the caustic concentration high. In high-temperature digestion the reactive silica dissolves, so lime is added and the silica is converted to hydrogrossite; the liquor is then given a short holding period during which the silica precipitates harmlessly. Every tonne of bauxite eats some caustic and some tens of kilos of lime that never come back.

###### Clarify the liquor and dam the red mud `metal.bayer.clarification`

The digested slurry is diluted with process water, cooled, and settled in a bank of gravity settlers with mechanical rakes; the red mud bottoms out and is pumped to the mud dam. A large plant produces 100-150 tonnes of red mud per tonne of alumina, which is why every alumina refinery has a mud dam engineered like a tailings facility.

###### Red mud (bauxite residue) `metal.red-mud`

A caustic, red, kaolin-rich sludge, typically 2.5-6 mol/L free NaOH, containing essentially all the iron, titanium and silica from the ore. A large refinery produces 100-150 tonnes of it per tonne of alumina. In 1982 the industry standard for handling it was to build a dam and pump it in; the search for a use was real academic work with no commercial outcome. Successful commercial red-mud use at scale did not arrive until the 2000s and later, so nothing in a 1982 C64 contains it.

###### Precipitate aluminium hydroxide from the cooled liquor `metal.bayer.precipitation`

The clear caustic aluminate solution is cooled from 100-110 C to 60-80 C and seeded with a few grams per litre of finely ground aluminium hydroxide already in the plant. The seed grows into the supersaturated solution as a hexagonal-plate alumina trihydrate over 24-48 hours, and the mud is filtered and washed. Washing matters twice over: to remove the caustic that would otherwise attack the kiln, and to recover the soda. The mother liquor goes back to digestion, and this recycle loop is what makes the caustic consumption manageable at all.

###### Rotary vacuum filtration and counter-current washing `metal.bayer.filter` _(medium)_

The hydrate is filtered on a rotating vacuum drum with cloth- or paper-covered segments, then washed on a multi-stage counter-current filter. By the time the wash water reaches the pregnant liquor the caustic is essentially recovered, so the caustic circuit closes to better than 95%. This single piece of equipment is why alumina refining has the caustic efficiency it does.

###### Calcine the trihydrate to smelter-grade alumina `metal.bayer.calcination`

The hydrate goes into a rotary kiln or, more often by 1982, a fluidised-bed calciner, and at 1000-1100 C it gives off its water of crystallisation and recrystallises from gamma through theta to alpha alumina. Alpha alumina is the hard, insoluble, spark-resistant form that will dissolve in cryolite. The rotary kiln burns 400-600 kg of fuel oil or gas equivalent per tonne of alumina and emits a lot of carbon dioxide; the fluidised bed is more efficient and was being adopted through the 1980s.

###### Fluidised-bed calciner `metal.bayer.calciner`

Hot gas from a multi-flash evaporator is blown through a bed of alumina hydrate on a distributor of alloy nozzles, holding the bed fluid at 1000-1100 C by balancing gas throughput against feed rate. The bed fluidises like a boiling liquid and every grain sees the same temperature, which is exactly why the alpha alumina comes out with a tight particle-size distribution. The 1980s smelter-grade alumina market effectively standardised on this machine.

##### Primary aluminium ingot, 99.7% `metal.aluminum.ingot`

The metal itself, and the deliberate convergence point of the electrolysis branch and the rolling branch. Tapped from the pot every 24-48 hours, brought up to about 720 C, filtered to remove the entrained alumina and metal droplets, alloyed if the customer wants it, and cast. In 1982 the standard product was the 20-25 kg P1020 ingot, or the 500 kg or 1.5 t minimum-content ingot that newer smelters preferred, 99.70% minimum aluminium with iron and silicon the main impurities. Rolling ingots for the foil mills were a different shape entirely - see the foil branch.

###### Hall-Heroult electrolysis of alumina in cryolite `metal.hall-heroult`

The cell is a steel shell the size of a bathtub lined with carbon, containing 300-500 t of molten cryolite at 950-970 C. Alumina dissolves in the melt and is reduced at a carbon cathode; current passes through the anodes, where the oxygen from the alumina burns the carbon away and makes carbon dioxide. The metal pools on the floor and is tapped every day or two. A pot takes 3-6 V at 100-200 kA, which is why a 200,000 t/year smelter is also a 2-3 GW power station.

###### Cryolite (Na3AlF6), the electrolyte solvent `metal.cryolite`

The white, insoluble, water-repellent mineral that makes aluminium electrolysis possible at all. Pure alumina melts at 2072 C; a bath of cryolite with excess aluminium fluoride and some calcium fluoride is liquid at 950-970 C, and the alumina dissolves in it at 6-10%. The other crucial property is that cryolite is not consumed stoichiometrically - it is a solvent - and only the fluorine lost as HF and in the fume has to be replaced. Correcting the brief: consumption was roughly 0.5-1.0 t of cryolite per tonne of aluminium in 1980s practice (theoretical about 0.5 t, higher in practice because of fluoride loss), not 'four tonnes of aluminium per tonne of cryolite'.

###### Synthetic cryolite from hydrofluoric acid `metal.cryolite.synthesis`

Because natural cryolite was one mine in Greenland, the industry made its own. Sodium carbonate or caustic soda reacts with hydrofluoric acid and aluminium hydroxide at 60-90 C: 6HF + 3Na2CO3 + Al(OH)3 -> 2Na3AlF6 + 3CO2 + 3H2O. So the electrolyte solvent of the aluminium pot is manufactured from fluorspar, caustic soda and alumina - three of this file's other endpoints in one reaction.

###### Aluminium fluoride and the bath `metal.aluminium-fluoride` _(medium)_

The excess AlF3 in the bath is not a deliberate additive so much as the consequence of the water and the fluorides in the alumina; smelters add it back to hold the bath at the composition that gives the best current efficiency, which is somewhere between 8 and 14% excess AlF3. Too little and the bath's freezing point rises and the pot freezes; too much and the current efficiency falls and the crust gets hard. Getting this balance right is the potline operator's entire job, and it is checked by sampling the frozen bath and analysing it in a laboratory.

###### Carbon pot lining and the cathodic block `metal.hall-heroult.pot-lining`

The steel shell is lined first with refractory brick, then with a monolithic carbon lining about 400-600 mm thick made of calcined coke, graphite and hot pitch, rammed in place. A block lining of graphitised carbon blocks is better and was common in newer cells. The lining is deliberately cathodic: the aluminium that seeps into the pores becomes a cathode of itself, and when the cell is finally relined after 3-8 years the spent lining is leached for the metal it swallowed.

###### Alumina dredges and the alumina crust `metal.hall-heroult.alumina-dredge` _(medium)_

Alumina fed into the pot floats and solidifies into a chilled crust on the bath surface, which is far more stable than loose powder. Machines called dredges or skimmers break holes in this crust and feed alumina down them at a controlled rate; the classic 1980 design was the dual-feed with pneumatic runners. The holes are also where carbon dust from the anode is skimmed off. A floating crust is good for the pot but insulates the bath, so the balance between a thick stable crust and a cool cell is the operator's whole job.

###### Aluminium dross and the skimmings `metal.hall-heroult.dross` _(medium)_

Two or three tonnes of dross and sludge per pot per year: oxide, carbon, and aluminium that never reached the cathode. Because aluminium dross burns spectacularly it must be handled under cover, and the smelter had a dross furnace to burn out the aluminium and get it back. The recovered metal is dirty and low grade, and in 1982 it went straight back into the pot - a small but real recycling loop, since remelted aluminium needs only about 5% of the energy of primary metal.

        - *Aluminium foil, 6-25 um, for capacitors* `metal.aluminum.foil` *(seen above)*
##### Aluminium sheet: the case and the shields `metal.aluminum.sheet` _(medium)_

Two uses in a C64: the heat-sink and shield material, and the case itself. The Commodore breadbin case is an aluminium extrusion with a stove-enamel finish, and the internal shields and the modulator compartment are plain sheet. Cold-rolled 1050A or 3003 sheet at 0.3-1.5 mm goes into drawing and stamping; the anodising or powder coating is the plastics-and-paint agent's business, but the substrate starts here. Also the convergence point for the die-casting branch: a 1982 C64 has several kilograms of aluminium foundry alloy in its key plungers and the joystick and case-bracket castings.

###### Alloying to 3003, 6063 or A13 `metal.aluminum.blending` _(medium)_

The rolling mill is not a refinery. It melts primary ingot, remelted can scrap and dross recovery in a reverberatory or an induction furnace, adds the alloying elements as lumps of master alloy, degasses with a rotating argon lance to strip hydrogen, and skims the dross. Manganese for 3003, magnesium and silicon for 6063, silicon for the A13 casting alloy. So the C64's case metal is partly recycled metal, and its chemistry is set in a small furnace rather than a pot.

##### Aluminium extrusion: the case and the heat sinks `metal.aluminum.extrusion`

A hot billet is forced through a steel die by a ram at 420-500 C, at 20-100 MN of pressure, at several metres a second, and the profile that comes out is straight and, if the die is good, dimensionally within a fraction of a millimetre. The Commodore case is a complicated extrusion: the cooling fins, the rail and the case walls are all one profile, and the visible finish is a consequence of the die geometry. The rectifier and regulator heat sinks are separate small extrusions or machined blocks.

###### Hydraulic extrusion press, 500-2500 t `metal.aluminum.extrusion.press` _(medium)_

The industry standard was the 2300-2500 t class press with a 200-500 mm container, driven by a hydraulic intensifier that gave a hard step change in speed at the start of the stroke. A heated soak furnace beside the press holds the billets, a shear cuts them to length, and the runout bench stretches the profile while it is still hot. A C64 case would have been pressed at a Taiwanese or Hong Kong extrusion shop on a machine of exactly this size.

###### The soak furnace and the billet's temperature history `metal.aluminum.soak-furnace` _(medium)_

Billet quality is set before the press ever sees it. The billets are heated in a gas- or oil-fired pit furnace to 420-500 C and held for 3-24 hours so that the temperature is uniform through the section, because a billet with a hot core and a cold skin extrudes with a surface tear and a soft interior. The furnace is a 3-5 m long box with a hot zone and a transition zone, and the entire extrusion industry's reputation for inconsistent profiles is mostly the reputation of its furnaces. A C64's case extrusion depended on the profile being within a fraction of a millimetre, because it had to fit a plastic moulding and a painted finish.

###### Steel extrusion die and its forging `metal.aluminum.extrusion.die` _(medium)_

The die is a disc of hot-work tool steel with a cavity machined into it, and it has to be made before it can be used: drilled, rough-machined, heat-treated, then finish-machined and nitrided. A case profile takes a lot of steel and a lot of hours, which is why the extrusion industry is full of small specialist shops rather than a few giants. The same die steel family, SKD61 and H13, is the tooling steel of the plastics agent's injection-moulding branch.

#### Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts `metal.copper`

The most-used metal after iron, and in a C64 it is everywhere the electricity goes and everywhere the heat has to leave. The PCB tracks are 35 um copper foil on 1.6 mm FR-4; the switch-mode transformer is wound with 0.2-0.4 mm enamelled magnet wire; the rectifiers and the regulator leadframes are copper; the edge connector fingers and the heatsink mounts are copper alloy. All of it starts as porphyry ore at 0.4-1% Cu, which is why copper smelters are, in the 1980s, as much sulfuric acid plants as they are metal plants.

##### Porphyry copper ore (0.4-1% Cu) `metal.copper.ore`

A porphyritic intrusion - a granite-textured quartz monzonite that has been split by its own crystallisation and had its cracks filled with hot copper-bearing fluids. The copper minerals are chalcopyrite CuFeS2, bornite and chalcocite Cu2S, covellite and enargite Cu3AsS4. The ore body is graded by porphyry systems but the grade is low and getting lower, which is the whole problem with the industry. In 1982 the great producers were Chuquicamata and El Teniente in Chile, Bingham Canyon in Utah, Butte, the Arizona porphyry belt, Oyu Tolgoi and the Escondida development, and the copper belt of northern Zambia.

###### Open-pit copper mine `metal.copper.mine`

An enormous terraced pit. Ore is drilled and blasted on 15 m benches, loaded into haul trucks by 3-6 cubic metre shovels or loaded onto a conveyor, and hauled in 100-150 tonne trucks out of the pit on ramps. The waste:ore ratio at a mature porphyry pit is often 2-5:1, which is why the waste dumps are larger than the pit. As the pit deepens into the ore, block caving takes over: a fracture zone is undercut and the ore caves into a series of drawpoints, and the mining cost per tonne collapses - El Teniente in Chile was the world's largest block-cave operation from 1958 onwards.

###### Block cave drawpoints and ore pass `metal.copper.block-cave` _(medium)_

The block cave is the deepest and most sophisticated piece of 1980s mining engineering anywhere near a C64: a slot is cut along the base of the ore block, the slot is blasted, the overlying ore fractures and subsides into the void, and a finger stoper trains stop releasing ore once the cave front has moved past a drawpoint, to stop surface subsidence from outrunning the cave. Ore falls 100-1000 m to a conveyor at the bottom. Throughput per drawpoint is low - a few hundred tonnes a day - so a big block cave has hundreds of them.

###### Tertiary porphyry intrusion `metal.copper.intrusion`

The leaf: a granodiorite or quartz monzonite stock, once liquid and now frozen, with the copper-bearing sulphide veins filling fractures and disseminated grains through it. Under a 100 m of leached, iron-stained capping lies the transition ore and then the primary sulphides, so the pit's first 50-150 m of material is nearly worthless and has to be hauled anyway.

###### The haul road, the ramp and the truck cycle `metal.copper.haulage` _(medium)_

The economics of an open pit are a haulage problem. A 130-tonne truck on a 2 km round trip from the loading point to the crusher, at about 25 km/h loaded and 40 km/h empty, takes 3-5 minutes per cycle including spotting and loading, so a shovel with a 4-second loading cycle needs about 6-8 trucks to keep it fed. The ramp grade matters enormously - every 1% of extra grade costs roughly 1-2% of the truck's payload - and so does where the crusher is put. A large porphyry pit moves 100,000-400,000 tonnes a day, and the fleet is 100-400 trucks.

###### Suppress the pit dust on the haul road `metal.copper.dust-suppression` _(medium)_

A 100,000 t/day pit with unsuppressed haul roads produces a very large tonnage of airborne dust, and by the 1970s that had become a legal problem: the Clean Air Act of 1970 and the 1974 federal mine-safety inspection regime both applied to metal mines, and the pit had to water its roads, restrict the speed on unpaved haulage, and in the worst cases stop blasting in a high wind. So the environment is a genuine node in the middle of the ore chain, not a decoration at the end of it, and it is the same regulation that produced the sinter-plant dust precipitator in the steel branch.

###### Crushing and grinding to 100-150 um `metal.copper.grinding`

The ore arrives at 1 m. It goes through a gyratory crusher, then a semiautogenous mill (which uses the ore itself as the grinding medium, so no steel balls to pay for at that stage), then one or two ball mills in a closed circuit with a spiral classifier and then a cyclone. Autogenous grinding came in during the 1970s and was fully established by 1982 because it both saved the grinding media cost and produced a much cleaner surface - less steel contamination matters when you are about to float it. Before the mill a 1500-4000 t/h gyratory with a screen at 25-50 mm does the primary crushing, and a 100 g charge goes to the fire assay for total copper while a leach assay of the fines gives the recoverable copper - the difference between the two, the oxide and the locked-up copper, is the number that becomes the contract between the mine and the mill. The grind has to be fine enough to liberate chalcopyrite but not so fine that the froth washes out.

###### Forged steel grinding balls `metal.copper.steel-grinding-media` _(medium)_

Even in an autogenous circuit the ball mills need some steel, and the balls themselves are a ferroalloy product: rail steel or scrap forged and quenched. Hardness matters more than anything - a 1982 ball mill ran 100-150 mm balls in the harder grind, and the wear rate was the plant's second-biggest cost after power. Nickel and chromium in the steel were deliberately kept low here, unlike in a crusher liner.

###### Froth flotation of chalcopyrite `metal.copper.flotation`

The slurry is conditioned with lime to a pH of 8-9.5 and with a xanthate collector, then aerated in a bank of 20-50 cubic metre rectangular cells. Air bubbles pick up the particles of chalcopyrite that the collector has made water-repellent and float them into a froth; the gangue stays in the water. Each cell in a bank is stage-controlled, with a froth of 100-300 mm. In 1982 the workhorse collector was sodium or potassium ethyl xanthate, made from carbon disulphide, caustic soda and ethanol, and the frother was pine oil or a synthetic such as methyl isobutyl carbinol.

###### Ethyl xanthate collector (SIPC) `metal.xanthate` _(medium)_

Xanthate is the workhorse flotation reagent, and it is a petrochemical in disguise: carbon disulphide (from natural gas or from coke-oven gas and methane) reacts with ethanol and caustic soda. Potassium and sodium ethyl xanthates were the standard 1980s collectors for sulphide copper, with a frother on top. So the flotation chemistry that recovers copper in 1982 depends on a sulphur-and-alcohol chain that ends in a gasworks, not a mine.

###### Carbon disulphide (CS2) `metal.cs2-synthesis` _(medium)_

Carbon disulphide, the feedstock for every xanthate collector and for the rayon and cellophane industries, was made in 1982 almost entirely from natural gas or from methane recovered from coke-oven gas: the gas and a fraction of hydrocarbon oil are passed over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C, and the carbon disulphide is condensed out. So the flotation collector that separated copper from a porphyry in Nevada was made from gas, and the same molecule went into the rayon that was in the 1980s' idea of a flame-retardant textile. It is a leaf of the copper branch that is unambiguously a chemical plant rather than a mine.

###### Lime and soda ash as pH regulators `metal.caustic-lime-flotation` _(medium)_

Flotation needs the ore surfaces clean of slime and the water at a controlled alkaline pH, or the xanthate decomposes to xanthic acid and carbon disulphide and evaporates. Lime from a limestone kiln is the cheapest and most common regulator; soda ash where lime is unavailable; and in the deep concentrators of Chile and Arizona the process water has to be lime-treated hard before use because the Andean water is very soft and very acid.

###### Pine oil and MIBC frothers `metal.pine-oil-frother` _(medium)_

Frothers are oily surfactants that stabilise the air-water interface. Until the 1970s the standard was pine oil distilled from pine stumps and mill residues - a forestry residue, not a mineral. Pine oil was being displaced by methyl isobutyl carbinol, a petrochemical, precisely because the natural supply was limited and the synthetic one gave a more stable froth.

##### Copper flotation concentrate (~25-30% Cu) `metal.copper.concentrate`

A damp, fine, almost black powder shipped by rail or truck to the smelter. What the smelter really wants is not the copper but the sulphur, because that is what makes the smelter a sulfuric acid plant. A 25% Cu concentrate is roughly 50% sulphur and 10% iron, and the smelter's job is to burn out the iron, keep a copper-iron matte, and send every tonne of SO2 to an acid plant.

###### Thicken, filter and ship the flotation concentrate `metal.copper.concentrate-handling` _(medium)_

The flotation concentrate at 25-30% Cu arrives as a pulp at 10-20% solids and has to be dewatered to 8-12% moisture to be shipped, because shipping water is shipping money. A 30,000 t/day concentrator produces 1,000-3,000 t of concentrate a day, and it is thickened in a 30-50 m diameter tank, filtered on a vacuum belt or a plate-and-frame press, and often dried to 8% on a steam belt dryer so it does not cake in a railcar. Copper concentrate that arrives wet is worth less per tonne and smelters charge for the water.

##### Flash smelting of concentrate to copper matte `metal.copper.smelting`

Concentrate, silica flux and limestone are dropped into a vertical reverberatory shaft where a hot gas blast, 40-60% oxygen-enriched, burns the concentrate as it falls. Three reactions happen simultaneously: the sulphides oxidise to copper oxide and iron oxide, the oxides react with each other to form a copper-iron matte, and the iron oxide reacts with the silica flux to make a slag. The furnace runs at 1250-1400 C and the products settle into three layers - matte at the bottom, slag above it, and offgas above that - which are tapped separately. By 1982 the flash furnace had largely displaced the reverberatory furnace: it is smaller, faster and needs less fuel, and it works on concentrate straight from the flotation circuit with only a small amount of dried concentrate added as fuel.

###### Silica flux from a sand quarry `metal.silica-flux` _(medium)_

The smelter adds sand or quartzite so that the iron in the concentrate can be thrown off as a slag instead of entering the matte. The quartz is often a cheap nearby dune sand - which is exactly the same material the glass industry buys, and the reason a copper smelter in the 1980s had a sand dryer and a small silica prep plant. The flux is dosed so the slag's silica content matches what the concentrate brings.

###### Industrial silica sand (quartz dune sand) `metal.silica-sand`

Siliceous sand from a dune or a beach, washed, screened and often magnetically separated to take out the heavy mineral concentrates that would be a nuisance. This is a distinct node from the silicon-grade quartzite: the purity required here is far lower, and this sand is a commodity that the foundry, the glass and the copper industries all pull on. The quartzite that goes into the silicon furnace is a different, much rarer rock.

###### Aeolian dune sand and beach placer `metal.silica-sand.dune`

The leaf: quartz grains rounded by wind or wave, in an unconsolidated surface deposit a few metres to tens of metres thick sitting on older sediment. Dunes along the Mississippi valley, the Great Lakes shorelines and the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States were the standard sources, mined with bucket-wheel or dragline dredges - a sand mine is the commonest kind of open pit in the world.

###### Sulphuric acid, 93-99%, from smelter SO2 `metal.sulphuric-acid`

The most-produced inorganic chemical in the world, and about half to three fifths of it was made not from burning sulphur but from the offgas of the copper, zinc and lead smelters in this file. The plants are the same: gas cleaning, drying, 10-14% SO2, 400-450 C over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, absorption in 98-99% acid in the first absorber, and then a second absorber with fresher acid - the double contact, double absorption process that was the industry standard by 1982. This node is the deliberate convergence point: the copper flash furnace, the zinc sinter plant, the lead sinter plant, the copper tankhouse and the zinc leach all feed or draw from the same acid plant.

###### Where the smelter acid goes `metal.sulphuric-acid.uses`

Roughly half of world sulfuric acid production is made from smelter offgas. In 1982 the biggest single use was fertiliser: phosphoric acid from Florida apatite, then superphosphate. The second was metal refining - the copper tankhouse electrolyte, the zinc plant leach circuit and the iron and steel pickling line, all of which are in this tree. The third was hydrofluoric acid. So a great deal of the world's phosphate rock was fertilised with acid made from the sulphur in somebody else's copper ore.

###### Apatite ore for phosphoric acid `metal.phosphate-ore`

The Florida pebble phosphate - a marine sedimentary phosphorite of fossil bones and excreta - is the classic source, and it is the end consumer of most of the sulfuric acid made in the copper and zinc branches of this file. It is mined by dragline or bucket-wheel stripping of 5-15 m of overburden over a 3-6 m ore layer, then crushed and slurry-piped to a beneficiation plant. Almost no phosphate rock in 1982 came from a chemical process: the whole fertiliser industry downstream of the copper and zinc smelters is a sedimentary rock mined out of a swampy coastal plain.

###### Marine phosphorite bed `metal.phosphate.rock`

The leaf: a 1-10 m bed of unconsolidated, often glauconitic phosphatic sand and clay in a marine or coastal plain sequence, sitting directly on limestone. It is dug, washed in a slurry pipeline, and floated or gravity-separated.

###### The flash furnace, its tuyeres and the concentrate burn `metal.copper.flash-furnace`

The furnace is a 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter vertical shaft with a refractory lining, fed by a few hundred tonnes an hour of dried concentrate through a hopper, and blown at the bottom by 30-60% oxygen-enriched air through tuyeres. The concentrate burns as it falls - it is the fuel as well as the charge - so the furnace needs almost no external heat. The reaction happens in the first metre above the tuyeres, the particles are spent, and the matte and slag settle into the two-deep bath at the bottom. The shaft above is used to preheat the charge with the rising offgas, and a flash furnace treats more tonnage in less volume than anything else in smelting.

##### Peirce-Smith converter to blister copper `metal.copper.converting`

The matte from the flash furnace is charged into a horizontal cylindrical steel converter with refractory lining and is blown with air through tuyeres along the side. The iron in the matte oxidises preferentially and goes into a slag that is skimmed off the top every few hours; once the iron is gone the copper sulphide itself oxidises to copper metal and gives off SO2. The blow takes 4-8 hours and takes 1 t of 60% matte to roughly 0.85 t of blister copper at 98-99% purity, still containing iron, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. The converter is a batch process and by the 1980s it was the target of the new continuous technologies (Noranda, Inductokemco) that were not yet commercial.

###### Fire-refine the blister copper `metal.copper.fire-refining` _(medium)_

Blister copper still carries arsenic, antimony and bismuth, and every one of them is a nightmare for the electrolytic tankhouse because they float to the cathode and destroy the deposit. So the blister is ladle-refined: an oxidising slag of sodium carbonate with the impurities skims off, and then the copper is under-oxidised by dropping in green charcoal to reduce the whole mass back to copper, with the arsenic floatationised out. Where the arsenic is high, the refinery buys a second, smaller furnace.

###### The Peirce-Smith converter and its tuyeres `metal.copper.converter` _(medium)_

The converter is a cylindrical steel shell, 3.5-4.8 m inside diameter and 8-10 m long, on trunnions so it can be tilted, lined with magnesite brick, with 20-40 tuyeres along one side at the trunnion line. Air at 30-50% oxygen is blown in at 5-10 bar through water-cooled tuyeres that must be cleared and re-cleared by hand every few hours as the lining erodes - and a tuyeres that is not cleared becomes a plug and the whole heat is lost. The operator tilts the converter so the slag runs out of the mouth, then charges back, and there is no continuous process anywhere else in smelting with quite that much manual involvement. It is the machine that has been unchanged since 1865, and it is still the standard.

##### Blister copper anode, 99.9%+ `metal.copper.anode`

Blister is poured into a horizontal straight-mould casting machine - a ladle of molten copper that pours into a row of cast-iron moulds on a moving chain, giving a rectangular anode of 200-500 kg, roughly 700-1000 mm long, 400-800 mm wide and 30-50 mm thick, with a hanging loop cast on top. In 1982 the standard anode assay was 99.5-99.9% copper, and the gold and silver in it - typically 5-30 g/t gold equivalent - is why anodes are not made to 99.99%: that would be throwing away money.

##### Electrolytic refining of copper to 99.99% `metal.copper.tankhouse`

The refinery's tankhouse is a building a couple of hundred metres long containing rows of concrete or rubber-lined steel cells. Each cell holds a 150-250 g/L copper, 200-250 g/L free sulfuric acid solution at 55-65 C, with one or two anodes and one cathode per cell. Current at 20,000-40,000 A per cell is passed through; copper dissolves off the anode and plates onto the cathode at 98-99% efficiency, and gold, silver, selenium, tellurium and the platinum group fall out as a sludge on the bottom of the cell - the anode slime - which is worth more per tonne than the copper. A refinery producing 100,000 t a year has 300-500 cells and about 100,000 MWh of DC power.

###### Electrolytic copper cathode, 99.99% `metal.copper.cathode`

The end product of the mine-to-metal chain and the shape in which essentially all world copper trades. A flat plate grown on a stainless steel or copper starter sheet, with a characteristic slightly rough surface because too many nucleation sites make a soft, dull deposit. Cathode mass is 45-125 kg depending on the refinery. Weighed, sampled, stamped and shipped. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tankhouse branch, the foil branch and the wire branch.

###### Anode slime: the real reason to smelt copper `metal.anode-slime`

The sludge on the tankhouse cell floor, 5-20 kg per tonne of copper refined, containing gold, silver, platinum, palladium, selenium and tellurium. It is dried and shipped to precious-metals refineries, where the gold is separated by cupellation, the selenium by roasting to SeO2 and volatilising, and the platinum group metals by solvent extraction and precipitation. By 1982 the anode slime was typically worth more per tonne than the copper in the anode, and a copper mine with good gold credits could be a gold mine that happened to have copper in it. This is a deliberate convergence node: the copper, gold and silver branches all meet in it.

###### Platinum-group metals from the anode slime `metal.palladium` _(medium)_

The anode slime also carries platinum, palladium, ruthenium, iridium, rhodium and osmium, at grams per tonne of copper rather than kilograms, so the volumes are tiny and the values are astronomical. In 1982 most of the world's refined palladium came from the nickel-copper ores of the Sudbury and Norilsk basins and from the Bushveld's platinum mines rather than from the copper anode slimes, but the slimes were a real secondary source for platinum and rhodium. The refining route is a solvent extraction and precipitation circuit followed by a final electrolytic or thermal refining, and by 1982 the platinum-group market was dominated by South Africa and the Soviet Union, whose platinum was the ore of choice for autocatalyst converters in the 1970s - which is a genuine and slightly absurd piece of industrial history, since the autocatalyst is a device for cleaning up the exhaust of a car and the platinum came out of the same layered intrusion as the chrome in the ignition plugs.

###### Cupellation of the gold-silver dross `metal.anode-slime.cupellation`

The slime is smelted with lead and flux into a litharge, then the litharge is blown with air in a cupellation furnace. The lead and everything else oxidises and is absorbed by a bone-ash or magnesite cupel, and what is left on the cupel is gold and silver together. This is the oldest refinery process in the book and it was still standard in 1982, because it is simple and it works.

###### Bone ash cupel from animal bone `metal.cupellation.cupel` _(medium)_
