Traditional cupels are made of calcined bone - tricalcium phosphate - ground and pressed into a shallow cup with a porous, low-density surface that absorbs the molten litharge. Bone ash is the reason cupellation is called what it is, and by the 1982 industry the major refineries had largely moved to magnesia and alumina cupels for the big furnaces, though bone ash was still in use. So a refinery furnace foot was, historically, a rendering-house product.

###### Selenium and tellurium from the anode slime `metal.anode-slime.selenide`

Two of the minor metals that pay for a copper smelter. The slime is roasted in a fluidised bed and the selenium volatilises as SeO2, caught in a hot cyclone or an electrostatic precipitator; the tellurium comes out of the roasted residue by leaching and electrowinning. Both are a few per cent of the slime's mass and both sell at a price per kilogram above the copper, so by 1982 a smelter could not afford to throw them away.

###### Copper ingot and rod casting `metal.copper.ingot-casting` _(medium)_

The cathode is melted in an induction furnace or a reverberatory with a controlled sulphur addition, then cast - either continuously into wire rod by the Properzi upcast method or into 250-450 kg ingots for further processing. The 1980s standard route to rod was continuous casting; the alternative, longer route was a DC casting machine feeding a wire rod mill. Melting loses almost nothing because copper does not oxidise appreciably; the real problem is gas absorption.

###### Upcast wire rod line `metal.copper.upcasting` _(medium)_

In the Properzi upcaster the melt runs out of a horizontal holding furnace into a vertical casting trough behind a steel die that is being drawn upward by a rotating carousel; the trough is water-cooled and the copper solidifies against the moving die face, giving a controlled solidification structure. It makes 6-9 mm rod very cheaply and was standard in the 1980s, though the resulting cast structure needs patenting before drawing.

            - *Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings* `metal.copper.wire` *(seen above)*
###### Copper foil: 35 um PCB and 6-18 um capacitor foil `metal.copper.foil`

Two completely different foils with the same name, and this is a deliberate convergence node. The PCB foil is 35 um copper (70 um on very old boards) electrolytically deposited or rolled; the C64's board is single-sided, so it is one sheet of foil laminated to 1.6 mm FR-4. The capacitor foil is electro-deposited drum foil, deposited 6-18 um onto a rotating stainless or titanium drum from a copper sulphate bath, stripped and wound, then roughened again for etching just like aluminium foil.

###### Electro-deposited drum foil `metal.copper.foil.ed-drum`

A rotating drum cathode, 1-2 m diameter and 1-1.5 m wide, dips into an acid copper sulphate bath and turns; copper plates onto it at 20-100 A/dm2. A scraper peels the foil off at the top of the drum as a continuous 6-18 um web, which is then slit and wound. The deposit is not bulk metal: it is a columnar, sometimes dendritic growth, which is exactly why it etches into foil capacitors so well and why, for PCBs, it needs a bonding treatment before the laminate resin will stick to it.

###### Nodular treatment for PCB foil adhesion `metal.copper.foil.bonding` _(medium)_

Bare copper foil will not bond to epoxy; it delaminates. So the foil is treated in a warm sulfuric acid bath with a silicofluoride or a silane - historically sodium silicofluoride, later silanes - which grows a forest of microscopic oxide nodules on the surface. The resin flows into the forest and locks in, and the peel strength goes from a few N/cm to about 20 N/cm. This etching of the foil surface is the single most important step in making a copper-clad laminate, and the silicofluoride comes from the same fluorochemical industry as the hydrofluoric acid in the aluminium and tantalum branches.

###### Rolled annealed copper foil `metal.copper.foil.ra` _(medium)_

The traditional foil: heavy copper strip rolled on a Sendimir mill to 35-105 um and slit. It has a rolled, fibrous grain that is anisotropic, so it is easy to form and easy to drill, and it was the foil of record for anything that needs to be bent rather than etched. By 1982 electronic-grade rolled foil had been mostly displaced by electro-deposited foil for PCBs because deposition was cheaper and the bonding treatment was more reliable, but rolled foil remained the foil of choice for fine pitch and for capacitor cathodes.

###### Anode casting and the anode scrap stream `metal.copper.anode.casting` _(medium)_

About 10-20% of the anode never makes it into a cell - it is broken in handling, or the bars are too thin, or the busbar is corroded away - and it goes back to be remelted and recast. Every tankhouse therefore has a stub and an anode scrap yard and a melt, and the plant's anode book is a mass balance between the smelter's output and the tankhouse's demand. At the end of its life an anode is a thin, perforated, gold-bearing skeleton of iron and lead oxide that goes back to the smelter, so the gold in the anode is in a closed loop with the refinery and the melt is where the loop is closed.

          - *Anode slime: the real reason to smelt copper* `metal.anode-slime` *(seen above)*
###### Starter sheets, seeding and the tankhouse floor `metal.copper.tankhouse.starters` _(medium)_

Everything in a tankhouse depends on nucleation. The cathodes start on stainless steel or titanium starter sheets, or on copper seed plates that have been roughened. If too many nuclei start, the deposit is dull and soft and hard to strip; if too few, it is bright and hard and needs a big shear force. The whole art is seeding the right number. The electrolyte is also circulated at 200-400 mm/s across the cell face, because the anode slime would otherwise build up and short.

        - *Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings* `metal.copper.wire` *(seen above)*
        - *Copper foil: 35 um PCB and 6-18 um capacitor foil* `metal.copper.foil` *(seen above)*
#### Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts `metal.tin`

Tin is the metal that made electronics solderable. On a 1982 C64 board there are roughly 3,500 through-hole joints and most of them are joined with a lead-tin alloy, so there is a couple of hundred grams of tin per machine. Tin also does two other jobs in the machine: it is the coating on tin-plated steel (tinplate, though a home computer case is not canned food) and it is the facing on tin-plated copper-alloy switch and connector contacts, where it stops the copper from tarnishing and gives a low and stable contact resistance.

##### Cassiterite concentrate (SnO2) `metal.cassiterite`

Cassiterite is a very heavy, very hard, brown-to-black mineral - the specific gravity of 7 makes gravity separation unusually effective on it, which is why tin mining has always had a placer tradition. The concentrates bought by an smelter in 1982 came from four very different operations: alluvial and offshore dredging in Malaysia and Indonesia, hard-rock lodes in the Bolivian and Brazilian Precambrian shields, hard-rock in Cornwall and the Pan, and shallow residual deposits in Thailand and Nigeria. Concentrates assayed 40-80% Sn with arsenic, iron, tungsten and fluorine as the problem impurities - fluorine in particular is the reason the Bolivian smelter needed a roast.

###### Alluvial cassiterite gravel: dredging and panning `metal.cassiterite.alluvial`

Tin gravel is a beach or stream deposit: pebbles and clay with a few grams of cassiterite per tonne. The classical recovery is the sluice and the jig, where a stream of water over an inclined riffled box stratifies by density and the heavy mineral stays behind. The Kinta Valley in Perak, Malaysia, was dredged on an enormous scale from the 1900s through the 1980s by suction dredges working a 100 m wide alluvial fan at 30-100 m depth, pumping gravel through a 3-6 inch suction pipe to a floating washing plant and a jig. Off Thailand and Indonesia it was offshore and shallow-sea dredging. Gravel is essentially quarried from a sea floor.

###### Stanniferous alluvium and laterite `metal.cassiterite.gravel`

The leaf: unconsolidated stony clay and gravel of a valley floor or a coastal plain, with cassiterite grains scattered through it and concentrated at the base of gravel layers where the wave or the stream action is right. In Malaysia it is a young alluvial fan over limestone; in Bolivia it is not alluvial at all but a hard-rock lode in Ordovician slates and granites, which is why Bolivia's process chain is longer.

###### Cassiterite lode in the Bolivian and Cornwall tin belt `metal.cassiterite.lode`

For contrast: the tin lodes of the Cordillera Real in Bolivia and of the Cambrian granite cupolas in Cornwall are hydrothermal cassiterite in quartz veins and greisens, and they have to be blasted and milled. Bolivia's Oruro and La Paz districts still supply a fraction of world tin from ore averaging 0.3-1% Sn, with the famous manioc mill and the hydraulic concentrator. Cornwall's industry was by 1982 essentially finished - the last deep mine closed in 1984 - a hundred years after the smelter industry had been moved to the East.

###### Greisen and quartz vein `metal.cassiterite.greisen`

The leaf for the hard-rock route: a pneumatolytic alteration halo of topaz-bearing greisen and milky quartz with cassiterite disseminated through it, around a granite cupola. It is a rock, it is in a hillside, and it is drilled.

###### Topaz and the greisen alteration `metal.cassiterite.topaz` _(medium)_

The leaf, geologically: a pneumatolytic alteration halo around the granite cupola in which the feldspars are replaced by topaz (Al2SiO4F2) and quartz, and in the interstices sit the crystals of cassiterite, wolframite and native bismuth. The fluorine in the topaz is the whole reason the alteration happened - it is a fluorine-rich hydrothermal fluid - which is a satisfying way for the tin branch to close, because the same fluorine chemistry that greened the rocks is the fluorine chemistry that made the cryolite in the aluminium pot and the hydrofluoric acid for the silicon plant.

##### Tin smelting: reduction of SnO2 with carbon `metal.tin.smelting`

Cassiterite is one of the easiest oxide ores to reduce: SnO2 + C -> Sn + CO2 goes at only 1200-1400 C, far below copper or iron, because tin's oxides are unstable. The Malaysian and Indonesian smelters in 1982 were reverberatory or electric furnaces on 5-20 t capacity, fired with coke, charged with concentrate and about 15% limestone as a flux, and tapped a crude tin at 99.5-99.8% in maybe eight hours. The furnace is a long, narrow, brick-lined box with a step grate at the firebox end, so the charge moves gradually forward and meets rising temperatures - a reverberatory used for a purely solid-solid reaction, which is why tin smelting smells of SO2 only when the concentrate is sulphide.

###### Roasting of fluorine-bearing Bolivian concentrate `metal.tin.bolivian-roast` _(medium)_

Bolivian concentrates carry fluorine, which would carry through into the tin as a stubborn impurity. So they are roasted at 600-800 C before smelting to drive off the fluorine as HF and the arsenic as arsenic oxide, and the hot gas is scrubbed with lime to make calcium fluoride before release. That lime scrub is a genuine environmental control fitted in the 1970s and 1980s, and it is one of the reasons the smelters are the only tin plants with a scrubber.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) ore `metal.fluorspar`

Calcium fluoride rock, the only commercial source of fluorine. A 1982 hydrofluoric acid plant buys 97-98% acid made by treating acid-grade fluorspar (97%+ CaF2) with sulphuric acid in a kiln, and the acid then goes into the aluminium fluoride and cryolite that the Hall-Heroult bath needs and into the fluoride digestion that turns coltan into soluble tantalum fluoride. The ore is mined in open pits and underground, in hydrothermal veins in limestone and as replacement bodies in dolomite.

###### Fluorite open-pit and underground mine `metal.fluorspar.mine` _(medium)_

Fluorite fills the cavities and fracture zones of limestone, so it is mined either as a replacement body in a working limestone quarry or as a vein. Mexican fluorite was underground at Naica - where it grows the famous 12 m transparent crystals in a cave - and in open pits in Chihuahua. The South African deposits are in the carbonate sequences of the Transvaal Group, and the Chinese and Mongolian ones, which became dominant in the late 1980s, are in greisen and vein systems related to granite.

###### Fluorite vein in limestone `metal.fluorspar.vein`

The leaf: a purple, green or white vein of CaF2 a few centimetres to a few metres thick in a fractured carbonate host, in a limestone hill.

###### Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar `metal.hydrofluoric-acid`

The corrosive reagent. Fluorspar plus sulfuric acid gives hydrogen fluoride in a kiln at 200-300 C; fluorspar plus concentrated sulfuric acid in a rotary kiln gives anhydrous HF directly, and the anhydrous route is what makes water-free fluorinations possible. HF is the reagent for silicon to trichlorosilane, tantalum to K2TaF7, glass etching, uranium hexafluoride, and the fluorochemical industry generally.

###### Dry, sieve and mix the smelter charge `metal.tin.charge-prep` _(medium)_

Cassiterite concentrates are roasted if they carry fluorine or arsenic, dried to remove the 8-12% moisture, and sieved - because a reverberatory furnace with fine charge in it just makes dust. The charge is then mixed with the limestone flux and the coke, in the ratio that gives 15-20% flux and 15-25% reductant. Nothing about this is clever and everything about it is critical: an Indonesian smelter that got the coke ratio wrong lost a few percent of its tin into the slag, which at 3% is a third of its margin.

###### The tin smelter's slag and its tin loss `metal.tin.slag` _(medium)_

A tin smelter loses 1-3% of its tin into the slag, and the slag is a silicate of iron and silica with tin locked up in it. Recovering that tin is a separate business: the slag is crushed and re-smelted, or in Malaysia and Brazil it was re-smelted in a small furnace to recover the tin. A tin smelter therefore has a second, smaller smelter, and the discipline of a tin plant is judged by its recovery, which is why the industry published recovery figures with a seriousness that most primary metals do not.

##### Fluid-bed reduction of fine cassiterite (post-1982 route) `metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor` _(medium)_

Worth noting as the direction the industry went in rather than as 1982 practice: the fine concentrates that a gravity circuit now produces reduce easily in a fluidised bed at 850-1000 C, which is a temperature no reverberatory furnace can hold at its hearth. This process is why the modern tin industry uses much less coke and produces much less CO. In 1982 essentially none of this existed.

##### Refine the crude tin to 99.9% `metal.tin.refining`

Crude tin at 99.5-99.8% still carries iron, copper and arsenic, and the difference between 99.5% and 99.9% matters enormously for solder because iron is a solder poison and raises the liquidus. Two routes. Liquation, the old one, melts the crude tin at about 400 C: tin melts at 232 C, so the iron and copper stay solid and bottom out, and the clean tin is drawn off. Electrolysis, the modern one, uses a stannic chloride or a fluorostannate bath and gives 99.97-99.99%. Malaysia ran electrolysis; Bolivia's low-grade concentrate still used liquation.

###### Refined tin ingot or tin powder, 99.9-99.97% `metal.tin.ingot`

Shipped as a 25-50 kg or 250 kg ingot at 99.9-99.97%, or - for the electronics industry - atomised into a fine powder. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tin smelting branch and the solder branch: the solder manufacturer needs the ingot, and the solder-paste manufacturer needs the powder. Iron is the impurity that matters, because iron is a solder poison that wets badly and raises the liquidus.

###### Air atomisation of tin to powder `metal.tin.atomisation` _(medium)_

Molten tin at about 1150 C is poured into a launder and a high-pressure air jet at the bottom of a vertical stack sprays it into a fog of droplets that solidify on the way down. It is cheap, it works for metals that do not oxidise much, and it gives a bimodal powder. Under nitrogen it gives the fine, oxide-free powder that solder paste needs. Every particle in the can came out of a slot in a nozzle.

###### Tin plating of steel and of copper alloys `metal.tin.plating`

Tinplate - a 1.1-11.2 g/m2 tin coating on 0.15-0.3 mm of steel - is made by electrolytic tinning of a continuous steel strip on a horizontal passivating line: the strip is degreased, pickled in acid, tinned in a sulphate or fluoroborate bath, rinsed, and then either passivated in chromic acid (food can) or - through the 1980s - given an electrolytic chromate or tin-oxide passivation to stop the tin growing dendrites during storage. Food can was the dominant market by mass. A C64 uses tinplate only incidentally, in a switch body or a shield; tin plating of copper-alloy contacts uses a different chemistry altogether and is the node that matters for the machine.

###### Tin plating of copper-alloy contacts `metal.tin.contact-plating` _(medium)_

Not tinplate on steel, but tin on brass or phosphor bronze - the plating on the contacts of a C64 switch or a keyboard connector. The 1980s chemistry was an acid stannate or an alkaline stannate bath: SnSO4 with sulfuric acid, or sodium stannate with caustic soda and a puller such as sodium gluconate. Tin is on a connector contact because it forms a soft, low-resistance, non-tarnishing intermetallic with the copper. The reason it fails is the tin whisker - a single-crystal filament of tin that grows out of the plating under compressive stress in humid storage and can bridge a 0.1 mm gap. Tin whiskers were the reliability nemesis of exactly this kind of contact.

#### Lead: the base metal of 63/37 solder `metal.lead`

Lead is the soft, low-melting, cheap half of the solder alloy, and it is the reason soldering works at all: pure tin wets copper badly and has no strength, and pure lead does not wet anything. Lead also has its own huge pre-electronics industrial life - storage batteries, cable sheath, pigment - and its 1982 smelting industry is the oldest continuous industrial process in the book. The C64 carries a couple of hundred grams of it, which is why the machine is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

##### Galena (PbS) concentrate `metal.galena`

Galena is cubic, bright grey when fresh and dull grey when oxidised, extremely heavy at 7.6 g/cm3, and it is one of the few common ores that a prospector could identify by eye. The great mining districts in 1982 were the Tri-State district of Missouri, Oklahoma and Kansas (which supplied most of the United States' lead and is a fossil limestone-hosted deposit), the Broken Hill and Mount Isa districts of Australia, Cerro de Pasco and Huancavelica in Peru, and the Iberian and Atlas belts. Concentrates assay 40-75% Pb and are always accompanied by enough silver and zinc to make a good deal of the mine's revenue.

###### Underground lead-zinc mine `metal.galena.mine` _(medium)_

The Tri-State district's galena bodies sit as veins and bedding replacements in Mississippian limestone only a few metres thick, and they were worked by room-and-pillar mining - essentially taking the limestone out and leaving the lead in place, because the ore grade at 3-6% Pb did not pay for selective mining. The mineral was hand-picked off the back of the working face and off the cars. This is a soft-rock, shallow, cheap mining operation, and its day had largely gone by 1982 as the deeper and lower-grade Missouri deposits took over.

###### Galenite replacement in carbonate rock `metal.galena.rock`

The leaf: galena crystals and veins in a fossiliferous limestone - literally the remains of a Carboniferous sea floor. The Tri-State district is one of the great fossil-mineral coincidences of industrial history: a lead-bearing limestone under a farm field.

###### Hand picking and gravity sorting `metal.galena.sorting` _(medium)_

The Tri-State district's ore was a 3-6% lead limestone that could not be selectively mined and could not be concentrated, so the technique was brute force: the rock was shot down, the lead-bearing rock was picked out of the face by hand by a face worker, and then the cars were run over a sorting table or a picking table where a sorter took out the visibly lead-coloured lumps from the limestone. In 1930 the Tri-State had about 15,000 sorters - a third of them children - and that is what made the district the largest lead producer on Earth. It is a labour technique rather than a machine, and it is a genuine leaf of the tree.

###### The sorting table `metal.galena.sorting-table` _(medium)_

A sloping table with a light on it and a raised lip, worked by two or three people, one on each side. Galena is bright and heavy and galena-bearing limestone is dark and light, so the visual contrast is real, and the sorter's job is to lift out the dark lumps at perhaps 2-4 tonnes per shift. It is the lowest-skill, lowest-pay, highest-volume job in the lead industry, and it is where a great many Missouri families started.

##### Roasting/sintering of galena to PbO `metal.lead.sintering`

The concentrate is roasted in a sinter plant: a travelling grate on which a 1-2 m bed of concentrate is ignited and slowly drawn through with the gas being pulled after the fire. The sulphide oxidises to lead(II) oxide: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. The point of sintering rather than fluidised-bed roasting is that the heat can be high and localised enough to sinter the fine particles into a coherent porous cake, which is exactly what the blast furnace needs to breathe. The sinter is 50-60% Pb and the SO2 - at 10-14% - goes to the acid plant, the same one the copper smelter uses.

###### Dwight-Lloyd sinter strand `metal.lead.sinter-plant`

A continuous chain of cast-iron pallets on an endless track about 1.2-1.5 m wide, with the ignition hood at the discharge end. Feed is a mix of concentrate, sinter returns, flux and coke spread to exactly 1-2 m - there is nothing clever about it and it works. The strand advances 1-2 m/min, the fire burns through the bed in about 20 minutes, and the hot sinter is broken off by a set of crusher jaws at the end and tipped into the blast furnace. One machine makes 200-400 t of sinter an hour and runs continuously for years.

###### Self-fluxing sinter mix `metal.lead.self-fluxing` _(medium)_

Sinter is not simply roasted concentrate. The mix is designed so the sintered cake is its own flux: the silica that comes with the concentrate is balanced with limestone so the blast furnace slag has a basicity near 1.5-2.0. Anything between about 1.0 and 2.0 works; outside that range the slag either freezes in the furnace or dissolves too much lead. The smelter's metallurgist is balancing silica, iron, calcium and lead every shift.

##### Lead blast furnace reduction to crude lead `metal.lead.blast-furnace`

A lead blast furnace looks like an iron blast furnace but is only 4-7 m tall, because lead reduces so easily. Self-fluxing sinter, coke and limestone are charged at the top; a blast of 200-350 C air is blown in at the hearth; the PbO is reduced to lead by CO at 1000-1100 C and the metal runs out. The sinter, coke and limestone charge comes down a shaft that is deliberately kept chilled so the metallic lead freezes before it goes further down - if it melted it would run into the tuyeres. Two outputs: crude lead bullion at 950-1050 C at the bottom, and a slag carrying off the iron and silica.

###### Crude lead bullion with silver and gold `metal.lead.bullion` _(medium)_

Tapped at 950-1050 C, the bullion is about 95-98% lead with 1-3% silver, a little gold, and copper, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. Silver at 1-3% is not a trace - it is often the difference between a viable mine and a marginal one, and the Parkes process that recovers it is the reason lead smelters have a refinery at all. By 1982 crude lead was increasingly sold as a low-grade bullion to the refinery and the smelter/ refinery was one continuous plant.

###### Parkes process: zinc drossing and desilverisation `metal.lead.parkes`

The genius step, invented in 1850 and still standard in 1982. The molten bullion is stirred with a few tenths of a percent of zinc, which has a much stronger chemical affinity for silver than lead does, so a zinc-silver intermetallic (AgZn2, Ag2Zn5) migrates to the zinc 'dross' floating on top. The dross is skimmed, and the now-silver-poor lead is treated again with fresh zinc until it is down to 10-30 g/t silver. The dross is then distilled in a retort: zinc boils at 907 C and is condensed, and the silver and gold stay behind, to be cupelled. The zinc is a sacrificial reagent and goes back into the alloy.

###### Betts process: electrolytic refining `metal.lead.betts` _(medium)_

The rival to the Parkes process, and the answer for the last fraction of a gram of bismuth. Anodes of impure lead are dissolved in a caustic soda solution containing sodium plumbite (Na2PbO3), and pure lead plates onto the cathode. The chemistry is unusual - the anode dissolves as plumbite and the deposit forms by the reaction of plumbite with metal, which is why the bath has to be kept in a narrow alkaline window. Cost is high, energy is high, so it was used only as a finishing step on top of the Parkes route, and in the 1980s it was being displaced by the Betterton-Krastchkow continuous drossing tower.

###### Vacuum-degass and dross the lead bullion `metal.lead.vacuum-degassing` _(medium)_

The modern version of both processes in one machine: a 6-10 m tall cylindrical steel vacuum vessel with an internal fractionating column. Molten lead is sprayed into the vacuum; the volatiles - hydrogen, oxygen, zinc, and the remaining silver on its way out - distil out and are fractionated, so the silver comes off as a separate metal rather than as a dross. It replaces two steps with one, cuts the labour, and gives 99.99% lead with under 5 g/t silver. It was the technology that spread through the lead industry in the 1980s, and it is a good marker for what was changing in smelting and what was not.

###### Cupellation of the silver dross to silver and gold `metal.lead.cupellation-lead`

The dross from the Parkes process is mixed with lead and flux and cast into a 30-50 kg charge, which is placed in a cupellation furnace at 1000-1150 C and blown with air. The lead oxidises to litharge, PbO, which melts at 888 C and is absorbed by the porous cupel, while the silver and gold do not oxidise and stay on the surface. When all the lead is gone the silver is 96-99% pure and the gold is 30-50% of it; the gold is then cupelled again, or electrorefined, to 99.9%. So every lead bullion makes a small pile of very pure silver - a deliberate convergence of the lead and silver branches.

###### Retorting the Parkes dross to recover the zinc `metal.lead.dross-smelting` _(medium)_

After the silver has been skimmed off as dross, the dross itself has to be processed, and it is done in a cast-iron retort: the dross is mixed with charcoal and a little limestone, charged into a retort at 800-950 C, and the zinc distils out - it boils at 907 C - into a condenser where it is collected as a crude zinc metal. The silver and gold stay in the retort. A dross retort holds 100-500 kg and takes 8-20 hours, and a refinery had six to a dozen of them. The recovered zinc is dirty and goes back into the next drossing cycle, which is why the Parkes process consumes no net zinc even though it uses some every time round.

###### The dross retort and its condenser `metal.lead.dross-retort` _(medium)_

A cast-iron or steel tube, 1.5-3 m long, charged at one end and heated in a coke-fired setting, with a condenser of iron pipes at the cool end into which the zinc vapour condenses and runs out as a crude metal. The retort has to be skimmed of oxide and it is a batch process, so a refinery ran a bank of them in shifts. It is an object that is essentially unchanged since the 1850s, which makes it one of the oldest continuous processes in this file.

###### Hot-dross the copper out of the lead bullion `metal.lead.copper-drossing` _(medium)_

Before the Parkes zinc drossing, the bullion is hot-drossed for copper. The blast-furnace bullion comes out at 950-1050 C holding copper, which is insoluble in lead at that temperature and forms a separate copper matte that floats on top; the refinery skims it off, cools it, and recovers the copper and its precious metals by further processing. It is the same physical principle as the zinc drossing - a metal that mixes preferentially with another - and it is done first because the copper dross would otherwise interfere with the silver dross.

###### Refined lead ingot, 99.99% `metal.lead.ingot`

Cast into 25 kg pigs or into 500 kg slabs. About two thirds of all the lead refined in the world was never made into a product in the refinery - it went straight into an alloy, most of it lead-acid battery plate and cable sheath. The solder industry took a small fraction, on the order of five to ten percent, and in 1982 that fraction was the entire basis of the electronics solder business. This is a deliberate convergence node: the blast furnace branch, the Parkes desilverisation branch and the solder branch all meet here.

            - *Cupellation of the silver dross to silver and gold* `metal.lead.cupellation-lead` *(seen above)*
#### 63/37 Sn-Pb solder: wire, bar, paste `metal.solder`

The alloy that makes electronics manufacturable. 63% tin, 37% lead is a true eutectic, so it melts and freezes at one temperature, 183 C, with no mushy interval - which means a joint goes from solid to liquid in milliseconds and the reflow time window can be measured in seconds. That property is why a decade of copper thicknesses and lead-free anxiety has not displaced it from the bench. A C64 has roughly 3,500 through-hole joints; at about 30 mg of solder per joint that is around 100 g of alloy per machine, in wire fed from spools and in a few kilos of bar in the wave-solder tank.

##### Casting the 63/37 bar `metal.solder.alloy-making`

The alloy is made in a handful of ways, all of them embarrassingly simple. The best is the cored wire method: rods of high-purity tin are cast inside a steel tube pre-filled with molten lead at exactly 37%, so the tube's own wall meters the lead; the tube and the core are then rolled and drawn out to wire in one operation, and the core forms down the middle as the flux. This is how most electronics solder wire is still made. The alternative, and what the solder manufacturer would do for its own bar stock, is simply to melt the two ingots together in a grease pot with a little antimony or phosphorus and pour into ingot moulds.

###### Antimony addition to stiffen the alloy `metal.solder.antimony` _(medium)_

Pure Sn-Pb solder creeps. A 1982 instrument or a through-hole joint under a hot component would push itself out of the joint over a few years, and the classic failure was a capacitor that walked out of its pads. Two tenths of a percent of antimony, as an Sb-Sn hardener or as a lead-antimony master alloy, makes the alloy's creep resistance about an order of magnitude better with only a small rise in melting point. So the solder in the C64 very probably contained 0.1-0.5% antimony, and none of it is on the bill of materials.

###### The cored-wire manufacturing method `metal.solder.cored-wire` _(medium)_

The standard way to make electronics solder wire, and the reason the alloy composition is so consistent. A steel tube with a wall thickness calculated for 37% lead by volume is filled with molten high-purity tin - actually with the exact alloy, but the wall does the metering - and the tube is cold-drawn and then drawn to wire in the same multiwire machine the copper industry uses. The core forms down the middle as the tube collapses. The result is a wire in which the flux core is in the middle of the metal rather than smeared along it, which is what stops the flux from being wiped off during handling. The alternative - extruding a bar of flux and then jacketing it in molten alloy - gives a worse wire and was being displaced by the cored method through the 1980s.

###### Fill the flux core with activated rosin `metal.solder.flux-core-fill` _(low)_

The flux core is a paste, not a powder: rosin dissolved in a solvent - turpentine, or in the 1980s increasingly a mild-rosin paste - with the zinc chloride activator, made viscous enough to hold a column. It is injected into the tube with a hydraulic filler in a batch, and the tube's ends are crimped and drawn closed. The viscosity and the shrinkage matter, because the core has to survive being drawn to 0.5 mm without either splitting out of the wire or shrinking away from the axis. So the flux chemistry in a C64's solder wire is a colloid and a rheology problem as much as it is a chemical one.

##### 63/37 solder wire with a rosin core `metal.solder.wire`

The wire that went through a C64 assembly line: a solid 63/37 core inside a flux core inside a tin-lead sheath, made by the cored-wire method and drawn on the same kind of multiwire machine the copper industry uses, in a smaller and more delicate setup. This is a deliberate convergence node: the solder alloy branch, the rosin branch and the wave-solder branch all meet here, and it is the single most identifiable material in the whole tree - it is why the C64 is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

###### Pine rosin (colophony) `chem.rosin` _(medium)_

The sticky amber solid left when turpentine is distilled out of pine resin. Most rosin is made from pine stumps - the resinous wood left behind when a tree is cut for pulp - by destructive distillation: the stump is chipped, heated in a still to about 150-200 C, turpentine and pine oil come over, and the residue is the rosin, which is then graded by colour and by softening point. About 700,000-800,000 tonnes of rosin were made in the early 1980s, mostly in China, the United States and Brazil. The black liquor from a kraft pulp mill carries resin acids and fatty acids - tall oil - which is distilled into fatty acids, tall-oil fatty acids and a pitch and can be processed further into rosin equivalents.

###### Stump distillation and grading `chem.rosin.distillation`

Rosin is made by distilling the resin out of pine stumps. The stump is chipped into 5-10 cm pieces, charged to a still, and heated; turpentine comes over first and is condensed and separated by distillation into alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and dipentene, and then pine oil and a heavy residue come over, and what is left in the pot is the crude rosin. The rosin is then graded - by colour (X, WW, WW, W) and by softening point (batter 75 C, fir 80 C, Norway 85 C, I 90 C, P 110 C, S 120 C) - and the Y grade, at about 165 C softening point and clear, is the one the flux core needs because it has almost no crystallisation and it does not go brittle. Grading is colour against a reference chip, softening point by the ring-and-ball method and acid value by titration, and the flux maker's specification is colour and softening point with the abietic acid content following from them.

###### Chipping and the still `chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping` _(medium)_

A whole-tree distillery burns about 1.5-2.5 tonnes of dry pine stumps per tonne of rosin plus its turpentine, and yields about 5-8% rosin, 3-4% turpentine and 1-2% pine oil by mass of dry wood. The stumps come from pine killed by beetle attack, from pine cut for pulp, and from the thinning of a plantation - so the rosin business is downstream of a forestry, and specifically of a beetle, in a way that is often overlooked when the flux is described as a petrochemical.

###### Retort and the batch cycle `chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.retort-and-still` _(medium)_

The classic stump still is a cast-iron or steel retort holding one to two tonnes of chipped wood, charged, closed, and fired with the turpentine vapour going to a condenser and the rosin staying in the pot. A cycle takes 12-20 hours and the still is charged by hand - which is why the business has barely changed since the 1850s in its mechanics while every other part of the 1980s chemical industry has been rebuilt twice. The 1980s changes were in the condenser and in the chip size, not in the process.

###### Pine resin from a plantation or a pulp mill `metal.pine-resin`

The leaf: resin bled from the trunks of Pinus species in managed plantations in the American Southeast, Brazil, India, Malaysia, Portugal and China. In the 1980s most rosin came not from tapping but from distilling pine stumps and pulping residues left over from the paper industry - a pulp-mill residue. So the flux in a C64 solder joint is, quite literally, a by-product of making pulp, which makes it a convergence point with the paper and pulp side of the organics chain.

###### Turpentine from the same stump `metal.turpentine` _(medium)_

When pine stumps are distilled for rosin, the first thing off is turpentine - alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene - and it is the solvent the flux paste is made with. So the same 5 kg of pine stump that ends up as the flux in a C64's solder joint first gives up its turpentine, and the two are the two halves of one stump-distillation plant. The turpentine went into the paint and printing-ink industry, which means the soldering branch of this tree converges with the coatings branch through a barrel of distilled turpentine.

###### The halide activator in the flux core `metal.rosin.activator` _(medium)_

Plain rosin is a weak flux. The electronics industry improved it by adding a small amount of acid activator - in 1982 almost always zinc chloride, or in the more aggressive grades a zinc chloride-ammonium chloride mixture - so the flux can remove oxides that rosin alone would leave. The trade is real: more activator means a better joint and a corrosive residue that, if it is not washed off, eats the copper. This is why the flux grade is a specification on the wire, and why the electronics-grade rosin wire of 1982 was normally a mildly activated (MA) or activated (A) flux rather than pure RMA.

##### Wave soldering with the alloy pot `metal.solder.wave-solder`

The board assembly method for a 1982 C64. The bottom of the board is swept across a standing wave of molten 63/37 at 250-280 C, the excess drains through a hot-air knife, and the whole board lives in a hood full of the vapour of flux decomposition products. A few kilograms of solder in the pot are held at a temperature just above the 183 C liquidus, and the pot is kept clean with a rotating skimmer. Wave soldering is why solder consumption in electronics manufacturing was measured in kilograms per day per line rather than grams per board, and why the flux vapour was a genuine occupational exposure that the electronics industry was only beginning to quantify in the late 1980s.

###### Intermetallics and lead leaching in the solder joint `metal.solder.joint-microscopy` _(medium)_

A good 1982 through-hole joint is a shallow concave meniscus filling the pad hole about 70-90%, with a fillet at the lead. The metallurgical reason it works is the intermetallic: copper and tin react to form Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn, and the joint is a composite of unreacted solder and intermetallic compound. On the PCB side the pad is tin-plated and forms a Cu-Sn intermetallic too. What nobody in 1982 was measuring was how much lead leached out of a solder joint into the copper land when the joint was at 200 C for an hour - and it is a lot, which is the mechanism behind the later 'solder fatigue' literature.

###### The hot-air knife and the solder wave `metal.solder.wave-solder.knife` _(medium)_

A pump throws molten solder up a nozzle to form a standing wave 3-8 mm high, and the board is dragged across it on a conveyor with fingers. As the board leaves, a 'hot-air knife' - a duct blowing 200-300 C air across the solder line - blows the excess solder off the pads and off the solder side of the board, and what runs off goes back into the pot through a trough. The whole operation is a temperature profile in space: preheat, flux activation, wave, drain, and the knife. Getting the four temperatures right - preheat, pot, board and cleaning - is the entire craft.

###### Preheater, fluxer and the thermal profile `metal.solder.preheater` _(medium)_

Before the wave, the board goes through a preheater - infrared lamps, a hot plate or hot air - to 100-150 C, and through a fluxer that lays a foam or sprayed layer of flux on the solder side. The reason for preheating is thermal expansion: a FR-4 board with a big hole pattern expands by a different amount in different directions, and if the solder side heats faster than the component side the board warps and the joints crack. A C64's mainboard is a large single-sided board with a lot of heat-generating parts on one side, so warp was a real yield problem. The preheater is the cheapest fix and it is a temperature-control problem.

###### Board warp, thermal stress and the epoxy `metal.solder.board-warp` _(medium)_

Why preheat exists at all. A single-sided 1.6 mm FR-4 board with a large hole pattern expands and contracts with a coefficient of about 14-18 x 10^-6 per K, and it is not isotropic - the copper layer and the epoxy cloth have different coefficients, and the weave gives the board different stiffness in the warp and weft directions. Warm the solder side faster than the component side and the board bows; cycle it and the board stays bowed; and on a double-sided board it can delaminate the copper from the epoxy. So the preheater is really an epoxy-handling device, and the epoxy is the resin agent's problem while the solder pot is the metals one, and they meet at the warp.

##### Solder paste: powder in flux `metal.solder.paste` _(medium)_

Solder paste is a mixture of atomised alloy powder at 60-90% by weight in a flux vehicle, and in 1982 it was the technology for surface-mount parts, which Commodore did not really use on the mainboard but which every other electronics maker in the world was. The powder particle size is controlled by the printing stencil: a 0.5 mm gap needs 20-45 um powder so the powder does not bridge the gap with two particles. Alloy powder is not made by atomising finished solder; it is made by atomising the melt and then the 63/37 particles are aged so they develop an oxide shell of a controlled thickness, so that paste sits on a pad for minutes without the paste shrinking or the surface going dull.

##### The leaded-solder problem in the 1980s `metal.solder.lead-hazard`

Lead in solder was the first workplace poison to arrive with electronics. It was already deeply regulated for the smelter workers - the whole lead industry is under air-monitoring and blood-lead surveillance - and by the early 1980s occupational-health attention had turned to the solder bench: solder fume is an aerosol of lead oxide particles, and the flux fumes carry it. The US OSHA lead standard covered soldering. The C64 is the emblem of this because it was sold by the million with a leaded-solder supply chain: the solder manufacturer, the wave-solder pot, the washing machines that washed the flux off, the drain water, and finally the landfill. Every one of those is a different regulatory jurisdiction and none of them was solved in 1982.

###### Silver-bearing solder and silver paste `metal.solder.silver-solder-paste` _(medium)_

A distinct and important thing in the 1980s electronics industry, which is easy to confuse with the lead-tin eutectic: high-temperature silver solder - 62Ag/38Cu, 50Ag/50Cd, 70Ag/30Sn - melts at 600-750 C and is brazed, not soldered. Silver-tin solder melts at 217-220 C and is used where lead-free behaviour is wanted. Silver brazing is how the heat sinks and the chassis joints were made. And separately there is the silver-filled epoxy and silver-filled ink of the electronics industry: real silver powder at 60-80% by weight in an epoxy or an organic vehicle, screen-printed or stencil-printed and fired, used for die attach and for the conductive ink of the keyboard membrane. That is a genuine and separate use of silver in a C64, and it is a chemistry, not a metallurgy.

##### The wave-solder pot and its dross `metal.solder.pot` _(medium)_

A 5-20 kg pot of 63/37 at 250-280 C with a pump and a wave-forming nozzle, plus a rotating skimmer and an oil skimmer. The surface of a working solder pot accumulates a metre of black oxide dross - tin oxide, lead oxide and flux residue - and it has to be skimmed off every shift and every night, and it is a genuine metallurgical waste stream: the dross contains most of the lead and a lot of the tin, and in 1982 the recovery options were poor. A dross reclaimer sold a few percent of the metal back and the rest went out as lead-containing waste. This is the point at which the solder chain and the lead chain close on each other.

###### The dross oxide film on the solder pot `metal.solder.dross-oxide` _(medium)_

At 250-280 C the surface of molten Sn-Pb oxidises continuously - tin oxide forms preferentially because it has the lower oxidation potential - so the pot grows a skin of SnO2 with lead oxide and flux in it. The skimmer takes it off, but the formation is unavoidable, which is why wave-solder lines had a person whose whole job was pot maintenance and why the flux was designed to keep the oxide mobile and floatable rather than letting it crust over.

##### Cleaning the flux residue off the board `metal.solder.cleaning` _(medium)_

A rosin-fluxed board is covered in a sticky, slightly acidic film of flux decomposition products that will corrode the copper and will not accept a conformal coating. In 1982 it was removed in an aqueous machine - a conveyor with spray bars and drying ovens - often followed by a trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degreaser. The cleaning water left the factory through the drain with the lead in it, which is the other half of the 1982 leaded-solder problem and the reason the electronics industry spent the late 1980s arguing about what to do about it.

###### The solder wash-water waste stream `metal.solder.waste-water` _(medium)_

A C64 assembly line's cleaning water carried dissolved lead, tin, flux residues and a lot of suspended solids. In 1982 the standard practice was dilute and discharge: a settling tank and a pH adjustment, then to the drain. The lead was almost all in the sludge, so the sludge went to a hazardous-waste landfill and the liquid went out. This is the last place the C64's lead leaves the factory, and it is the reason leaded solder became a regulatory object rather than merely an occupational one.

###### Lead in landfill leachate `metal.solder.waste-leachate` _(low)_

Landfill leachate is where the lead problem stops being a factory problem. Dross and baghouse dust that could not be recycled went to a hazardous-waste landfill, and a landfill that takes metal-bearing waste generates leachate in which lead concentrations are routinely orders of magnitude above the drinking-water limit, so the liner, the leachate collection sump and the treatment plant are the last line of defence. By the early 1980s this was the reason several countries began classifying lead-bearing wastes separately from general industrial waste.

##### The solder factory's own waste streams `metal.solder.waste` _(medium)_

A solder pot, a dross heap, a flux residue stream, a wash-water drain and a baghouse for the flux fumes. The dross goes to a reclaimer or to a hazardous-waste disposal contract; the baghouse dust is lead oxide and rosin and is genuinely hazardous; and the wash water goes to the drain with the lead in it. In 1982 this was the least regulated part of the whole electronics industry, and it is the reason the United States' lead exposure limits for electronics workers - which were set at a time when electronics was not a regulated industry - exist at all. The waste stream is a leaf of this tree and a genuinely uncomfortable one.

###### The flux fume baghouse and its dust `metal.solder.waste-baghouse` _(medium)_

The wave-solder hood has an extraction duct and a baghouse, because the fume is an aerosol of lead oxide and of rosin-acid degradation products. The dust is 30-60% lead oxide and it is collected as a hazardous waste. A big 1982 line threw away tens of kilograms a week. The control measure was local exhaust ventilation with a capture hood about 100 mm from the wave, and the compliance measure was an area respirator, which was why electronics assembly was one of the more heavily respirated occupations of the period.

#### Zinc: die-cast alloy, plating, brass, varistor `metal.zinc`

Zinc is the fourth non-ferrous metal and the most recycled one. In a 1982 C64 it appears as a die-cast zinc alloy for the case-mounted parts and the key plungers, as a plating on steel for EMI shields and chassis fasteners, as brass (copper-zinc) for the bus-bar and connector bodies, and as zinc oxide in the varistor that clamps the supply spikes off the mains input. The smelting industry in 1982 was in the middle of its biggest change in a century: the roast-leach-electrowin zinc-iron plant was replacing the horizontal retort furnace.

##### Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate, 50-60% Zn `metal.sphalerite`

Sphalerite is one of the few ores that is not visually recognisable: it is a black to honey-brown cubic crystal whose colour depends on the iron substituting in the lattice, so the industry grades it in grades of iron - a 4% iron concentrate looks black and a 12% iron concentrate looks ruby red-brown. Concentration is by flotation with an amine or xanthate collector. The great districts were the Red Dog and the Sullivan mine in British Columbia, Broken Hill, the Cerro Rico of Potosi, the Rammelsberg of Goslar, and the Appalachian and Midwestern US zinc districts such as the Bartlesville and the Tennessee mines.

###### Underground zinc-lead mine `metal.sphalerite.mine` _(medium)_

The Red Dog and Sullivan type deposit: a massive sulphide body in a sedimentary basin, mined underground from a ramp or a shaft, with the ore hoisted in a friction hoist or a skip, and the mill right at the portal. Broken Hill's Broken Hill Proprietary was the other archetype, an open pit above a very large primary orebody that was mined for sixty years. Where the zinc and lead are in separate veins, gravity and flotation split them: galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 do separate well on a dense-medium separator.

###### Massive sulphide in a sedimentary basin `metal.sphalerite.massive-sulphide`

The leaf: a lens-shaped body of fine-grained sulphide - sphalerite, galena, pyrite, with chalcopyrite and arsenopyrite - conformable with the bedding of a marine shale or carbonate, and sitting at a specific stratigraphic horizon. The Red Dog deposit is exactly this: a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin. The ore is not in a vein you can see from the surface; it is a stratigraphic layer you have to know is there.

###### Zinc concentrator: differential flotation `metal.sphalerite.mill` _(medium)_

The ore is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground to 50-100 um in a ball or autogenous mill, and floated in stages. The classic circuit is differential: copper and lead sulphides are floated first with a stronger collector and a higher pH, and then the sphalerite is floated from the tailings with a weaker collector at a lower pH, with copper sulphate added as an activator because sphalerite does not float on its own. That gives a 50-60% Zn concentrate at 85-92% recovery. The Red Dog and Sullivan concentrators were among the largest in the world and are the reason those two mines could be mines at all.

###### Dense-media separation of galena from sphalerite `metal.sphalerite.dms` _(medium)_

Galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 are separable on a shaking table or, much faster, in a dense-medium separator using a ferrosilicon or magnetite suspension at a cut density of about 3.0-3.5. The lead concentrate and the zinc concentrate are thereby split before flotation, which lets the flotation plant be small. Dense-medium separation of a polymetallic ore is one of the great quiet successes of twentieth-century mineral processing.

###### Ferrosilicon powder for dense-media separation `metal.dms.fe-silicon` _(medium)_

The liquid in a dense-medium separator is ferrosilicon - an alloy of iron and silicon made in exactly the submerged arc furnace described in the electrical-steel and metallurgical-silicon branches of this file. So a 1982 concentrator that separated galena from sphalerite by density was running a slurry of metallurgical silicon, and the silicon branch of this tree reaches a zinc concentrator as well as a power transformer. Silicon really does end up everywhere: 60-90% of all ferrosilicon production goes into the steel and aluminium branches, but the rest goes into heavy-media separation, and it is the sharpest possible illustration of why a tree like this has cross-links.

###### Ferrosilicon in the submerged arc furnace `metal.ferrosilicon`

Ferrosilicon at 45-75% silicon is made in a submerged arc furnace very like the one that makes metallurgical silicon, but with more coke and a much higher silica ratio in the slag: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO, with the silicon going into the ferroalloy instead of condensing as dust. The largest producers make it in 60-100 MVA three-electrode furnaces, and the furnace is a genuinely different beast from the silicon one - the slag is liquid and the electrode has to tap through it. So the electrical-steel transformer in a C64 and the quartzite in a silicon plant converge at two different kinds of arc furnace.

                    - *High-grade quartzite (97-99% SiO2)* `metal.quartzite` *(seen above)*
###### Coke and coke oven gas: the reducing agent `metal.coke`

Coke is the black, porous, 90% carbon solid that makes the blast furnace possible, and it is also the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, manganese, ferrochrome and ferrosilicon furnaces. A tonne of coke is roughly 70% of the fuel and 30% of the reductant in a blast furnace charge, and nothing works without it. By 1982 the coke oven was a mature and much-diagnosed industry: the air pollution from coking, and the fact that a coke oven is the largest single source of coal tar and benzene in the industrial world, were the reasons the Clean Air Act of 1970 and its amendments hit coal and coke first.

###### Coking coal, caking and prime coking blends `metal.coking-coal`

Not any coal: a blend of coals that fuse and solidify into a coherent cellular cake when heated. The caking power comes from the vitrinite, and the best coking coal is a low-volatile, medium-bituminous coal that goes plastic around 350-450 C. The 1982 sources were the Appalachian basin (the US steel industry ran on Appalachian coal shipped up the Great Lakes and the Mississippi), the Ruhr, the Donbass, the Kuzbass, the Bowen Basin in Queensland, and the Gondwana coals of India, which are so low in caking power that India had to import coking coal to make coke for its own steel - a good illustration of how coal rank, not just coal carbon, is the relevant property.

###### Longwall coal mine at 300-1000 m `metal.coal-mine`

A coking coal mine in 1982 was almost always a mechanised longwall: a shearer cuts a 1.5-3 m thick seam across the face, the roof is allowed to collapse, the coal is loaded onto a pan chain conveyor and a main belt carries it to a preparation plant and up the shaft. The seam is a few metres thick, so the mine is a thin dark ribbon of coal a kilometre wide. Pennsylvania, the Ruhr and the Kuzbass are the three great coking coal provinces, and they are the geological reason those three places have both the coke ovens and the blast furnaces - the coal is too bulky to ship, so the steel industry grows where the coal is.

###### Bituminous coal seam (Middle and Lower Kittanning) `metal.coking-coal.seam` _(low)_

The leaf: a 2-3 m band of bright, banded, caking bituminous coal lying within a cyclothemic sequence of sandstone, shale and fireclay - the same sequence that holds the Pennsylvanian iron ore, coal and limestone together in the Appalachian basin, and the reason Pittsburgh is the steel capital of America. The Kittanning and the Freeport seams were the premium coking coals; the coal is Carboniferous, about 320 million years old, and it was deposited in a swamp.

###### Coal preparation: crushing, washing, blending `metal.coal-preparation` _(medium)_

Run-of-mine coking coal is crushed to under 50 mm and washed, because the ash that matters is the mineral matter - clay bands and pyritic nodules - that can be taken off by a dense-media wash at about 1.4-1.6 specific gravity. The washed coal then goes to a blending yard, because a coke oven wants a consistent blend and no single seam is consistent. Blending is done by a stacker-reclaimer in a yard, and the recipe is a metallurgical decision that is still made on the basis of the dilatation and the sulphur.

###### The wash plant tailings and the creek `metal.coal-tailings` _(medium)_

The other end of the coal preparation. Dense-medium washing rejects 15-30% of the mined tonnage as a fine waste with a high ash content, and in the Appalachian coal country in the early 1980s that waste was routinely placed in the creeks. The valley fills and the stream failures - the Buffalo Creek disaster in West Virginia in 1972 killed 125 people - were the reason the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 exists and why by 1982 a coal mine had to have a reclamation plan and a bond. So the coke chain in a 1982 C64 has, at its far end, one of the first major environmental regulations in the United States.

###### Rehabilitate the spoil by valley fill `metal.valley-fill` _(medium)_

The deep end of coal preparation's waste problem. In a contour mine the seam outcrops along a hillside, the coal is taken off along the contour and the overburden is pushed into the valley below, so the terrain ends up as a stream of grey waste from the highwall to the toe. It is cheap mining - no stripping, no trucks - and it is the reason the Appalachian coalfield has a hundred kilometres of dead grey creeks. In 1982 the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 required the mine to backfill and revegetate, with a bond per tonne, and that is the direct ancestor of the reclamation practices that the rest of the extractive industries adopted later.

###### Coking in a battery of by-product ovens `metal.coke.oven`

Two hundred and fifty horizontal chambers, 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide and 3.5-5 m high, arranged in a brick battery 40-100 m long, heated in the flues between them by coke oven gas and reheated to 1100-1300 C. A charging car pushes 20-30 tonnes of crushed coal through a hopper into each chamber in about 30 seconds; the chambers are then sealed, and 16-20 hours later the doors are opened and the red-hot coke is pushed out by a pusher machine onto a quenching car. That cycle, 16-24 hours, is the heartbeat of the plant and it never stops. In the meantime the gas coming off the coal - the raw coal gas, typically 15-20% hydrogen, 20-25% methane, 15-20% CO, 5% CO2, 20-30% nitrogen - has been drawn off, cooled, and cleaned of tar and ammonia.

###### Quench the hot coke, wet or dry `metal.coke.quenching`

The coke comes out of the oven at 1000-1100 C and must be cooled fast or it will keep burning. Wet quenching sprays it with 3-4 m of water in a 30-60 s tower; the water flashes to steam, the coke is cooled to about 200 C and comes out wet with 3-8% moisture, which the blast furnace operator hates. Dry quenching pushes the coke into a sealed horizontal chamber and cools it with nitrogen or recirculated coke-oven gas. In 1982 nearly every coke plant in the world was wet, and the change to dry came later, mostly driven by the same air-pollution regulation that hit the oven itself.

###### The coke quench blow tank and its drain `metal.coke.quench-blow` _(medium)_

Quenching has three products, not one: the coke, the water with the fine carbon in it, and the coke breeze - the 3-10 mm fraction that the blast furnace cannot use because it would be blown through the burden. Breeze is worth something: a coke plant sells it for sinter-plant fuel, for foundry moulding sand, and in 1982 increasingly for the electrode and anode pitch trade as a cheap carbon filler. So the coke oven's smallest product feeds three of the other branches in this file, and the water carries 1-3 kg of suspended carbon per tonne of coke quenched.

###### Coke oven gas and its by-products `metal.coke.gas`

The gas is the profit centre as well as the fuel. After cooling it goes through a primary cooler and a benzol washer, which strips out benzene, toluene and xylenes; then a saturator removes tar and ammonia; then a Quinolining or electrostatic precipitator removes the last of the dust. What is left is coke oven gas, which is burnt in the battery flues to supply exactly the heat the ovens need - the plant is roughly self-sufficient - and the surplus goes to the steelworks as fuel and to a chemical works as a benzene and ammonia feedstock. Crude benzene from the benzol washer is one of the most valuable by-products in the plant, and it is where the aromatic chemistry of the plastics agent's chain starts.

###### Coke oven benzene `chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar` _(medium)_

Byproduct benzene from the coking of coal in an integral coke plant: the coke oven gas is cooled and the aromatics stripped out with a wash oil, which is then steam-stripped, giving a crude benzole with toluene and xylenes. In 1983 coal tar benzene was still a major share of world benzene - more so in Europe and Asia than in the United States - and it is the one benzene of that era that is not a petrochemical at all.

###### The quench tower and the coke push `metal.coke.quench-tower` _(medium)_

The physical heart of the battery: a tall steel tower with spray nozzles fed by a 300 mm main, a receiving pan, and a surge hopper from which a 2-3 m pusher car pushes the cooled coke onto a belt. Behind it stands the battery, bricked with about 20,000 refractory bricks per oven chamber in the modern design and castable in the older one, all of which has to survive 1300 C cycling every twenty hours forever. The doors are the coke-side door on top and the charging door below, and the charging machinery is driven by a single large winch.

###### Coal tar and pitch: the binder under everything `metal.coke.tar-pitch` _(medium)_

The tar that comes off a coke oven condenses as a dense black liquid, and it is the source of three of the most important carbonaceous materials in this file. Distilled, it gives crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and pitch - the binder in the carbon anode, the coke-battery electrode, the extrusion die lubricant and the aluminium pot lining. A tonne of coke gives roughly 30-50 kg of crude tar, and a tonne of that tar gives a few tens of kilos of soft pitch. So the coke oven is upstream of the aluminium pot, the coke battery and the graphite electrode, and the carbon-anode branch of this file is not an independent industry at all - it is the coke oven's tar still.

###### Soft pitch and hard pitch `metal.soft-pitch` _(medium)_

Pitch is classified by softening point: soft pitch around 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard pitch above 110 C. The carbon anode wants a medium-to-hard pitch for the extrusion binder; the pot lining wants a softer grade that can be rammed hot. Pitch is also a dense, black, aromatic, carcinogenic material that has to be kept hot at every stage, so the anode plants had their own pitch melting and storage tanks. It is one of the dirtiest materials in the metals tree and one of the least replaceable.

###### Crude coal tar and creosote `metal.coke.tar` _(medium)_

The tar is separated into a light fraction (benzol wash oil and crude benzene), a middle fraction of heavy oils used as a coking-plant quench medium and a wood preservative, and a heavy pitch fraction. Creosote as a wood preservative is a genuinely large market and it is the same molecule family as the pentachlorophenol and the coal-tar pitch that the board and case coatings used. So the coke branch of this tree touches the plastics, the coatings and the timber-preservation branches as well as the metals one.

###### The coke oven feeds six branches of this tree `metal.pitch.from-pitch` _(low)_

Putting the carbon branch together as one loop. Coal is distilled for rosin and turpentine on one side and for tar and pitch on the other; the pitch becomes the binder in the carbon anode, which becomes aluminium; the coke from the same oven becomes the fuel for the silica reduction that becomes the metallurgical silicon that becomes the polysilicon; the coke breeze becomes the sinter plant's fuel; and the benzene becomes the styrene and the phenol and the epoxy resin. One oven on a 1982 coking plant therefore feeds at least six branches of this tree, and it is the single most connected node in the file after the quartzite.

###### Carbon anode for the Hall-Heroult cell `metal.carbon.anode`

Calcined petroleum coke at 90-95% carbon, ground to 1-20 mm, mixed with 25-30% of crushed and baked coke returns and 25-30% coal-tar pitch as the binder, extruded through a die with a threaded stud on the end, and roasted at 1000-1100 C for 20-30 hours. The point of roasting rather than baking is to drive the volatiles out before the anode goes into the cell, because an anode that gases in the pot poisons the metal. Consumption is 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium, and the anode is consumed continuously - which is what makes aluminium smelting a carbon business as much as an electrochemical one.

                            - *Coke oven benzene* `chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar` *(seen above)*
                            - *Soft pitch and hard pitch* `metal.soft-pitch` *(seen above)*
###### The battery, its flue and the chimney `metal.coke.battery`

A coke battery is a long brick building - 50-100 ovens in a row, 40-60 m long, with a 60-70 m chimney at one end and a quenching tower at the other. Between every pair of ovens is a heating flue, so there are twice as many flues as ovens, and the gas from the ovens is burned in those flues and the hot gas is then drawn up the chimney. The chimney is the tall thing on the coke works skyline, and it is there for the combustion products, not for a draft. A battery is a piece of 1880s engineering that has been continuously rebuilt ever since and is essentially the same machine today.

###### The cold-strip push and the bench `metal.coke.cold-strip` _(medium)_

The hottest, ugliest machine in the coking plant: a horizontal bar on a chain, 3-5 m long, permanently red, that pushes red coke out of the chambers onto the collecting bench. Its life is measured in weeks and its water-cooling is the operator's main concern. Everyone who worked on a battery in the 1980s had a job that was hot enough to need its own PPE rotation, which is the reason the whole industry has a 'coke oven man' occupational category and a very specific set of burn scars.

                      - *Quench the hot coke, wet or dry* `metal.coke.quenching` *(seen above)*
                      - *Coke oven gas and its by-products* `metal.coke.gas` *(seen above)*
###### The host basin and its caprock `metal.sphalerite.host`

The final leaf of the zinc chain is not a rock but a structure: a sedimentary basin with a metal-bearing horizon in it. The Red Dog deposit is a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin on the Tukarakka Peninsula; Broken Hill is a metamorphosed, deformed massive sulphide in a sequence of Proterozoic metasediments. In both cases the orebody sits at a specific stratigraphic level, and the mine is a series of ramps and stopes chasing a bedding-parallel body a few metres thick. So the zinc in a C64's die-cast key plunger came out of a bed that happens to lie a kilometre beneath a river delta.

##### Roasting of sphalerite to zinc oxide `metal.zinc.roasting`

The concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed or on a sinter strand, 850-1000 C, with the result 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. The 1980s plant that grew out of this is the roaster-sinter plant, in which the hot ZnO and Fe2O3 sinter together into a porous 'dead roast sinter' that is a much better feed for an acid leach than a fine powder. The SO2 at 8-12% goes to the acid plant. This roasting step is where a zinc smelter became a sulfuric acid producer of the same order as a copper smelter, and where the sinter plant's dust catch and its dewpoint control - keep the gas above about 150 C or the zinc and lead fume plasters the plant - became a real engineering discipline.

###### Fluidised-bed roaster `metal.zinc.roaster` _(medium)_

Concentrate is fed into a bed of 1-3 m of the roast itself on a distributor of tuyeres, held at 850-950 C by the fluidising air, and the bed overflows continuously into a hot cyclone and then a sintering conveyor where the last 100-150 C of roast and the sintering happen together. The whole thing was invented at the Balotelawezwa plant in South Africa and Canadian Calumet in the 1960s and was standard new-plant practice by 1982. An older plant would instead have used a multiple-hearth roaster or a sinter strand and produced a fine, un-sintered ZnO.

###### Catch the cadmium and lead in the roaster gas `metal.zinc.fume-catch` _(medium)_

The roaster gas carries a fine zinc oxide fume and, in the vapour phase, the cadmium and the lead. Economically the cadmium is the point: the fume goes to a baghouse, and the cadmium is recovered in a separate cadmium plant. The lead in the same gas is a nuisance and an occupational hazard, and in 1982 the zinc plants of North America were beginning to worry about it for exactly the reason they would later worry about it in the environmental context. The dust is one of the more awkward solid wastes in metallurgy because it is both valuable and toxic.

###### Copper-cadmium residue `metal.cadmium-residue` _(medium)_

A 1980s cadmium plant roasted the residue in a retort at 600-800 C: the cadmium volatilised off (it boils at 767 C) and was condensed in a condenser, giving 99.9% cadmium metal, while the copper stayed behind. This is the only major industrial source of cadmium, and it is a zinc by-product. It matters here only as a consequence of zinc refining; a C64 has no cadmium.

###### Zinc oxide sinter: the smelter's intermediate `metal.zinc.oxide` _(medium)_

The dead-roast sinter is the actual feed to the leach circuit, and its specification is a compromise between the roast and the leach. It wants to be as completely roasted as possible so that the zinc is all in the oxide, but it also wants to be porous enough for the sulphuric acid to reach it, which is what the sintering stage of the roaster-sinter plant is for. Between 5 and 10% of the zinc stays locked up in the silicate matrix and is lost in the leach residue, which is the second big reason a zinc plant's recovery is not higher than it is.

##### Acid leach and purification of the zinc sulphate solution `metal.zinc.leach-purify`

The dead-roast sinter is leached in spent electrolyte diluted with water, at pH about 4.5 and 40-60 C, in a series of leaching tanks. Then the solution must be purified, because almost every impurity that reaches the cell either consumes current or plates out on the cathode as a short circuit. Iron is removed by air oxidising the pH up to 5.2 so it precipitates as jarosite or goethite - a step that consumes zinc as well and is where most of the zinc plants' zinc loss is. Then copper, cadmium and cobalt are removed by adding zinc dust, which by cementation throws those metals out of solution. Chloride is kept down by jarosite precipitation. Every one of these is a chemistry rather than a metallurgy, and every one of them costs zinc.

###### Zinc dust for cementation `metal.zinc.dust` _(medium)_

The purification step uses zinc metal itself, atomised from a small kettle, as the reagent that throws out copper, cadmium and cobalt. The cemented metals - a black sludge heavy with copper and cadmium - is filtered off and shipped to a cadmium refinery, which is where the world's cadmium came from in 1982. So the zinc plant's purification residue is a cadmium ore in all but name.

            - *Copper-cadmium residue* `metal.cadmium-residue` *(seen above)*
###### Jarosite residue and the zinc it costs `metal.zinc.jarosite-residue` _(medium)_

The iron precipitation step that makes the zinc plant's chemistry work is also its biggest single loss. Oxidising the iron out at pH 5.2 throws down jarosite or goethite, and both of them carry zinc in their lattice - typically 4-10% Zn. At 1-3 tonnes of residue per tonne of zinc made, and 5-10% of the contained zinc never recovered, the iron removal step is where a zinc plant loses a million dollars a year. It is also a waste stream: acidic, iron-rich, and in the 1980s dumped in a lined pond. This is the residue the modern jarosite and goethite processes are designed to shrink.

###### Iron removal by the jarosite and goethite routes `metal.zinc.iron-removal` _(medium)_

The purification chemistry in one process. The leach liquor's pH is raised with limestone and the iron is oxidised with air in a bank of aeration tanks at 90-100 C. Whether the precipitate is jarosite (the older route, at pH 5.2 with sodium sulphate added, at 90-100 C over 10-20 hours) or goethite (the newer route, at 80-95 C with less retention time) decides how much zinc the residue holds and how much sulphate the plant makes. Every zinc plant in 1982 had made a choice between these two, and the choice is the single biggest determinant of its cost.

##### Electrowinning of zinc on aluminium cathodes `metal.zinc.electrowinning`

Zinc is one of the few metals won by electrolysis out of an aqueous solution at industrial scale. The reason is that zinc is more negative than hydrogen and would just deposit hydrogen from water if it were not for the high hydrogen overvoltage on aluminium; each cathode is an aluminium plate of 1-2 m2 and 10-25 mm thick, and the scraper at the top of the cycle knocks off a 5-25 kg slab. The slabs are melted in a small induction furnace and cast into 25 kg ingots at 99.995%. The energy is 3,000-3,500 kWh per tonne of zinc - high, but the purity and the by-product recovery make the route worth it for ores that cannot be smelted. This is the convergence point of the roast, leach, purification and ingot branches.

###### Lead-silver anode in the tankhouse `metal.zinc.anode-mb`

The insoluble anode is a lead alloy - 99% Pb with 0.5-1% Ag, cast as 10-40 mm thick plates - which works because when it does corrode slowly, the lead dioxide layer that forms is a perfectly good anode surface. Silver is added because it slows the corrosion. So the zinc tankhouse is structurally a lead operation: it consumes lead anodes at a rate of a few kilograms per tonne of zinc, which is one of the more elegant hidden cross-links between the lead and zinc branches in this file.

###### The single-deck electrolysis cell `metal.zinc.electrowinning-cell` _(medium)_

The 1980s zinc tankhouse cell was a plain open-top concrete or rubber-lined steel box, 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, with an aluminium cathode every 15-25 mm and a lead anode between them. The electrolyte is fed in at one end and pulled out at the other; the plates go in, run for 24-72 hours, come out, get scraped, and go to the melting furnace. A modern plant with 300,000-400,000 m2 of cathode area is a building the size of a football pitch. This is one of the least mechanised and most manually-intensive electrolysis plants in the industry, because the plate handling has never lent itself to automation.

###### Strip the cathodes and melt the SHG ingot `metal.zinc.stripping` _(medium)_

At the end of the cycle each cathode is lifted out, tipped against a steel plate that shears the zinc slab off, and the slabs are charged to a 100-500 kg induction furnace. The furnace has to be held at 450-470 C and under a cover flux because zinc oxidises readily and every gram of oxide is a loss. Two refinements came in during the 1980s: induction furnaces with better stirring and better control, and the move to a single large furnace rather than a fleet of small ones, which cut the oxide loss and the labour.

###### Special high grade zinc ingot, 99.995% `metal.zinc.ingot`

Twenty-five kilogram ingots, or the 500 kg minimum-content ingot that the bigger plants preferred by 1982. Special high grade at 99.995% was the grade specified by the galvanising industry and by die-casters, because both are very sensitive to lead, cadmium and iron. Two thirds of world zinc goes into galvanising and roughly a sixth into die casting. The four markets below are the whole of the demand: galvanising, die casting, electroplating with a chromate passivate, and brass. An ingot that misses any of the four impurity limits is unsellable, which is why the smelter spends its margin on the assay rather than on the metal.

###### Hot-dip galvanising of steel strip `metal.zinc.galvanising`

Steel sheet, strip or fabric is pickled in hydrochloric acid, fluxed in an ammonium chloride-zinc chloride bath, and dipped in a kettle of molten zinc at 450-470 C. The zinc wets the steel, forms an iron-zinc intermetallic, and the kettle surface is skimmed of dross by a wiper roll. Every galvanising line in the world consumed thousands of tonnes of zinc a year this way, and a big continuous strip line used 50-300 t a day. The C64 itself is not galvanised, but its chassis and any sheet-metal bracket, and much of the world around it, was.

###### Recover the zinc from the galvanising dross `metal.zinc.dross-recovery` _(medium)_

The iron-rich dross and the bottom ash skinned off a galvanising kettle are picked out, and the metal is recovered in a specialised horizontal crucible furnace, where the dross is heated with a flux and the iron drops out as Fe-Zn hard zinc. The remaining zinc is pumped out. A galvanising line therefore recovers most of its zinc, and in 1982 the galvanising industry was also the main secondary source of zinc, second only to galvanised scrap.

###### Zamak die-cast alloy and the pressure die-caster `metal.zinc.die-cast`

Zinc's most interesting product for this tree. A zinc alloy with 4% aluminium and a little copper - Zamak 3 is Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5, Zamak 5 with 5% aluminium for better die-castability - is injected into a steel die at 380-430 C under 20-150 MPa by a cold-chamber machine with 200-800 tonnes of clamping force. It fills the thinnest sections any metal can fill - 0.8 mm walls, and details you could not machine - and it holds a fine surface as cast. The 1982 pressure die-caster was a 350-800 tonne machine, and the seconds per shot multiplied by the shots an hour is the number that set the cost of a key plunger or a case bracket.

###### Zinc alloy melting furnace `metal.zinc.ingot-furnace` _(medium)_

The die-caster does not melt its own alloy from primary metal; it buys 10-25 kg alloy ingots of a certified composition and melts them in a thermostatically controlled holding furnace - typically a 100-500 kg crucible furnace with an immersed resistance heater and a lead bath to keep the alloy away from air.
