A crucible furnace full of molten zinc is the classic source of metal-fume fever among die-casters, because zinc oxide fume is generated wherever the surface is disturbed.

###### Electrolytic zinc plating of steel `metal.zinc.electroplate` _(medium)_

For small plated parts - chassis fasteners, brackets, EMI shields - zinc is electroplated rather than dipped. An alkaline cyanide bath, a non-cyanide acid chloride bath, or in the barrel a simple sulphate. The deposit is sacrificial: even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially and protects the steel underneath. A chromate passivation on top gives the characteristic yellow or olive colour and much better corrosion resistance, and by 1982 chromate was already being restricted because of hexavalent chromium.

###### Chromate conversion coating `metal.chromate-passivation`

A nitric acid or chromic acid bath - most often a sodium dichromate bath in 1982 - converts a zinc, tin or cadmium surface to a chromium oxide-hydroxide film a few hundred nanometres thick. Yellow is dichromate, olive is chromic acid, and the black 'iridium' used on some zinc die castings is a different chromate chemistry altogether. This is where the electronics industry met hexavalent chromium: not only in the plating baths but on every chromate-passivated steel part, on every tin-plated part that went through a passivation tank, and in the anode foil formation treatment. It is the reason the OSHA hexavalent chromium standard, published in 1971, was one of the first such rules in the United States, and it is a deliberate convergence point of the zinc, tin, aluminium-foil and chromium branches.

###### Brass (Cu-Zn) `metal.zinc.brass`

Zinc's largest engineering use is as the alloying element in brass and bronze. Brass is 60-95% copper with zinc, and the connector bodies, bus bars, shield cans and some switch frames in a C64 are brass, often brass plated with tin or nickel. Brass is melted and cast from cathode copper and zinc ingots in a small reverberatory or induction furnace, then extruded or rolled and machined. It is included because roughly a third of the world's refined zinc goes into brass, and because it is a genuine convergence of the copper and zinc branches.

###### Zinc oxide varistor: the mains spike clamp `metal.zinc-oxide-varistor`

The C64's power supply faces the mains directly. A zinc oxide varistor disc - ZnO powder pressed and sintered between two fired electrodes - sits across the input, and its resistance is astronomically high until the mains edge is exceeded, at which point it conducts and clamps the surge. ZnO is essentially a doped semiconductor ceramic: zinc oxide powder mixed with a few mol percent of the oxides of bismuth, cobalt, nickel, manganese and antimony, calcined, granulated with a binder, dry-pressed at 100-200 MPa, fired at 1100-1300 C, and cooled under a reducing atmosphere so the grain boundaries become the non-stoichiometry that gives the voltage knee. So the surge protection on the input filter is a zinc metallurgy product - and, incidentally, the same powder metallurgy as the ferrites.

###### Zinc oxide powder `metal.zinc-oxide-powder` _(medium)_

Zinc oxide for ceramics was, in 1982, made by burning high-purity zinc in air, by calcining high-purity zinc carbonate, or - for the highest grades - by the vapour-phase oxidation of high-purity zinc metal, which gives spherical sub-micron particles with a very tight size distribution. A varistor powder needs high-purity ZnO because any foreign phase at the grain boundary changes the voltage knee. So the varistor in the C64's power supply starts with 99.99% zinc.

#### Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless `metal.nickel`

Nickel is small in mass and enormous in function. In a C64 it is the plating on the connector shells and the gold-plated edge connector fingers' underlayer, the constantan and nichrome of the thin-film resistors on the board, the Invar of the composite-video circuit's chroma delay, and the bulk of AISI 304 and 430 stainless in the audio jack and the shield cans. 1982 was the year nickel was in a price crisis - the 1982-83 LME collapse, following the Escondida-adjacent and the Sherritt expansions of the late 1970s, took nickel from about $4/lb in 1980 to under $1.30/lb by 1983.

##### Nickel laterite (garnierite ore) `metal.nickel.laterite`

A soft, earthy, red-brown clay-and-laterite ore, really a weathering product of ultramafic rock: olivine and pyroxene in a serpentinised peridotite are altered from scratch, and nickel substitutes for magnesium in the clay lattice, giving garnierite. There is no nickel mineral to concentrate; the whole ore body is the ore. The great deposits in 1982 were the Cuban Moa and Nicaro operations - where the ore was shipped to the United States and Japan for the nickel limit of the United States Defense Production Act of 1981 made government stockpiling a political event - the Philippines' Surigao and Bacojo operations, the New Caledonian laterite, and the Queensland laterite. Laterite is mined in the open pit in soft, wet ground with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline, and often leached in place.

###### Bucket-wheel excavator laterite mine `metal.nickel.laterite-mine` _(medium)_

The soft, wet, deeply weathered ore is the ideal bucket-wheel material. A walking or rail-mounted bucket-wheel excavator with a 20-40 m boom cuts the overburden and the ore bench itself, dropping it onto a belt conveyor, and the ore goes to a long washing and screening plant rather than to a crusher. The Philippine and Cuban operations had bucket-wheel excavators with booms over 50 m by the early 1980s. The ore arrives at the plant as a slurry, which is why the pressure leach of the 1980s was designed for a pumped pulp and not for a dry concentrate.

###### Serpentinised peridotite `metal.nickel.peridotite`

The leaf: an ultramafic igneous rock, mostly olivine, now largely converted to serpentine, that has been chemically weathered for tens of millions of years in a warm wet climate. The nickel is in the clay and in the limonite, not in a crystal. Cuba, New Caledonia and the Philippines all have large serpentinite bodies, and that is why the island arcs of the Pacific are the nickel map.

###### The laterite washing and screening plant `metal.nickel.ore-washing` _(medium)_

The laterite arrives from a bucket-wheel excavator as a slurry, and it goes through a log washer, a scrubber, a screen tower and a series of hydrocyclones, and the -0.5 mm fraction is rejected outright as low-grade clay. The coarse fraction is dewatered on a screen and stacked in a concrete bin. In the Cuban and Philippine operations the stacked ore was then leached in place on a pad, in the Queensland operations it was dried in a rotary dryer and shipped to a furnace. The whole plant exists because the ore is a soft, wet, variable, low-grade bulk material, and the plants are mostly about handling water.

###### Limonite and garnierite: the two nickel minerals `metal.nickel.limonite-garnierite`

The leaf of the nickel branch, and it is a mineral solution rather than a mineral. There is no nickel mineral in a laterite. Nickel substitutes for magnesium in the smectite and kaolinite clays - the mineral is garnierite, which is really a mixture - and it substitutes for iron in the goethite of the limonite, so a limonite laterite's nickel is spread through amorphous iron oxide at a few percent. The two grades of laterite that matter commercially are the high-iron limonite ore and the low-silica saprolite ore, and the difference between them is the grade of the nickel-bearing lattice, which is why the pressure leach was developed for one and not the other.

###### Dry the laterite before smelting `metal.nickel.drying` _(medium)_

A laterite arrives at 30-45% moisture and the submerged arc furnace cannot take it wet, because the water costs more steam than the reaction releases. So the dewatered ore is dried in a rotary dryer or - in the Cuban and Philippine operations of the 1980s - in a suspension dryer with the hot flue gas, to below 1-2% moisture, and the drier's exhaust is the source of the dust and the fuel consumption that dominated the cost. Some plants solved the problem differently: the Queensland operations calcined and reduced the ore on the pad and then shipped a nickel oxide, which moved the water problem upstream to the leach.

##### Sherritt-Gordon ammonia leach and hydrogen reduction `metal.nickel.sherritt-gordon`

The process that unlocked the laterites in the 1970s and 1980s. The slurry is leached at atmospheric pressure with concentrated ammonia and oxygen at 50-70 C: nickel and copper form soluble ammine complexes while the iron precipitates as hematite. The pregnant liquor is heated in a pressure autoclave with hydrogen and more ammonia, and the nickel comes out of solution as a metal powder while the copper stays in solution as the ammine, so the two separate in one vessel. The powder is filtered, washed and dried in a rotary vacuum dryer. This is genuinely a 1980s technology - the first commercial laterite plant, at Browns River in Queensland, started in 1974 and Sherritt licensed the process to the Cubans and the Japanese in the second half of the decade.

###### The ammonia-hydrogen autoclave `metal.nickel.autoclave` _(medium)_

A 10-15 m long, 3-5 m diameter, titanium or 316L-lined pressure vessel in a 6-10 stage cascade. In each stage the liquor is contacted with hydrogen and stirred, and the nickel comes out onto the walls and the cooling surfaces. The whole chemistry depends on the fact that ammonia complexes nickel and copper so strongly that hydrogen alone cannot reduce them at atmospheric pressure; the autoclave gives the extra pressure to push the equilibrium over. Removing the ammonia and boiling the slurry then precipitates basic nickel carbonate, which is calcined to nickel oxide.

###### Nickel oxide (NiO) `metal.nickel.nickel-oxide` _(medium)_

The commercially traded intermediate. The pregnant solvent is stripped of ammonia and boiled, basic nickel carbonate NiCO3.2Ni(OH)2.4H2O drops out, it is filtered and washed, and it is calcined at 400-600 C to green-black nickel oxide at 99.0-99.5% Ni. In 1982 the overwhelming majority of nickel oxide went to ferronickel smelting; pure nickel oxide was a smaller but growing market for stainless steel and for plating.

###### Ferronickel, the laterite iron-nickel alloy `metal.ferronickel`

The dominant way nickel actually became metal in 1982. Dried laterite and quartzite are fed with coke into a large submerged arc furnace, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, running at 1350-1500 C. The laterite's iron is already present as hematite, so the whole charge reduces together and the product is not nickel metal but an alloy of about 60-75% Ni and 25-40% Fe, plus a slag of magnesium, silicon and aluminium oxides. The ferronickel is tapped and either refined in the same operation to pure nickel or - more commonly in the 1980s - sold straight to a stainless steel mill as a charge, which is why the whole ferronickel industry is really a stainless steel industry.

###### Nickel electrowinning from a pure sulphide circuit `metal.nickel.electrowinning` _(medium)_

Where the ore is sulphide rather than laterite, Sherritt's original ammonia-pressure process dissolves the concentrate in ammoniacal ammonium sulphate at 160-190 F (70-90 C) with oxygen, and then electrowins the nickel directly out of the pregnant liquor onto titanium cathodes in diaphragm cells at a very low voltage, about 0.5-1.0 V, because hydrogen evolution competes and the current efficiency is only 70-85%. This is the Sherritt-Gordon route as it was licensed in 1969-1972, and it is why the company is called after two towns in Manitoba. The cathodes are stripped, briquetted and remelted.

###### Nickel sulphide concentrate (Sudbury) `metal.nickel.sulphide-concentrate`

The Sudbury basin of Ontario was the world's nickel capital and it is a genuinely strange deposit: an impact structure full of shock-melted, metal-rich breccia at the base of a 1.8 billion year old impact crater, with pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8 and millerite NiS. The INCO operation mined both underground and, from 1962, from the open pit at the south end of the basin, and roasted the ore in fluidised beds to make 'fines' - a nickel-copper matte rather than a concentrate - before smelting. The tree therefore continues down through the Sudbury ore to a shocked sulphide breccia in an impact melt sheet, which is as geologically interesting an endpoint as this tree has.

###### Impact melt sheet at the base of the Sudbury crater `metal.nickel.impact-melt`

The leaf: a foot-thick to 20 m layer of rock melted and shock-altered by the impact, in which the nickel and copper sulphides were disseminated as droplets. It is a metamorphic and melt rock, not an igneous intrusion, and it is a band about 60 km long and 20 km wide across northern Ontario. The mining is ordinary room-and-pillar or open-pit on a sheet that lies only a few hundred metres below the Huronian cover.

###### Mond carbonyl refining (nickel from 99.9 to 99.999) `metal.nickel.mond`

Ludwig Mond's 1890s process, still used in the 1980s for the last nines. Nickel carbonyl Ni(CO)4 is formed at 50-60 C in a saturator, distilled off as a colourless liquid boiling at 43 C, and decomposed in a decomposer column at 200-230 C onto 99.99% nickel pellets. The trick is that the carbonyl of cobalt is much less volatile and iron forms a non-volatile carbonyl, so the distillation separates the three metals in one operation - the same volatility trick as the trichlorosilane column in the silicon branch. Cobalt is recovered from the residue as Co2(CO)8.

###### Dicobalt octacarbonyl, Co2(CO)8 `metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl` _(medium)_

The cobalt in a Mond residue is a genuine industrial source, and an unusual one: the residue left after the nickel has been volatilised as Ni(CO)4 still contains the cobalt as Co2(CO)8, and the two carbonyls are separated by exploiting the fact that dicobalt octacarbonyl is solid and will crystallise out while nickel carbonyl boils off at 43 C. In the classical route the residue is treated with copper at about 200 C under hydrogen to reduce both carbonyls, and then re-carbonylated to re-form Co2(CO)8, which is filtered and decomposed to metal. The consequence for the wider market is that every tonne of nickel refined by the carbonyl process is a tonne of cobalt that did not have to be mined, which is why the two nickel carbonyl plants at Sudbury and Kokkola were influential in the cobalt market well beyond their own output.

###### Why nickel carbonyl is the deadliest room in metals `metal.nickel.mond.safety` _(medium)_

Nickel tetracarbonyl is a colourless, volatile liquid that boils at 43 C and is lethal by inhalation at concentrations far below anything that can be smelled. A Mond refinery therefore runs on a rule that no one enters a carbonyl area without a respirator, that the vapour is continuously monitored at the floor and at breathing height, and that the whole plant is vented through a high-temperature incinerator that destroys the carbonyl before releasing it. The 1980s occupational-hygiene literature on nickel carbonyl is a case study in how a process can be kept running at all when the material is that toxic, and the number of fatal poisonings in nickel refineries over the century is a reminder that this is one of the most dangerous processes in the metals industry.

##### Electrolytic or cathode nickel, 99.9% `metal.nickel.ingot`

Nickel metal arrives at the user as a cathode or a briquette: 99.8% for ferronickel-grade stainless, 99.9% for stainless and for plating. For a plating line the metal arrives as matte or as a soluble anode, but in 1982 the majority of nickel plating anodes were still the insoluble carbon steel anode, with the nickel actually coming from the electrolyte as nickel sulphate made from nickel oxide. This is a deliberate convergence node: the laterite branch, the Mond branch, the plating branch and the stainless branch all meet here.

###### Nickel electroplating and the gold underplate `metal.nickel.electroplating`

The single most important metallurgical fact about nickel in a 1982 C64: gold plating does not sit on copper. It sits on a nickel underplate of 1-3 um, and the reason is electrochemistry - gold will not plate directly onto copper because the copper dissolves faster than the gold deposits, and a gold-copper diffusion couple makes a brittle, corrosion-prone joint. So the connector fingers and the IC leads get nickel and then a thin gold flash, or electroless nickel - a nickel-phosphorus deposit from a hypophosphite bath - followed by gold. The electroless route was standard in the semiconductor industry of the era and was how the die-attached gold on a hybrid IC was built.

###### AISI 304 and 430 stainless steel `metal.stainless.304`

The iron-chromium-nickel family, and a deliberate convergence point of three branches in this file. 304 is 18% chromium, 8% nickel, the balance iron - austenitic, non-magnetic, non-hardenable. 430 is 16-18% chromium with no nickel - ferritic, magnetic, and cheap. Both are made the way any steel is made: blast furnace for the iron, then a stainless steelmaking step that decarburises in an argon-oxygen decarburisation vessel, and the key is that the melt must not pick up more than about 0.05% carbon or the chromium goes into carbide and the metal loses its corrosion resistance. Stainless is the audio jack shell, the shield cans, some of the chassis and any fastener. Its cost is driven almost entirely by the chromium and the nickel, which is why the nickel price crash of 1982-83 directly cheapened stainless.

###### Cold rolling, bright annealing and finishing of stainless `metal.stainless.cold-work` _(medium)_

Stainless is rolled and formed by the same equipment as mild steel - a Sendimir mill, a continuous annealing line, a Timesaver - but the tooling is different, because austenitic stainless work-hardens violently and needs much more force, and because a bright anneal must be carried out in hydrogen or in a vacuum to avoid discolouration and to avoid needing a thick pickling. A 1982 bright annealing line used hydrogen at 1000-1100 C with dewpoint control, which is a very refined piece of metallurgy for a machine that cost $395.

###### Where a 1982 C64's stainless actually is `metal.stainless.jewel-audio` _(low)_

Not much: the outer shell of the composite or RCA connector, the shield cans over the analogue sections, some of the tuner and modulator housings, the hinge hardware, and any stainless fastener. In practice much of what looks like stainless in 1982 consumer electronics was nickel-chrome electroplated or tin-plated mild steel, because solid 304 in a thin stamping cost several times what a plating operation cost. The distinction matters and cannot be settled without the part.

#### Manganese: the steel deoxidiser `metal.manganese`

Manganese has no visible place in a C64, but without it the steel the case and the shielding are made from would have inclusions and blowholes in it. Almost all manganese ore is used to make ferromanganese, which is added to the steelmaking furnace as a deoxidiser and desulphuriser and as an alloying element. It is a branch included because the steel branch cannot honestly stop without it.

##### Pyrolusite and manganiferous ore, 25-50% Mn `metal.manganese.ore`

Manganese ore is almost never a clean manganese mineral. The Groote Eylandt and South African supergene ores are a hard, black, sooty mass of MnO2 cryptocrystalline material - wad and psilomelane - interbedded with iron formation. Grade is 25-50% Mn, and low-grade ore needs beneficiation: the South African ores were washed and jigged to reject the iron, and Groote Eylandt is washed in a scrubber and on a sluice. Silica and phosphorus are the two impurities that destroy value. This is a convergence node: the ferromanganese furnace, the ferrite branch's manganese carbonate and the steel deoxidiser all hang off it.

###### Supergene manganese mining in the Kalahari `metal.manganese.laterite-mine` _(medium)_

The Transvaal and the northern Cape were the world's largest producers in 1982 by a wide margin, and the operation was surface mining on a 5-20 m ore layer over a 100 m thick band of black manganese-bearing sandstone. Drag hoists, belt conveyors, and a scrubber-and-jig beneficiation plant, then a sinter belt. The ore is a black, hard, siliceous rock and it is dug out of a 30 m face.

###### Scrubber, sluice and jig beneficiation `metal.manganese.washing-plant` _(medium)_

Groote Eylandt and the South African operations do not smelt the raw lump: they wash it. The ore is dumped on a heap, a high-pressure water monitor scrubs off the fines and the clay, and the coarse goes over a sluice and a jig where the density difference between the manganese minerals (4.5-5.1) and the iron formation (5.0-5.3 but with a very different mineralogy) and the waste gangue separates the product. That is why a 30% Mn ore can make a 40% Mn product at low cost: the operation is a placer operation with a shovel in it.

###### The oxide and carbonate phases of the ore `metal.manganese.oxide-phase`

The leaf of the manganese branch's rock: the manganese in a supergene ore is not one mineral but four. Pyrolusite MnO2 is the black, soft, fibrous one; psilomelane is a barium-bearing cryptocrystalline mixture; braunite Mn2O3 is the hard brown one; and rhodochrosite MnCO3 is the pink carbonate in the primary zone. The refractory braunite is the one the smelter hates, because it takes three times the reductant and gives a high slag. Which phase a shipment is made of determines whether it goes to a ferromanganese furnace or to a chemical plant, and the assay is a chemical analysis, not a visual test.

###### Abyssal manganese nodule dredge `metal.manganese.nodule`

The other, entirely different source: polymetallic nodules lying in thousands of square kilometres of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone and the Peru Basin at 4,000-6,000 m depth, containing 30% Mn, 2% Ni, 1% Cu and 25% Fe. Collecting them means a 10,000-tonne ship dragging a pipe across the seabed for 20,000 hours a year. It was never commercial in 1982 - technology trials were running but no mine was producing - and the incentive that eventually made it real was nickel, not manganese. This node is here because the 1980s seabed mining industry was built by exactly the people looking at the ore as a nickel resource, and by 1982 the C64's nickel supply chain and this geological curiosity were the same corporate conversation.

###### Manganese oxide concretions on pelagic clay `metal.manganese.nodule-rock` _(medium)_

The leaf: millimetre-to-centimetre potato-shaped concretions of Mn-Fe oxide lying unattached in a soft abyssal red clay. The metal has precipitated out of seawater around a nucleus, slowly, over millions of years. It is the most extraordinary leaf in this tree: the manganese in a C64's steel is, in principle, available from the floor of an ocean.

###### The abyssal red clay beneath the nodules `metal.abyssal-clay` _(medium)_

The true bottom of the manganese branch: a soft, red, pelagic clay that covers the abyssal plains at 4,000-6,000 m and that took the better part of 100 million years to accumulate, one centimetre at a time. The nodules sit on top of it. So the deepest leaf in this tree is a handful of dark potatoes on a carpet of red mud at the bottom of the Pacific, and the entire industrial-manganese question of whether to mine it is a question about that carpet.

###### Why the 1970s nodule trials were abandoned `metal.manganese.nodule-tech` _(low)_

By 1982 seabed nodule mining was a real programme with real money behind it, and the money is the interesting part. The incentive was not manganese - the grades were assumed recoverable but nobody had proved it at scale. The incentive was nickel and cobalt, because the strategic metal studies of the 1970s and early 1980s concluded that the West had too little nickel and too little cobalt and that the seabed was the answer. The trials - the French Nodule, the American DOMES and NOAA work, the Japanese and the German programmes - put a collector on the bottom and brought up tonnages. Nothing commercial resulted before the 2000s, largely on legal grounds, but the 1982 assessment was optimistic, and that is a genuine piece of the 1982 story rather than hindsight.

###### The hydraulic collector head `metal.collector` _(low)_

The machine the whole idea rests on: a manifold of suction nozzles, 10-30 m across, towed along the seabed at 1-3 knots, that lifts the nodules into a riser pipe and up to a ship 4,000-6,000 m above. The 1970s trials worked at the point where the ocean is deepest to learn whether nodules survive being lifted - the attrition of the nodules on the way up turned out to be a genuine engineering problem - and the riserless concepts that would have solved it were still on paper. It is a beautiful illustration of how much of deep-sea mining is really a fluid mechanics problem.

##### High-carbon ferromanganese, Mn 65-80%, C 6-8% `metal.ferromanganese`

Made in a submerged arc furnace, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, at 1400-1600 C with the electrode tips submerged in the slag. The charge is sintered manganese ore, coke, limestone and often a good deal of iron ore, because the aim is an alloy of about 70% manganese at 6-8% carbon, and manganese is expensive enough that the industry buys more ore than stoichiometry requires in order to reach the assay. The manganese comes out as a carbide, Mn7C3, not as the metal, which is why the alloy has a carbon content at all. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: high-carbon ferromanganese is 6-8% C, not 13-15%; medium-carbon is 1-4% and low-carbon is under 0.5%, so 13-15% is not a real grade.

###### Sintering the manganese ore `metal.manganese.sintering` _(medium)_

Manganese ore is very fine and very friable, so it cannot be blown into a submerged arc furnace as a powder; it is sintered first, on a travelling grate exactly like the lead sinter, to make a 30-50 mm porous cake. The sinter belt at a manganese works is a zinc-works sinter plant or a lead-works sinter plant wearing different clothes, which makes it a nice example of a single machine serving three of the branches in this file.

###### Deoxidation and desulphurisation in the steel ladle `metal.manganese.deoxidiser`

Where the alloy is actually used. During tapping, ferromanganese is added to the steel. Manganese has a higher oxygen affinity than iron, so it combines with the dissolved oxygen to form MnO inclusions - which is the point: the oxygen is now safely tied up in an oxide the steelmaker can float out instead of being trapped as a gas bubble or an oxide stringer. Manganese also lowers the sulphur by forming MnS. The cost is that every kilo of manganese added becomes an inclusion unless the steel is properly deoxidised and the slag properly cleaned, which is why the amount is carefully calculated and why clean, low-inclusion steel is a specific technical achievement.

###### Aluminium and silicon deoxidation `metal.manganese.melt-deoxidation` _(medium)_

The last step in the ladle is the one that actually decides the steel's quality. Manganese ties up the bulk of the dissolved oxygen as MnO inclusions, and then a calculated addition of aluminium - 0.5-2 kg per tonne - ties up the rest as Al2O3. Those inclusions have to go, and in a well-run plant they are floated out in the ladle or removed later by degassing and filtering. Manganese is what makes the aluminium deoxidation work: without manganese in solution, aluminium would oxidise preferentially as Al2O3 straight out of the bath and never reach the steel.

###### Removing the inclusions: degassing and filtration `metal.manganese.inclusion-removal` _(medium)_

A modern low-sulphur steel has few MnS inclusions but a lot of fine Al2O3, and that is a different problem: fine alumina does not float out, so it has to be filtered. A 1980s plate mill that wanted clean, formable sheet for deep drawing or for tinplating ran a ladle through a vacuum degasser to flush hydrogen and nitrogen and then through a ceramic foam filter in the ladle, or poured through a tundish filter. This is the technology that made the C64's chassis panel and the tinplate base material reproducible rather than lucky.

###### The submerged arc furnace and its refractory `metal.manganese.furnace-lining` _(medium)_

A ferromanganese furnace is 25-100 MVA with three electrodes 1.5-2.0 m in diameter, and the difference from a silicon furnace is the slag: the ferromanganese process makes a large volume of a liquid, low-basicity slag, so the furnace is a slag vessel with an electrode in it. The shell is steel with a refractory lining of magnesite or magnesite-carbon, and the lining is eroded by the slag at 1500 C faster than in a silicon furnace. Carbon pastes, electrode paste made of the same coke-and-pitch as the aluminium anode, are rammed into holes in the roof around each electrode. So a ferromanganese plant is a coke-and-pitch shop as much as a manganese shop, which is the same convergence as the ferrochrome and ferrosilicon branches.

###### Graphite and carbon electrodes `metal.graphite.electrode`

The EAF electrodes, the submerged arc furnace electrodes of the ferrosilicon, ferrochrome and ferromanganese industries, the aluminium pot anodes, the silicon furnace electrodes and the large carbon blocks of a blast furnace hearth all consume the same two feedstocks: calcined petroleum or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as the binder. A 'graphite' electrode is green-milled from petroleum coke, extruded, and baked above 2500 C; a 'carbon' electrode stops at 800-1200 C. Pitch coke dominates for the graphite grades because it gives the higher density and the lower ash.

###### Why a ferroalloy smelter is built beside its power station `metal.manganese.smelter-electricity` _(medium)_

A 100 MVA submerged arc furnace draws about 80-90 MW continuously and cannot be stopped without destroying the furnace. So it needs a long-term supply contract and, in most cases, its own generating plant or a dedicated hydro or coal share. In the 1980s several ferroalloy industries - Norway's ferrochrome and ferrosilicon, South Africa's ferrochrome, Norway and Quebec's ferrosilicon - were built around cheap hydropower, and the industry's geography is essentially a map of where the cheap electricity was. It is the same fact as the aluminium smelter's, and the reason the same two or three countries dominated both.

##### Charge the ferromanganese into the steel ladle `metal.manganese.ladle-charging` _(medium)_

A ladle of steel is a bad place to drop a lump of ferromanganese, because the lump floats, the reaction is violent and the steel is left with unreacted alloy inclusions. So the FeMn is added in sized lumps and, increasingly in the 1980s, in cored wire - a steel tube filled with powdered ferromanganese and flux, fed into the ladle on a lance and dissolved by the passage of the steel through it. Cored-wire charging was a genuine 1980s development in secondary metallurgy and it improved the yield of the manganese, because it puts the metal into the steel rather than onto it.

#### Chromium: stainless, ferrochrome, hard chrome `metal.chromium`

Chromium does three separate jobs: it makes stainless steel stainless, it is the alloying element in the NiCr film resistors on the board, and as hexavalent chromium it is the hard chrome plating on switch contacts, the keyboard frame hinges and the RF shielding. The plating chemistry is the one with a body of regulation attached to it, and the ferrochrome industry is a South African monopoly that gave apartheid-era South Africa its nickname 'Chrome City'.

        - *Chromite ore (FeCr2O4), 38-46% Cr2O3* `metal.chromite` *(seen above)*
##### High-carbon ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr `metal.ferrochrome`

Chromite ore and coke are charged into a submerged arc furnace at 1400-1600 C with a chromite self-fluxing slag, and the result is an alloy of 60-70% chromium, 1-3% silicon and 5-8% carbon. It consumes about 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome - a fifth of aluminium's energy per tonne but on a much smaller tonnage. In the 1980s the industry was the classic vertically integrated single-industry town: the chromite mine, the power station with its 400 MW supply contract, and the smelter were all owned by the same company in the same town. The 1982-85 US and European voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome were aimed squarely at the market power of one country, and it is why ferrochrome is one of the very few metals where the 1982 price environment is a real story.

###### The self-fluxing chromite slag `metal.ferrochrome.slag` _(medium)_

A ferrochrome furnace is self-fluxing, which means the ore's own silica is balanced by the ore's own magnesia and there is nothing to add - the chromite is 16% MgO and 20% SiO2 and the ratio of the two is already about right for a liquid slag at 1500 C. That is why the smelter does not need lime, and it is also why the ore is smelted as it is rather than being beneficiated: a ferrochrome plant is a furnace and a power station, and the beneficiation happens in the ore dressing only if the ore is too fine to charge.

##### Argon-oxygen decarburisation and the stainless vessel `metal.chromium.aod`

The step that makes stainless steel possible. A 300-450 tonne ladle is fitted with a lance that injects a mixture of argon and oxygen under the steel surface. The argon stirs the melt and dilutes the carbon, the oxygen burns carbon to carbon monoxide, and because the gas is argon rather than air the melt does not pick up nitrogen - and nitrogen is exactly what stops 304 from being fully austenitic. At the end the gas is switched to pure oxygen and then back to argon to dilute the carbon without oxidising the chromium. The whole cycle takes 40-90 minutes and takes carbon from about 0.6% down to 0.03%, and it is why a stainless melt shop looks like nothing else in the steel industry. A deliberate convergence point of the chromium, nickel, ferrochrome and steel branches.

###### Where the chromium ends up in a 1982 C64 `metal.chromium.stainless-use` _(medium)_

AISI 304 in the audio jack shell, the shield cans and any stainless fastener or bracket; 430 where a magnetic ferritic grade was wanted. Chromium at 18% is above the roughly 11% needed for the surface to passivate, which is the whole trick: chromium forms a self-healing chromium oxide film about 2 nm thick, and that film is why stainless does not corrode. The passivation step in nitric acid is what removes the free iron that welding and machining leave on the surface, and without it the stainless rusts.

###### The AOD lance and its tuyere block `metal.chromium.aod.lance` _(medium)_

The lance is a 10-25 cm carbon-molybdenum or refractory tube lowered into the metal on a mast, and it carries both the argon and the oxygen. Around it sits a refractory tuyere block in the ladle lining with a single small hole through which the gas is injected into the melt, so the gas is introduced a few hundred millimetres below the surface and the stirring is far more effective than a surface lance. The lance itself is a consumable: the oxygen attacks the tip, and a lance lasts one heat or a few hours, so there is a pile of spent lances outside every AOD vessel.

###### The refractory ladle lining `metal.refractory-ladle` _(medium)_

The AOD vessel is lined with magnesia or with magnesia-carbon, and the slag at pH 5 or higher eats a basic lining - which is why a stainless ladle lining is more expensive and more carefully maintained than a mild steel one. The lining is a consumable of its own, replaced every few hundred heats. So the chromium branch reaches the bottom not only in an ore body but in a sea of magnesia sand, and the magnesia is from seawater or from a magnesite mine.

        - *Electrolytic chromium metal from chrome alum* `metal.chromium.metal` *(seen above)*
        - *Chromate conversion coating* `metal.chromate-passivation` *(seen above)*
#### Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts `metal.gold`

A C64 contains perhaps 0.2-1 g of gold. It is the flash on the edge-connector fingers, the plating on the IC leads, the ball or wedge bond from the die pad to the package, and the contacts in the 'jewel' switch mechanisms. Gold is the only metal that does not tarnish and does not form an insulating oxide, which is the entire reason it is used where an electrical contact has to survive years untouched. All of that gold is refined to 99.99% from an ore averaging a few grams per tonne, and in 1982 essentially all of it came out of a cyanide leach.

##### Low-grade gold ore (0.5-5 g/t) `metal.gold.ore`

Gold at a few parts per million is not visible and not dense in a hand specimen - it is in the ore as discrete grains, often only microns across, or in tellurides. Most of it is in quartz veins, often with sulfides. The 1982 world had two completely different industries: the deep underground Witwatersrand, where a 15 cm face of reef at 10-40 g/t gave 100,000 tonnes a day through mills, and the Carlin trend and the Nevada heap leaches, where 0.5-2 g/t in oxide rock was stacked in 10 m heaps and leached in place. The heap leach was a genuine 1970s invention and by 1982 it had become a third of Nevada's production.

###### Heap leaching with cyanide, 10 m pads `metal.gold.heap-leach`

Run-of-mine ore, after a cyanide spray test, is crushed to a few centimetres and stacked in 100,000-tonne heaps on an impermeable pad. It is flooded with 0.02-0.05% NaCN solution, allowed to percolate for 30-60 days, and then drained and sprayed again. The pregnant solution is sent through a carbon bed and then an electrowinning cell. A heap-leach pad is a piece of civil engineering first and a chemical plant second: the entire economics depend on the liner holding and the pad draining properly, and the cyanide inventory on a large heap is the largest single cyanide hazard in mining. After the leach the cyanide is destroyed with lime and ferrous sulphate and the pad is detoxified before closure.

###### Witwatersrand underground gold mining `metal.gold.wits-mine` _(medium)_

The other end of the industry. A 15 cm to 3 m band of gold-bearing conglomerate called 'the reef' lies at 1000-6000 m below the Witwatersrand, and from 1886 to 1982 the industry sank shafts and drove long decline haulages and ventilation and cooling galleries into it. Ventilation was the limiting factor: rock at 3000 m is at 40-50 C because of the geothermal gradient and because the rock is 3-6 C warmer than surface, so a mine 4 km deep needed refrigeration and a shaft fan development that took hours to boost air through the raises. Each shift broke perhaps 30,000 tonnes of reef in the mine and treated 100,000 tonnes in the plant, so the metallurgy was crushing a very hard quartzite and recovering maybe 60-70% of a 10-40 g/t ore.

###### Witwatersrand gold reef conglomerate `metal.gold.reef` _(medium)_

The leaf: a 2.9 billion year old quartzite with rounded pebbles of quartz and jasper in a fine matrix - a fossil beach. The gold is in the matrix, as discrete grains a few microns across, and the deepest part of the deposit has the highest grade because it is the oldest and the most distal. It is one of the largest gold concentrations ever formed and it is a sediment.

###### The uraninite in the Witwatersrand reef `metal.gold.uraninite` _(medium)_

The gold reef is also the world's largest gold-uranium conglomerate, and the same reef that was being mined for gold was being mined for uranium by a separate set of shafts from the 1950s onwards. The uraninite is present as discrete grains on the carbon seams, and it recovers in the gold plant's gravity circuits and in the tailings retreatment plants. So the uranium in the C64's power supply - in a 1982 it might have been a South African or Canadian utility's grid, but the fuel cycle is the same one - began in the same bed as the gold on the edge connectors. It is the single best example in this tree of one layer of rock supplying two unrelated metals.

##### Cyanide leaching of gold ore at pH 10-11 `metal.gold.cyanide-leach`

The reaction is 4Au + 8NaCN + O2 + 2H2O -> 4Na[Au(CN)2] + 4NaOH, and it needs three things: cyanide, lime to hold the pH at 10-11 so the cyanide does not protonate into deadly hydrogen cyanide gas, and dissolved oxygen. The pulp - ground ore plus lime, at 25-50% solids by mass - is agitated in an aerated pachuca tank or a Dorr agitator for 12-48 hours. The design variables are all about cyanide consumption, most of which is not gold dissolving but the cyanide reacting with the copper, iron and zinc minerals in the ore. In 1982 the plant that won was the one that kept the concentration as low as possible and the oxygen pressure as high as possible, which is the lesson of the 1986 Carbonin/Small's Pouso Bello mine disaster in Brazil, where 5-6 tonnes of cyanide went into the environment through a tailings dam failure and poisoned a river.

###### Pachuca tank and the Dorr agitator `metal.gold.pachuca` _(medium)_

The 1982 standard leach vessel was either a Pachuca tank - a tall cylindrical tank with a cone at the bottom and a compressed-air rising pipe that boils the pulp like a carbonated drink - or a Dorr agitator, a vertical tank with a rotating central shaft and radial arms and baffles. A typical circuit was 4-8 tanks of 30-60 m diameter in series, 6 m deep, with the air line serving as both the agitator and the oxygen supply. Life before the mid-1980s the industry moved to Dorr thickeners and to the large rectangular Dorr-Oliver leach tanks.

###### Carbon-in-pulp and activated carbon adsorption `metal.gold.cip`

Gold is present in the pregnant solution as the cyanide complex at only about 1 mg/L, far too dilute to precipitate or to recover directly. The industry fix is adsorption onto activated carbon: the slurry after leaching goes through a bank of 4-8 tall columns of 1.5-3 mm coconut-shell carbon, which takes up the gold. In carbon-in-pulp the carbon is instead added directly to the leach tanks and separated by a static or centrifugal screen. The carbon is then stripped in a hot caustic solution - with a few parts in a million of cyanide and, from the late 1970s, acetonitrile, which is what makes the strip efficient - and the gold is electrowon off a lead or stainless cathode, or smelted.

###### Activated carbon from coconut shell `metal.activated-carbon` _(medium)_

The adsorbent is a botanical product, not a mineral: coconut or palm-kernel shell, or coal, carbonised at 500-900 C and steam-activated at 800-1000 C until the pore volume is about half the material's bulk volume. The pore structure is what holds the gold cyanide. So the carbon in the carbon-in-pulp column is a plantation or coal-mill product, and by the 1980s activated carbon was becoming an industrial commodity in its own right.

###### Hard coal and petroleum coke as activated carbon feed `metal.activated-carbon.coal` _(medium)_

By 1982 the industry was moving off coconut shell, which had become scarce and expensive as the plastics and activated-carbon markets grew, onto hard coal and - as the process matured - onto delayed petroleum coke, which has the right isotropic pore structure and essentially no ash. The activation is the same: carbonise, then blow steam at 800-1000 C to burn out the carbon and open the pores, giving a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. So the carbon in a carbon-in-pulp gold plant in the 1980s was often made from the same coke as the aluminium anode and the coke battery electrode, which is one of the more unexpected places this tree's carbon converges.

###### Activate the carbon with steam at 800-1000 C `metal.steam-activation` _(medium)_

The step that makes charcoal into activated carbon. A bed of coke or coal is held at 800-1000 C while steam and carbon dioxide are passed over it, and the gas burns the carbon away, opening a pore structure with a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. The rate of the burn is the whole process: too fast and the structure collapses, too slow and the pores are too small to admit the gold cyanide complex. The gold is adsorbed as the ion-pair Au(CN)2- at the carbon surface, so the carbon's chemistry is an ion-exchange chemistry rather than a physical adsorption, which is why the carbon has to be chemically clean and why it has to be regenerated before its capacity falls too far.

###### Miller chlorination and the Aubure process `metal.gold.miller`

The refinery end. Gold doré - typically 90-95% gold with 5-10% silver - is fluxed with borax and litharge and blown with chlorine gas in an MRL (Mineral Resources Limited) chlorinator, heated by a propane torch, for 1-3 hours. The chlorine dissolves the gold as AuCl3 and the silver as AgCl, and the silver chloride precipitates as a crust. The gold is then stripped of the silver by the Aubure process - a hot parting - which reduces the silver chloride with wet wood chips and wet clay, a piece of technology that had not changed since the Middle Ages: the organic matter reduces the AgCl to metallic silver. What is left is gold at 99.5-99.9%, which is then electrorefined to 99.99% or cast directly into an anode.

###### Electrorefine the gold to 99.99% `metal.gold.electrorefining`

The Doré is cast into anodes and dissolved in an aqueous solution of gold chloride in hydrochloric acid at 50-60 C. The electrolyte is the Wohlwill process electrolyte, with a little silver nitrate added to make the silver chloride stay solid and drop out. Gold plates onto a pure gold or platinum cathode at 99.99% and the whole refinery runs at 2-5 V with a very high current efficiency. Every gold refinery in the world in 1982 used the Wohlwill process and it is essentially unchanged today.

###### Melt the dore bars `metal.gold.dore-melting` _(medium)_

Before the gold can be chlorinated it has to be melted, and the doré - whatever mixture of gold and silver the refinery is holding - is melted with a little borax and litharge in a clay or graphite crucible to 1000-1200 C and poured into a dore ingot weighing 20-50 kg. The litharge is what makes the dore pour cleanly, because it fluxes the oxide skin; it also means a little lead comes along, which is harmless because the next step takes it out. The dore is weighed and assayed, and that assay is the number on which the refinery is paid for the month's production.

##### Sodium cyanide from natural gas `metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis`

Cyanide is an industrial chemical, not a mined material, and its feedstock is the same natural gas that makes hydrogen cyanide for acrylonitrile. The Andrussow process is the cheap one: natural gas plus ammonia plus oxygen over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at 900-1000 C gives hydrogen cyanide, which is absorbed in caustic to give sodium cyanide. So the cyanide that leaches the gold that plates the connector comes out of an ammonia-and-air reactor fed with methane.

###### Ammonia (NH3) `metal.cyanide-precursor` _(medium)_

The nitrogen source for the cyanide that dissolves the gold. Ammonia is made in enormous tonnage for fertiliser and the cyanide plant buys a small part of it: natural gas and steam are reformed to hydrogen and nitrogen, the mixture is shifted, and about 15-20 MPa of hydrogen with nitrogen passes over a promoted iron catalyst at 400-500 C to give ammonia. The ammonia is then oxidised with air over a platinum or manganese dioxide catalyst to hydrogen cyanide and hydrolysed to sodium cyanide. The same ammonia is what the Sherritt-Gordon nickel leach and the potash-ammonia Solvay works buy.

###### Iron catalyst for ammonia synthesis `metal.habers-catalyst` _(medium)_

The hydrogen in the cyanide comes from ammonia, and the ammonia's Haber-Bosch reaction runs over a promoted iron catalyst made from magnetite or from mill scale. So the cyanide that leaches the gold, and the chlorine that makes the hydrochloric acid, and the aluminium in the case all hang off an iron-ore-derived catalyst in a gas works. This is the last of the deliberate cross-branch loops in this file, and it is a real one: the Haber-Bosch catalyst is a 1980s version of the same magnetite that this tree mines for steel.

###### Magnetite (Fe3O4) and the taconite route `metal.magnetite`

The other main ore. Magnetite is magnetic, so it can be separated from a low-grade run of rock by magnetic separation, and that changes the economics of the whole business. The Mesabi taconite of Minnesota at 25-32% Fe is ground to 30-45 um and concentrated to 65-70% Fe pellets on a concentrator with a 3 m diameter separator. Krivoy Rog and the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly in the Soviet Union are magnetite districts at 55-65%, worked down to 100 m depths with sublevel stoping. The magnetite is also roasted in a fluidised bed to hematite before magnetic separation, or sintered and reduced.

###### Magnetic separation and the taconite concentrator `metal.magnetite.separators` _(medium)_

The separator is a rotating drum 1-2.5 m in diameter with a 4-10 pole magnet of 400-1,200 gauss at the drum surface, or a high-gradient can of ferrite pole pieces that achieves 10,000-20,000 gauss on the tips. Slurry flows past and the magnetic grains are held to the drum and carried around until they fall off the other side. With the magnetoferrite in the drum the recovery of a 30-45 um magnetite grain is above 95%. A taconite concentrator at 20-40 Mt a year is one of the largest single streams of water and solids in the world, and the tailings are a billion-tonne deposit in their own right.

###### Ferrite magnets in the separator `metal.magnetite.ferrite-magnets` _(medium)_

A short and important cross-link: the permanent magnet inside a magnetic separator is a ferrite - barium ferrite or strontium ferrite, sintered like the power ferrites but with a different composition and without the permeability requirement. So the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace contains ferrite magnets, and the ferrite branch of this file is the same powder metallurgy.

###### Deep underground magnetite mining `metal.magnetite.underground`

The Soviet iron ore industry - Krivoy Rog, the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly, and the Khibiny - mined massive magnetite bodies at 300-1000 m with sublevel stoping, sublevel caving and room-and-pillar, on a scale with no real comparison anywhere else. The magnetite ore was magnetic enough that the mine was lit by the ore's own remanence in the early shafts. It is included to mark that the iron chain has two completely different mining geometries: a 300 m wide surface pit in Western Australia, and a 100 m thick tabular body a kilometre down in Ukraine.

###### Fluidised-bed roasting of magnetite concentrate `metal.magnetite.roasting` _(medium)_

The Krivoy Rog and Finnish magnetite concentrates were roasted before magnetic separation and before the blast furnace, because a magnetite concentrate that has been oxidised to hematite sinter is far easier to reduce - hematite is the reducible oxide, magnetite is not. A fluidised bed of concentrate with a magnetite-gangue composition can be held at 700-800 C indefinitely without sintering, and it is the only economical way to oxidise a hundred thousand tonnes of fine concentrate. The plant is a tall rectangular refractory-lined box with a bed of nozzles on the floor and water-cooled walls, and its throughput is enormous.

###### Oxide pellets and the direct reduction route `metal.magnetite.speciality` _(medium)_

A different branch of the same ore: magnetite concentrate is the only ore that can be reduced to sponge iron directly, without coke, by a hydrogen-nitrogen mixture at 1100-1200 C in a shaft furnace. That is the MIDOR and HYL processes, which by 1982 were the strategic reserve of the steel industry in the oil shock years - a few per cent of world steel but a hedge, and the reason a Soviet or Brazilian or Venezuelan integrated steelworks would spend a decade building an ore-based direct-reduction plant. It is also the only ore that can be shipped as a pellet and reduced at a distant site without smelting.

##### Refined gold anode, 99.99%, and the plated flash `metal.gold.ingot`

The gold that reaches the electronics industry is 99.99% minimum, as a rolled sheet or an anode, and it is used in three ways. Flash plating for connector fingers and IC leads: the gold is dissolved in a cyanide gold bath - typically a gold cyanide, potassium cyanide, gold hydroxide bath at 0.5-2 g/L gold - and deposited on the nickel underplate at 0.1-1 A/dm2 for a few seconds, giving 0.05-0.25 um. Wire bonding: 15-50 um pure gold wire, drawn through diamond dies like copper, is welded from the die pad to the package lead with a thermosonic bonder. And sputtering: thin film resistors and the gold metallisation on some hybrid ICs were gold, sputtered from a cathode.

###### Gold wire bonding of the die `metal.gold.wire-bonding`

Each die has to be electrically connected to the package. The 1982 method was wire bonding: a 25 um gold or aluminium wire is threaded through a ceramic or carbide capillary, the tip is melted by a discharge or by a heated work holder, and the first weld is made to the die's aluminium pad. The wire is then run out and the second weld is made to the package bond pad, and the wire is cut. A 40-pin chip has 80 of these welds per package, each under a milligram of gold, and the whole thing happens a thousand times a minute. Aluminium bonding wire was already displacing gold on most logic parts by 1982 for cost reasons, but gold remained the default for anything requiring a conductive epoxy or a eutectic die attach.

###### Gold-plated contacts: the edge connector and the switches `metal.gold.contact-jewel` _(medium)_

Two very different gold contacts in the C64. The 62-way edge connector at the rear has gold-flashed fingers - a 35 um copper-alloy finger with 0.1-0.5 um of gold and a nickel underplate, inserted in the board by a wipe in the card guides. The keyboard and the rocker switches use either gold-plated copper-alloy leaf springs or, in the better keys, solid silver or silver-alloy contacts. The gold flash on the edge connector is the only place where gold must survive thousands of insertions, and it does so because the nickel underplate stops the copper from diffusing into the gold and the gold itself never oxidises.

#### Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing `metal.silver`

Silver is the most electrically conductive of any element, and it is used in a C64 where the contact has to carry current at low force: the contacts of the rocker switches and of many of the keyboard switches, the silver-bearing solder and brazing alloys for the heat sinks and chassis joints, the silver-filled epoxy and silver ink of the keyboard membrane, and the silver that comes out of the lead and copper refineries as a by-product. Most of the world's silver is mined as a by-product - of lead, of copper, of zinc - and only about a fifth comes from a primary silver mine.

##### Silver ore and the by-product sources `metal.silver.ore`

Silver behaves chemically like lead, so it substitutes for it in galena, and the world's most productive silver mines are really lead mines. The primary ores are native silver, argentite Ag2S, pyrargyrite Ag3SbS3 and stephanite Ag5SbS4 - the last two are why silver is also a lead-bysulphide metallurgy problem. The Cordillera Real of Potosi in Bolivia and Zacatecas in Mexico were the great producers, and Cobalt in Ontario is the historical outlier where silver was the target. Silver at 500-1000 g/t is a very good ore and at 5-50 g/t it is a credit.

###### The Zacatecas-Potosi silver vein mines `metal.silver.mine-mexican` _(medium)_

Mines like the Fresnillo, the Zacatecas and the San Luis Potosi: an underground operation on steeply dipping epithermal quartz veins carrying native silver, argentite and the antimony sulphides, worked in the Spanish colonial era by water-driven mills, mercury amalgamation and patio amalgamation, and by 1982 by mechanised narrow-vein mining and flotation. The Fresnillo mine is a silver mine that also happens to be the world's largest producer of antimony, which is a neat illustration of the interpenetration of these branches.

###### Mercury amalgamation of small silver operations `metal.silver.amalgamation`

Before cyanide, silver was recovered by amalgamating the crushed ore with mercury: 4Au + 8Hg -> 4AuHg4 and 4Ag + 4Hg -> 4Ag2Hg, then squeezing the amalgam in a heated press and retorting the sponge at 500-700 C to drive the mercury off and recover the metal. The process left 10-100 grams of mercury per tonne of ore behind in the tailings, and it is one of the largest anthropogenic mercury dispersals in history. In 1982 it was in decline in the large mines and still widespread in artisanal operations; in the small artisanal miners' union of Guanajuato it outlived the century.

###### Mercury: cinnabar from Idrija and Almaden `metal.mercury-source` _(medium)_

Amalgamation consumes mercury and does not give it back, so a silver mine that amalgamated needed a mercury supply. Cinnabar, HgS, the vermilion pigment mineral, came from Idrija in Slovenia - the largest mercury mine in the world for 500 years - and from Almaden in Spain, and from the New Idria and New Almaden mines in California. The leaf is a mercury deposit, which is itself a strange one: cinnabar forms in shallow hydrothermal systems, and the Spanish and Yugoslav mines are in exactly the kind of fractured carbonate and volcanic rocks that the precious-metal branches of this file have already been through.

###### The cinnabar vein `metal.cinnabar.bed`

The leaf: a scarlet vein of cinnabar in brecciated limestone, sometimes 10 m wide, worked by open pit and by fire-setting underground since Roman times. It is the only mercury ore that has ever mattered commercially, and it is a beautiful and rather grim example of a metal that exists in one mineral, in one setting, in a few places on Earth.

###### Silver mill: crushing, grinding and flotation `metal.silver.mill` _(medium)_

Ore at 300-1500 g/t is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground in a ball mill to 50-100 um, and floated with a xanthate or a thio compound collector at pH 8-10. Silver sulphides float with the lead and zinc sulphides they are intergrown with, so the circuit produces a bulk concentrate that the smelter treats as a lead concentrate. The recovery is 60-85% and the tailings are the reason the Zacatecas and Guanajuato districts look the way they do - a very large volume of finely ground rock in long, engineered tailings impoundments.

###### Why silver concentrate goes to a lead smelter `metal.silver.concentrate-shipping`

A silver concentrate is not a product anybody wants to buy; it is a concentrate to ship to a lead smelter 500 km away, because the only economical way to separate silver from lead is the Parkes process, and that needs a lead smelter. So the silver chain leaves the mine, joins the lead chain inside a smelter that may be in a different country, and comes back out at 99.9%. This is the practical meaning of silver being a by-product metal, and it is why the silver price has so little to do with the silver mines.

              - *Lead blast furnace reduction to crude lead* `metal.lead.blast-furnace` *(seen above)*
##### Refine the silver to 99.9-99.99% `metal.silver.refining`

Most silver never gets a refinery of its own. It is separated inside the lead smelter and refinery, or the copper anode slime, and refined there. The copper route: the slime is dissolved in nitric acid or in an aqua-regia type circuit, silver precipitates as silver chloride which is then reduced with copper and melted, and gold is recovered separately. The lead route: the Parkes process and the cupellation furnace described in the lead branch deliver silver at 96-99%, and it is electrorefined in a small silver tankhouse with a silver anode and a silver cathode in a nitric acid or a copper nitrate electrolyte at 2-4 V. In 1982 perhaps 60% of the world's refined silver was made at a handful of silver refineries and the rest was by-product metal refined alongside lead and copper.

###### Silver ingot, 99.9%, and silver contact material `metal.silver.ingot` _(medium)_

A 99.9% ingot is the standard commodity grade, cast as 0.5-1 kg bars or as a 15-30 kg or 1000 troy ounce bar. For the contacts of the C64's switches and keys the relevant alloy is not pure silver but a silver-cadmium-oxide or silver-tin-oxide electrical contact material - a silver matrix with 5-15% of a refractory oxide that reduces the contact resistance rise caused by metal transfer, at the cost of a bit of conductivity. Silver-graphite is a related and very common sliding contact material: 50-95% silver in graphite, sintered and infiltrated, used where the contact has to rub.

###### Electrolyse the silver and the dore loop `metal.silver.electrorefining` _(medium)_

The silver from the Parkes cupellation or from the anode slime is cast as anodes and dissolved in a nitric acid electrolyte with a little silver nitrate, at 2-4 V with a pure silver cathode. The electrolyte's job is to hold the silver as the nitrate while the gold and the base metals either stay in the anode mud or fall out as slime. A small refinery might have 20-40 cells and make 5-20 t a month. The silver cathode is then melted and cast, and the whole cycle - cupell, electrorefine, cast, cupell again - can run three times to get five nines.

###### Silver contact powder: Ag-SnO2 and Ag-graphite `metal.silver.contact-powder` _(medium)_

A switch contact is not silver metal. It is a powder metallurgy composite: 80-95% silver powder mixed with 5-15% of a refractory oxide - tin oxide, cadmium oxide or graphite - pressed at 200-400 MPa and sintered at 700-950 C. The oxide breaks up the silver grain boundaries and suppresses the metal transfer that otherwise builds up on a small, low-force contact, at the price of some conductivity. Silver-graphite is the same idea for sliding contacts, and silver-graphite in a rotary encoder or a potentiometer is the single most common use of silver powder in electronics.

###### Fire assay with borax and litharge `metal.silver.borax-flux` _(medium)_

A refinery that also assays needs a cupellation furnace and a borax flux, because silver is assayed by cupellation: the sample is mixed with borax and litharge, cupelled, and the silver bead that is left is weighed. So the assay and the refining process are the same process, which is why a small refinery has a cupel furnace whether or not it refines. It is also why the assayer's skill and the refiner's skill are the same skill, and why the price of silver has always been set by a weighing scale on a furnace roof.

#### Tantalum powder for electrolytic capacitors `metal.tantalum`

A 1982 C64 has a handful of tantalum capacitors on the mainboard, in the analogue filter section, and tantalum beads in small packages. Each one is a sintered porous tantalum anode with a tantalum oxide dielectric and a solid manganese dioxide or a liquid electrolyte. The tantalum metal is won from columbite-tantalite, a refractory oxide ore, through a hydrofluoric-acid digestion that is one of the most corrosive industrial processes in existence. In 1982-83 there was a real tantalum supply crisis - the Congo and Brazil supply, the Botswana and Zimbabwe expansions, the US stockpile, and a price that doubled - and it is the one place in this tree where a commodity shock from a mining country touched a home computer.

##### Columbite-tantalite concentrate `metal.columbite`

A hard, black, sub-conchoidal mineral - (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 - that in practice is never a pure species but a solid solution, and that is the whole problem of the tantalum industry: tantalum and niobium are chemically almost identical and always occur together, with the tantalum content ranging from a few percent to more than 50% of the total. The separation is the entire industry. The main 1982 sources were the Greenbushes and Wodgina pegmatites in Western Australia, the Cat Creek and Oarkopper operations in Brazil, and the columbite-tantalite concentrates from the Congo, Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Tantalum-bearing tin slags from Malaysia and Brazil were a secondary source.

###### Pegmatite open pit with sluicing `metal.columbite.mine` _(medium)_

The tantalum ore is in a pegmatite dyke, a very coarse-grained granite intrusion, and the extraction in the small operations is almost artisanal: the dyke is blasted, the rock is crushed and hand-sorted, and the heavy tantalum minerals are concentrated on a sluice or a jig. The Greenbushes operation, at the time one of the largest, mined a 3 km pegmatite by open pit with a 200,000 t/year plant. So the tantalum in a 1982 C64's capacitors very plausibly came out of an Australian open cut in a pegmatite, hand-sorted and sluiced.

###### Granitic pegmatite dyke `metal.columbite.pegmatite`

The leaf: a coarse-grained, quartz-feldspar-mica rock so coarse that individual crystals are centimetres across, with the tantalum-bearing minerals in small pockets of rare-metal enrichment. Pegmatites are the last-crystallising fraction of a granite magma, so they are the natural home of every incompatible element - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, rare earths. There is no more apt end point for the tantalum chain than a dyke of crystals bigger than your fist.

###### The crystals and the rare-metal pockets `metal.pegmatite-crystals`

The leaf of the tantalum branch. A pegmatite is the last thing a granite magma crystallises, and because it is water-rich and volatile-rich it can hold elements that have no business being in a granite at all - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, tin, the rare earths - at hundreds of times their normal concentration. Those elements concentrate in the last pockets to crystallise, and a pocket 30 cm across can hold a few kilos of coltan worth more than the whole pegmatite around it. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor came out of small pockets in a last-stage granite pocket, hand-sorted out of a rock whose crystals are bigger than your fist, in a pegmatite that is less than 0.1% tantalum.

###### Coltan concentrator: gravity, magnet and electrostatic `metal.columbite.concentrator` _(medium)_

The coltan upgrade in a small operation is a classic three-stage gravity and magnetic plant: a shaking table or a jig throws away the quartz and mica, a magnetic separator takes off the magnetite and ilmenite, and a second gravity stage with a dense-medium separator makes a 20-30% Ta2O5 concentrate from a 0.05-0.1% pegmatite. Electrostatic separation takes out the zircon. The mass yield is under 1%, so the concentrator's job is mostly to throw away 99.5% of the rock, which is why a coltan operation is a small, cheap, labour-intensive plant sitting next to the pit rather than a large mill.

###### Coltan tailings `metal.columbite.tailings` _(low)_

A coltan concentrator throws away over 99% of the mass it treats, and in the artisanal operations of the 1970s and 1980s that was put into the creek bed without any attempt at settling, and the creek carried it away. The ecological consequence of that was small compared to what followed - the coltan rush of 2000-2008 - but the mining itself was the problem and the tantalum industry spent most of the 1980s designing a better process and a better tailings facility precisely because it was planning for exactly the kind of scrutiny it eventually got. A node whose importance is only visible in hindsight.

##### Hydrofluoric acid digestion at 100-200 C `metal.tantalum.hf-digest`

The concentrate is digested in a mixture of hydrofluoric acid, nitric acid and hydrochloric acid at 100-200 C in a Teflon-lined or Monel vessel with a condenser to keep the HF in the loop. Ta2O5 and Nb2O5 both dissolve as pentafluorides, while iron, tin, thorium and most of the rare earths stay as insoluble fluorides or oxides and are filtered off. Thorium in particular is a problem: it is a radioactive alpha emitter that comes with the coltan and has to be separated and disposed of carefully. The mixed HF/HNO3/HCl digestion was the industry standard for decades; the Bayer process digest, using anhydrous HF with calcium fluoride at 150-200 C, arrived later.

          - *Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar* `metal.hydrofluoric-acid` *(seen above)*
###### Thorium in the coltan: a radioactive by-product `metal.tantalum.thorium` _(medium)_

Columbite-tantalite carries thorium and uranium in solid solution, typically 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2, and because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths it follows them through the whole fluoride circuit and reports with the rare-earth product. It is an alpha emitter, so the refinery's thorium residue is a radioactive waste that has to be stored, and in 1982 the disposal arrangements in most producing countries were informal. The leaf is a radioactive waste site, which is a legitimate if slightly grim terminus for a branch of the metals tree.

###### Monazite concentrate and the beach-sand placer `metal.rare-earths.monazite`

Monazite, (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4, is a heavy placer mineral from the beach sands that carry ilmenite, zircon, rutile and xenotime with it - the Kerala and Queensland and Cape Breton sands, worked by a dredge and a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnet and an electrostatic separator. It holds 20-30% rare-earth oxides and, because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths', 5-30% ThO2 as well. That thorium is the practical difficulty and the reason monazite had been worked mainly for its heavy minerals: it follows the rare earths through the whole separation chemistry and has to be parked in a radioactive residue. Monazite is mined for thorium, for the heavy minerals and, in a few places, for the rare earths themselves. It is also an impurity that a coltan refinery has to filter off its fluoride solution.

###### The heavy-mineral beach and its dredge `metal.monazite.beach`

A beach on the east coast of Queensland or on the Malabar coast of Kerala where the wave has concentrated ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite and xenotime into a dark, 1-10% heavy-mineral band a metre or two thick in the sand. It is worked by a cutter-suction dredge or a walking dredge on a barge, which pumps the sand onto a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnetic separator and an electrostatic separator. This is the shared geological endpoint of a surprising amount of this file: the titanium dioxide, the coltan, the thorium residue, the rare earths and the zircon all came out of a band like this one, which is why a capacitor's tantalum and a television's red phosphor can be argued about at the same beach.

###### Caustic soda bake to split the rare earths from the thorium `metal.rare-earths.monazite.caustic-bake` _(medium)_

Monazite is a refractory phosphate, so the industrial split between the rare earths and the thorium is a matter of finding a lye that will dissolve one and not the other. A 50% caustic soda solution is mixed with the sand and taken to about 140-150 C for several hours; the phosphate is broken down and the rare-earth elements go into solution as hydroxides, while thorium and uranium stay behind as comparatively insoluble hydroxides in the residue, where they concentrate into a radioactive waste that has to be stored. The pregnant liquor is then diluted, filtered and taken to the separation plant. An acid digestion at 150-200 C does the same job more cheaply on some ores and worse on others, because it dissolves the thorium too and puts the separation problem downstream.

            - *The heavy-mineral beach and its dredge* `metal.monazite.beach` *(seen above)*
###### The fluoride digestion vessel `metal.tantalum.digest-vessel` _(medium)_

The digestor is the most aggressively corrosive piece of equipment in the metals tree. Anhydrous hydrofluoric acid at 100-200 C attacks glass, attacks most metals, and attacks concrete; so the vessel is Monel, nickel, or Teflon-lined, with the condenser and the piping also in Monel, and there is a continuous fluoride leak problem because HF is off-gassing from a boiling slurry. The industry answer through the 1980s was the Monel plant, with a steam stripping system to recover the HF and a caustic scrubber on the vent, and it was the single largest reason the industry needed a process chemist rather than a metallurgist.

###### Monel: nickel with copper `metal.nickel-monel` _(medium)_

The alloy that made the fluorine chemistry of the 1980s possible: 60-70% nickel with 30% copper, and sometimes molybdenum, made in the same vacuum-melted, cast-and-rolled route as any nickel alloy. Monel resists hydrofluoric acid better than almost anything because the nickel fluoride film that forms is protective while aluminium fluoride and steel fluoride are not. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor was separated in a vessel made of a nickel alloy that came out of the nickel branch of this same file, and the aluminium capacitor in the power supply is made with an acid that would destroy it.

##### Separation of tantalum from niobium: K2TaF7 `metal.tantalum.separation`

From the fluoride solution the tantalum is selectively precipitated as potassium heptafluorotantalate, K2TaF7, by adding potassium chloride and hydrofluoric acid at 70-90 C - and this is the step that separates it from niobium, because K2TaF7 is far less soluble than K2NbF7. The K2TaF7 crystals are filtered, washed and dried. Then the metal is won from it in one of two ways. The potassium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with liquid potassium metal, or with sodium, at 700-800 C, giving a coarse tantalum powder. The aluminium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with aluminium in an induction furnace, and the charge is self-separating by particle size - the tantalum comes out as the finer powder and the aluminium-fluoride slag on top. The capacitor industry wanted the sodium-reduction powder specifically, because it could be made much finer.

###### Tantalum powder `metal.tantalum.powder`

The anode of a tantalum capacitor is a pressed and sintered tantalum pellet of porous sintered tantalum powder, sintered at 1200-1400 C under vacuum, then anodised - electrolytically grown Ta2O5 - to a formation voltage of about 2-4 times the working voltage. The dielectric is the anodised oxide itself, which is why a tantalum capacitor is a bipolar electrolytic part with no liquid. The powder must be pure and must be milled and classified so the particle size is right for the pellet's porosity: a sintered pellet has to have a tortuous pore path, or it will short.

###### Recycling the potassium and fluorine `metal.tantalum.kcl-cycle` _(low)_

The potassium in K2TaF7 and the fluorine in it both come back. The mother liquor from the precipitation is evaporated and the potassium is recycled, and the fluoride is recovered from the aluminium fluoride slag in the metal reduction by hydrolysing it to fluoride and re-fluorinating. A modern tantalum plant's fluorine and potassium consumption is a small fraction of its theoretical requirement because of this loop, and the 1980s plants were learning it. It is a small detail that says something about how tight the tantalum business economics were - and the answer is that they were tight enough to make the 1982-83 supply crisis severe.

      - *Coke and coke oven gas: the reducing agent* `metal.coke` *(seen above)*
#### Steel: sheet, stainless, tin plate, tool steel `metal.steel`

Steel is the machine's frame, its shields, its fasteners and its tooling, and in mass it dominates everything else in the C64. The route is: iron ore plus coke plus limestone into a blast furnace for hot metal; hot metal plus oxygen plus scrap into a steelmaking vessel; steel through a continuous caster into a slab; slab through a hot mill and a cold mill into sheet. Then three specialties matter for this tree: grain-oriented electrical steel for the power supply transformer, stainless for the jack and the shields, and hardened tool steel for the injection moulding dies and the extrusion dies.

##### Blast furnace hot metal (4.3% C) `metal.iron.hot-metal`

A 25-30 m tall, 8-11 m wide stack, charged at the top with sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and limestone, and blown at the bottom through 3-4 tuyeres with 1000-1300 C blast at a pressure of 2-4 bar. The iron oxide is reduced in stages on the way down - hematite to magnetite at 400-600 C, magnetite to wüstite at 700-900 C, wüstite to iron below 1000 C - and the carbon goes out as CO. The iron arrives at the hearth as a liquid at about 1450-1550 C, containing 3.5-4.5% carbon, 0.3-1% silicon, 0.1-0.2% manganese, 0.05-0.1% phosphorus and about 0.5% sulphur, and it is tapped every 4-6 hours. The slag floats on top and is tapped separately. A 1982 furnace made 5,000-15,000 t of hot metal a day on 3,000-4,500 m3 of volume and consumed about 400,000 m3 of blast a minute.

###### Blast furnace burden: sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and flux `metal.iron.burden` _(medium)_

The furnace eats a precisely weighed blend, batched in 1-3 t bins and dumped in a rotating order around the bell-less throat so the burden descends evenly. Sinter is 55-65% Fe and 8-12% gangue; pellets are 62-66% Fe and are nearly always the majority of the iron-bearing burden in a modern furnace because they are uniform and permeable; lump ore is 45-60% Fe and is in retreat. The blend is sized and ground so it is permeable enough for the gas to reach the burden and rigid enough not to collapse into the raceways.

###### Sinter the fine ore on a travelling grate `metal.sinter`

Fine iron ore cannot be charged into a blast furnace - it would be blown away or it would pack. So it is sintered: mixed with 8-12% returning sinter fines, 5-7% coke and 10-20% lime, moistened to 6-8%, spread in a 0.7-1.0 m bed on a travelling grate, and ignited. At 1200-1400 C the bed self-fuses into a porous 100-150 mm cake. A modern sinter strand produces 3,000-6,000 t of sinter an hour and consumes about 1 GJ of fuel per tonne. It is the same machine as the lead sinter and the manganese sinter, and it emits a great deal of dust.

###### Coke breeze: the sinter fuel `metal.coke-breeze` _(medium)_

The 3-10 mm fraction of coke, screened out at the coke plant, that would be too small for the blast furnace. A steelworks' sinter plant is therefore a consumer of its own coke plant's fines - a neat example of an internal recycling loop in the iron and carbon chain that closes from the coke oven's quench, through the sinter plant, back into the blast furnace's burn.

###### Pelletising the concentrate on a disc or a pelletiser `metal.pellet`

Very fine concentrate - under 45 um - is mixed with 5-8% bentonite binder and 0.5-1% limestone, moistened, and fed to a rotating disc pelletiser or a drum pelletiser where 3-10 mm green pellets are rolled up by capillary action. The green pellets are then fired on a travelling grate at 1200-1350 C in an oxidising atmosphere, which sinters the surface, gives the pellet its compressive strength and, if the furnace is properly controlled, magnetises it - the hematite becomes magnetite, which means the pellet can itself be recovered magnetically, and its reduction in the blast furnace is faster. Pelletising is what made the 1970s and 1980s post-and-tensile steel possible and it is the reason Brazil and Canada have a modern steel industry at all.

###### Bentonite binder from a clay pit `metal.bentonite` _(medium)_
