A sodium bentonite with a high swelling capacity, mined from a montmorillonite clay bed and used as the binder that makes a pellet roll up instead of shatter. In 1982 the world bentonite market was dominated by Wyoming and by Italy and the Balkan sources, and it was also the drilling mud of the oil industry, so the two applications competed for the same tonnage. The particular clay a pelletiser wants is a sodium montmorillonite, which is a specific alteration product of volcanic ash - the leaf of this little branch is a bentonite bed in a Tertiary volcanic sequence.

###### The furnace stack, throat and bustle pipe `metal.iron.burden-shaft`

The 20-30 m stack is lined with 1,000-2,000 mm of refractory and carries the burden down through a rotating throat seal into a stock column. The burden rests on a 'ledge' in the wall where the gas changes from upward to horizontal flow - the place every blast furnace operator watches, because if the burden descends too fast the gas gets through and the furnace races. At the bottom, the bustle pipe wraps the furnace and delivers the blast through the tuyeres, with the hot blast stoves - Cowper stoves, 8-12 per furnace, each 8-12 m tall - heating the air to 1000-1300 C on the gas from the previous cycle. A 1982 furnace is a machine about 25 m tall and 9 m wide with a 3,500 m3 working volume, and it holds about 100 tonnes of burden in flight at any moment.

###### Copper stave hearth cooling `metal.iron.copper-cooler` _(medium)_

The stave coolers that protect the hearth from 1500 C molten iron are made of copper or copper alloy with a water passage cast into them, because copper conducts heat far better than cast iron. They are a copper industry product, and they are one of the more elegant cross-links in this tree: the blast furnace cannot survive without a copper casting technology. On a modern furnace the stave is cast as a composite with a cast-iron backing and a copper water-cooled front, and about 400-900 staves are fitted.

##### Basic oxygen furnace steelmaking `metal.steel.bof`

Hot metal is charged into a 40-60 t vessel - a pear-shaped converter with a refractory lining - together with about 20-30% scrap, and then a lance lowered into the bath on a boom blows 99.5% oxygen at 40,000-80,000 Nm3/h for 15-25 minutes. Three things happen at once: the carbon burns, the silicon and phosphorus oxidise, and the carbon monoxide boils the bath. The phosphorus removal is the reason the process is called basic: the lining is doloma, calcined dolomite, and the phosphorus ends up as calcium phosphate in the slag, which is why BOF slag is a genuine phosphorus fertiliser. The chemistry is violent and self-accelerating - the bath heats itself to about 1600 C from the oxidation reactions alone, so no fuel is added at all.

##### Open hearth furnace steelmaking, in decline `metal.steel.open-hearth`

A 200-500 t rectangular basin of refractory with a hearth at 1300-1400 C, in which pig iron and scrap were melted while fuel gas or oil was burned above them and air was blown across the surface. It was dominant in 1920-1960 and it took 6-10 hours for a heat, produced a lot of nitrogen (so it could not easily make low-carbon steel) and consumed a lot of fuel. In 1982 it was a historical footnote in most of the world, still running in India, in Japan at a few works, and in a handful of Eastern European plants. It is included because it is the process the industry left, and because the heat-transfer engineering of the open hearth was the same furnace that the BOF was designed to eliminate.

##### Electric arc furnace on scrap `metal.steel.eaf`

The other route, and the one that was growing fastest in the 1980s. Three carbon electrodes are lowered into a 30-100 t shell furnace and an arc struck, melting scrap with 600-1,500 A at 30-50 V - a physically brutal heat transfer that lets a small furnace melt steel quickly. In 1982 the units were mostly the smaller, older 'three-phase' EAFs of 30-50 t; the 100 t+ DC furnace that transformed the industry came at the end of the decade. The EAF makes about 20% of US steel and rather less of world steel, and it is the route that makes the recycling loop of car scrap back into new sheet possible.

###### Carbon electrodes from needle coke and pitch `metal.carbon-electrode`

The EAF, the submerged arc furnaces of the ferroalloy industries, the aluminium pot anodes and the large carbon blocks of the blast furnace all consume the same two materials: calcined petroleum coke or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as a binder. An electrode is milled green - coke, pitch and sometimes a sulphur or metal additive - extruded, and baked at 800-1200 C in a graphitising furnace to above 2500 C. The 1980s problem was exactly the nickel crisis showing up here: the EAF plants had no electrodes of their own in Japan, and when the 1979-80 nickel spike also hit electrode prices, Japanese steelmakers found that making steel required nickel, in the electrodes. UHP electrodes and the shift to larger electrode sizes was the industry response.

##### Choosing the steelmaking vessel in 1982 `metal.steel.vessel-choice` _(low)_

Three vessels made the world's steel in 1982 and only one of them was winning. A short parent node so the basic oxygen furnace, the dying open hearth and the scrap-based electric arc furnace sit side by side instead of inside one another.

###### Ladle treatment, degassing and the steel's last chemistry `metal.steel.ladle` _(medium)_

In 1982 the most important development in steelmaking was not the furnace but the ladle. A 1980s steel ladle is a 100-200 t vessel on a rotating turret, and it is where three things happen in sequence. Secondary metallurgy: argon is stirred in to homogenise the temperature and composition and to flush hydrogen and nitrogen. Desulphurisation: calcium or a calcium-bearing reagent is added and stirred, taking the sulphur out as calcium sulphide in a basic slag. Deoxidation and inclusion control: aluminium is added as the last deoxidiser, and in a bottom-pour ladle the whole ladle is streamed through a nozzle to collect the inclusions in the nozzle. This is the technology that made clean, low-inclusion, low-carbon steel a reproducible product, and it is why modern sheet steel for tinplate and for deep drawing exists at all.

##### Continuous-cast the steel slab `metal.steel.caster`

Steel is not poured into moulds one heat at a time; it is cast continuously. Liquid steel at 1600 C is fed from a tundish through a nozzle into a water-cooled copper mould 1-2.5 m long, where the shell freezes in seconds. The strand then passes through a series of spray headers that remove the rest of the heat, and finally through a torch-cut or a flying shear, and is coiled. The whole point is yield: continuous casting replaced ingot casting in the 1980s across the industry, and a modern continuous caster turns out better than 95% of its steel while ingot casting threw away the 10-20% of each ingot that was the crop - the ends, the segregation, and the shrinkage void. The C64's steel exists because of this machine.

###### The copper mould wall of the continuous caster `metal.steel.mould-wall` _(medium)_

The copper alloy plate - phosphor bronze in most designs - that does the single hardest job in the whole of steelmaking, withdrawing heat from 1600 C steel at a rate that makes a millimetre of metal freeze in a second, and doing it hundreds of thousands of times. The plates are thin, 5-30 mm, and are cooled internally by high-pressure water, and they are plated and re-ground as they wear. Their thermal-fatigue cracking is the plant's central maintenance problem, and every crack means a slab defect that a tinplate maker will find on the inspection line.

##### Hot and cold rolled sheet steel `metal.steel.sheet`

The slab goes to a reversing hot rolling mill at 1150-1250 C - first through a roughing stand, then a rail mill or a continuous mill - and comes out as strip 2-12 mm wide. Then the cold mill, a Sendimir or a multi-high cluster mill with a Sendzimir Z-High line upgrade, takes it to 0.2-0.5 mm, with the rolling oil and the annealing line in between. Annealing in a hydrogen or hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere gives the recrystallised, equiaxed grain structure that makes a stamping possible. Cold-rolled sheet at 0.3-1 mm is the C64's case panel, the shield cans, the brackets and the heat-spreader, and the tinplate branch below is the same mill with a different end.

###### Steel rolling oil: emulsion and hydraulic oil `metal.rolling-oil` _(medium)_

Hot rolling of steel uses water emulsion; cold rolling uses a neat oil or a water-in-oil emulsion, chemically similar to the aluminium rolling lubricant but with a much higher base oil viscosity and a lot of boundary additives. So the C64's steel mill and its aluminium mill are the same kind of lubricant plant, and both are quietly downstream of crude oil.

###### Anneal and temper the sheet to its specification `metal.steel.heat-treatment` _(medium)_

Cold-rolled low-carbon steel is hard and full of internal stress, so it is annealed in a continuous line - a few seconds to a few minutes at 700-850 C in a hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere - to recrystallise it into soft equiaxed grain, and then, if it is going to be drawn rather than stamped, given a temper mill pass to raise the yield point by 50-150 MPa. The temper mill is a roll that puts in a deliberate rolling reduction that the temper roll locks in as a dislocation structure the anneal will not remove. The 1982 temper mill was a three-high Sendimir with a work-roll diameter of about 300 mm, and it is the reason a can and a deep-drawing panel are different products from the same mill.

###### Pickle, oil and specify the surface `metal.steel.surface` _(medium)_

Cold-rolled sheet is covered in mill scale and must be pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to remove it, or the next operation cannot stick to it. Then it is oiled or lacquered so it does not rust in storage. On the 1980s tinplate line the acid was hydrochloric, which put a genuinely dangerous hydrogen into the atmosphere, and the 1982 line ran its pickling tanks under a hood with an acid fume scrubber using sodium carbonate - which is another place the sodium chain of this file enters. The surface specification is a contract: roughness, cleanliness, and oil film weight in grams per square metre.

##### Tinplate: the tin-coated steel sheet `metal.tinplate`

Tinplate is 0.15-0.3 mm of low-carbon steel with 1.1-11.2 g/m2 of tin on both sides, made on a continuous electrolytic line at 4-8 m/s. The strip is degreased and pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, rinsed, then tinned in a stannous sulphate bath with a fluoroborate additive, rinsed, and either given a food-can passivation in chromic acid or - in the electronics and tinplate trade - an electrolytic passivation in a chromate or tin-oxide bath. A C64 uses a few square metres of tinplate a year at most, in switch bodies and shields, but tinplate is worth a node because it is the one place where tin and steel and electrochemistry all meet, and because the chromate passivation is the same chemistry as the zinc chromate passivation in the plating branch.

###### The tinning line: greening, tinning, soaking `metal.tinplate.tin-pots` _(medium)_

The line has four electrolytic tanks in series - a 'greening' or pretreat tank to strip the last oxide, two or more tinning tanks with soluble tin anodes, and a 'soaking' tank to heal any bare spots. The strip runs through as a ribbon, and the tin is applied at a controlled thickness by the current and by how long the strip spends in the stannate bath. The mechanical complexity is in the handling: a 0.2 mm ribbon travelling at 6 m/s has to be threaded, cleaned and welded end to end several times a shift.

##### Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) `metal.electrical-steel`

The C64's power supply transformer is the one place where the metal of the machine is deliberately not stainless or mild steel. Grain-oriented electrical steel is a 3.2% silicon low-carbon steel whose grains have been given a preferred orientation - the classic route is a 700-1000 C anneal in hydrogen in a field or, in the modern continuous process, a high-temperature final anneal with a bias field - so that the flux runs along the grain and the core losses and the magnetostriction both fall. The 1982 transformer in a C64 used M4 to M6 grade GOES, somewhere around 0.3-0.5 mm thick, wound as E-E laminations. Without the silicon the core would saturate, the transformer would be too big, and the whole switching supply would not fit. Silicon steel is therefore not a speciality of this tree - it is load-bearing.

###### E-E laminations and the stamping `metal.electrical-steel.lamination`

The 0.3 mm strip is blanked and stamped into E and I shapes - or, in a cheaper 1982 supply, into E-E pairs and then stacked and interlocked - on a 400-800 tonne mechanical or hydraulic press with a compound die that does the whole lamination stack in one stroke. The stamping is heavily lubricated and the edges are deburred and then given a magnetic insulation treatment: a thin epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an 'insulation coating' of an inorganic glassy film, applied so that the laminations do not short-circuit each other. The core of the C64's transformer is about 30-60 stamped laminations, and the number is set by the stack height and the available die.

###### Make the ferrosilicon and add it to the steel `metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source`

How does 3% silicon get into sheet steel at all? Ferrosilicon is added to the ladle, or - in the parent process - the ore is smelted with silica and coke in a submerged arc furnace to give 45-75% Si ferroalloy, and that alloy is added to the steel in the ladle or in the EAF. So the silicon steel branch intersects the ferrosilicon furnace, which is a carbon-reduction electric furnace just like the ferromanganese and ferrochrome furnaces in this tree, and which ultimately runs on the same metallurgical silicon and quartzite chain as the semiconductors. One of the more satisfying loops in the tree.

          - *Ferrosilicon in the submerged arc furnace* `metal.ferrosilicon` *(seen above)*
###### Continuous casting and the Goss texture formation `metal.electrical-steel.casting` _(medium)_

Electrical steel is continuously cast, hot rolled, and then given the two anneals that make it grain-oriented. The first, at 800-1100 C, is an ordinary recrystallisation anneal in wet hydrogen; the second, at 1100-1200 C, is the orientation anneal, in which the steel is held just below the Curie point in a magnetic field aligned with the rolling direction so the alpha-iron grains with their [110] axis along the field grow preferentially. The second anneal takes a week or more in a hydrogen atmosphere, which is why GOES costs three or four times what mild sheet costs and why a C64's transformer was one of the most expensive parts in it.

        - *AISI 304 and 430 stainless steel* `metal.stainless.304` *(seen above)*
##### Tool steel: SKD61 / H13 / D2, the moulds and dies `metal.die-steel`

The C64's case, the keycaps, the key plungers and the disk-drive and modulator housings were all made in injection-moulding dies, and every one of those dies and every aluminium extrusion die was cut from tool steel. SKD61 in Japan and H13 in the US and DIN X40CrMoV51 in Europe are the same alloy: 5% chromium, 5% molybdenum, 1% vanadium, 0.4% carbon, air-hardening to about 50-54 HRC. It is made in a small vacuum arc or vacuum induction furnace, forged, annealed, and then given three heat treatments - austenitising at 1000-1050 C, air cooling, and double tempering at 500-550 C - before it goes near the machine. A single C64 case die weighs 1-4 tonnes and cost tens of thousands of dollars, and it is the reason the tool steel branch is in this file at all.

###### Molybdenum: a tool steel alloying element `metal.molybdenum` _(medium)_

Molybdenum is in the tool steel, in the stainless and in the hydrodesulphurisation catalyst, so it belongs in this tree, but its own branch is short because in 1982 almost no molybdenum came from a molybdenum mine: about half came from the molybdenite recovered as a by-product of the porphyry copper concentrators, where it is a few hundred ppm of the concentrate and reports to a separate flotation circuit, and the other half came as molybdic oxide from roasting. The ore is molybdenite, MoS2, in the Climax and Henderson porphyry in Colorado and in the Bingham Canyon concentrate. Molybdenum and tungsten share the greisen hydrothermal environment, so scheelite CaWO4 and molybdenite are sometimes intergrown in the same vein and the two metals can be recovered from one orebody. The leaf is a porphyry or a granite vein.

###### Molybdenite in a porphyry `metal.molybdenite`

Soft, greasy, platy flakes of MoS2 in the quartz and feldspar of a granitic porphyry, associated with the copper minerals of the Climax and Henderson molybdenum operations or with the Bingham copper concentrate. The leaf is the same porphyry intrusion the copper branch ends in, which is a genuine shared endpoint.

###### Vanadium: a small alloying element `metal.vanadium` _(medium)_

Included only because tool steel and the AOD of stainless steel both use it, and because the source is genuinely unusual. Most vanadium came from vanadiferous titanomagnetite - a magnetite containing 1-6% vanadium - which was a problem in the iron ore of the Panzhihua district in China and in the U.S. and Canadian Mesabi ranges until somebody worked out how to separate it. By 1982 the US route was slag processing: the titanomagnetite went into a blast furnace or an oxygen converter, and the vanadium reported to the slag, and the slag was ground and reprocessed. The other source is spent petroleum catalyst, which by the late 1980s was a genuine and growing vanadium source. Both of those are consequences of processes elsewhere in this tree.

###### Vanadiferous titanomagnetite `metal.vanadium.titanomagnetite`

The leaf: a magnetite with the iron partly replaced by titanium and vanadium, occurring as an iron ore in itself. At Panzhihua it is a magnetite-ilmenite ore in a vanadium-bearing magnetite gabbro; in the Mesabi it was a nuisance component of the taconite. Either way it is an iron ore, and the vanadium is a consequence of somebody mining iron.

###### Vacuum melting and the purity of tool steel `metal.die-steel.vacuum` _(medium)_

A tool steel that contains a hundred parts per million of sulphur will embrittle, and one with two hundred ppm of oxygen will pit. So the melt for a die is made in a vacuum induction or a vacuum arc furnace rather than in an air-melted crucible, and the ingot is remelted by the VAR or the EB process - electron beam - which gives a fine equiaxed grain with no inclusions and no segregation. The vacuum arc furnace is a modified version of the vacuum-arc remelting process that the titanium industry invented, and by 1982 the extrusion die industry and the mould industry both bought them.

#### Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain `metal.iron`

The bottom of the steel branch. Iron ore is dug, concentrated, reduced and never appears in a C64, and this branch exists so that the steel branch terminates in a mine rather than in an abstraction. The 1982 iron ore trade was dominated by three names: Mount Whaleback and the Pilbara in Western Australia, the Carajas and Quadrilatero Ferrifero in Brazil, and the Labrador Trough and the Mesabi range in North America. The ore is hematite, or magnetite, or both in a metamorphic banded iron formation - a rock that is 2 billion years old and was originally a chemical precipitate out of seawater.

##### Hematite (Fe2O3) and the Pilbara `metal.hematite`

Hematite is a steel-grey to red mineral that occurs as specular crystals, as kidney ore, and - the mass of the world's supply - as itabirite and hematite replacements in a banded iron formation. The Pilbara ore bodies in Western Australia are the richest hematite in the world at 62-66% Fe with almost no gangue, and the Brockman and Hamersley ranges were being mined at full rate by 1982. The ore ships from Port Hedland, where the ore handling and ship loaders are among the largest machines ever built.

###### Pilbara open-pit iron mine and the ore loader `metal.hematite.pilbara`

The Pilbara mines in 1982 were the mining engineering standard for the industry. A 15 m bench, 100-250 tonne haul trucks, 3-4 cubic metre shovels, and - this is the part everybody photographs - the huge travelling ore loaders that straddle the width of a haul truck and scoop up a 40-60 tonne load in one pass. The ore is crushed to 250 mm and conveyed up a 1.5 km incline to a stockyard, and then a 3-4 million tonne bulk carrier is loaded in about 20 hours at Port Hedland. One Pilbara mine shipped 40-100 Mt a year in the mid-1980s.

###### Banded iron formation: a chemical precipitate from seawater `metal.banded-iron-formation`

The leaf of the whole iron and steel branch, and one of the great ones. Around 2.0-1.8 billion years ago, the oceans contained dissolved ferrous iron and oxygen appeared in the atmosphere as a result of an earlier generation of photosynthetic organisms. Wherever the oxygen-rich surface water sank and met the anoxic iron-rich deep water, the iron oxidised and precipitated, as a jelly of iron oxide that settled as a chemical mud. It compacted into alternating silica and iron bands, and it is that banding which gives the rock its name and which makes the high-grade hematite ore bodies on the Hamersley Range the size they are. So the iron in a C64 chassis began, two billion years ago, as an oxide precipitating out of an ocean.

###### The silica and iron oxide banding `metal.bif-banding` _(medium)_

The leaf, described properly: a stack of alternating 1 mm to 10 m bands of chert (cryptocrystalline silica) and iron oxide, the whole thing metamorphosed, with the hematite in the oxidised upper part and magnetite in the reduced lower part and the P-rich band - the band that gives the Sudbury nickel deposit and the Phalaborwa copper - where fossil bacteria oxidised the iron. Each band is a single depositional event or a group of them, and the ore-to-waste ratio of a Banded Iron Formation is often 1:2, so the pit that produces a tonne of iron ore has to move three tonnes of rock.

###### Crushing, screening and the lump/fines split `metal.hematite.crushing` _(low)_

The ore is crushed in a gyratory and then on a screen, and the product is split three ways: lump ore above 6.3 mm that goes straight into the blast furnace, fines below 6.3 mm that must be sintered or pelletised, and a reject stream of the banded iron formation that is too low grade to smelt. The lump/fines split is a commercial decision rather than a metallurgical one: in 1982 the steelmakers wanted as much direct-shipping lump as possible because it avoided the sintering plant's capital and its fuel.

###### The ore stockyard and the ship loader `metal.hematite.stockyard` _(low)_

Because the ships are 180,000-250,000 dwt and the mine's output is lumpy, the ore goes into a 1-2 million tonne stockyard with a stacker and a travelling shiploader. The shiploader is a 100 m long gantry on rails with a slewing chute that trims the ship's hold as it loads, so a 250,000 dwt vessel is filled flat without a bulker or a trimming machine. The whole Pilbara export chain - mine, conveyor, stockyard, loader, ship - was built to move one commodity in enormous tonnage at very low cost, and it is the reason Australian iron ore is the cheapest iron in the world.

        - *Magnetite (Fe3O4) and the taconite route* `metal.magnetite` *(seen above)*
#### Ferrite: transformer and choke cores `metal.ferrite`

The C64's power supply transformer, the filter chokes, the RF modulator coil and the ferrite beads on the board are all ceramic magnetic materials, not metal. A power ferrite is a spinel - either MnO.Fe2O3.ZnO or NiO.Fe2O3.ZnO - pressed as a powder and fired to 1200-1300 C, which is powder metallurgy in the truest sense: the magnetisation is not in the metal particles, it is in the magnetic domain walls of a ceramic. This is the branch where the metals tree stops being about metal and starts being about oxide chemistry, and the raw materials are iron oxide, manganese carbonate, zinc oxide and nickel oxide.

##### MnZn power ferrite `metal.ferrite.mnzn`

The material of the C64's transformer core, the rectifier choke and the bulk filter chokes. Its job is to carry a large alternating flux at 15-65 kHz with as little loss and as little audible noise as possible, and that is a tight compromise: MnO raises the permeability and lowers the magnetostriction (which is what stops the transformer singing), ZnO raises the resistivity and pushes the Curie point up but lowers the saturation, and the two oxides partly cancel. A 1982 E-core for the C64's supply would be MnZn at roughly 0.2-0.35 W/cycle at 16 kHz and about 0.35 T saturation.

          - *E/EI/EE core geometry and the transformer* `metal.ferrite.e-core` *(seen above)*
###### Filter chokes and the common-mode choke `metal.ferrite.choke` _(medium)_

The bulk filter chokes in a 1982 linear-supply C64 are 470 uH to a few millihenry with a current rating of 1-3 A, wound on an EE or a bobbin core of the same MnZn material. The switch-mode version instead has a common-mode choke: two windings on a single core, arranged so the two currents are equal and opposite, so the flux cancels and the choke does not need to store any energy - its only job is to present a high impedance to the common-mode noise on the mains lead. Both are the same pressed ceramic with a different winding.

###### Dopants: calcium, silicon, cobalt and the grain boundaries `metal.ferrite.dopants` _(medium)_

The last half percent of the ferrite recipe does most of the work. A small calcium and silicon addition forms a grain-boundary phase that makes the grain boundaries insulating and therefore suppresses eddy-current loss. Cobalt raises the anisotropy and the permeability at low field, which matters for a filter inductor. Lithium prevents wall-jumping in a high-coercivity ferrite. These additions are 0.1-2% each and they are why a power ferrite's chemistry is a trade secret and why the same nominal composition from two suppliers will not behave the same way.

##### NiZn ferrite `metal.ferrite.nizn`

The second family. Substituting nickel oxide for most of the manganese oxide raises the resistivity of the grain boundary by a factor of a hundred, so the eddy-current loss at high frequency collapses and NiZn is usable to about 100 MHz instead of 1 MHz. The price is a permeability of only 15-100 where MnZn gives a thousand, and a low saturation. In the C64 it is the RF modulator transformer and the video output circuitry, and off the board it is the small cylindrical bead slipped onto a wire to kill EMI. NiZn is pressed and sintered the same way; the only real differences are the raw material and the sintering atmosphere.

          - *Ferrite bead: a small cylinder of NiZn or MnZn* `metal.ferrite.bead` *(seen above)*
###### The RF modulator coil `metal.ferrite.modulator` _(medium)_

The C64's TV modulator, which puts the composite video onto the RF of channel 3 or 4 so a television could display the machine, contains a small ferrite-loaded coil - a few turns of enamelled copper wire on a ferrite core or threaded through a ferrite bead. This is the one place in the machine where nickel-zinc ferrite is genuinely a radio-frequency component rather than a filter. The modulator itself and the television are the optics/television agents' business; the core is this branch's.

###### NiZn dopants: copper, cobalt and calcium `metal.ferrite.nizn.doping` _(medium)_

The NiZn family is doped with copper and cobalt to shape the grain-boundary physics, and with calcium to control the sintering. The NiZn product of the 1980s was deliberately split by composition into a high-permeability low-loss grade for transformers below 1 MHz and a very high-permeability grade for read heads and for antenna cores, and the difference between them was a fraction of a percent of dopant. It is a good example of a material in which the last tenth of a percent of the recipe is the difference between two products.

###### The nickel and cobalt raw materials for NiZn `metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source` _(medium)_

The Ni-Zn family's nickel does not come as metal. It comes as nickel oxide, or as green nickel hydroxide precipitate from a laterite leach, and the cobalt comes as metal, as oxide, or - much more cheaply - as a cobalt hydroxide carried out of the nickel refinery's ammonia circuit. Which is the point: the cobalt in a NiZn ferrite, the cobalt in a superalloy and the cobalt binder in a tungsten-carbide drill cone all came out of the same few refineries, so the price a ferrite maker paid for its dopant was set by the nickel market rather than by anything to do with ferrite. By 1982 that price was falling rather than rising - cobalt was about $12.50/lb in May, down from $25/lb in 1980, and about $5/lb by 1983-84 as new supply arrived.

              - *Nickel oxide (NiO)* `metal.nickel.nickel-oxide` *(seen above)*
##### Ferrite raw materials: the oxide blend `metal.ferrite.raw-materials`

The three powders that get blended, and each one has its own industrial route. The iron oxide is either mill scale from the aluminium or the steel mill - washed, dried and milled, and the cheapest source - or a precipitated oxide made by acid leaching hematite. The manganese is manganese carbonate, a chemical precipitate from a manganese sulphate solution. The zinc is zinc oxide, made by roasting zinc ore or by burning zinc metal. The blend has to be accurate to about 0.2% in each component, because the magnetic properties are extremely sensitive to it, and by the 1980s the oxide suppliers were selling pre-blended 'master mixes' to the smaller ferrite makers precisely because the blending was the hard part.

###### Iron oxide from mill scale or from a precipitate `metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source` _(medium)_

The cheapest ferrite iron oxide is the mill scale from an aluminium rolling mill or a steel mill - but it comes as a mix of FeO, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 plus the alumina or silica the original metal carried, so it is milled and then passed over a strong magnetic separator to take out the magnetite, and the residue is calcined in air to convert all the iron to Fe2O3. The higher-purity route is to leach fine hematite in sulfuric acid and precipitate goethite or ferric hydroxide, wash it, and calcine it to a very pure Fe2O3 of 0.02% or less impurity - which is what the RF NiZn grades and the high-permeability grades need.

###### Manganese carbonate `metal.manganese-carbonate` _(medium)_

Not a mined material: a chemical precipitate. High-purity manganese sulphate solution is treated with sodium or ammonium carbonate at 60-90 C and pH 5-7, and manganese carbonate drops out as a pale pink powder. The iron must be kept out because MnCO3 with 1-2% iron pushes the ferrite's Curie temperature up and its permeability down. So the manganese chemistry of the ferromanganese branch in this file and the manganese chemistry of the ferrite branch share a plant but not a product, and a manganese mine does not touch either.

          - *Zinc oxide sinter: the smelter's intermediate* `metal.zinc.oxide` *(seen above)*
          - *Nickel oxide (NiO)* `metal.nickel.nickel-oxide` *(seen above)*
###### The mix house and the recipe book `metal.ferrite.mix-house` _(medium)_

The place where a ferrite formula is actually executed. A blend of perhaps 300 kg of oxide is weighed into a mixer - a ribbon blender or a ball mill - to 0.1 kg, sampled, analysed, and then the result is used to correct the next batch. The correction logic is where the manufacturer differs: some makers blend to the analysis and some blend to the recipe, and the argument between them is an old one. The mix house also holds the master recipes, and the confidentiality around them is a matter of pride rather than of deep mystery. A 1980s small ferrite factory had one mix house, one kiln line and one grinding room, and made a few hundred tonnes a year.

##### Ferrite powder metallurgy from blend to fired core `metal.ferrite.manufacture`

Five steps, all of them inherited from the ceramic industry, none of them changed since the 1950s. Blend: the oxides are mixed wet in a ball mill or a vibrating mill to a few tenths of a percent. Calcine or pre-sinter: the blend is heated in air to about 900-1100 C, which drives off the moisture and the carbonate carbon dioxide and starts forming the spinel; the material comes out as a hard, sintered cake. Granulate: the cake is crushed and screened, and about 1-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or polyethylene binder is added with a little water so the powder will press. Press: a dry press - a 100-250 tonne hydraulic press - forms the shape at 100-200 MPa, with the tool steel die giving the final dimensions. Fire: the pressed part is sintered in air at 1200-1350 C, and the part shrinks about 1% linearly, which is why the die is made oversize and why every ferrite part in the world is ground afterwards. Finish: the fired part is ground on a double-disc or planetary grinder to final dimension, because the press cannot hold the tolerance.

###### Wet mixing and the ceramic ball mill `metal.ferrite.mixing` _(medium)_

The oxide blend is mixed wet in a rubber-lined ball mill or a vibrating mill, because water is the only way to get all three oxides into intimate contact within half a percent. A 1982 MnZn blend ran in a 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or in a ball mill with a few hundred kilos of zirconia or rubber-lined steel balls. The wet slip is then dried on a spray dryer or a rotary dryer to a granulated powder with the right moisture and the right particle size. The whole discipline of the ceramic industry is really about this step, and the blending tolerances of the finished core are set here.

###### Granulation and the binder `metal.ferrite.granulation` _(medium)_

Free powder flows; a pressed ferrite part needs the powder to fill the die uniformly, so the powder is granulated with 0.5-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or a PVA-polyethylene glycol binder and 8-12% water, on a spray granulator or a pan granulator, into 100-400 um granules. The granule has to survive being filled at a few grams per stroke and being pressed at 200 MPa, which is a tough mechanical requirement for a granule of ceramic powder.

###### Calcination and the spinel formation `metal.ferrite.calcination`

The chemical heart of the branch. Below the calcination temperature the blend is a mechanical mixture; by 900-1100 C the oxides have reacted and the cubic spinel lattice - which has three cation sites and eight for every 32 oxygen atoms - has formed, with the zinc on the tetrahedral sites, the manganese on the octahedral sites and the iron distributed across both. That distribution is why MnZn has a high permeability: Mn2+ and Fe2+ on opposing sublattices give an antiparallel but nearly equal spin arrangement, so the magnetisation can be tipped by a small field. It is an oxide chemistry result, and it is why a C64's transformer is ceramic and not iron.

###### Dry pressing in a tool steel die `metal.ferrite.pressing` _(medium)_

The pressed shape is the finished shape - an E, an EE, a toroid, a drum core - and the tool is a hardened steel die in a 100-250 tonne press. Ferrite presses in 1982 were 100-250 t, usually with a single or double action upper punch, and the cycle time for a small E core was 0.3-2 s. The part is pressed dry, which is why the powder has to be granulated first: free powder flows, granulated powder fills a die uniformly. The tooling is the same tool steel as an extrusion die, so the SKD61/H13 branch serves the ferrite industry too.

###### Firing at 1200-1300 C and the shrinkage `metal.ferrite.sintering`

The pressed part is fired on a belt or in a tunnel kiln in air, and in the last stage of the sintering it goes through the Curie temperature - about 200-250 C for MnZn - which is a magnetic transition, and above it the permeability of the material is irrelevant because it is paramagnetic. That is why a fire that goes too fast or spends too little time above the Curie point produces a core with poor low-frequency properties even though its density looks fine. During firing the part shrinks about 1% linearly, so a 20 mm E core comes out of a 20.2 mm die, and the finished dimension has to be set by grinding.

###### Grinding the fired part to size `metal.ferrite.grinding` _(medium)_

Because the fired part cannot be held to a useful dimension by pressing, it is lapped and ground. An E core is face-ground and the bore is ground; a toroid is OD and ID ground. In 1982 this was a double-disc or a planetary grinder with a diamond wheel, and it was expensive enough that a great many ferrite parts were still sold with a loose dimension tolerance and machined by the customer. The final steps are the coating: a thin epoxy or phenolic coat, or a dry lacquer coat and bake, which holds the core together, insulates it from the winding, and gives it a corrosion-resistant surface.

###### Control the firing atmosphere and the schedule `metal.ferrite.quality` _(medium)_

The most closely guarded part of the whole ferrite industry is the firing curve: the ramp rate, the hold times, and the oxygen partial pressure through a 12-30 hour cycle. Too fast through the Curie point and the grain boundaries form in the wrong order and the core is lossy; too oxidising and Mn2+ becomes Mn3+ and the losses double; too reducing and the Fe becomes FeO and the permeability collapses. The kiln in 1982 was a tunnel kiln or a continuous belt with a controlled-atmosphere section and a dewpoint-controlled atmosphere, and the recipe was the plant's only real asset.

##### Hard ferrites and permanent magnet materials `metal.ferrite.hard` _(medium)_

The same pressed-and-fired powder metallurgy as the power ferrite, but with no permeability requirement and a coercive force instead. Barium and strontium hexaferrite, BaFe12O19 and SrFe12O19, are sintered into magnet blocks for small motors and, in this tree, for the permanent magnets inside a magnetic ore separator. None of it is in the C64; it is here because the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace is full of ferrite magnets, and because the separator is the one place the barium branch and the ferrite branch meet.

###### Strontium ferrite magnet `metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite` _(medium)_

SrFe12O19 pressed and fired like a power ferrite, then cooled through the Curie point in a magnetic field so the hexferrite grains line up. It is brittle, it is an oxide, and its key property is that it does not need any rare earth at all - which is exactly why barium and strontium ferrite are the standard cheap magnet, and why the two-share-the-mill argument makes this branch's economics obvious.

###### Strontium carbonate `metal.strontium-carbonate` _(medium)_

The only geologically interesting part: strontium is the rarest of the three alkaline-earth metals used in ferrites and ceramics, because it has no ore of its own that anyone uses. Strontium sulfate (celestine) is mined in Spain, Mexico and Iran, and almost all of it is converted to strontium carbonate. A C64 contains no strontium, so this is a dead end, but it is a real example of a mineral that exists only to make a ceramic.

##### Radio-frequency and rod ferrite `metal.ferrite.radio` _(low)_

A third shape family: ferrite rod and toroid for antenna and RF applications, pressed with an anisotropic die so the ferrite is oriented in the pressing direction. An isotropic pressed ferrite has half the usable permeability along the pressing axis as across it, because the pores are flattened; a ferrite maker who wants an antenna rod presses it in a die that aligns the grains. This is the ferrite in a portable radio's antenna, and it is the same powder as the transformer core, pressed in a different die.

###### The anisotropic pressing die `metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die` _(low)_

A ferrite pressed in an ordinary die has its pores flattened in the pressing direction, and flattened pores cut the permeability in that direction roughly in half - so a plain-pressed ferrite rod is a poor antenna core along its length. To avoid that, a rod core is pressed in a die with a fine central punch, so the powder is displaced radially and the pores and the grains align across the rod instead of along it. The same die idea is behind the toroid's oriented product and behind ferrite for read heads. It is a small piece of die engineering with a large effect, and it is why ferrite die makers were a specialist trade in the 1980s.

#### Barium titanate: the ceramic capacitor dielectric `metal.barium`

The disk and multilayer ceramic capacitors on a 1982 C64 mainboard are barium titanate - BaTiO3 - and barium titanate is an industrial material made from barite, the same heavy white mineral that makes the drilling mud. The chain is barite to barium sulphide to barium carbonate to barium titanate, and then a 1000-1400 C calcination and a ceramic pressing. It is the most complete oxide-mineral chain in this file: a sulphate ore, a carbothermal reduction, a carbonate, a perovskite, and a dielectric constant of several thousand.

##### Barite (BaSO4) ore, 90-98% `metal.barite`

Barite is a very heavy, very white, chemically inert mineral - specific gravity 4.5 - which occurs as veins, as replacement bodies in limestone, and as a residual clay. It has two completely separate markets. The drilling-mud market is by far the biggest and takes barite that has simply been crushed and graded to 200 mesh, because all it needs is density and a low quartz content. The chemical-grade market, which is where the barium titanate comes from, needs the barite to be low in iron and low in silica, because those impurities end up in the ceramic. In 1982 the chemical-grade barite was a small, carefully selected part of the output, and China and Morocco were the dominant suppliers.

###### Barite vein and replacement mine `metal.barite.mine` _(medium)_

Barite is mined as a primary vein mineral - a gangue mineral of many lead-zinc hydrothermal deposits - or as a replacement of limestone. The processing is simple: crush, wash off the clay, and either float or just size and sell. A barite plant of the 1980s was a jaw crusher, a log washer and a deslimer, and the quality specification was almost entirely about the Fe2O3. The chemical-grade plants did a rougher job: a flotation and an acid leach to take the iron down.

###### Barite vein in limestone or as a hydrothermal gangue `metal.barite.rock`

The leaf: white bladed or massive barite filling a fracture, or replacing a fossiliferous limestone bed. The barite has essentially no use as a rock - it is only ever interesting where it happens to be 90% or better and low in iron.

###### Barite, bentonite and lime: the drilling mud system `metal.barite.mud-system` _(medium)_

A drilling mud is not one material; it is a designed composite. The barite is the weight - it is the only cheap, abundant mineral dense enough to hold back formation pressure at a density of 1.5-2.0. The bentonite is the viscosity and the filtration control, and it works because its sodium montmorillonite swells in water to several times its dry volume. The lime and the lime-soil inhibitors control the calcium contamination that comes up with the cement and that would flocculate the bentonite. So the barite branch of this tree converges with the bentonite branch of the steel branch, and both converge on the drilling of the oil and gas wells that produce the crude oil the plastics agent starts from.

              - *Bentonite binder from a clay pit* `metal.bentonite` *(seen above)*
              - *Lime (CaO) and calcium* `metal.lime` *(seen above)*
###### Drilling grade barite and its mud `metal.barite.drilling-mud` _(medium)_

The larger half of the barite market, and the reason a chemical-grade barite supplier has to be selective. Drilling mud needs a barite that is dense, grindable to a very fine size, low in soluble salts and above all low in cadmium and other toxic heavy metals, because the drill cuttings go into a mud pit and the barite is not recovered. In 1982 the drilling grade specification was a gravity of at least 4.2 and a particle distribution such that 90% passed 45 um. A 1982 rig's mud for a deep well used 100-300 tonnes of barite per kilometre.

##### Barite to barium sulphide, then barium carbonate `metal.barite.reduction`

The chemical reduction of barite. Barite plus coke at 900-1100 C in a rotary kiln gives barium sulphide: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO. That reaction needs about 1100 C to proceed at a useful rate, and the kiln is a long steel tube, 2-3 m diameter and 30-50 m long, rotating at 0.5-1 rpm, heated by a gas or oil burner at one end. The barium sulphide is leached out of the cooled cake with water, giving a solution of BaS, and that solution is carbonated with carbon dioxide - from a coke oven, from the sinter plant, from anywhere - and barium carbonate precipitates: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S. So the barium carbonate is made from a sulphate ore, a coke-oven gas and a stream of hydrogen sulphide, and the H2S is either burned to sulphur or sent to a Claus plant.

          - *Ceramic-grade barium carbonate* `metal.barium-carbonate` *(seen above)*
###### Hydrogen sulphide from the carbonation `metal.hydrogen-sulfide` _(medium)_

The barium carbonate process makes hydrogen sulphide as a by-product, roughly 0.2 t of H2S per tonne of barium carbonate, and H2S is an acutely toxic gas that a 1982 barium plant either burned in a flare or sent to a Claus plant for elemental sulphur. It is also, if you are unlucky, a gas that kills by olfactory paralysis: at high concentration you cannot smell it, which is why a barium works had an H2S alarm on the roof and why the workers carried a supplied-air respirator. It is the least well-known hazard in this tree and a real one.

##### Barium titanate powder (BaTiO3) `metal.barium.titanate`

The solid-state reaction of barium carbonate with titanium dioxide: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2. It happens in a calcination at 1100-1350 C, in a rotary kiln or a batch furnace, and the outcome is a powder of perovskite-structured grains - a cubic cell with the titanium atom at the centre of an octahedron of six oxygens and the barium in the twelve-fold site between them. It has to be de-aerated and it must be calcined in an atmosphere that keeps the titanium from being reduced to the +3 state, because a reduced titanate is a semiconductor and a lossy dielectric. This is a real problem in the ceramic industry and the reason the calciner is sealed and the oxygen partial pressure controlled. The bulk material is then ball-milled to sub-micron before the powder is pressed or cast into a film.

###### Titanium dioxide from rutile sand `metal.titanium-dioxide`

The titanium dioxide half of the equation, and it comes from a beach sand. Ilmenite, a titanium-iron oxide, is dredged from the heavy-mineral beach sands of the Cap York coast in Queensland, of Kerala in India, of the Mozambique coast and of the Richards Bay area of South Africa; it is separated from the zircon and the rutile by gravity and electrostatic separation; and it is then either chlorinated with coke and chlorine at 900-1000 C to give TiCl4, which is oxidised in a flame to give the pigment TiO2, or sulfided and digested to give synthetic rutile and then the pigment. Rutile, the TiO2 mineral itself, is also separated directly from the sand and is the higher-grade feed for ceramic-grade titanium dioxide. The pigment industry is by far the biggest user of titanium dioxide in 1982, and barium titanate is a small, very high-value user of the same commodity.

###### Heavy mineral beach sand and the dredge `metal.ilmenite-sand`

The leaf: a beach or dune sand a few metres thick carrying 1-10% heavy minerals - ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite, tourmaline - in a strip along the shoreline. A concentrator dredges a cutter suction pump from the shallow water, washes and upgrades on a shaking table and a spiral, then on gravity and electrostatic separators, recovering 200,000-300,000 t of ilmenite a year from a single operation. So the barium in a 1982 disk capacitor, having gone through a rotary kiln and a hydrogen sulphide stream, ends up in a titanium atom that came out of a Queensland beach.

###### The ceramic capacitor and its dielectric classes `metal.barium-titanate-capacitor` _(medium)_

The finished use. A 1982 C64 mainboard carries perhaps 30-60 ceramic capacitors, mostly small discs and a few multilayer blocks. The disc is a pressed or cast barium titanate body, sintered at 1250-1350 C, silver-coated on both faces and fired to make the electrodes, and dipped in an epoxy or phenolic encapsulant. The multilayer capacitor stacks hundreds of microns-thick dielectric layers with internal nickel or palladium electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired - a technology that was genuinely new in 1982 and was the reason a 10 nF 50 V part started to fit in a 1.6 mm-tall package. The dielectric classes are named by their temperature coefficient: X7R and Z5U for the general-purpose 1980s parts, Y5V for the high-capacitance low-stability ones.

###### Grade the barium titanate powder into a dielectric class `metal.dielectric-grading` _(medium)_

The same powder cannot make a Y5V capacitor and an X7R one. Y5V is made from a fine, uniform, high-surface-area powder near the Curie point, where the dielectric constant is enormous and wildly temperature-dependent - a huge capacitance that changes by a factor of five over the working range. X7R is made from a coarser powder with barium zirconate or barium strontium titanate added, which flattens the temperature curve at the cost of the peak. So the capacitor 'class' is really a powder specification, and the class marking on the part is a statement about the ball mill that ground it.

###### Co-fire the internal electrodes in a low-oxygen atmosphere `metal.dielectric-grading.mlc` _(medium)_

A multilayer capacitor's internal electrode is nickel or palladium, printed as a paste and co-fired with the ceramic. That will not work in air - the ceramic would reduce and become a lossy semiconductor - so the whole stack is fired in a low-oxygen atmosphere at 1200-1350 C in hydrogen or in a nitrogen-hydrogen mix, and then re-oxidised afterwards so the barium titanate goes back to being an insulator. The oxygen partial pressure is controlled to a few millibars. It is the most metallurgically demanding step in the whole electronics supply chain that nobody ever sees, and it is a barium carbonate problem.

#### Tungsten: filaments, carbide and alloying element `metal.tungsten`

Very little tungsten is inside a 1982 C64, and almost all of what there is sits in capital equipment and consumables rather than in the machine: the heater filament in a television's electron gun, the cemented-carbide cutters that drill the mainboard and route the glass-epoxy laminate, the carbide dies that draw the power-supply transformer's magnet wire, the tungsten-rhenium needles of a wafer probe card, and a percent or two of it in the simple tooling and stamping steels. What it is: the highest-melting-point of all metals at 3422 C, boiling at 5930 C, density 19.25 g/cm3 - a metal that is essentially never found as native metal, because wolframite and scheelite carry it at 0.3-2.5% WO3 and it has to be chemically opened before it can be reduced. It is not in the case mould: SKD61 and H13 are chromium-molybdenum-vanadium steels with no tungsten in them at all, and the alloying element in that family is molybdenum.

##### Wolframite and scheelite ore `metal.tungsten.ore`

The two ores are chemically different and are opened differently, which is why the mine and the mill are designed separately. Wolframite, (Fe,Mn)WO4, a solid solution of ferberite FeWO4 and huebnerite MnWO4, is a dense black mineral of specific gravity 7.1-7.9 that sits in the quartz veins of a granite cupola with cassiterite, topaz and native bismuth; being that heavy and weakly magnetic it concentrates on a shaking table and on a magnetic separator. Scheelite, CaWO4, is the calcium equivalent - too light and too non-magnetic for gravity, so it is froth-floated, and it is the ore of the Climax and Pine Creek skarns in Colorado and Montana and of the Felbertauern in Austria. Neither commonly exceeds about 1.5% WO3, so a tungsten mine is a large mill for a small product and it is usually a by-product operation. Molybdenum and tungsten share the greisen hydrothermal environment, so scheelite and molybdenite MoS2 are sometimes intergrown in one vein.

###### Tungsten mine and concentrator `metal.tungsten.ore.mine` _(medium)_

Wolframite is dense and refractory, so the ore is mined, crushed and gravity-concentrated or floated to a 60-70% WO3 concentrate, which is roughly a hundredfold upgrade on a 0.6% head grade. Because the ore is so often a by-product of a tin or molybdenum mine rather than the main product of its own, tungsten supply followed the fortunes of tin mining for most of the twentieth century, and the price spiked hard whenever the tin market wobbled. The supply map changed abruptly around 1980: China had been a minor producer whose entire output went to its own steel industry, and from 1980 its production rose sharply on an export surge, while South Korea's Sangdong was the other new large source. Korea and China were becoming the dominant suppliers just as the electronics industry started buying filament wire.

##### Ammonium paratungstate (APT) `metal.tungsten.apt`

The intermediate every other tungsten product starts from. The concentrate is digested with sodium hydroxide or with soda ash at about 900-1000 C, which brings the tungsten into solution as sodium tungstate while the calcium, iron and fluorine stay behind as insoluble residues that are filtered off; ammonium chloride then precipitates ammonium paratungstate. APT is a stable, dry, freely soluble white solid, and that is the whole point of it: it can be shipped a long way without absorbing moisture or picking up anything from a wooden crate, so APT rather than concentrate is what crosses an ocean. Calcining it at 500-600 C drives off the ammonia and leaves yellow tungsten trioxide, the one stable oxide and the universal feedstock for the metal.

##### Reduce the trioxide to tungsten powder `metal.tungsten.reduction`

WO3 + 3 H2 gives W + 3 H2O. Hydrogen is the reducing agent because carbon would give tungsten carbide, which is a different and also valuable product rather than the metal anyone wants here; the reaction is carried out on a boat of fine powder in a hydrogen tube furnace at 500-1000 C. What comes out is not yet a usable metal: it is a porous mass of interlocking crystallites a few microns across that can be crushed but not drawn. Tungsten is brittle at room temperature - its ductile-to-brittle transition sits near 200 C - so no amount of powder metallurgy alone gives a workable solid, and the grain boundary chemistry of the powder has to be fixed before the metal can be made at all.

###### Doped tungsten powder `metal.tungsten.powder`

Undoped tungsten powder has almost no grain boundary strength, and a filament drawn from it sags as it heats and burns out where the sag is greatest. The fix, worked out in the 1920s and universal by 1982, is to add a few tenths of a percent of potassium as potassium hydroxide or potassium carbonate, with a little alumina alongside, during the reduction itself: the potassium ends up as finely dispersed potassium bubbles along the grain boundaries, and it is those bubbles that pin the boundaries so the wire can be drawn to 0.04 mm without slumping. Alumina refines the grain as well. The doped compact is pressed and sintered, then hot-worked, and the final filament metal is 99.9-99.95% pure with the potassium content controlled to control the grain.

            - *Drawn tungsten wire* `metal.tungsten.wire` *(seen above)*
##### Tungsten carbide and the WC-Co cemented carbide `metal.tungsten.carbide`

Tungsten carbide, WC, is made by heating tungsten powder with carbon above 2000 C, and pressed and sintered on its own it is brittle and useless. What the industry actually buys is the composite: 6-12% finely divided cobalt powder mixed with WC grains of 0.5-30 microns, pressed and vacuum-sintered at 1400-1600 C, then ground and lapped to shape. The molten cobalt wets the carbide grains and holds them in a continuous binder, which is why the two metals are inseparable inside one object - a rock bit cone is a tungsten product and a cobalt product at once. By the 1980s cemented carbide was the largest single use of tungsten, ahead of filament, and oil-well drill cones were among its largest markets, so the bit on the rig producing the crude is a tungsten product just as much as the end mill cutting a C64 mainboard is.

#### Cobalt: the carbide binder, the ferrite dopant and the magnet alloy `metal.cobalt`

Cobalt is the element nobody thinks of and cannot do without. In a 1982 C64 and its peripherals it is the metal that holds tungsten carbide together in a drill cone, an end mill and a stamping die; the grain-boundary dopant that makes NiZn ferrite behave; the balance element in the iron-nickel-cobalt lid sealed onto a memory chip's ceramic package; a few percent of an Alnico correction magnet; and, at the top of the price range, half of a samarium-cobalt magnet. The mass in any one machine is a few grams. What is worth tracing is where it comes from, because cobalt is almost never mined for itself: it is overwhelmingly a by-product reporting out of somebody else's circuit, most often a copper-cobalt orebody or a nickel refinery, so the cobalt supply chain is largely a set of attachments to the copper and nickel branches.

##### Cobalt ore: heterogenite, carrollite and asbolane `metal.cobalt.ore`

Most cobalt never appears as a cobalt mineral at all. In the Copperbelt - the Shaba and Nkana strata of Zaire and Zambia - it sits in the sulphide ores as carrollite, Cu(Co,Ni)2S4, and it is recovered by flotation alongside the copper sulphides, so its output tracks the copper mine's. Where the deposit weathers, the same cobalt is oxidised to heterogenite, CoO(OH), a black manganese-rich oxide in the near-surface ore, and it is the oxide that the later hydrometallurgical flowsheets treat. A third source is asbolane, (Ni,Co)2-xMn4+(O,OH)4.nH2O, the cobalt-nickel-manganese oxide that forms in New Caledonian laterite. Grades are low: laterites run 0.1-1.5% Co, and the oxide zones are mined at a few percent.

###### Leach the copper-cobalt oxide ore `metal.cobalt.ore.hydromet` _(medium)_

The oxide ores of the Copperbelt are not smelted for their cobalt: they are leached. The ore is crushed and agitated in a sulfuric acid solution, which dissolves the cobalt and copper as sulphates while the iron stays in the residue as hydroxide, and the pregnant liquor is then taken to a solvent-extraction circuit that pulls the cobalt and copper apart from each other. What comes out of that circuit is a cobalt sulphate solution and, from it, a cobalt hydroxide intermediate that is shipped to a refinery. This is why the cobalt in a 1982 tungsten-carbide drill cone is a chemical-plant product rather than a smelter product, and why the Copperbelt's cobalt followed the fortunes of its acid plants and its export routes.

##### The Sherritt-Gordon ammonia pressure leach `metal.cobalt.ammoniacal-leach` _(medium)_

The second big route takes cobalt out of a nickel refinery rather than out of an orebody, and it exists because the nickel circuit was already there. Nickel concentrate or matte is leached with ammonia and ammonium sulphate in horizontal autoclaves under air at elevated pressure, which dissolves the nickel, cobalt and copper as metal-ammine complexes while the sulphide sulphur is oxidised and leaves as ammonium sulphate - a saleable fertiliser, which is what made the process pay. Cobalt is then separated from nickel on the fact that the cobalt ammine is far more stable: it is held in solution while the nickel is thrown down, and the cobalt stream is finished separately to metal. Because the feed is somebody else's concentrate, every tonne of cobalt this route makes is a tonne that did not have to be mined.

##### Electrolytic refining to 99.8% cathode `metal.cobalt.electrolytic`

Almost all cobalt metal on the market is won by electrolysis, and that is a deliberate choice about purity rather than about cost. The cobalt hydroxide or the crude metal is dissolved in sulfuric acid to make a cobalt sulphate solution; that solution is fed to an insoluble anode and a cobalt starter cathode, and metal grows on the cathode at a controlled current density while the impurities that are not plating out stay in the bath. The result is a cobalt cathode of about 99.8% - the grade trade calls Falconbridge cathode - and it is the standard feed for the tungsten-carbide industry, because a carbide's cobalt binder has to be fine, uniform and free of the copper, iron and lead that would poison the sintering. Electrolytic cobalt is also how the high-purity metal for superalloys and for the samarium-cobalt magnets was made.

          - *Dicobalt octacarbonyl, Co2(CO)8* `metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl` *(seen above)*
##### Cobalt(II) oxide, the additive grade `metal.cobalt.oxide` _(medium)_

The oxide a component maker actually buys is neither the ore nor the metal but a calcined powder, and in 1982 electronics the grade in question was a few percent of a zinc oxide varistor disc and a trace in a ferrite body. Heating cobalt metal in oxygen gives the blue-black spinel Co3O4, which is the oxide most of the industry actually trades; the green rocksalt CoO underneath it is a different substance with a different stability range, oxidising back to Co3O4 at 600-700 C and reappearing only when the temperature goes above 900 C. That is why the calcining route is described as reducing to the metal by way of Co3O4, and why a supplier's 'cobalt monoxide' and 'cobalt oxide' can be the same powder. The varistor is why this matters - a few percent of cobalt lets a zinc oxide disc hold a wide voltage range without failing, by making the grain boundaries and the grain interiors drift to their breakdown voltages at different rates.

#### Rare earths: fifteen metals out of two concentrate ores `metal.rare-earths`

The lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium are a single mining and refining industry that supplies fifteen elements which are chemically almost identical and economically almost unrelated. What a 1982 machine actually asks for is a gram-scale pinch of several of them: europium to make the red of a television phosphor, samarium for a correction magnet, neodymium for the catalyst that sets the cis content of a butadiene rubber, lanthanum and dysprosium as the donor dopants of an X7R ceramic dielectric, and lanthanum and neodymium exchanged into the zeolite of a refinery's cracking catalyst. All of them leave the same two concentrate ores and the same solvent-extraction plant, and after that plant the only question is which of the fifteen fractions a customer asks for.

##### Bastnasite concentrate and the Mountain Pass carbonatite `metal.rare-earths.bastnasite`

Bastnasite - usually written bastnaesite in commercial and metallurgical use, and bastnäsite in mineralogy - is (Ce,La)CO3F, a light-brown carbonate fluorosilicate carrying 6-9% rare-earth oxides. It was found in 1878 at Bastnas in Sweden and worked in quantity from 1949, but the ore that supplied the western industry in 1982 was a carbonatite in the Clark Mountains in California. It is an open pit in a 1.4-billion-year-old carbonatite intrusion, 8-12% rare-earth oxides in bastnasite with calcite, barite and dolomite as gangue, and it is dredged, floated and sent to its own separation plant on the same site. Mountain Pass is the clearest single example in this tree of an ore mined for an element nobody can see in it: barium is the gangue, iron is what comes out of the separation circuit, and the rare earths are what it is for. Production rose steeply through the 1960s to supply europium for the red of colour television. The other giant, Bayan Obo in Inner Mongolia, is different in kind: it is an iron-ore mine first, with monazite and bastnasite in the ore and the rare earths and niobium recovered as by-products, its concentrate travelling 150 km to the separation works at Baotou.

        - *Monazite concentrate and the beach-sand placer* `metal.rare-earths.monazite` *(seen above)*
##### Cracking, leaching and solvent extraction `metal.rare-earths.separation`

Fifteen elements that differ only in the number of electrons in one inner shell cannot be separated by any normal chemical operation, because they all want the same compounds. The industry separates them by arithmetic instead: a long train of mixer-settler stages in which a hydrocarbon solvent and an aqueous phase pass counter-current and the partition coefficient between them is exploited a hundred times over, walking cerium, lanthanum, neodymium and the rest off the stream one at a time. Hundreds of stages and several tonnes of solvent per tonne of oxide is what it costs, which is why the whole business sits behind one or two plants per ore rather than being spread around, and why the ore's owner and the plant's owner are usually the same company. Cerium is the one that comes out cheaply and in bulk, and cerium is a nuisance: there is far more of it than anyone can use.

###### Separated rare-earth oxides `metal.rare-earths.oxides`

The output of the separation plant is a set of individual oxides rather than a mixture: europium oxide for the red activator in a colour television phosphor, samarium oxide for the samarium-cobalt magnet, neodymium oxide for the lanthanide rubber catalyst and for the cracking-catalyst zeolite, lanthanum and dysprosium oxides ground to sub-micron as the donor dopants of a ceramic dielectric, and yttrium oxide as both a dopant and a stabiliser. Grades are quoted by purity - 99.9% or 99.99% for the phosphor and magnet grades - and the price differences between them are large enough that the tonnages are shaped by which grade happens to be wanted, not by how much of the element there is in the ground.

### Petrochemicals and process chemistry `chem`

Everything on the C64 that began as crude oil or natural gas: the polymers of the case and the keyboard, the solvents of the assembly plant, the wet chemicals and photoresists of the silicon fab, the laminate resin and flux of the board, and the fuels that moved all of it. Traces roughly a tonne of hydrocarbons per kilogram of plastic back to a barrel of light sour crude. The two feedstocks are named as ingredients, not children, because a petrochemical complex does not contain the oilfield it buys from.

#### Crude oil: finding it, drilling it, lifting it `chem.crude`

The upstream end of the chain. Seismic surveys pick a structure, a rig drills a 5-7 km hole through rock, casing and cement line the hole, the well is completed and perforated into the reservoir, then often artificially stimulated. An 8 kg C64 case corresponds to only 1-3 litres of crude oil, but that crude was found under 5-10 km of overburden using a drilling rig that cost tens of millions of dollars.

##### Petroleum exploration `chem.crude.exploration`

Finding a commercial accumulation of oil before spending the exploration well. In 1980s practice this was reflection seismology over regional grids, closed by wildcat drilling. Cost per barrel discovered had fallen from tens of dollars to roughly $2-8 by the early 1980s. A mud-logging unit beside the rig sampled cuttings and gas continuously with a hot-wire or infrared hydrocarbon detector, and it was the shows it found that decided whether to run a full log suite.

###### Reflection seismic survey `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey`

A surface source sends a pressure wave down through the rock section; reflectors return it to hydrophones and the travel times are stacked into a two-dimensional depth section. Seismic is a time-domain method: it maps reflectivity contrasts (sandstone/shale, gas-sand amplitude dimming) and gives no direct information about fluid type. The record was stacked and migrated on a mainframe or minicomputer: common-midpoint stacking, normal-moveout correction from velocity analysis, deconvolution and depth conversion, with the 1980s emphasis on multiple suppression and on early 3-D, where a single field cost $1-3 million per acre-foot. A log response indicating oil or gas - high resistivity, low neutron density, a gas effect on the seismic - is a test, not a discovery: a discovery needed a producing well, and industry experience was one test in eight to one in thirty commercial.

###### Seismic vibrator truck `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.vibrator`

A truck-mounted hydraulic vibrator sweeps 10-80 Hz into the ground under hold-and-hold conditions; on land it replaced explosive shot holes because it gave repeatable, higher-energy sources with no shothole cleanup. Regionally a 1,000-2,000 m shotpoint spacing was normal in 1980s 2-D work.

###### Airgun and marine seismic source `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.airgun-array`

Offshore and in shallow water the source was a 1,000-10,000 cu-in (16-160 litre) airgun array fired every 10-15 s from the stern of a seismic vessel. Compressed air from compressor trucks on deck; a single 1980s 3-D crew vessel carried up to four sources.

###### Dynamite shothole source `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.explosive-shot`

Still used for small onshore surveys in the early 1980s: 0.5-5 kg of packaged explosive in a borehole, fired from a firing truck, with the shot hole re-drilled for the next shot. Cheap per shot but slow, noisy and it polluted a producing field's drill cuttings.

###### Seismic shot-hole explosive ammunition `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.explosive-shot.ammo-case`

Cast or pressed explosive in aluminium or paper shells with electric or vacuum-fire detonators, supplied on the same chemical logistics as any blasting operation. This is a one-off consumable of a survey, not part of any C64 material.

###### Marine seismic streamer and hydrophone cable `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.streamer-cable`

A towed cable up to 3 km long carrying hundreds of hydrophone elements at 12.5-25 m groups; it was a synthetic-fibre-wrapped, oil-filled or water-filled analogue/digital telemetry line whose integrity was the limiting factor on data quality. Hydrophone elements used piezoelectric ceramic (PZT-5) discs coupled to silicone oil in a pressure-compensated housing.

###### PZT-5 piezoelectric hydrophone element `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.streamer-cable.pzt-element`

Lead zirconate titanate ceramic discs, typically 25-50 mm diameter, epoxied onto a diaphragm and back-electrode in a silicone-oil-filled housing; sensitivity about -190 dB re 1 V/uPa in the 10-60 Hz band. Silicone oil here is one of the petrochemical elastomers/fluids, unrelated to the case material.

###### Seismic geophone array `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.geophone-array`

On land, 12 to 48 groups of 10-60 Hz moving-coil geophones per station, each on a spike planted in a levelled hole, cabled and buried. In 1980s 2-D the fold of coverage (usually 6-fold to 24-fold) was chosen by geophone group interval and source spacing, not by 3-D binning.

###### Moving-coil geophone `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.geophone-array.geophone`

A 1-2 kg mass suspended in a magnetic field inside a case 3-5 cm across; coil movement induces a signal proportional to ground velocity. A second coil acts as a position feedback for the servo. Cost per channel in the early 1980s was several hundred to a few thousand dollars.

###### Geophone takeout cable and junction box `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.geophone-array.takeout-cable`

Polythene-insulated multi-pair takeout cable to a junction box, then a line-trap and telemetry radio link to the recording truck. Cable insulation here is polyethylene from the same steam-cracking chain as the C64's power cord jacket.

###### Seismic recording system `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.recording-truck`

Field recording on 1/2 in or 1 in nine-track magnetic tape (typically 2000 inch/s, 12.5-50 Hz bandwidth) or, from the early 1980s, 12-bit digital field recorders writing 3M/IBM-compatible cartridges. The whole array recorded simultaneously; it was common for the record to be demultiplexed and copied to a computer tape for onshore stacking.

###### Exploration (wildcat) well `chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well`

The first hole into a prospect. Cheap success-failure logging with mud logging and core, drilled to the deepest prognosis rather than the shallowest pay. Exploration wells in the early 1980s averaged about 3,000-5,000 m of hole and took 30-90 days offshore.

###### Wildcat cost and success statistics `chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well.wildcat-cost` _(medium)_

A North Sea or Gulf of Mexico wildcat cost $3-20 million in the early 1980s; the historical industry success rate was about 1 in 10 wells dry, 1 in 15 total wildcats a commercial discovery, and about 1 in 8 wildcats found non-commercial hydrocarbons. Exploration cost per barrel discovered was roughly $2-8.

###### Reserve estimation `chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate` _(medium)_

Volumetric and material-balance estimates, presented to a board and to governments as proved, probable and possible reserves. Rules of thumb: recovery factor 15-35% of oil-in-place for a sandstone reservoir, higher (35-60%) for a fractured carbonate. Reserve booking was and remains a commercial and legal judgement, not a measurement. The volumetric calculation behind all of it is pore volume x oil saturation x formation volume factor, and B_o for a light crude at reservoir temperature is 1.1-1.3, so reservoir barrels convert to stock-tank barrels at a meaningful ratio; saturation is the least measurable input and the most sensitive.

###### Reserve uncertainty and contingency `chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate.uncertainty` _(medium)_

Undiscovered reserves behind existing fields were treated as of similar magnitude to proved reserves. The industry view of world ultimately-recoverable oil in 1983 was around 1,500-2,000 billion stock-tank barrels, versus about 700 billion produced or proved.

##### The reservoir: where the oil sits `chem.crude.reservoir`

Oil exists in pore space between grains of sandstone or in fractures and vugs of carbonate, held down by an overburden of rock and by an overlying gas cap or water. This is the physical thing that the whole upstream industry is trying to reach. Oil squeezed out of the source rock moves updip along a permeable sandstone or through a fault until it is trapped, driven by a buoyancy of roughly 0.2-0.4 degrees API per 1,000 ft, with the column height set by the capillary entry pressure of the seal.

###### Sedimentary basin `chem.crude.reservoir.sedimentary-basin`

A subsiding basin in which organic mud is buried, buried deeper, cooked and squeezed; the whole petroleum system is source, maturation, migration, reservoir, seal and trap, and it takes 1-100 million years of that history. By 1983 the world's producing basins were a few hundred in number, with the Middle East and the Gulf of Mexico dominating reserves.

###### Source rock and kerogen `chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock`

Organic-rich marine shale. Type I and type II kerogen give oil; type III, humic and mainly terrestrial, gives gas. Maturation is measured by vitrinite reflectance, with the oil window at roughly 0.6-1.3% Ro and the gas window above about 1.3%. Between about 60 and 160 C the kerogen breaks down into oil and at higher rank into wet and then dry gas: the same thermal-cracking chemistry, far slower and uncatalysed, that a steam cracker performs in seconds.

###### Geological trap `chem.crude.reservoir.trap`

Anticline, fault, pinch-out or stratigraphic trap. The Ghawar field in Saudi Arabia, discovered in 1948, remained the largest oil field on earth for decades, holding some 100+ billion stock-tank barrels in a stacked series of Arabian carbonate reservoirs.

###### Reservoir rock: sandstone and carbonate `chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock`

Porosity 15-35% and permeability 50-2,000 mD for a good sandstone; carbonate reservoirs have most of their porosity as vugs and fractures and typically 5-25% matrix porosity. Around 60% of world oil reserves and 80% of world gas reserves were in carbonate rock, most of it fractured Arab-type in the Middle East.

###### Marine carbonate (Arab-type) reservoir `chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.marine-carbonate`

Dolomitised limestone and dolomite of the Arabian shelf: high initial productivity, typically 4,000-10,000 bbl/d per well with strong water drive, but rapid flow assurance decline and high water cut. Saudi production was essentially all of this rock type in 1983.

###### Oil column in the pore space `chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column`

An oil column of tens to hundreds of metres stands between a gas cap and a water contact, with oil saturation in the pay zone often only 50-80% of pore volume. That gap, plus the reservoir rock and the seal, is why recovery factors are 15-35% and why hydraulic fracturing and acidising exist.

###### Oil in place `chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-place`

The volume of hydrocarbons physically present in the rock, before any recovery factor. Multiply it by the C64 scale: the entire world shipped about 200,000 Commodore 64s in 1983, so the machine is a rounding error on a single wellhead's hourly output.

###### Asphaltenes and resins `chem.petroleum.asphaltene`

The heavy, aromatic, high-molecular-weight end of crude. Roughly 2-20% of crude, soluble in the light ends and precipitated by heptane in the standard n-heptane asphaltene test. Asphaltenes are the coke precursors in every thermal cracker, coker and reformer, and their content is what decides whether a crude makes a good or bad feedstock.

##### The drilling rig `chem.crude.rig`

Rotary drilling: the drill string is rotated from the surface, the bit mills a hole, mud circulates to carry cuttings out and to control formation pressure. Offshore this is a jack-up, a semisubmersible or a drillship; onshore it is a land rig with a derrick. 1980s rigs reached 6,000-7,500 m total depth on routine programs.

###### Rotary drilling `chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling`

A rotary table or top drive turns the string at 30-150 rpm with 10-40 kN-m torque while 200-450 kN of weight is set off the bit. Weight-on-bit and torque are the two variables the driller steers with; the drilling engineer watches torque and bit exponent while the driller watches penetration rate.

###### Drill string `chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstring`

Drill pipe, drill collars and a bit, threaded or coupled API 5-1/2 in and 6-5/8 in in the 1980s, with 3-1/2 in drill collar subs. Length is a queue of 5,000-7,000 m of 5 in pipe plus 200-400 m of collars; the string must be strong enough for tensile load at the maximum string weight yet remain within the derrick.

###### Mud circulation system `chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.mud-system`
