The 1980s specification was that irradiance from 350 to 500 nm should stay below roughly 0.5 W/m2 at the work surface, with the rest of the spectrum unrestricted. Resists of the period were sensitive to the mercury g-line (436 nm), h-line (405 nm) and i-line (365 nm).

##### Photolithography area `facility.cleanroom.litho-area`

Mask aligners, coat/develop tracks, bake ovens and the mask storage cabinets. In a 1980s 1-micron NMOS fab the lithography bay was Class 100 with the amber lighting, the operators wore yellow-room coats and face shields, and the photoresist was spun from a solvent (Shipley AZ1350, based on a novolak resin sensitised with a diazonium salt) with xylene or cellosolve acetate.

##### Passivation and packaging areas `facility.cleanroom.passivation` _(medium)_

Passivation (the final silicon nitride or phosphosilicate glass over the completed aluminium) and then the back-end: wafer probe, dice, die attach, wire bond, and the moulding of the ceramic or plastic package. The back end in 1983 was Class 10000 to Class 1000, not Class 100 - the contaminating work (bonding, moulding compound) happened there.

##### Make-up air and air change rate `facility.cleanroom.makeup-air`

The fab's single largest utility load. Because the Class 100 rooms were almost entirely recirculating, the make-up air was only the leakage plus the exhaust: the acid and solvent fume hoods, the furnace exhaust, the ion-implant exhaust. Even so, a 1980s fab typically ran 100-1000 air changes per hour in the clean bays and 20-60 in the support areas, and the air-handling plant cost tens of millions of dollars and dominated the energy bill.

##### Temperature and humidity control `facility.cleanroom.hvac`

20-22 C and 40-60% relative humidity, tighter than any other building of the era, and the single most expensive thing in the building to get right. The 1980s control was a system of pneumatic controllers and a mechanical chart recorder; a modern fab uses thousands of sensors and a BMS.

##### Gowning and airlock `facility.cleanroom.airlock`

A two-stage airlock - a 'dirty airlock' for incoming components and personnel in street clothes, and a 'clean airlock' with a cross-over bench for gowning. The costume of the era was a hooded coverall plus boots; in the amber room a yellow-coated garment as well.

##### What the building cost (1983 dollars) `facility.cleanroom.cost`

For scale: a small 4-inch fab cost about $4 million in 1970 (about $31 million in 2024 money); a full production fab in 1983 ran from roughly $100 million to several hundred million dollars - National Semiconductor announced a $100 million, 290,000 sq ft plant in August 1983, and UMC spent about $200 million on a 1.2 micron fab in the same year. That is why owning a fab was only ever available to very large firms.

##### Pre-filter bank `facility.cleanroom.prefilter`

Bag or panel filters (2-5 micrometre) ahead of the HEPA units, on the make-up air ducts and on the return air. The 1980s standard pre-filter was a 5-ply disposable bag of coarse glass fibre in a steel frame, or a V-bank of 1-inch washable aluminium-header panels. It existed because a HEPA that gets loaded with dust is an expensive mistake.

###### Coarse glass-fibre filter media `facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media`

Glass melted and blown into coarse fibres and felted into a mat. The same glassfibre technology as the HEPA medium but 100-1000x coarser and far cheaper. Ends at the glass batch.

##### Garment and consumable supply `facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies` _(medium)_

Garments were not laundryable in the era - a hooded coverall was worn once and destroyed. The plant bought enormous quantities of spun-bonded polypropylene garments, hoods, overshoes, gloves, wipes and tacky mats, and washed nothing. One 1980s 5,000-person fab burned something like a million garments a year.

###### Spun-bonded polypropylene `facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp` _(medium)_

Polypropylene melt-spun into continuous filaments and laid down in a random web, then bonded by heat or needle punching. Cheapest possible cleanroom garment material, and the raw material for the 'tacky mat' that caught shoe-borne particles at every airlock.

##### Wafer carriers and handling hardware `facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools`

In 1983 a wafer still travelled in a quartz boat inside a plastic carrier, or hand-carried in a PTFE-wafer cassette from process to process. The SMIF FOUP - the sealed nitrogen-purged single-wafer container that made the whole modern fab possible - arrived with SEMI E10 in the early 1990s. Before that, every transfer was an opportunity for a particle, and a large fraction of the total defect budget.

###### Fused-quartz wafer boat `facility.cleanroom.quartz-boat`

A slotted quartz holder that carries 25-50 wafers through the diffusion furnace. Fused quartz is used because it survives 1000 C, expands predictably, and is chemically inert to the dopants. Made from high-purity synthetic quartz rod, ground and flame-polished.

##### Fab workforce, 1980s `facility.cleanroom.workforce` _(medium)_

A large 1983 fab ran 5,000-10,000 employees, of whom the majority working on the wafer lines were women - the largest single female industrial workforce in many of the regions where the plants went, because the tool operators and the wafer handling were culturally coded as women's work even though they were skilled and tightly controlled.

#### The Commodore supply-chain geography `facility.foundries`

Where a C64 physically came from, and the only place in this tree where the map is Commodore-specific rather than industrial. Commodore owned one fab, in Pennsylvania. The boards were printed in Hong Kong. The boxes were assembled in Hong Kong, Japan, West Germany, the United States and - from 1984 - Britain. The corporate records that survived the bankruptcy are unusually detailed and are the best source for this branch.

##### The corporate chain that owned all of it `facility.foundries.corporate-structure`

From the US Tax Court record: Commodore Holding B.V. (Netherlands) at the top; Commodore International Ltd (Bahamas); Commodore Electronics Ltd (CEL, Bahamas) as the principal operating corporation; Commodore Business Machines Inc (CBM, West Chester PA) as the US sales subsidiary and the site of the semiconductor division; Commodore Japan Ltd (CJL); Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd (CE(HK)L) and, after April 1982, the Hong Kong branch of CEL; Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH (West Germany); and CBM International Sales Inc, the DISC. MOS Technology became a division of CBM on 1 January 1981 - which is why all the chips were still stamped with the MOS logo until 1989.

###### Vertical integration as a strategy `facility.foundries.vertical-integration`

Tramiel's thesis, and the reason the whole tree looks the way it does: if you own the chip, you do not pay a merchant supplier's margin, you control the schedule, and nobody can raise your price. The concrete results: a $135 initial production cost against a $595 retail price, and a production cost driven down to $35-50 by 1985.

##### MOS Technology / Commodore Semiconductor Group fab, Norristown PA `facility.foundries.mos`

The fab that made the 6510, the 6567/6569 VIC-II, the 6581 SID, the 6526 CIA and the ROMs. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 by John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin as a second source for Texas Instruments' calculator chips, was majority-owned by Allen-Bradley from 1970, and built its own plant on 14 acres of the Valley Forge Corporate Center, 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania. It was a 1-micron NMOS fab running 4-inch wafers, and it is the only place the C64's silicon came from - none of the five custom chips could ever be second-sourced. Commodore bought MOS outright for a 9.4% stake in CBM in November 1976 and merged it in 1981. The fab was closed in 1992 after Commodore's bankruptcy.

###### The captive fab as a prototyping advantage `facility.foundries.mos.captive-prototyping`

The reason Commodore could design a chip in nine months: the fab was not full, the mask shop and the processing line were on site, and a designer could pull a test chip in a few weeks - or, in an emergency, four days. Ziembicki's line is the whole story of Commodore's speed: 'We were using people who were there anyway... You waste a little bit of silicon, but silicon's pretty cheap. It's only sand.'

###### After Commodore: GMT Microelectronics `facility.foundries.mos.csg-successor` _(medium)_

The fab was bought out of bankruptcy in December 1994 for about $4.3 million plus $1 million of liabilities (including the EPA licence), reopened in 1995, ran a 1-micron process for third parties, and was shut down by the EPA in 2000-01. 183 employees and $21 million of revenue in 1999. It is a rare, well-documented instance of a 1970s fab surviving the death of its owner.

##### CBM Santa Clara, California `facility.foundries.santa-clara`

Commodore's US assembly line, where production of the C64 began in late summer 1982. It had automated component-insertion equipment. It went badly: excessive video and audio noise, excessive heat, and semiconductors incompatible with the design, so yield was low, cost high and returns came back. Only a limited number of units came out of Santa Clara before responsibility was shifted to Commodore Japan in the autumn of 1982.

###### The automated-insertion board layout fight `facility.foundries.board-layout-dispute`

Commodore's US plant used automatic component insertion; the Japanese plant did not, and the two wanted different component spacing. Charpentier's group won: the C64 board was laid out for automated insertion, and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools. This single decision is why every C64 motherboard was made in Hong Kong.

##### The Hong Kong operation (CE(HK)L and the CEL Hong Kong branch) `facility.foundries.hong-kong`

Where the C64 really got built. Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd had been making watches and calculators since 1979, and manufactured VIC-20 units from April 1982; later the Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd took over. Mass production of the production-redesigned 'C-64A' began at the Hong Kong branch in March 1983, and that branch employed approximately 2,500 people. Commodore's Hong Kong operation bought or produced watches, calculators and computers, and by 1983 it was the assembly centre for the whole company's output. Commodore had Hong Kong subsidiaries listed as Commodore Business Machines Ltd (Hong Kong) and Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd.

###### Hong Kong PCB fabricator `facility.foundries.hk-pcb`

All sixteen versions of the C64 motherboard were manufactured in Hong Kong. Hong Kong in the early 1980s was a genuine centre of bare-board fabrication - dozens of small plants doing gold-impregnated or tin-lead plated FR-4 double-sided boards on a 0.3-0.4 mm grid with the pads drilled and plated by a subcontractor. Commodore did not own one; it bought them.

###### Hong Kong / Taiwan injection moulding sub-contractor `facility.foundries.hk-injection` _(medium)_

The ABS case, the keyboard keycaps and the cassette-port door were moulded by a sub-contractor, not by Commodore. Hong Kong and Taiwan each had hundreds of small toolrooms and presses in 1983, and Commodore used both. The case cost an estimated $1-2 in 1983 prices.

###### Power supply / transformer sub-contractor `facility.foundries.psu-maker` _(medium)_

The linear power supply inside the C64 - the big orange or black transformer, the rectifier and the linear regulators - came from outside suppliers, cost an estimated $5-10 including connectors, and one of Ziembicki's complaints was that a supplier that had passed engineering approval then quietly changed the design without telling anybody.

##### Kentron Co., Ltd., Ina, Japan `facility.foundries.kentron`

The small Japanese production-engineering company that Commodore Japan acquired in October 1982 and that actually fixed the C64. Kentron had about 150 employees at its height and expertise in production engineering, quality control, work standards, purchasing and materials control. Commodore Japan substantially redesigned the machine into the 'C-64A' with Kentron's help; Kentron produced prototypes in late 1982 and began mass production in January 1983 - two months before the Hong Kong branch started, which is why Kentron, not Hong Kong, is where the machine was made buildable. Kentron was a CJL subsidiary from October 1982 to June 1986, when it was sold to an unrelated party.

##### Japanese assembly vendors for the VIC-20 `facility.foundries.japan-vendors` _(medium)_

The VIC-20 - the machine whose case, board size and BASIC the C64 inherited - was first built in Japan by Shinwa Electric Company, then by Japanese Cash Register (JCR), both assembling and manufacturing to Commodore Japan Limited's specifications and under its direction. Japanese Cash Register also owned a factory on Ina road; CJL's engineering headquarters was at Isaka.

##### Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH, Braunschweig, West Germany `facility.foundries.braunschweig`

The European production base. Commodore launched production for the European market in Braunschweig in 1980 and it once employed up to 2,000 people. Commodore GmbH also designed products. The PET had been imported from Braunschweig, and Commodore UK in the 1970s bought calculators at a factory on Teesside. After the 1983 Corby decision, the more expensive business systems stayed in Braunschweig.

##### Commodore Business Machines (UK), Corby `facility.foundries.corby`

The British end. Commodore UK's head office was in Slough and it built calculators at a factory on Teesside; in 1983 it announced a new GBP 20 million home computer factory at Corby, Northamptonshire, as the European manufacturing and distribution centre for the C64 and VIC-20, expecting 300 jobs by the end of 1984 and 700,000 units a year by then. The Corby plant was in place by September 1984 with 850 jobs on a ten-acre site, ran flat out sixteen hours a day, and was closed as a manufacturing base in January 1986.

##### The rest of the manufacturing map, 1983 `facility.foundries.other-sites`

By 1983 Commodore described itself as an international company with manufacturing in Japan, Hong Kong, West Germany, the UK, Pennsylvania and California in the United States, and Scarborough in Metropolitan Toronto. C64 units carried the MADE IN HONG KONG, West Germany or England marks, and were assembled in at least 11 factories worldwide over the model's life. Commodore did not, at this stage, have a Commodore Taiwan plant - the Taiwanese supply chain in this story is the sub-contractor base, not a Commodore factory.

##### The sub-contractor geography: Japan, Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines `facility.foundries.subcontract-network` _(medium)_

Commodore's own factories were few; its supply base was enormous. Japan supplied the disks and a great deal of the precision mechanics and passives. Taiwan and Korea supplied the display-grade passives, the transformers, the coils, the keyboards and the power supplies, through the export processing zones. The Philippines and Malaysia supplied the switching power supplies and the magnetics by the late 1980s. Hong Kong was the assembly and test node, sitting between them, with the boards printed locally and the chips arriving from Pennsylvania.

#### Moving 100,000 C64s `logistics.shipping` _(medium)_

The C64 was assembled in East Asia and sold in North America and Europe. In 1983 that was containerised cargo on liner services, not break-bulk: a 40-foot box holds 250-350 C64s depending on how they were packed, and the whole industry's economics were shaped by the 1966-1980s transition from weight/measurement cargo to box rates.

##### Containerisation (40-foot box) `logistics.shipping.containerisation` _(medium)_

ISO 40-foot general purpose container: 12.192 m x 2.438 m x 2.591 m internal, holding up to about 32-36 tonnes. One TEU is a 20-foot box; a 40-foot box is two. Box rates had replaced weight rates on the main east-west lanes by the end of the 1970s, so a low-density, high-value cargo like a C64 paid per box rather than per tonne.

##### The volume Commodore was moving `logistics.shipping.c64-count` _(medium)_

By March 1983 the C64 was shipping at about 25,000 units a month and had passed the Apple II in monthly unit sales; roughly half a million had sold in the first six months. At 300 units a 40-foot box, that is about 83 TEU a month - about four to five ships' worth of containers a month, which sounds trivial until you remember it was compounding 20-30% a month.

##### The ports `logistics.shipping.ports`

Kaohsiung was Taiwan's largest container port and was ranked the world's fifth-largest container port in 1982; its first container terminal was built 1969-70 and Container Terminal No. 4 in the Zhongxing Commercial Harbor Area was built from 1983. Keelung, on the northern approach to Taipei, opened the first Taiwanese container ship movements in January 1972 and worked on a filled jetty because of the terrain. Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour terminals, Rotterdam, and Long Beach or Oakland on the US West Coast, plus New York and Newark on the East Coast, completed the set.

##### Route times: transpacific and Europe-Asia `logistics.shipping.routes` _(medium)_

Kaohsiung or Hong Kong to Long Beach is about 4,500-5,000 nautical miles via the Luzon Strait and the great circle; at 16-18 knots that is roughly 12-14 days port to port, plus 3-7 days in the terminal on each end. Hong Kong to Rotterdam via the Suez Canal is about 11,000 nautical miles, 22-26 days, with 5-7 days of canal transit and waiting. These were the numbers that set Commodore's inventory position: eight weeks of sea transit each way on the Pacific route, eleven to twelve weeks each way on the Europe route.

##### The bill of lading `logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading`

The negotiable document that made containerised trade possible: a carrier-issued contract of carriage naming the shipper, the consignee, the port of loading and discharge, the freight terms, and the description of the goods. Without it the goods did not move; with it, the bank paid on presentation. The 1983 electronic BOL did not exist - the paper document was the mechanism.

##### Air freight for the high-value parts `logistics.shipping.air-freight` _(medium)_

Customs values tell the story: a box of 300 C64s entered at, say, $150-200 declared value each would carry $45,000-60,000 of electronics inside a container whose ocean freight was a few hundred dollars. The ICs were the opposite case: a 6510 and a VIC-II at internal transfer value were a tiny fraction of the customs value of the finished case, so nobody flew the chips - the chips came by sea inside the container, and the container moved once. Air freight was for prototypes, for a replacement part in an emergency, and for the tape and the spares.

##### Demurrage, detention and the inventory cost `logistics.shipping.demurrage` _(medium)_

Two separate costs. Demurrage is the charge for leaving a container on the terminal beyond the free time; in 1983 free time was commonly four to five days and the daily charge escalated. Detention is the charge for keeping the container beyond the time allowed at the other end. On top of both sat the real cost: eight to twelve weeks of sea transit each way meant Commodore had to hold inventory in transit and in the destination warehouse, which is exactly the cost structure that rewarded the 'just-in-time' port-to-port discipline and punished Commodore's famous spotty availability in 1983.

##### US import duty on a computer in 1983 `logistics.shipping.import-duty` _(medium)_

The C64 entered the United States under the Tariff Schedules of the United States (the TSUS - the HTS did not exist until 1989), classified as an accounting, computing and other data processing machine incorporating a calculating mechanism, item 676.15, dutiable at 5.5% ad valorem. Separately, item 807.00 gave a duty allowance for the US components shipped out for assembly abroad - which for Commodore meant a deduction for the value of the MOS chips and the case shipped to Hong Kong, so only the value added in Hong Kong paid duty.

##### Customs valuation and the paper trail `logistics.shipping.customs-valuation`

US customs value was the transaction value - the price actually paid or payable - which is why Commodore's transfer-pricing between Commodore Electronics Ltd (Bahamas), Commodore Japan Ltd and the Hong Kong branch became the subject of a US Tax Court case that ran from 1991 and shifted $116 million of income between entities. The same transfer prices determined the duty. The documentation for a 1983 shipment would have included a commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading and, in a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal, a certificate of origin.

###### Commercial invoice, packing list and certificate of origin `logistics.shipping.commercial-documents` _(medium)_

The three documents that travelled with the container besides the bill of lading. The invoice stated the price actually paid or payable, which is the number customs used; the packing list was the count and weight the carrier checked against the manifest; the certificate of origin was what made the 807.00 assembly-relief deduction claimable. In a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal all three had to be issued and retained for years - which is why the tax case could reconstruct Commodore's internal transfer prices two decades later.

#### The labour content of a C64 `logistics.people`

Two labour populations with almost nothing in common: a tiny, very senior, very expensive American engineering team in Pennsylvania and Japan, and a large, low-paid, mostly female production workforce in Hong Kong and Japan. The design labour is amortised over millions of units and is invisible in the $35-50 bill of materials; the assembly labour is a few dollars per unit and is the reason Commodore could hit a $135 production cost. The Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd employed approximately 2,500 people when mass production of the production-redesigned C-64A began there in March 1983 - the single best-documented headcount in the whole Commodore manufacturing story.

##### The bill of materials (1983 estimate) `logistics.people.bom`

Brian Dougherty of Berkeley Softworks gave the most-cited contemporaneous breakdown, used as a production cost of $35-50 by 1985: three ROMs at $1 each; eight 64K DRAMs at $1.85 each; SID and VIC-II at $4 each; RF modulator $3; 6510 at $1-2; TTL, buffers, regulators and capacitors together $5; keyboard under $10; PC board $1-2; plastic case $1-2; power supply and connectors $5-10; packaging and manual $1-2. Note what this says: the eight DRAM chips alone were $14.80, more than the case, the board and the modulator combined.

##### Direct assembly labour per machine `logistics.people.direct-labour` _(low)_

Roughly 0.5-1.5 person-hours per machine across population, insertion (automated), wave-solder, assembly, test and packing, plus a share of the test and rework. At 1983 Hong Kong and Japanese electronics wage levels of roughly HK$9-14 or JPY 500-700 per hour, that is about US$1-3 per machine of direct labour - between 3% and 8% of the $35-50 production cost. Direct labour is genuinely tiny compared with the IC content, which is exactly the point Commodore's vertical integration strategy rested on.

##### Hong Kong electronics wages, 1983 `logistics.people.hk-wages` _(medium)_

The Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department's Quarterly Report of Wages, Salaries and Employee Benefits Statistics carried explicit occupational breakdowns for the electronics industry in 1983 - assembler, soldering worker, tester/aligner, quality control operator, packer, machine operator - with average daily wages and normal hours, and it separately flagged that piece rates were common in manufacturing and that the survey therefore reported them on a time basis. Operative daily wages across manufacturing generally sat around HK$60-100 in 1983, so an assembler earned roughly HK$9-14 per hour at a 7-8.5 hour day. Hong Kong had no statutory minimum wage at all in 1983.

##### The worker at the wave-solder line `logistics.people.wave-solder-worker` _(medium)_

The single most recognisable job in a 1980s electronics factory. She stood or sat at one end of a 2-3 m wave-solder machine, fed pre-inserted boards into the conveyor, watched for bridging and dry joints, pulled the rejects, and often did the visual inspection and the component-insertion handwork at the same station. Almost always female, usually in her twenties or thirties, on a piece rate or a small hourly premium for yield, and living within an hour's bus ride of the plant in a New Territories squatter village or a public housing block. Hong Kong's 1983 wage survey listed 'soldering worker' as a distinct occupational category for exactly this reason.

##### The C64 chip design team `logistics.people.design-team`

A team of about seven people, working in parallel on two chips, in nine months. Al Charpentier designed the VIC-II with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Bob Yannes designed the SID with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Charles Winterble, then director of worldwide engineering, authorised and managed the project. The whole effort began in January 1981, spent about two weeks studying the Mattel Intellivision, the TI 99/4A and the Atari 800, and finished with first-pass silicon in November 1981 that worked except for one bad sprite. The chips were designed in a modular, deliberately uncompact style - Yannes built one oscillator module and repeated it rather than multiplexing - because design time was the scarce resource, not die area. Neither designer had a modern CAD workstation; logic was simulated by hand.

##### The C64 system design team `logistics.people.c64-system-team`

After Tramiel decided in late November 1981 that the VIC-II and SID would go into a 64 KB home computer rather than a game console, the machine itself was designed in about five weeks. The architecture was laid out on paper in two days; five working prototypes were finished just before the new year. The team was Bob Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki, with Yash Terakura of Commodore Japan involved on the Japanese variant. They worked over Thanksgiving and Christmas. Charlie Winterble had set the deadline; Tramiel had decided the machine had to be at the January 1982 CES.

##### Nobody knows what the C64 cost to develop `logistics.people.development-cost`

Winterble's answer to the question was direct: 'I had no formal budget accountability, other than Jack watching me. Jack said that budgets were a license to steal.' The reason the answer was 'nothing much' is that the fab was not running at full capacity and the design chips were absorbed into existing overhead with no supplier margin at all. Ziembicki: 'We were using people who were there anyway.' Software, per Charpentier, 'wasn't tangible - you couldn't hold it, feel it, or touch it - so it wasn't worth spending money for.'

##### The production engineers who fixed it `logistics.people.production-engineering`

The unsung labour in Commodore's story: David Ziembicki (production engineer, then Commodore West Chester), Bruce Crocket and Charles Winterble, who had to debug the project and bring it into production, and Robert H. Lane, who became president of Commodore Business Machines Inc in November 1982 and was fired by Tramiel after the June 1983 CES. Kentron's 150 Japanese engineers and technicians - brought in specifically because Commodore Japan's production engineering had worked on the VIC-20 - are the documented reason the C64 was eventually manufacturable at all.

##### The labour cost of the quality problems `logistics.people.qa-defects`

Commodore's labour did not just build machines, it found and reworked other people's mistakes. The 'sparkle' defect was traced after three weeks to a ROM - not the VIC-II - with a pre-charging circuit that was sensitive to a bus contention spike; three million such ROMs were already in service. A logic error put 64 clock cycles on a scanline instead of 65 and took about five months into production to fix. Assembly-line workers over-adjusted the colour potentiometer until it saturated the colour and wiped out the luma. Electric screwdrivers cut traces on the disk-drive connector, and because those traces went to a connector nobody tested, they passed final inspection. Charles Winterble: 'It takes a very tough person to say I'm not shipping these because they're not as good as they could be - especially when people are clamoring to buy them.'

#### Factory and engineering test equipment `facility.test-equipment`

Every C64 that left the Hong Kong line had been through a functional test, and the boards had been tested electrically before population and after soldering. In-circuit testers and flying probes were the technology of the era; the automated ATE industry of the 1990s did not exist yet. The capital equipment here was made by the test-and-measurement industry, which is why it is categorised `industry` rather than `assembly` - assembly is reserved for the operations themselves.

##### In-circuit tester (ICT) `facility.test-equipment.ict`

A bed-of-nails fixture pressing 1000 or so spring-loaded probes onto the bare board's pads, measuring resistance, capacitance, diode voltage and, at an increasing share, functional signatures at each node - all in a few seconds. By 1983 the analogue resistance-only tester was giving way to the analogue-plus-functional 'in-circuit functional tester' that could catch an unpopulated IC or a wrong-orientation part without a board-level functional test.

##### Functional tester `facility.test-equipment.functional` _(medium)_

A powered-up test station running a test program from ROM that exercised the VIC-II registers, checked the RAM, drove the keyboard matrix and read back the RAM. On a Commodore line this was a dedicated fixture with a monitor and a keyboard, and the operator's job was to load, run, read the result, box or quarantine.

##### Test ROM in the final-test fixture `facility.test-equipment.test-rom` _(medium)_

A dedicated test ROM - the '501' diagnostic ROM is the one most C64 owners meet - loaded into the machine's own ROM socket during factory final test so the machine could self-test its own RAM, character ROM, CIA timers and VIC registers. It is the same object a user later used to prove the machine worked.

##### Burn-in oven and sockets `facility.test-equipment.burn-in` _(medium)_

A forced-air oven at 70-100 C with burn-in sockets, holding hundreds of boards for 24-72 hours so that early-life component failures - bad solder joints, marginal ICs, leaky capacitors - showed up on the line instead of in the customer's house. Commodore's 1982-83 quality record suggests it was not always run long enough.

##### Bare-board test and flying probe `facility.test-equipment.bare-board`

Bare PCB test came first: a bed-of-nails grid fixture to prove every net was etched and plated correctly, catching a shorts-heavy board before it was populated and therefore before the parts were on it. The flying probe - a robot or CNC head with a moving needle that touched nets individually without a fixture - existed by the early 1980s as an engineering diagnostic, and only later became the standard production tester once it got fast enough.

###### Spring probe and tungsten needle `facility.test-equipment.needle-probe` _(medium)_

The bed-of-nails is a field of sprung tungsten-rhenium or beryllium-copper pins on a 2.54 mm grid, each pressing a few grams onto a pad to make contact. The 1980s fixtures were drilled and wired by hand or on a numerical-control machine from the Gerber artwork - which is why a board layout change meant a new fixture.

### Published but unlinked materials `unlinked.catalogue` _(medium)_

These 10 nodes were written as canonical, reusable subtrees — a fragment's "made from" chains in full detail — but no other branch ended up referencing them, so nothing linked them into the tree. They are collected here rather than deleted. Where a component subtree inlines its own shorter version of the same material chain, this is the long one.

#### E-glass fibre `chem.glass-fiber`

Continuous glass filaments about 5 microns across, drawn in thousands from a tank furnace and woven into cloth. The C64 needs it twice on the board side of the machine: as the reinforcing cloth in the FR-4 mainboard laminate, and as the laminate core of the keyboard matrix board. E-glass is a lime-alumino-borosilicate, and the 15-19% of its weight that is not silica exists for one reason - it brings the working temperature down far enough that a 5 micron filament can be drawn from an affordable non-lead melt. That is why it is made in millions of tonnes a year and why it is the cheapest structural reinforcement known. Everything it is made of is weighed once, in a batch: silica sand, limestone, soda ash, a borate and a clay.

##### Mix the batch `chem.glass-fiber.batch`

The raw materials are weighed and dry-blended to about +/-1% on each constituent before a single tonne is melted. The tolerance matters more than it looks: the melt fixes the viscosity curve, and the viscosity curve decides whether 5 micron filament can be drawn from the bushing at all. A modern batch is tens of tonnes, and it is the last point at which the composition can be corrected.

          - *Industrial silica sand (quartz dune sand)* `metal.silica-sand` *(seen above)*
          - *Limestone (CaCO3) quarry* `metal.limestone` *(seen above)*
          - *Soda ash (Na2CO3)* `metal.soda-ash` *(seen above)*
###### Borax (sodium borate) `chem.glass-fiber.borax`

The boron source, and the reason E-glass is a borosilicate at all. Borax decahydrate, Na2B4O7.10H2O, goes into the batch either as the decahydrate or as boric acid made from it; either way the boron ends up in the glass network as B2O3. A few per cent of B2O3 lowers the liquidus and widens the working range enough to draw fine filament at a temperature the bushing alloy can survive, and it improves chemical durability - which is what stops the finished fibre dissolving in the warm caustic etch bath the board house puts it through.

###### Boric acid from colemanite `chem.glass-fiber.borax.acid`

Colemanite ore is crushed and boiled with sulfuric acid, which drives the calcium out as gypsum and leaves boric acid in solution: Ca2B6O11.5H2O + 2 H2SO4 + 2 H2O -> 2 CaSO4 + 6 H3BO3. The liquor is filtered hot and crystallised by cooling, and the crystals are dried at low temperature because boric acid dehydrates to B2O3 above about 100 C. Glass makers bought either this acid or the crude ash from dry lakes such as Searles Lake; the acid was the easier way to get a clean batch.

###### Colemanite and borate ore `chem.glass-fiber.borax.ore`

The borates are mined from evaporite deposits and altered limestone-tuff beds, in Turkey (Bigadiç, Emet) and California's Boron and Kramer districts. Ore is 25-35% B2O3 and is shipped as run-of-mine lump, so this is as close as the boron in a C64 mainboard gets to the ground.

          - *Kaolin (china clay)* `facility.power.kaolin` *(seen above)*
        - *Borax (sodium borate)* `chem.glass-fiber.borax` *(seen above)*
##### Melt, refine and condition the batch `chem.glass-fiber.melt`

The batch is charged into a regenerative tank furnace held at 1400-1500 C - hot enough to keep the viscosity low enough to draw a filament through a 10 micron hole, and then held in that narrow window for tens of hours. What comes out is not merely molten: it is refined until every bubble larger than a few microns has risen out or been broken by a rotating stirrer, and then conditioned - held just above the liquidus so that beta-eucryptite crystallises out on the refractory. That conditioning is the slowest step in the plant and the one that makes continuous fibre possible: without it the drawn fibre devitrifies into a crystalline, brittle mass the moment it cools.

##### Forehearth and bushing plate `chem.glass-fiber.bushing`

The glass leaves the furnace through a refractory forehearth and arrives at a bushing plate: a small alloy block, a couple of hundred millimetres across, drilled with 200 to several thousand holes of 10-40 microns. Gold-platinum-rhodium is the usual alloy because nothing else survives 1400 C in contact with a boron-bearing melt; the cheapest bushings are rhodium-plated nickel. Pressure pushes the melt through each hole, surface tension rounds the emerging cone, and gravity and attenuation do the rest.

##### Attenuate and size the strand `chem.glass-fiber.attenuation`

A blast of air at constant pressure across the wicket pulls the emerging cone out to about 5 microns before it has travelled half a metre, and the filament is wound onto a rotating package at 10-25 m/s. As it passes the sizing apron it picks up a thin film - starch or oil for the textile trade, and a light dose of silane for laminate grade. Continuous filament is not chopped: chopped strand is a separate product made by running the same strand through a hammer mill, which is what the glass-filled phenolic and glass-filled nylon parts elsewhere in this tree are made from.

##### Spin, rove and weave the cloth `chem.glass-fiber.packaging` _(medium)_

The attenuated strand is wound onto a rotating package at high traverse speed, then a few hundred filaments are gathered into a roving and woven on an air-jet loom into plain-weave cloth. The loom is the reason a laminate is isotropic: a plain weave with a square fill puts equal glass in both directions, so the board does not creep along one axis when it is heated. That is why PCB cloth is woven rather than chopped or randomly matted. The kraft liner in the finished laminate panel is paper, not glass - a softwood pulp sheet - and belongs to the resin and liner branch, not here.

##### Size the woven cloth with silane `chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing`

For laminate grade the woven cloth is desized and then treated with an organosilane coupling agent - sprayed or dipped, dried and cured at 100-150 C - before it is impregnated with epoxy. The molecule has one end that hydrolyses and bonds to the silanol groups on the glass surface and an organic end that reacts with the resin, so the glass is covalently joined to the epoxy instead of merely being wetted by it. That chemical bond across the cloth is what keeps a mainboard from delaminating along its own reinforcement when the assembly goes through a solder pot, and the 0.3-1.0 wt% of silane that buys it is invisible in the finished part.

#### Silane and organosilane chemistry `chem.silane`

Monosilane, SiH4, is a gas made by redistributing trichlorosilane, and it is the precursor for the polysilicon films deposited inside the fab that made the 6510 and the 4164s. Organosilanes are the opposite: a methyl- or ethylchlorosilane that has been reacted with methanol or ethanol instead, so the molecule ends up carrying an alkoxy group and an organic group and is a liquid rather than a gas. They are the surface chemistry that bonds glass fibre to epoxy resin, and every FR-4 board in the world contains them. Both families come out of the same silicon-chlorine-hydrogen chemistry; that shared feedstock is the only relationship between them, and conflating the two is the usual first mistake.

##### Monosilane (SiH4) `chem.silane.monosilane`

The polysilicon precursor: a colourless, pyrophoric gas that decomposes on a hot surface to lay down a conformal silicon film. A fab in 1982-84 that used it ran a small silane plant, because the gas is both too dangerous and too cheap to ship far. It goes into the machine's own logic: the polysilicon gate of the 6510, and the second of the three polysilicon levels in each 4164 DRAM, were deposited from silane by low-pressure CVD. It did not make the 9N polysilicon charge for the crystal pullers - that was still the Siemens trichlorosilane process until the late 1980s.

###### Disproportionate the trichlorosilane `chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route`

The industrial route to monosilane: trichlorosilane redistributes into silane and tetrachlorosilane, catalysed, with the whole reaction run in a hydrogen atmosphere: 4 HSiCl3 -> SiH4 + 3 SiCl4. It suits a fab because the trichlorosilane it consumes is the same material the polysilicon plant already makes by the ton, delivered in bulk ISO containers or road tankers, and the tetrachlorosilane that comes back out is reclaimed by hydrogenation at the same plant. The silane leaves the reactor diluted to roughly a tenth or a quarter in hydrogen, which is what the crackers and the adsorption columns downstream were designed for and is far easier to handle than neat silane.

###### Deposit polysilicon by low-pressure CVD `chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd`

Silane decomposes on hot silicon in a diffusion tube at 600-850 C, laying down a conformal film of polycrystalline silicon. This is the step that changed how the C64's own chips were made. A self-aligned gate needs a gate material that survives ion implantation into the source and drain on either side of it, and that can be laid down and then oxidised around; aluminium can do neither, because it is destroyed by the implant and it diffuses into the oxide at the temperatures every later step needs. So once implantation replaced diffusion for source and drain doping, polysilicon won, and with it a gate that is chemically bonded to its own dielectric rather than merely resting on it.

##### Organosilane coupling agents `chem.silane.coupling-agent`

Bifunctional organosilanes: a hydrolysable alkoxy or chloro group that bonds to the silanol groups on a glass surface, and an organic group - vinyl, amino, epoxy or methacrylate - that reacts with the resin. Aminopropyltriethoxysilane and vinyltrimethoxysilane are the workhorses; methacryloxypropyltrimethoxysilane and 3-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane were the ones chosen where the resin was an epoxy. They are made from the same silicon-chlorine chemistry as monosilane by substituting an alcohol for the hydrogen: methyltrichlorosilane plus methanol gives the trimethoxysilane and releases HCl. Applied to woven glass cloth at a few tenths of a per cent by weight, they are the reason epoxy bonds to glass rather than merely wetting it - and therefore the reason a C64 mainboard does not delaminate in a solder pot.

#### Helium over the CZ melt `si.cz.atmosphere` _(low)_

High-purity helium, bled over the melt to carry off the intense blackbody heat and to sweep volatile boron compounds away. Argon, or a helium-argon mix, was the cheaper alternative and produced more oxygen precipitation in the finished boule.

#### Quartz sand melted into crucible glass `si.cz.crucible-sand` _(medium)_

High-purity quartz sand, acid-leached to remove aluminium and iron, is melted in a flame or arc furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel at about 2000 C into a clear, annealed vitreous silica blank. The graphite is then burnt off in air at 800-1000 C.

#### Seed crystal for CZ pulling `si.cz.seed`

A short (100)-oriented sliver cut from a previous ingot, used to set the orientation and the defect-free growth of the new boule. Its diameter has to match the finished boule, so a seed is cut and ground for each crystal-pulling station.

#### Chlor-alkali brine electrolysis `si.polysilicon.brine` _(low)_

Salt dissolved in water and electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 3-4 V to make chlorine and hydrogen. The hydrogen is what reduces the trichlorosilane, and the chlorine is one half of the hydrochloric acid that chlorinates the metallurgical silicon in the first place.

        - *Rock salt and solar salt brine* `metal.salt-brine` *(seen above)*
#### Anthracite coal as a coke substitute `si.polysilicon.coke.anthracite` _(medium)_

The other traditional reductant for the submerged arc furnace, mined from the hard coal fields of Pennsylvania, Wales and Shanxi. Lower carbon, higher ash and higher iron than petroleum coke, so it was used as a blend component.

#### Delayed coking and calcination of petroleum coke `si.polysilicon.coke.calciner` _(medium)_

Vacuum residue from crude oil distillation is heated in a battery of delayed-coking heaters to 500 C and held in a large coking drum for 12-24 hours; the green coke is then calcined in a rotary kiln at 1200-1350 C to drive off volatiles and leave needle coke at 0.5-2% sulphur. Silicon furnaces blend petroleum coke with anthracite coal.

##### Sour crude residue, vacuum distilled `si.polysilicon.coke.crude` _(medium)_

Heavy Venezuelan or Middle East crude sent to a vacuum tower at 350-400 C and 30-50 mmHg; the bottoms are a dense black pitch of asphaltenes and metal porphyrins, and are the feed for the coke. Vanadium and nickel concentrate in this residue, so coke made from it carries trace vanadium that the silicon plant has to tolerate.

        - *Anthracite coal as a coke substitute* `si.polysilicon.coke.anthracite` *(seen above)*
      - *Sour crude residue, vacuum distilled* `si.polysilicon.coke.crude` *(seen above)*
#### Feldspar and mica gangue, hand-picked away `si.polysilicon.gangue` _(medium)_

The pegmatite that hosts the quartz veins contains albite and K-feldspar with muscovite and biotite. Alumina in feldspar is the enemy - it survives all the way to the aluminium metallisation - so the lump is sorted by hand and by hydrofluoric-acid washing before it is even shipped.
